In the decades before 1914, the fashionable application of Darwin's "struggle for existence" to nations and races taught statesmen, soldiers and intellectuals that international life was an inevitable contest in which strong peoples must expand and weak ones were doomed to decline — an outlook expressed in works like Friedrich von Bernhardi's *Germany and the Next War* (1911) and in Berlin's talk of an inescapable racial struggle between Teuton and Slav. War was therefore seen not as a catastrophe to be avoided but as a natural, even healthy and purifying, test of national fitness. This fatalistic and belligerent mentality lowered the moral and psychological barriers to conflict, encouraged leaders in 1914 to view a great-power showdown as unavoidable and even desirable, and made them far readier to gamble on war than to compromise during the July Crisis.

The legacy of the Franco-Prussian War (1870–71) and the German annexation of Alsace-Lorraine. Bismarck's newly unified German Empire seized these French provinces in the Treaty of Frankfurt, humiliating France and creating a permanent structural enmity at the heart of Europe. For over forty years French politics was shaped by revanchism — the determination to recover the "lost provinces" — which drove France to seek the 1894 alliance with Russia and the 1904 Entente Cordiale with Britain, encircling Germany and hardening Europe into two hostile camps. It also meant that in 1914 France had no interest in restraining Russia or in a compromise that would leave German power supreme, so that when Germany declared war on Russia, France willingly went to war, converting an eastern quarrel into a general European conflict.

Austria-Hungary's own deliberate choice for a "preventive war," pushed by Chief of the General Staff Franz Conrad von Hötzendorf. Conrad had urged war against Serbia dozens of times in the years before 1914 (and also against Italy), arguing that the Habsburg monarchy was a decaying multi-national state whose prestige and very survival demanded that it crush the South Slav threat before it grew stronger. After Franz Ferdinand — the leading restraining voice at court — was assassinated, Conrad and Foreign Minister Berchtold used the murder as the long-awaited pretext, framing an ultimatum designed to be rejected so that a military reckoning with Serbia could not be avoided by diplomacy. This determination in Vienna to settle the Serbian question by force, regardless of the risk of Russian intervention, was the decision that actually began the fighting on 28 July 1914 and set the wider European war in motion.

Economic rivalry in the Near East, epitomised by the Berlin–Baghdad Railway. From 1903 German banks and engineers, backed by the Kaiser's government, pushed a rail line from Constantinople through Anatolia and Mesopotamia to the Persian Gulf, tying the Ottoman Empire economically and militarily to Berlin. Britain saw the project as a threat to its sea route to India, its oil interests in Persia and the Gulf, and to the naval supremacy on which its empire depended; Russia feared German influence over the Straits and its own Caucasian frontier; France resented the challenge to its financial stake in Turkey. The disputes over concessions, loans and the Ottoman military mission under Liman von Sanders (1913–14) deepened Anglo-Russian-French distrust of Germany, drew the Entente powers closer together, and fed the atmosphere of great-power economic and strategic competition that made the crisis of 1914 escalate into a general war.

The Bosnian Annexation Crisis of 1908–09. When Austria-Hungary unilaterally annexed Bosnia-Herzegovina (which it had merely occupied since 1878) in October 1908, it violated the Treaty of Berlin, enraged Serbia — which had hoped to claim the province's South Slav population for a Greater Serbia — and humiliated Russia, whose foreign minister Izvolsky felt tricked by Aehrenthal and who was then forced by a German ultimatum in March 1909 to accept the annexation without compensation. The consequences poisoned European relations for the next six years: Serbian nationalist societies such as Narodna Odbrana and the Black Hand were founded or reinvigorated to agitate against Habsburg rule; Russia, determined never to suffer such a diplomatic defeat again, accelerated its army reforms and pledged firmer backing to Belgrade; and Vienna concluded that bullying tactics backed by German support worked. Thus, when the same constellation of issues reappeared after Sarajevo in July 1914, Russia would not back down a second time and Austria-Hungary saw force as the proven remedy — turning a Balkan quarrel into a general European war.

The Balkan Wars of 1912–13. In the First Balkan War the Balkan League (Serbia, Bulgaria, Greece, Montenegro) drove the Ottomans almost entirely out of Europe, and in the Second Bulgaria turned on its former allies and was defeated. The results were destabilizing for the whole continent: Serbia doubled its territory and population and emerged as a confident, battle-hardened regional power whose South Slav ambitions Vienna regarded as a mortal threat to the Habsburg monarchy; Austria-Hungary was forced to intervene diplomatically to create Albania and block Serbian access to the Adriatic, humiliating Belgrade and deepening its hostility; Russia, as patron of the Slavs, was drawn ever more deeply into Balkan affairs; Bulgaria and the Ottomans were pushed toward Germany and Austria; and the ease of these short, victorious campaigns reinforced the belief that war was a usable instrument of policy. By 1914 the Balkans had thus been left an armed, embittered "powder keg" of unsettled claims in which Vienna concluded that only force could stop Serbia — so the Sarajevo assassination detonated a general European war.

The collapse of the international peace movement and of socialist internationalism in July–August 1914. Before the war, the Second International had repeatedly pledged (at Stuttgart in 1907 and Basel in 1912) that Europe's mass workers' parties and trade unions would resist a capitalist war with strikes and protest, and liberal internationalists placed similar hopes in the Hague Conferences, arbitration treaties and arguments (like Norman Angell's *The Great Illusion*) that war had become economically self-defeating. These restraints proved illusory: national loyalty overwhelmed class solidarity, the French socialist leader Jean Jaurès — the most determined advocate of a coordinated Franco‑German general strike against war — was assassinated in Paris on 31 July 1914, and within days the German SPD voted for war credits while French and British socialists rallied to their governments in a "sacred union." Because the one force that might have imposed a domestic veto on mobilisation disintegrated, governments discovered they could go to war with the enthusiastic backing rather than the resistance of their peoples, removing the last practical brake on the escalation of the July Crisis into a general European war.

The dysfunctional structure of German decision‑making — the "personal rule" of Kaiser Wilhelm II and the dominance of the military over civilian government. Under the Bismarckian constitution the Kaiser, not the Reichstag, controlled foreign and military policy, and an erratic, insecure monarch surrounded himself with rival courtiers, admirals and generals (Tirpitz, Moltke, Falkenhayn) who reported to him separately, with no cabinet or prime minister to coordinate them. The result was an incoherent, blustering foreign policy (the Kruger telegram, the Daily Telegraph affair, the Moroccan crises) that alarmed Germany's neighbours, and a situation in which the General Staff could plan the invasion of Belgium and France without the Chancellor or Foreign Office being properly consulted. In July 1914 this meant that Bethmann‑Hollweg's belated attempts to restrain Vienna were undercut, and once the crisis turned military, Moltke's timetable overrode the civilians' diplomacy — a state in which soldiers effectively made policy pushed Europe into general war.

The role of the armaments industry and the pro-war pressure groups it financed. In the decades before 1914 great private arms firms — Krupp in Germany, Vickers and Armstrong in Britain, Schneider-Creusot in France, Škoda in Austria-Hungary — grew enormously wealthy from state orders and had a direct financial interest in continual rearmament. They cultivated close ties with generals, admirals, ministers and monarchs, subsidised nationalist and militarist lobbies such as the German Navy League, the Army League and the Pan-German League (and their British and French counterparts), and helped fund newspapers that publicised foreign "threats" and demanded ever bigger fleets and armies. Scandals such as the Krupp/Kornwalzer affair of 1913, in which the firm was shown to have bought war-ministry secrets and planted alarmist stories in the French press to boost orders at home, illustrated how these interests manufactured war scares. By profiting from and actively stoking the arms race, this military-industrial-nationalist nexus made huge armaments and an atmosphere of imminent conflict seem normal and necessary, strengthened the hand of the war party in every capital, and thus helped make the general European war of 1914 possible.

The secret Anglo‑French military and naval "staff conversations" (1906–1912). Although the 1904 Entente Cordiale was only a colonial settlement and carried no formal obligation to fight, from 1906 onward British and French general staffs quietly planned the dispatch of a British Expeditionary Force to the French left flank, and in 1912 the Grey–Cambon letters formalised a naval division of labour whereby the French fleet concentrated in the Mediterranean while the Royal Navy guarded the Channel and France's northern coast. These arrangements were kept from most of the British Cabinet and Parliament, yet they created a powerful "obligation of honour": by August 1914 Britain's leaders felt they could not leave France's coasts and armies exposed after having induced her to rely on them. At the same time, because the commitment was informal and unpublicised, it failed to deter Berlin. Thus the staff talks simultaneously bound Britain to intervene and left Germany gambling on British neutrality, helping turn a continental quarrel into a world war.

Why might the United States government n.answer:
Because superintelligence would be, above all, a national‑security asset rather than an ordinary commercial product. An ASI would confer decisive military, economic and strategic advantage — potentially enough to determine the global balance of power — so Washington would be unlikely to leave it in the hands of private companies. Key motivations include:

- **Beating adversaries (especially China):** ensuring an authoritarian rival doesn't get there first or steal a lead, treating the effort like a Manhattan/Apollo‑scale project.
- **Security of model weights and algorithmic secrets:** startups and labs cannot realistically defend against state‑level espionage; only government‑grade security and classification could protect the "crown jewels."
- **Accountability and legitimacy:** the power to reshape war, the economy and society (and to control something that could be catastrophically misused) shouldn't rest with a handful of unelected CEOs; it should sit with democratically accountable institutions with civilian/military oversight and checks and balances.
- **Safety and control:** managing existential/alignment risks, preventing a reckless race in which commercial pressure leads labs to cut safety corners, and having the authority to slow down or impose safeguards at the critical moment.
- **Marshalling resources:** the sheer scale of compute, energy, infrastructure and defense integration required may exceed what private firms can build or coordinate alone.

Beyond the obvious race dynamics, a key reason is that the *transition* to superintelligence would be an extraordinarily unstable, wartime‑like period that only a sovereign can manage. An ASI would trigger a compressed military revolution — obsoleting existing deterrents, potentially enabling a decisive first‑strike advantage — creating exactly the kind of volatile situation that invites sabotage, espionage, or even preemptive attack on the labs and data centers themselves. Only the U.S. government can put such a project on a genuine wartime footing: give it physical and military protection (bases, classified facilities, air defense, counterintelligence), place it under a proper chain of command with the same seriousness applied to nuclear weapons, and hold the authority to negotiate arms‑control-style deals or escalate/deescalate with rivals. Relatedly, no private CEO or board should hold what amounts to a controlling stake in the world's future military power — nationalization is a way to prevent any single unaccountable actor from being in a position to seize unprecedented, unchallengeable power, whether by design or by accident.

How might you use a brick and a blanket?.answer: Use them together for an outdoor picnic or camp‑out: spread the blanket on the ground to sit on, and set the brick (or several) on the corners as a weight so the wind can't blow the blanket up or away. At night you could also warm the brick by the fire, wrap it in the blanket, and use it as a bed‑warmer.

Turn them into a padded weight: wrap the blanket tightly around the brick and tie or tuck the ends, creating a soft-covered block you can use as a homemade dumbbell/kettlebell for exercise, or as a doorstop/paperweight that won't scratch floors or furniture — the fabric cushions your grip and muffles any bumps.

In an emergency escape or rescue, pair them: use the brick to smash a stuck or barred window, then drape the folded blanket over the jagged sill so you (or someone you're pulling out) can climb through without getting cut by the broken glass — and the blanket can double as protection over your head/arms while you swing the brick.

Make a quiet, portable work surface: lay the folded blanket down as a pad, set the brick on top, and use the brick as a mini anvil — cracking nuts, flattening or straightening a bent piece of metal, tapping in tent stakes, or pounding meat. The blanket absorbs the shock and noise and keeps the hard brick from scratching or denting the table or floor underneath (and you can fold a corner of it over the brick to protect whatever you're striking).

Rig a quick shelter or privacy screen: string the blanket over a rope, branch, or between two chairs as a wall/roof, then hang bricks in the bottom hem (tie or fold the edge around them) so the fabric stays taut and doesn't flap in the wind — instant lean‑to, sun shade, changing room, or room divider.

Turn them into an improvised throw‑line/anchor: twist or cut the blanket into a long rope (braiding the strips for strength), tie one end securely around the brick, then hurl the weighted end over a tree limb, roof beam, or fence. The brick's mass carries the line where you can't reach, and once it's over you can use the blanket‑rope to hoist a food bag away from animals, rig a clothesline or tarp ridgeline, haul gear up to a height, or lower items down safely.

Make a "haybox" (retained‑heat) cooker: heat a brick in a fire or oven until it's very hot, set it beside your covered pot of nearly‑cooked stew or rice in a box or hole, and bundle the whole thing tightly in the blanket. The brick keeps radiating heat while the blanket traps it, so the food finishes cooking and stays hot for hours without any fuel — handy for camping, power outages, or keeping a meal warm on the drive to a potluck.

Use them as an improvised clamp/press while glue dries: after re‑gluing a broken chair rung, veneer, or a craft project, lay the folded blanket over the piece to protect its finish and spread the pressure evenly, then set the brick on top as a dead weight to hold everything tight and flat overnight. The same trick works for flattening a curled rug, warped photo, or pressing flowers between sheets of paper.

Keep them in your car trunk as a roadside kit: if you get stuck in snow, mud, or sand, jam the folded blanket under the spinning drive wheel to give it grip, and wedge the brick behind another tire as a chock so the vehicle can't roll back while you dig out or change a tire (a jack can also sit on the brick to keep it from sinking into soft ground, and the blanket keeps you warm and clean while you kneel and work).

Use them as a rust‑removing polish kit: rub the brick's rough face over rusty tools, a grimy grill grate, or a stained stone step to scour off the crud, then crumble some of the brick into fine red powder, sprinkle it onto a damp corner of the blanket, and rub it over metal (a classic brick‑dust abrasive polish) to bring back a shine — finish by buffing with a dry patch of the blanket, which also works as a cleaning rag and as a mat to kneel on while you scrub.

Use them as a furniture‑moving rig: tip a heavy dresser, fridge, or piano up by levering it with a board over the brick (the brick acts as the fulcrum/block that holds the load while you work), slide the folded blanket underneath, then lower it and drag the whole thing across the floor on the fabric — the blanket glides like a furniture slider and protects the floor and the finish from scratches, while the brick can also be kicked under a leg to chock it and stop it rolling or tipping mid‑move.

Use them in the garden as a bed‑protection combo: spread the old blanket over a garden bed as a breathable weed‑suppressing mulch/frost cover (cut slits for your seedlings), and lay bricks along the edges to pin it down and outline the bed. The bricks soak up sun all day and release that warmth under the blanket at night, protecting tender plants from a late frost, while the blanket keeps moisture in and weeds out — and the bricks double as stepping stones so you don't compact the soil.

Make a DIY weighted (therapy) blanket: sew or pin a row of pockets across the blanket and slip in bricks — ideally wrapped in cloth and evenly spaced — so the weight is distributed over your body. Draped over you at bedtime, the deep, even pressure has a calming, "swaddling" effect that can ease anxiety and help you fall asleep (and if you warm the bricks first, it doubles as a heat therapy wrap for sore muscles).

Build a no‑electricity evaporative cooler ("desert fridge"): set the brick in a shallow pan or bucket of water and stand your food/drinks container on top of it so it stays above the waterline, then drape the blanket over the whole thing with its bottom edge dipping into the water. The porous brick and the fabric both wick water upward, and as it evaporates off the blanket's surface in the breeze it pulls heat away, keeping milk, produce, or drinks noticeably cooler than the surrounding air during a heatwave, power outage, or camping trip — just re‑wet the blanket and top up the pan as needed.

Use them as a hands‑on physics demo: put the brick on a bare floor and pull it with a rubber band or spring scale, then repeat with the blanket under it (and again with the brick wrapped in the blanket) to compare how much force each surface takes — a simple, vivid way to measure friction. Tilt a board until the brick slides on wood versus on wool to find each surface's angle of repose, or drop the brick onto the folded blanket versus the bare ground to show how padding spreads impact force over time. It turns two ordinary objects into a whole afternoon of teaching friction, momentum, and cushioning to kids.

Turn them into a DIY sound booth: hang the blanket on the wall (or over a window/closet doorway) to soak up echo and deaden reflections while you record music, a podcast, or a video call, and lay the brick along the bottom of the door as a heavy draft-stopper/mass barrier that blocks street and hallway noise from leaking under it. The brick can also weight the blanket's bottom hem so it hangs flat and taut instead of billowing, and sit on a stack of books as a stable, non-vibrating base for your mic stand.

Use them as a home conservation kit: drop the brick into your toilet's tank, where it displaces water so every flush uses less, and wrap the blanket around your water heater (and any exposed hot‑water pipes) as an insulating jacket so the tank loses less heat and the burner or element cycles on less often — two throwaway items quietly shaving money off your water and energy bills.

Use them to keep a compost pile "cooking" through cold weather: drape the old blanket over the top of the heap or bin like a duvet so the microbes' own heat is trapped instead of blowing away, and set bricks around the edges to pin the blanket down against wind and to stop raccoons or rats from nosing under it. The bricks also soak up daytime sun and radiate that warmth back into the pile at night, so decomposition keeps going in freezing weather — and you can stand on the bricks as stepping pads when you come to turn the pile so you don't sink into the mud.

Make a winter shelter/bed for an outdoor pet or a stray cat: set a few bricks on the ground under a crate, tote, or sturdy box to lift its floor off the cold, wet earth (and to keep it from blowing away), tuck the folded blanket inside as insulated bedding, and lay another brick on the lid so wind or raccoons can't pry it open. The bricks also absorb daytime sun and radiate a little warmth up into the nest at night.

Use them as a bread‑baker's kit: put the (clean, unglazed) brick on the oven rack and preheat it as a cheap baking stone — it stores and radiates steady heat, giving loaves, pizza, and flatbreads a crisp, well‑risen bottom crust. Meanwhile, wrap the blanket around your covered bowl of dough (or drape it over the dough on the counter) to make a cozy proofing box that holds in warmth so the yeast rises quickly and evenly, and use it again over the cooling loaves or around the pot on the way to the table to keep them warm.

Build cheap furniture with them: stack the bricks in two piles and lay a plank or old door across them to make a bench, low table, or bookshelf, then fold the blanket over the plank as upholstery — a padded seat cushion (or a soft, dust‑free liner for the shelf). Tucking the blanket's edges down between the bricks also keeps it from sliding and hides the rough block ends, and it doubles as a lap throw for whoever's sitting there.

Turn them into a field water filter: cut off the bottom of a bucket or big bottle, stretch a piece of the blanket across the opening as the fine straining cloth, then layer smashed-up brick inside — coarse chunks on the bottom, gravel-sized pieces above, and the powdery brick dust on top — with another folded square of blanket between each layer to keep them from mixing. Pour muddy creek water in the top and it seeps down through the porous brick and wool, coming out the bottom clear of silt, leaves, and grit (boil it afterward to make it safe to drink). The leftover blanket also works as a pre-strainer over your collecting pot and can be wrung out to squeeze water from dew-soaked grass, while a whole brick weights the setup so it doesn't tip.

Use them as yoga/stretching props: stand the brick on end as a block to bring the floor up to you — rest a hand on it in triangle or half‑moon, sit on it to lift your hips in a cross‑legged seat, or place it under your sacrum for a supported bridge — and fold the blanket into a firm pad to cushion your knees, elbows, and head, to sit on for better spinal alignment, to slide under your shoulders in shoulderstand, or to roll up under your knees/lower back in savasana. Draped over you at the end, the blanket also keeps you warm while you relax.

Turn them into a fermenting/pressing kit in the kitchen: set the (clean, bagged or plastic‑wrapped) brick on top of the cabbage in your sauerkraut or kimchi crock — or on the plate over a block of tofu, a wheel of homemade cheese, or a terrine — so its steady weight keeps everything pressed down under the brine and squeezes out excess liquid. Then wrap the crock or jar in the blanket to shield it from light and hold its temperature steady through cool nights, so the ferment works evenly instead of stalling or souring. The blanket also cushions the counter and muffles the clink when you lift the brick out.

Use them as a beekeeper's over‑wintering kit: wrap the hive body in the blanket (leaving the entrance and vents clear) as an insulating jacket so the cluster doesn't have to burn through its honey stores just to stay warm, and set the brick squarely on top of the outer cover to hold the lid — and the wrapping — down against winter gales, the way beekeepers traditionally do. The brick's angle on the lid can even serve as your at‑a‑glance code for that colony's status (e.g., turned sideways = needs feeding), and it soaks up daytime sun to radiate a little extra warmth into the box at night.

Keep them together as a fire‑safety kit for the fire pit or campfire: stand bricks in a ring (or stack a small wall on the windward side) to contain the embers, block gusts and give you a stable ledge for a pot or kettle — and keep the wool blanket, soaked in water, right beside it as your fire smotherer. If a flame jumps the ring, a pan flares up, or someone's clothing catches, you throw the wet blanket over it to cut off the oxygen and beat it out, then use a brick to weight the blanket down over the smothered spot so it can't reignite while you fetch water. Afterward the damp blanket doubles as a mat for scooping and carrying cooled ashes, and the warm bricks can be pulled out of the ring to take the chill off your tent.

Turn them into a swim‑training/lifesaving kit at the pool or lake: toss the brick into the deep end and practice the classic rescue drill — surface dive down, retrieve the heavy brick from the bottom, and swim it back to the wall (holding it overhead or on your chest builds huge lung capacity, leg strength, and confidence underwater; it's the standard lifeguard certification test). Between attempts, the blanket is your dryland gear: spread it on the deck or shore as a clean, warm spot to rest and stretch, and wrap it around the swimmer's shoulders after each dive so they don't get chilled and shivery — the same wrap you'd use to rewarm someone pulled out of cold water for real.

Build a backyard trebuchet with them: lash the brick to the short end of a pivoting beam as the counterweight, and cut a strip of the blanket into a sling pouch (plus leather-like straps and a padded bearing wrap for the axle) on the long end. Drop the brick and the beam whips the blanket sling around, launching water balloons, tennis balls, or pumpkins across the yard — a great physics/engineering project for kids, and the leftover blanket makes a soft landing target or a pad under the frame so it doesn't chew up the lawn.

Make a photographer's stabilizer kit: wrap the blanket loosely around the brick to form a firm "beanbag" pad, set it on a fence rail, rock, or your rolled-down car window, and nestle the camera lens (or binoculars/spotting scope) into the folds — the brick's mass kills vibration while the fabric cradles and grips the barrel, giving you tack-sharp long-exposure or telephoto shots without hauling a tripod. The same padded brick doubles as a counterweight hung on a tripod's center hook or laid on a light stand's leg so wind can't topple your gear, and the spare blanket can be draped as a plain backdrop, a reflector-diffuser, or a dark hood over your head to see the screen in bright sun.

Use them for a small masonry job: soak the brick in water first (a dry brick sucks moisture out of the mortar and gives a weak joint), lay it into your garden wall, step, or fire‑pit edge, then dampen the blanket and drape it over the fresh work as a curing blanket. Keeping the mortar wet and shaded for a few days lets it hydrate slowly so it sets hard instead of drying out, cracking, or crumbling — and in cold snaps the blanket insulates the joints from frost, while in sun it stops rapid drying. The same damp blanket can be laid over a fresh concrete patch or wrapped around leftover bricks to keep them clean, and a spare brick pins its corners down so wind doesn't peel it off.

Make an emergency flood barrier for a doorway: roll or fold the blanket into a thick sausage and jam it tight along the bottom of the door (wetting it first so the fibers swell and seal the gap), then set the bricks in a row against the blanket so the water's push can't shove it out of place — the blanket soaks up and blocks the seepage while the bricks give it the weight and backing it needs. The same trick works on a low‑lying vent or floor drain: lay the folded blanket over the opening and pin it down with a brick so backflow can't come up through it.

Use them as a survival trapping kit: cut the blanket into strips for cordage and rig a figure‑4 or Paiute trigger under the brick to make a deadfall trap — bait the trigger stick, and when a squirrel, rat, or rabbit nudges it, the brick drops and dispatches the animal instantly. The rest of the blanket serves as camouflage draped over the set (and over you while you watch from a distance), as a game bag to carry the catch back to camp, and as a clean mat to work on while you dress it.

Turn them into an improvised chimney (or duct/flue) sweep: tie a rope securely around the brick, wrap and lash the blanket loosely around it like a big shaggy swab so the fabric bulges out to the flue's width, then lower the bundle from the roof and work it up and down the chimney. The brick's weight pulls the rig down and keeps it plumb while the blanket scrubs soot and creosote off the walls, and repeated passes knock the deposits down into the firebox — where you can lay a spare corner of the blanket across the hearth opening to catch the falling soot and keep the mess out of the room.

Make a no‑power "cold box" for a heat wave or blackout: soak the porous brick in water and freeze it (or chill it in a snowbank/freezer beforehand), then stand it in the bottom of a cooler, box, or picnic basket under your milk, meat, and drinks, and wrap the whole container in the folded blanket. The waterlogged brick holds a huge amount of cold and gives it up slowly — like a reusable ice pack that won't leak or need refreezing as often as loose ice — while the blanket's trapped air acts as insulation that keeps the outside heat from getting in, stretching the cold for many extra hours. Wrapped alone in the blanket, the frozen brick also makes a cool "bed brick" to tuck by your feet on a sweltering night, the mirror image of the hot brick you'd use in winter.

Make an ice‑and‑snow kit for winter: smash the brick into coarse grit and scatter the red gravel over icy steps, the driveway, or under a spinning tire for instant traction — unlike salt it won't corrode concrete, kill plants, or burn a dog's paws. The blanket goes over your car's windshield the night before a freeze (tuck its top edge inside the closed doors, or lay a leftover half‑brick on each end to keep the wind from stripping it off), so in the morning you just peel it away and drive off with no scraping. The same blanket can also be laid flat over a slick patch of ice on the walkway as a temporary non‑slip mat, pinned at the corners by bricks, until you get the grit down.

Turn them into a craft/dye project: crush a corner of the brick into fine red powder, sift it and stir it with a little water and binder (glue size, milk paint, or acrylic medium) to make a rich terracotta pigment, then use the brick's flat face as a giant stamp — dip it and press repeating blocks along the blanket, or brush the paint through a stencil — to turn a plain, stained old blanket into a patterned throw, wall hanging, or floor rug. The rough face of a second brick also works as a "sanding block" to distress and soften the fabric for a worn, vintage look, and a whole brick makes a handy weight to hold the blanket flat and wrinkle-free while the pigment dries.

Make an improvised sauna/steam tent: build a small frame of bent branches or set up a chair‑and‑pole frame, drape the blanket over it to seal in the air, then heat the brick in a fire (or on a stove) until it's very hot, carry it in on a shovel or in a metal pan, and set it inside on stones. Trickle water over the glowing brick and it flashes into steam, turning the blanket‑covered space into a sweat lodge for warming up after a cold, wet day outdoors or loosening sore muscles. On a smaller scale, put the hot brick in a bowl of water on the floor, sit with the blanket tented over your head and shoulders, and breathe the steam to clear a stuffy nose and chest — then wrap the same blanket around yourself afterward to stay warm while you cool down.

Rig them as sailing gear for a small raft, canoe, or dinghy: lash a spar across the mast and hoist the blanket as an improvised square sail (its tight weave catches wind well, and you can cut grommet holes or tie the corners with strips torn from its hem for sheets), giving you free propulsion downwind so you can save your arms. The brick does double duty on board — set it low in the middle of the hull as ballast to lower your center of gravity and keep the craft from tipping when the sail catches a gust, and tie it to a line as a drop anchor so you can hold position over a good fishing spot or keep from drifting while you rest. When the wind dies, strike the sail and the blanket becomes your dry seat cushion and a wrap to keep off the spray-chill.

Make a DIY Foley (sound‑effects) kit for a film, radio play, or podcast: scrape and grind the brick against another hard surface to create convincing footsteps on gravel, crumbling rubble, or a stone door grinding open; drop or thump the brick onto the folded blanket for a muffled "body fall," punch, or distant explosion thud; and flap and shake the blanket near the mic for wind gusts, beating wings, billowing sails, or a cape swirling. The blanket also lets you tune each sound — more folds for a softer, deeper thud, fewer for a sharp crack — and you can wrap the brick in it and slide it across a table for a low rumble or drag.

Make an old‑fashioned ironing setup: fold the blanket into a smooth, thick pad on a table (that's exactly how ironing boards are padded — the wool cushions the fabric, stops seam impressions, and protects the table from heat), then heat the brick on a stove, in the oven, or by the fire, brush off any grit, wrap its face in a scrap of cloth or a fold of the blanket so it won't soot or scratch, and use it like a sadiron — its mass gives both the weight and the stored heat needed to press out wrinkles in shirts, tablecloths, or quilt seams. Sprinkle the cloth with water and the hot brick steams it flat, and when the pressing is done the still‑warm brick can go back in the blanket to warm your bed.

Turn them into a garden pest trap / wildlife "cover board": dampen the old blanket and lay it flat on the soil beside your vegetable beds overnight, weighted at the corners with the brick (and a couple of half‑bricks) so it stays snug against the ground. Slugs, snails, earwigs, and pill bugs crawl under the dark, moist cover to hide by morning — you just lift the blanket and collect or squash them (the brick's flat face works fine for that), then re‑set the trap the next night. The same setup doubles as a harmless survey tool for kids or naturalists: leave the weighted blanket out for a few days and check under it to see which beetles, worms, toads, or garter snakes are living in your yard, and it can be laid over a fire‑ant mound or weedy patch and left a week to smother it.

Turn them into a blade‑sharpening kit. Wet the brick and use its flat, gritty face as a coarse whetstone — draw a dull knife, machete, axe, chisel, or scissors across it at a steady angle to grind a fresh bevel (rubbing two bricks together first will flatten the face and give you a truer surface). Then stretch a section of the blanket taut over a board (or over the brick itself, which makes a firm backing) and use it as a strop, dragging the edge backwards along the wool a dozen times to remove the burr and bring it to a shaving polish — wool's natural lanolin and a smear of any fine abrasive make it work like a leather strop. Afterwards, roll the tools up in the blanket like a knife roll so the edges are padded and can't cut anyone or get nicked in transit, and keep a corner of it as an oily rag to wipe the blades down against rust; the brick doubles as a weight to hold the roll shut or as a steady rest to work over your lap without dulling the edge on a hard table.

Turn them into an improvised first‑aid rig for a badly injured person: spread the blanket flat and log‑roll the casualty onto it, then roll its long edges up tight against them to make handles — that's a serviceable stretcher/drag sheet for carrying or sliding someone out of danger, and the wool also keeps them from going into shock from cold ground. Once you've got them somewhere safe, tear a strip off the blanket to pad and lash a splint on a broken leg, and tie the brick to a cord run over the foot of the bed (or a stick footrest) so its dead weight hangs and applies steady traction to the fracture, easing the muscle spasm and keeping the bone aligned until help arrives. Spare folded pieces of blanket become head blocks either side of the neck to stop the head rolling, wound padding to press on bleeding, or a sling — and the brick can prop the stretcher's foot end up to raise their legs.

Rig a self‑watering system for your houseplants while you're away: fill a tub or sink with water, set the brick in it as a pedestal so the pot bottoms sit just above the waterline, and lay strips of the blanket over the brick with one end trailing deep into the water and the other tucked into each pot's soil. The wool wicks water up by capillary action at exactly the rate the soil dries out, so the plants stay evenly moist for a week or two without drowning — and a spare piece of blanket draped over the tray keeps the reservoir from evaporating too fast, with the leftover brick used to hold that cover in place or to prop taller pots to the right height.

Use them as a ground‑to‑air signal panel if you're lost or stranded: spread the blanket (dark or brightly colored side up) in the biggest open clearing you can find so it contrasts with the surrounding terrain, and pin its corners down with the brick and a few rocks so wind can't fold or carry it away — then break the brick into chunks and arrange the red pieces beside it in a big "V" or "SOS" (or an arrow pointing toward your camp) so searchers overhead see both the fabric flash and the shape. A brick can also be used to smash/scrape a shiny surface for extra glint, and once a plane passes you snatch the blanket up and wave it overhead as a flag, then wrap it back around yourself to stay warm while you wait.

Use them as a potter's kit: smash the brick and grind it into fine red powder to make "grog" — the traditional temper that potters mix into wet clay so it shrinks less, dries evenly, and can survive firing without cracking (coarser chips can also be used to line and insulate a pit kiln, and a whole brick makes a flat, absorbent slab for wedging and drying clay on). The blanket is the other half of the job: lay a folded piece down as a padded, non-stick surface for coiling and building your pots, use a damp strip of it to smooth and burnish rims, and — most importantly — drape the moistened blanket over the finished greenware so the pots dry slowly and uniformly instead of splitting in the sun. Afterwards it becomes the padding you wrap the fired pieces in for carrying, with a brick set on top to keep the bundle from shifting.

Use them to build a small garden pond or water feature. Dig your hole, then lay the old blanket down inside it as the protective underlay — the thick fabric cushions the pond liner from sharp stones, grit, and root stubs so it can't be punctured (this is exactly what commercial pond underlay does, and old blankets are the classic cheap substitute). Then use bricks to stack a shallow planting shelf around the edge for marginal plants, to hold the liner's folds and rim in place while you fill it, and to weight the overlapping edges under the border stones. Finally, lean a brick as a stepped ramp from the bottom up to the rim so frogs, hedgehogs, and birds have a safe way in and out, and any leftover scrap of blanket can be tucked under the ramp bricks so they don't chafe the liner.

Set up a safe backyard target range with them: hang the blanket loosely from a rope or fence as a "curtain" backstop behind your target — a slack blanket swallows the energy of stray arrows, darts, or thrown knives so they drop harmlessly instead of skipping off into the yard (and the missiles don't get bent or blunted the way they would hitting a hard wall). Stack the bricks as the pedestal/base under the target itself so it stands at the right height and won't tip in the wind, and drop one into the bottom fold of the hanging blanket so it hangs plumb and doesn't billow when the wind blows or when a shot hits it. Afterward, roll the gear up in the blanket and set the brick on top of the bundle to keep it from unrolling in storage.

Turn them into a backyard blacksmith's forge: stack bricks (or set the one brick as the fire-back/wall) to build a small hearth that contains the charcoal and reflects the heat inward, then fold and stitch the blanket into a simple bag bellows — sew it into a pouch with a wooden nozzle at one end and two slat "handles" at the mouth, and pump it to blast air into the coals. That forced draft is what takes a charcoal fire from campfire heat up to forging/melting temperature, so you can heat rebar or scrap steel to shape a hook, knife, or nail (or melt down aluminum cans in a small crucible). A spare fold of the wool blanket also makes a scorch-resistant lap apron and a pad for gripping hot handles, and the brick doubles as your anvil face and as a weight to hold the bellows flat between strokes.

Use them to tame a noisy, "walking" appliance: fold the blanket into a thick pad and slip it under your washing machine, dryer, or compressor (or under a rattly generator/air conditioner) so the fabric absorbs vibration and keeps the racket from drumming through the floor, and slide the brick under a low corner as a solid shim to level the unit — or set it snugly against the side so the machine can't creep across the room during a hard spin cycle. The blanket also keeps the brick from scuffing the floor, and it protects the appliance's finish if you ever need to tip it back to work on it.

Use them as a grain-processing (threshing and milling) kit: spread the blanket flat on the ground as a clean threshing floor and beat or tread your harvested wheat, oats, or sunflower heads on it so the seed falls onto the fabric instead of being lost in the dirt. Then gather the corners, toss the grain up in the breeze from the blanket like a winnowing sheet — the heavier kernels fall back onto the cloth while the wind carries the chaff away. Finally, use the brick as a mano/grinding stone, rubbing and crushing the cleaned grain against a flat rock or its own flat face to make coarse meal or flour, and use a folded corner of the blanket to sift and pour the flour into a container. Afterward the blanket becomes the sack you bundle the grain in, with the brick set on top of the tied bundle to keep rodents from nosing in.

Use them to fix up a bed: slide a brick (wrapped in a fold of the blanket so it can't scratch or scar the floor) under each leg at the head end as a cheap bed riser — it tilts the mattress a few inches to ease acid reflux, snoring, or swollen legs, and lifts the frame high enough to store bins underneath. The rest of the blanket goes folded flat between the mattress and slats to shore up a sagging, dipped spot so the mattress lies level again, and it keeps the raised frame from rocking or squeaking on the bricks.

Turn them into a wool‑felting setup: lay the old wool blanket out (or pull it apart into loose fiber layers), soak it with hot soapy water, then use the brick as your fulling tool — rub the fabric back and forth over its rough, flat face and roll the wet bundle under the brick's weight. The heat, soap, friction, and steady pressure mat the fibers together, shrinking the thin, worn blanket into a dense, sturdy felt you can cut into slippers, pot holders, seat pads, tool rolls, or a thick floor mat. Afterward, set the brick on top of the damp felt while it dries so it stays flat and doesn't curl at the edges.

Use them as an off‑grid laundry kit: at the creek or in a tub, scrub the wash on the brick's flat, gritty face and pound the dirt out of jeans, socks, and work clothes against it (the traditional washing‑stone/beetling method), using a corner of the brick to work stubborn stains. Then wring the clothes out by rolling each piece up tightly inside the blanket and pressing or standing on it — the wool soaks up most of the water so garments come out damp instead of dripping and dry in a fraction of the time. Finally, spread the blanket over a bush, fence, or hot rock as a drying rack/clean surface for the laundry, and set the brick on the pile so a gust of wind doesn't send your clean clothes down the riverbank.

Make an improvised balance scale for weighing things where there's no scale. Pivot a stick or plank over a fulcrum (a log, a rope loop, or a chair back), tie the blanket's four corners to a cord and hang it from one end as the weighing pan, and hang or set the brick on the other end as your standard weight — a common brick is a known, consistent mass (roughly 4–5 lb / 2 kg), and you can chip it into halves and quarters to get smaller increments, or add pebbles for fine tuning. Pile produce, fish, grain, or scrap metal into the blanket sling until the beam levels, and you know what you've got: handy for trading at a market, portioning out food rations, splitting a harvest fairly, or checking that a package is under a shipping weight limit. Slide the brick along the beam and you've even got a steelyard for a range of weights, and when you're done the blanket knots up into a bundle-sack to carry everything home, with the brick sitting on top to keep the load from shifting.

Make a homemade heavy bag for boxing/kicking practice: roll the blanket up tight and stuff it into a duffel or sturdy canvas sack, burying the brick deep in the middle of the roll (wrapped in several layers of fabric so it can never work its way to the surface) to give the bag real mass and a solid core. Lash the top shut, hang it from a beam or sturdy branch with rope, and you've got a cheap heavy bag for conditioning punches, elbows, and kicks — the wool absorbs the impact so it's firm but not bone-jarring, and the brick's weight keeps it from flying around like an empty sack. If you'd rather not hang it, leave the bundle on the floor as a ground-and-pound/kicking dummy, or set a spare brick on the base to stop it sliding across the room.

Turn them into a backyard game. Spread the blanket out flat on the lawn (or on ice/a smooth floor) and mark scoring rings or zones on it with chalk, tape, or string — it's your target mat. Then take turns tossing, rolling, or sliding the brick at it from an agreed throwing line, curling/horseshoe/shuffleboard style: closest to the bullseye wins the point. The blanket does double duty as the scoreboard and as a cushion, absorbing the brick's impact so it doesn't chip, bounce off, or gouge the ground, and its weight keeps the blanket from sliding around once the brick lands on it. You can scale it up into a strongman-style "brick throw for distance" contest (blanket laid down as the landing zone so nobody has to guess where it hit), or scale it down for kids by having them slide the brick gently along the fabric like a shuffleboard puck. Afterwards, everything rolls up together — brick inside the blanket — for easy carrying and storage.

Set up a drum kit with them: stuff the folded blanket inside your bass drum, resting lightly against the heads — that's the classic muffling trick that kills the boomy ring and gives you a tight, punchy "thud" instead of a hollow roar (a corner of it can also be laid over a snare or tom to dampen overtones for recording). Then lay the brick on the floor right in front of the bass drum hoop, or against the pedal's base plate, so the kit can't creep forward across the floor as you play; wrapping the brick in a flap of the blanket keeps it from scratching the floor or rattling. Between gigs, the blanket becomes the padded wrap for your cymbals and hardware, with the brick set on the rolled bundle to keep it from unrolling in the car.

Turn them into a dog‑training kit. Spread the blanket out as a portable "place" mat — teaching your dog to go to it and settle means you can carry that same square of fabric to a friend's house, a café patio, or a campsite and instantly give the dog a familiar boundary to relax on instead of pestering guests. The brick becomes the training object: wrap it in a fold of the blanket and tie it off so there are no rough edges, and use it as a weighted retrieve/carry item to build a confident, steady hold and some real muscle (or clip it to a harness line as a light drag weight for conditioning a working dog). It's also great for nose work — let the dog sniff the wrapped brick, then hide it under the folded blanket or beneath one of several blanket corners and cue them to find it; the fabric masks the visual so they have to use their nose, and the brick's weight keeps the game from sliding around as they paw at it. A plain brick set on the mat's corners also stops the blanket from bunching up or blowing away outdoors, and at the end of the session the blanket rolls up around the brick into one tidy bundle you toss in the car.

Make a seed‑starting/sprouting nursery: stand the (clean, unglazed) brick in a shallow tray of water so it constantly wicks moisture up through its pores, scatter cress, wheatgrass, mustard, or chia seeds over its damp top face — or set your seed pots on it so they self‑water from below — then drape the blanket over the whole tray as a cover. The blanket blocks light and holds in humidity and warmth, which is exactly what most seeds need to break dormancy and sprout evenly, and it protects them from drafts on a chilly windowsill or in a cold shed. Peek under it each morning, and once the shoots appear, whip the blanket off and move the tray into the light (the brick keeps them watered while you're at work), then use the blanket again at night as a frost cover over the seedlings when you harden them off outdoors.

Use them as a papermaking press. Tear up scrap paper, blend it into pulp, and lift a sheet on a screen; then flip ("couch") each wet sheet onto a piece of the blanket — wool felt is exactly what hand papermakers use, because its nap grips the fragile sheet and wicks water out of it. Build a stack of blanket‑sheet‑blanket‑sheet, lay a board on top, and set the brick on it as your press weight: its steady mass squeezes out the excess water so the sheets come out flat, dense, and strong instead of buckled and crumbly. Peel the pressed sheets off the felts to dry on a window or line (a brick on a board keeps them from curling as they dry), and wring and re‑use the blanket for the next batch — great for making handmade cards, notebook paper, or seed paper from junk mail.

Use them as a painting/decorating kit when you're redoing a room: spread the old blanket out as a drop cloth over the floor and furniture — unlike plastic sheeting it soaks up drips instead of letting them puddle or slide underfoot, and it won't slip when you step on it. Use the brick as your all-purpose helper for the job: set it on the corners/edges of the blanket so it can't creep or bunch as you move around, wedge it under the door to prop it open for ventilation (and to keep it from swinging into wet paint), stand it under one foot of the ladder on soft or uneven ground so the ladder doesn't sink or wobble, and stack it under a can or tray to keep it steady at the right height. When you're done, lay a scrap of the blanket over the resealed paint-can lid and thump/press the brick down on it to seat the lid airtight without denting it, then roll your brushes and rollers up in the blanket for storage.

Turn them into a stone‑carving project: common brick is soft enough to shape with a nail, chisel, rasp, or old screwdriver, so clamp/steady it on your lap or a table and carve it into a small garden gargoyle, a house‑number plaque, a set of bookends, or a relief block you can ink and use as a printing stamp. The blanket is the workshop half of the setup — spread it under and around the brick to catch all the red dust and chips (so cleanup is just a matter of carrying the blanket outside and shaking it out), to deaden the noise and keep the brick from skating or scratching the table, and folded into a pad it cradles the block at whatever angle you need while you cut. Bunch a corner of it over the brick as a grip so your hand doesn't get scraped, use a dampened patch to wipe away dust and burnish the finished surface smooth, and when you're done wrap the carving in the blanket to protect its edges until you set it in the garden.

Use them as an aquarium/pond‑keeper's combo. Scrub and soak a clean, unglazed brick to leach it out, then drop it in the tank as a hardscape base — it makes a cheap cave/ledge for cichlids or catfish, a weight to hold down driftwood or a plant pot that keeps floating up, and a rough surface you can rubber‑band moss or anubias to until it takes root (it also gently buffers hardness for African cichlid setups). The blanket is the other half: drape it over the whole tank for a 3–4 day total blackout to starve out a green‑water or algae bloom, use it to shade a stressed fish or a newly medicated tank, and wrap it around the glass during a winter power outage so the water holds its heat for hours instead of crashing. It's also your safety layer during maintenance — a folded pad under the bucket and on the stand catches drips and stops the brick from chipping the glass while you position it, and it doubles as a lint‑free wrap for storing the heater and equipment afterward.

Use them as a grill‑and‑hold cooking rig: wrap the (clean) brick in foil and preheat it, then set it on top of a spatchcocked chicken, a pork belly, or a sandwich on the grill or in a heavy skillet — the classic "chicken under a brick" press. Its weight forces the whole surface into contact with the hot pan so the skin crisps up evenly and the meat cooks faster and flatter (great for paninis and smash‑style cooking too). When the meat comes off, wrap it in butcher paper or foil and bundle it in the blanket to rest for an hour: the wool holds the heat in like a restaurant holding cabinet, so the juices redistribute and the food is still steaming hot when you carve and serve it.

Make a drag mat for grooming ground: lay the blanket flat, roll the brick into one end and tie it in (adding more bricks along the hem if you have them) so the fabric stays down and taut, then hitch a rope to the two front corners and drag it behind a lawn tractor, ATV, bike — or just by hand. The weighted blanket skims along, knocking down clods, filling in hoof prints and tire ruts, and smoothing out a gravel driveway, a ball-field infield, a freshly seeded lawn or a spread of topdressing/sand into a level finish. The same rig works to smooth a sledding hill or backyard skating patch after a snowfall, to sweep up loose grass clippings, leaves and dust off a big shop floor or patio in one pass, and — dampened first — to lay down dust on a dirt drive. When you're done, untie the brick and use it to weight the blanket while it dries on the line.

Turn them into a mushroom‑growing incubator. Soak the porous brick in water and stand it in the bottom of a plastic tub or box next to your inoculated substrate jars/bags — as it slowly gives up that moisture it keeps the air inside humid without soaking the substrate. Then wrap the whole tub in the blanket: the wool holds the temperature steady through cold nights and drafts and blocks the light, which is exactly the dark, warm, damp environment mycelium needs to colonize fast instead of stalling or drying out. Peek in every few days, and when the block is fully white, pull the blanket off, crack the lid and start misting for pinning — using the brick as the weight that holds the lid or a humidity tent open at just the gap you want, and the blanket as a screen to shade the fruiting chamber from direct sun.

Set them up as a still‑life for drawing or painting practice: stand the brick on a table under a single lamp and drape the blanket around and over part of it so the fabric falls in folds. It's an ideal beginner's subject because it pairs the two hardest problems in one setup — the brick is a rigid rectangular solid for practicing linear perspective, edges, and its rough, matte texture, while the blanket gives you soft, flowing drapery with all its curves, cast shadows, and gradual value shifts. Move the lamp to change the light, cover more or less of the brick to vary the composition, and you have endless free studies; the blanket can also be hung behind as a plain backdrop, and the brick used to hold your paper or canvas flat while you work.

Keep them by the back door as an animal‑rescue/handling kit. If a panicked stray cat, an injured bird, or a bat gets into the house or is hurt in the yard, toss the blanket gently over it — the sudden darkness calms the animal and stops it thrashing, and the thick wool lets you scoop it up without being bitten, scratched or spurred (and without damaging feathers or fur). Bundle the wrapped animal into a cardboard box or laundry basket, then set the brick squarely on the lid so it can't nose or push its way out on the drive to the vet or wildlife rescue, and lay a fold of the blanket in the bottom as warm, absorbent bedding to keep it from going into shock. The brick is also handy for propping the box lid open just a crack for air, wedging the door open while you carry everything out, and holding down the blanket if you have to lay it over a hole or gap to keep the animal from bolting back in.

Turn them into a cold‑smoker for preserving fish and meat: stack bricks into a small firebox on the ground and set a smoldering pan of damp hardwood chips on top of one (the brick keeps the fire off the dirt, radiates steady low heat, and lets you choke the smoke down to a smolder rather than a flame). Build a tripod or box frame over it, hang your split fish, sausages, or thin strips of meat inside, then drape the blanket over the whole frame like a tent so the smoke is trapped and drifts up around the food instead of blowing away — pin the blanket's hem down with more bricks and lift one edge to control the draft. Hours later you've got smoked, preserved food, and the same smoke leaves the blanket smelling like a campfire (which also makes it a handy cover to hang meat under to keep flies off while it air‑dries).

Turn a bathroom or closet into an improvised darkroom: tack the blanket over the window (or hang it across the doorway) as a blackout curtain and lay the brick along its bottom hem so the fabric hangs flat and no stray light creeps in around the edges — with a second brick set against the door to hold it shut. In the resulting darkness you can load film onto reels, develop prints, or make cyanotype/photogram exposures, and the brick doubles as a steady weight to hold your paper or negatives flat under a contact-print glass while the leftover fold of blanket cushions the counter and soaks up chemical drips.

Keep them as an improvised self‑defense/home‑security pair. Drop the brick into one corner of the blanket and twist the fabric into a handle — you've made a flail/sap you can swing with real reach and force (and let go of instantly), far safer to hold than a bare brick, which would tear up your hand. The rest of the blanket is the defensive half: hold it spread in front of you like a matador's cape to tangle up a lunging dog or an attacker's arm or knife, throw it over someone's head to blind and smother them while you get away, or wrap it around your forearm as padded armor against bites and grabs. At home, the brick can be wedged under the door or set against a sliding window track so it can't be forced open, while the blanket hung over the glass keeps anyone from seeing in — and afterwards you fold the brick back inside it so it stores quietly in a closet instead of looking like a weapon.

Build a scarecrow/bird‑scarer for the garden: drive a stake or cross‑frame into the ground and set it in a bucket or ring of bricks (the brick at the base is the ballast that keeps the whole thing from blowing over), then dress the frame in the old blanket — stuff a bundle of it for the head and body and let the rest hang loose as a "coat." The loose fabric flaps, billows and rustles in every breeze, which is what actually spooks crows, pigeons and deer off your seedlings, and you can cut the blanket into ribbons or a cape for even more movement. A spare half‑brick tied to a dangling strip makes it swing and thump against the post for noise, and the same brick can be moved to pin the hem of a blanket laid over a seed row when you want the fabric flat instead of flying.

Turn them into a weaving setup for a rag rug. Cut or tear the old blanket into long strips (winding them into balls) to serve as your weft, then rig a simple warp‑weighted loom: string your warp threads from a horizontal bar (a broom handle lashed between two chair backs or a door frame) and tie the brick — plus any half‑bricks or chunks you break off it — to the bottom of the warp bundles as the tensioning weights. The brick's steady pull keeps the threads taut and evenly spaced, which is exactly what the ancient warp‑weighted looms did, so you can pass the blanket strips over‑and‑under by hand and beat each row up snug. The result is a thick, durable rag rug, mat, or seat pad made entirely from a blanket that was too worn to sleep under. The brick's flat face also works to press and smooth the finished weaving flat, and it makes a fine weight to hold the roll of finished rug (or the loose warp) in place between sessions.

Build a backyard root‑cellar "clamp" for storing your harvest: lay bricks on the ground as a raised platform (with gaps between them for air) so the potatoes, carrots, beets and apples piled on top stay off the wet, freezing soil, then drape the blanket over the whole heap as an insulating quilt and pin its edges down with more bricks so wind can't lift it and rodents can't burrow under. The blanket keeps the pile dark (so potatoes don't green or sprout) while trapping just enough of the earth's warmth to hold the produce a few degrees above freezing through a cold snap, and the brick mass buffers the daily temperature swings so nothing gets frost‑bitten or overheats. Peel the blanket back on mild days to let moisture escape and pull out what you need, then tuck it back down.

Use them for erosion control on a bare slope or washed‑out gully: spread the old blanket flat over the bare, seeded soil as a biodegradable erosion mat — it breaks the force of falling rain, keeps the seed and topsoil from washing away, holds moisture in, and the new grass roots grow right through the weave. Pin it down with bricks laid along the edges and seams so wind and runoff can't peel it up, and stack a few bricks across the bottom of the gully (with a fold of blanket tucked behind them) as a small check dam that slows the water and traps the silt it's carrying. By the time the blanket rots away, the bank is knitted together with roots and the bricks can be pulled out and reused.

Use them to build a winter snow shelter: pack wet snow into a box or scoop it up and use the brick as a mold/tamper — press and pound it to form and square up uniform snow blocks, then stack the blocks into a wind wall or the spiral dome of an igloo (the brick's flat faces also work to shave and trim each block so it seats tightly, and to chink the seams). Once the shelter is up, the blanket becomes the door: hang it over the entrance tunnel, weighting its bottom hem with the brick so wind can't blow it aside, and lay the rest of it on the sleeping shelf as insulation between you and the snow. Come morning, the brick knocks the ice off the blanket and the frozen doorway so you can pack up and move on.

Use them as a wood‑bending rig: soak the blanket in water, heat the brick in a fire or oven until it's very hot, then lay the wet blanket over the strip of wood you want to curve (a chair rung, snowshoe frame, hoop, or bow limb) and set the hot brick on top, wrapping the whole bundle up. The brick's stored heat turns the blanket's water into steam that soaks into the fibers and makes the wood limp and pliable in minutes — no steam box needed. Bend the softened piece around a form or between pegs, and then leave the brick sitting on it as a dead weight (with a fold of blanket underneath so it doesn't mar the wood) until it cools and dries locked in its new shape.

Set up a kids' puppet/shadow theater with them: hang the blanket across a doorway (or between two chairs) as the stage curtain and backdrop, and run a cord from one top corner over a hook or nail with the brick tied to the other end — the brick's weight acts as a counterweight so the curtain glides smoothly open and shut, or drops closed on cue at the end of a scene. A second brick set on the blanket's bottom hem keeps it hanging flat and still so shadow puppets read crisply against it, and the brick offstage doubles as a stable base for the lamp or as the "curtain-up" bell you tap. Afterwards, roll the props inside the blanket with the brick on top of the bundle for storage.

Use them as a soap‑maker's kit: after you pour your cold‑process soap batter into its mold, set the (foil‑ or plastic‑wrapped) brick on the lid as a steady press weight so the loaf settles level with no air pockets and the lid stays sealed, then swaddle the whole mold in the blanket. The wool traps the heat the saponifying lye and oils generate so the batch goes fully through "gel phase" — giving a harder, smoother, more vividly colored bar instead of a partial gel with a chalky ring. Leave it bundled for 24 hours, unwrap, unmold and cut, then stand the bars on the brick's porous, absorbent face to cure, since it wicks moisture away from the bottoms so they dry evenly without sweating or soft spots.

Use them as a hide‑tanning kit. Work the raw skin over a log and use the brick's hard edge and gritty face as your scraper/fleshing tool — its weight and abrasive surface strip off fat, membrane and hair, and rubbing the brick over the dried hide breaks and softens the fibers the way a staking tool does. The blanket is the wet‑work half: wrap the soaking or brain‑dressed hide in it to keep it evenly damp while the solution penetrates (instead of letting the edges dry stiff), lay it under the hide as a padded, non‑abrasive work surface, and later drape it over the smoking frame to trap the smoke that sets the tan. Afterward the finished leather rolls up in the blanket with the brick on top to keep the bundle flat.

Use them as a tree‑transplanting kit: after you dig around the roots, tip the tree over onto the spread blanket, gather the fabric up around the root ball and tie it off — that's the classic "ball‑and‑burlap" wrap, which holds the soil and fine feeder roots together and keeps them from drying out while you drag the (surprisingly heavy) ball to its new hole on the blanket like a sledge, without wrecking your back or the tree. Set it in the new hole, cut the ties and slide the blanket out, then put the brick to work: bury it flat a foot or so down beside the tree with a wire or rope looped around it as a "deadman" anchor for the guy line that holds the young trunk upright against wind, and use any leftover brick pieces to ring a shallow watering basin around the trunk so irrigation soaks in over the roots instead of running off. A strip of the blanket makes soft padding where the guy line touches the bark, and the rest can be laid on the soil as a mulch/moisture blanket, pinned by the bricks, while the tree settles in.

Make a mudroom setup at your back door: stand the brick outside on the step with its rough, gritty face and sharp edge exposed and use it as a boot scraper — drag your soles and heels across it to knock off caked mud, snow, and manure before you go in. Just inside the door, spread the folded blanket as a mud mat to catch whatever's left, so wet boots and paws get wiped and dry there instead of tracking grit through the house (fold a corner of the blanket over to wipe the dog's feet, too). Shake the blanket out over the garden when it's filthy, and set the brick on its edge indoors on windy days so the mat doesn't curl up or slide when the door swings open.

Make hand‑cranked ice cream at a picnic: put your bagged ice inside a folded corner of the blanket and smash it with the flat of the brick to crush it fine (the fabric contains the shards and muffles the noise), pack the crushed ice and salt around the cream canister, then bundle the whole bucket in the blanket so the slush stays cold and freezes the custard faster instead of melting away in the sun. Once it's churned, keep the canister wrapped in the blanket with the brick set on the lid to hold it shut, and the ice cream will still be firm by the time you serve it.

Set them up as an improvised printing press for block prints or etchings: lay your inked lino/carved block (or plate) face‑up on a table, place your dampened paper on it, then put a folded piece of the blanket on top as the press "felt" — wool blankets are exactly what etching presses use, because they cushion and push the paper down into every cut and line so the ink transfers evenly. Instead of a roller, put the brick on top of the blanket and press/rock its flat face over the whole area with your body weight, working section by section, to get a crisp, fully inked pull. The same brick then holds the finished prints flat between blotter sheets while they dry (weighted on a board over the blanket pad), and a corner of the blanket doubles as your ink rag and as a non‑slip mat that keeps the block from shifting while you work.

Make a sun clock/navigation tool out of them: spread the blanket flat on an open, level patch of ground as your "dial face" (weight or stake its corners so it can't shift), stand the brick upright on end in the middle as the gnomon, and mark the tip of its shadow on the fabric with chalk, pins, or pebbles every hour through the day. Connect the marks and label them and you've got a working sundial you can roll up and re-lay in the same spot; the shortest shadow of the day marks local noon and gives you a true north–south line, so the same setup doubles as the classic shadow-stick compass for orienting a map when you have no phone or watch. It's a great, cheap astronomy lesson for kids — and the blanket keeps the marks all in one place instead of scratched into the dirt, while the brick's flat faces make it easy to stand plumb and to hold a straightedge against when you draw the hour lines.

Make an improvised oil lamp out of them: common brick is soft and porous, so gouge or drill a shallow bowl into its top face (a nail, screwdriver, or the corner of a second brick will do it) to make a stable, fireproof lamp body that won't tip or burn a table. Twist a narrow strip torn from the wool blanket into a tight cord for the wick, lay one end in the hollow with the tip draped over the notch you've cut in the rim, and fill the bowl with cooking oil, rendered fat, or melted candle stubs — wool wicks fuel beautifully and burns slowly, and the brick's mass soaks up and re-radiates the heat while keeping the flame off anything flammable. Hang the rest of the blanket behind or beside it as a windbreak/blackout curtain so drafts don't gutter the flame and the light doesn't spill where you don't want it, and keep a damp corner of the blanket handy to snuff the wick or smother a spill. It's a cheap, reusable light source for a power outage, a camp, or a shed with no wiring — and when the fuel's gone you just re-fill the hollow and twist a fresh strip of blanket for a new wick.

Set them up as a worm‑composting (vermiculture) bin. Lay the old blanket — dampened — flat over the bedding surface inside the bin: it keeps the top layer moist and dark so the worms come right up to feed instead of hiding at the bottom, blocks fruit flies, and you just peel it back to add scraps. The brick does three jobs: crush a small amount of it into coarse red grit and sprinkle it in, since worms need grit in their gizzards to grind food (it also sweetens acidic bedding); stand the bin up on a whole brick or two so air can reach the drainage holes and the tray underneath catches the "worm tea"; and set another brick on the lid so raccoons, rats, or the wind can't get it open. In a cold snap, wrap the spare length of blanket right around the outside of the bin as a duvet so the worms keep working through the winter.

Turn them into a garage‑parking kit: set the brick on the floor at exactly the spot where your front tire should stop, so you can pull in each night until you feel the wheel touch it and know you're far enough in without nosing into the wall or shelves (it also acts as a chock so a car on a slight slope can't creep). Then hang the folded blanket on the garage wall (or the pillar/car beside you) at door‑handle height with a couple of nails or hooks — it becomes a padded bumper so swinging doors hit soft wool instead of concrete, saving your paint and the neighbor's car. The blanket can be pulled down whenever you need to kneel on the cold floor or cover the fender while you lean over the engine, and the brick keeps it from blowing around when the garage door is open.

Use them as a stable/horse kit: fold the blanket into a saddle pad (or throw it over a hot, sweaty horse as a cooler rug after a ride so it doesn't chill while it dries), and set the brick on end beside the horse as a small mounting block to give you the extra few inches to get a foot in the stirrup — the same brick then props the barn or stall door open while you lead the horse through, chocks the wheel of the muck cart or trailer on a slope, and weights the corner of the blanket when you hang it over a rail to air out.

Turn them into an improvised incubator/brooder for hatching eggs or newly hatched chicks (or an orphaned litter of kittens/puppies): warm the brick gently in the oven or by a fire until it's hand-hot — not scorching — wrap it in a fold of the blanket so nothing touches the bare, hot surface, and set it in the corner of a cardboard box or tote. Nestle the eggs or chicks in the rest of the blanket beside it; the brick's dense mass releases its stored heat slowly and steadily for hours, while the wool traps that warmth and blocks drafts, holding the box in the brooding temperature range. Swap in a freshly warmed brick every few hours, drape a corner of the blanket loosely over the top to hold the heat while leaving an air gap, and lay a second brick on the box lid or against its side so it can't be nosed open or tipped over. It's a lifesaver when the heat lamp or incubator loses power, or for keeping a chilled chick alive on the drive to the vet.

Turn them into a fire‑starting kit. Use the brick as a hard anvil/hammer: smash a piece of flint, quartz or chert against it to knock off a sharp‑edged flake, then strike that flake against the back of a knife or steel to throw sparks. Cut a few squares from the blanket (cotton works best) and slow‑cook them in a sealed tin over the coals to make char cloth — it catches a spark instantly, and fluffed‑up fibers teased from the blanket's nap serve as the tinder nest you blow into flame. The brick then becomes the dry, insulated hearth you build the little fire on so ground damp doesn't kill it, and it makes a heat reflector to bounce warmth back at you, while the rest of the blanket shields the new flame from wind and keeps the char‑cloth tin dry in your pack.

Use them as a casting setup: because common brick is soft and heat‑proof, carve a cavity into its flat face (with a nail, chisel, or screwdriver) to make a reusable ingot/figure mold — then pour in melted candle wax, crayons, lead sinkers, pewter, or aluminum from a crucible and let it set in the brick's hollow. The blanket is the safety and finishing half: fold it into a thick pad as a heat‑proof mat under the mold, wrap a corner around your hand as a hot pad for handling the brick, and once the pour has skinned over, bundle the whole brick and casting up in the wool so it cools down slowly and evenly — which anneals metal so it doesn't crack or go brittle, and keeps wax from shrinking and cracking. Afterwards, rub the cooled casting against the brick's rough face to file off the sprue, and buff it on the blanket.

Use them as an entomologist's "beating sheet" for pest scouting: hold or spread the blanket flat under a shrub, fruit tree, or berry bush, then rap the branches sharply with the brick a few times. The jolt knocks caterpillars, weevils, aphids, Japanese beetles, stink bugs, and spider mites off the foliage and they drop onto the pale fabric, where they're easy to see, count, identify, and tip into a jar of soapy water — a quick way to know exactly what's eating your plants before you decide to spray. The brick's mass delivers a firm thump without bruising or snapping the limbs (wrap it in a corner of the blanket for extra cushioning), and set on the blanket's corners it keeps the sheet from blowing or curling while you work. It's also a great kids' nature activity: beat a branch, then examine the spiders, lacewings, and ladybugs that land on the blanket before letting them go.

Make a poor‑man's weight sled for conditioning: fold the blanket into a thick square, set the brick (or a stack of them) in the middle, tie a rope through the folded corners, and then push, drag, or sprint‑pull the bundle across a carpet, gym floor, lawn, or driveway. The blanket glides like a furniture slider and protects the floor while the brick supplies the resistance — add or remove bricks to change the load, or slide the whole rig hand‑over‑hand for a rowing‑style pull. Flip it over and the same folded blanket works as a pair of "sliders" under your feet or hands for mountain climbers, lunges, and pike slides, and the brick doubles as a low step/platform for calf raises or a marker for shuttle runs. When you're done, roll everything up in the blanket with the brick inside and stash it in a closet.

Set them up as a backyard bird station. Snip the blanket into short, loose strands (2–4 inches of wool works best) and stuff them into a mesh bag, suet cage, or the fork of a shrub — nesting birds will pull the fibers out all spring to line their nests, and the leftover fabric can be draped over a shrub as a windbreak. Stand the brick on end in the yard as a sturdy pedestal for a shallow water dish or a saucer of seed, and drop a second brick into the bottom of a birdbath so it doubles as a shallow "wading step" that lets small birds and bees perch and drink without drowning. The brick's weight also keeps the dish, and the blanket you spread beneath as a seed-catching mat, from blowing away in the wind.

Take them ice fishing as a "dark house" rig.
