**The structural move — unbundle the school.** Instead of one building that owns a child's day, create a local learning network in which the school is the hub but libraries, museums, labs, farms, hospitals, workshops, small businesses, civic bodies, and nonprofits are all credentialed learning sites. Students earn credit wherever real learning happens. A teenager could spend mornings on core academics and afternoons in a clinic, a machine shop, a newsroom, or a watershed restoration crew. This solves the deepest problem with the current model — that school is a simulation of life rather than participation in it — and it multiplies the number of adults invested in each young person.

**The curricular move — teach on a 100-year time horizon.** Organize learning around the durable, civilization-scale challenges students will inherit rather than around the 19th-century subject silos: energy and climate, food and water, health and biotechnology, machine intelligence, migration and demographic change, and the maintenance of self-governance. Math, writing, history, biology, and chemistry are taught *inside* these problems, where they gain obvious purpose. Crucially, add what's almost entirely missing today: **long-term thinking** — exponential growth, compounding, feedback loops, second-order consequences, risk under deep uncertainty, and obligations to people not yet born. A generation that intuitively reasons across decades rather than quarters is the single greatest gift we could give the 22nd century.

**The moral move — restore the formative purpose of education.** Every student engages in sustained service and stewardship work, contributes to something in their community that outlasts their enrollment, and studies ethics and moral reasoning seriously — not as abstraction, but as practice, because the technologies coming (gene editing, synthetic biology, artificial minds, geoengineering) will hand ordinary people powers that previously belonged to no one. Technical capability without formed judgment is the central danger of the next century.

**The economic move — replace the one-shot degree with a lifelong entitlement.** Give every citizen a publicly funded learning account, drawable across an entire life, and make credentials modular and stackable. If people will live to 100 and change careers six times, the idea that education concludes at 22 is already obsolete. This also removes the crushing pressure that forces 17-year-olds to bet their future on a single irreversible choice.

**The human move — measure what matters.** Judge schools not by test scores but by longitudinal outcomes: are graduates, at 30, healthy, employed in work they find meaningful, civically engaged, capable of sustaining relationships, and still learning? Design backward from that.

The underlying wager is that the 22nd century will not reward those who know the most, since knowledge will be ambient and instantly retrievable. It will reward those who can direct attention wisely, judge well under uncertainty, cooperate with strangers across difference, and care about consequences beyond their own lifespan — and none of those are learned by sitting in rows.

**Redesign the system to evolve rather than to be redesigned — treat American education as an adaptive, self-correcting portfolio of models instead of a single blueprint.**

The honest premise: nobody in 2025 can specify what a 22nd-century citizen needs. Every confident curriculum we write today will look as quaint as 1925's typing and penmanship requirements. So the real failure of American education isn't any particular content choice — it's that the system has almost no capacity to learn from its own results. It changes by political fashion, not evidence, and it changes at the speed of textbook adoption cycles.

**The core mechanism:** decouple funding, provision, and quality control, which are currently fused in the district monopoly.

- *Funding follows the child*, weighted heavily upward for poverty, disability, and English-learner status — so the students hardest to serve become the ones providers most want to serve, reversing today's incentive.
- *Provision becomes plural and small-scale*: district schools, charters, microschools, hybrid homeschool co-ops, career academies, tribal and religious schools, online providers. Not because markets are magic, but because a monoculture cannot discover anything. Variation is the raw material of improvement.
- *Quality control becomes public, rigorous, and outcome-based*: a genuinely independent national assessment infrastructure with transparent, longitudinally tracked results — including growth measures, graduate earnings, college persistence, civic participation, and wellbeing at 30 — published for every provider. Freedom to design, no freedom to hide results, and swift closure of persistent failures.

**Build the missing R&D layer.** Education spends roughly 0.1% of its budget on research; pharmaceuticals spend twenty times that share. Create a DARPA-scale education research agency with authority to run large randomized trials in real schools, fund high-risk pedagogical bets, and — critically — fund replication and publish failures. Pair it with a national implementation corps that carries proven practices into classrooms, because the gap between "known to work" and "actually done" is where most educational value dies.

**Professionalize teaching through licensure by demonstrated effectiveness**, not credit hours in ed schools. Let engineers, nurses, and machinists teach after supervised residency; pay far more; make tenure a genuine achievement rather than a three-year default; create master-teacher roles that let the best practitioners stay in classrooms while shaping others.

**Guard the commons.** Pluralism without a floor becomes fragmentation, so hold a small, non-negotiable core: literacy, numeracy, scientific reasoning, American constitutional history and civics, and integration incentives that prevent the system from sorting children into sealed ideological or class enclaves. Democracy requires citizens who can still talk to each other.

**Rebuild the on-ramps.** Fund apprenticeships at European scale so that the non-college path is a genuine path rather than a consolation prize, and make credentials modular and stackable so a 40-year-old can re-enter without starting over.

The wager: a system with fast feedback loops, honest measurement, real variation, and the institutional courage to kill what fails will outperform any fixed design we could impose today — and it will still be improving in 2100, when our specific curricular guesses have long since expired.

**Redesign schools around human biology and cognitive science — build them as attention sanctuaries that cultivate deep knowledge, not as information-delivery pipelines competing with the internet.**

The premise most reform proposals get backwards: in a world of infinite, instantly retrievable information and machines that can generate any text on demand, the scarce resources are *attention, memory, and the capacity for sustained, difficult thought*. Those are biological capacities that atrophy without deliberate training. A 22nd-century education should therefore be countercultural — it should build precisely what the surrounding environment erodes.

**Protect attention as the core asset.** Phone-free campuses, bell to bell. Long uninterrupted work blocks instead of fragmented 45-minute periods. Sustained silent reading of full books — not excerpts, not summaries — as a daily, protected practice, because the ability to hold a complex argument in mind across hundreds of pages is the substrate of every other intellectual capacity, and it is disappearing. Explicit training in single-tasking, boredom tolerance, and voluntary attention control, treated as seriously as we once treated handwriting.

**Take memory seriously again.** "Just look it up" is cognitively false: reasoning, insight, and creativity all operate on knowledge held *in* long-term memory, not on a screen. So build a coherent, cumulative, knowledge-rich curriculum — history, literature, science, geography, art — sequenced so that each year's learning has something to attach to, and delivered through spaced retrieval practice, interleaving, and cumulative examination rather than cram-and-forget units. A student with a richly furnished mind can evaluate an AI's output; a student with an empty one can only accept it.

**Align the schedule to developing bodies.** Start high school after 8:30 a.m. — adolescent circadian biology is not negotiable, and the sleep debt we impose is one of the largest unforced errors in American schooling. Restore daily physical movement, outdoor time, and recess at every grade level, not as a reward but as a cognitive intervention. Prioritize small classes and expert phonics-based reading instruction in the early years, where the returns are largest, and accept larger classes later if that's the tradeoff.

**Redesign adolescence around the drives it actually has.** Teenagers are wired for status, risk, belonging, and contribution — and we respond by seating them in rows for six more years. Instead, structure ages 15–18 around real apprenticeship, performance, and public accountability: work with adult mentors, oral examinations and disputation before audiences, competitions, productions, published research, paid workplace placements. Let them earn genuine standing among adults, which is what they are neurologically hungry for.

**Rebuild the social organism.** Loneliness and anxiety are now the binding constraint on learning for millions of students. Design for stable relationships: keep cohorts with the same teacher for multiple years, keep schools small enough that every child is known by name, restore singing, theater, team sport, and shared ritual — the embodied, synchronous, in-person experiences that build the emotional regulation and trust no software can supply.

**Assess through performance, not proctoring.** When AI can write any essay, take-home written work loses its evidentiary value. Shift to oral defenses, timed in-person writing, laboratory and studio practicals, and public demonstrations — assessments that measure what a student can actually do with their own mind, in real time.

The wager: the 22nd century will be saturated with machine intelligence, so the differentiating human capacities will be the ability to concentrate deeply, to hold a large store of knowledge in mind, to think clearly under one's own power, and to be well-attached to other people. Schools should be the one institution in society deliberately engineered to build exactly those things.

**Break the diploma's monopoly: separate the *teaching* of things from the *certifying* of things, and let credentials become open, granular, and earnable by anyone, at any age, from any path.**

The hidden architecture distorting American education isn't pedagogy — it's the fact that a handful of institutions hold a legal and cultural monopoly on the signals that unlock adult life. Because a K–12 diploma and a bachelor's degree are the only currencies employers trust, schooling becomes a 13-to-17-year tollbooth that students must pass through regardless of whether learning occurs inside it. That single fact produces almost everything we complain about: seat-time instead of mastery, grade inflation, the admissions arms race, credential inflation that pushes ever more years of schooling in front of ever more jobs, and the crushing of anyone whose talents don't fit the one approved route.

**The redesign:**

- **Build a public, open credentialing infrastructure** — a national library of fine-grained, rigorously validated competency certifications (statistical reasoning, technical writing, machining, wound care, conversational Mandarin, financial modeling, constitutional reasoning, welding to spec) that any person can attempt at any age, free of charge, without regard to where or how they learned it. Assessment is done by independent bodies with no stake in enrollment — secure, in-person, performance-based, and AI-resistant by design: oral defense, timed production, supervised practicum, verified work product.
- **Make learning provision fully plural and unregulated on the front end.** Once the exit signal is trustworthy, it no longer matters whether a student learned from a public school, an AI tutor, a machine shop, a parent, a bootcamp, or a library. Regulate the *credential*, not the *route*. This immediately legitimizes the enormous amount of learning happening outside classrooms and lets talent from any background prove itself directly.
- **Attack the demand side too**: restrict degree requirements as legal proxies in hiring and licensing (as several states have begun doing for public jobs) and require employers to state the competencies they actually need. This deflates credential inflation and stops forcing families to buy four years of tuition to signal traits a two-hour exam can verify.
- **Let this run over a whole lifetime.** Credentials stack and are re-earnable, so a 45-year-old displaced by automation can re-credential in months rather than restarting a degree — essential in a century of 60-year careers and repeated technological displacement.

**What happens to schools:** relieved of their role as gatekeepers, they become what they're uniquely good at and nothing else can replace — places of mentorship, apprenticeship, argument, performance, teamwork, and belonging, with adults who coach rather than certify. Teachers stop being the judges students must please and become allies against an external standard, which is a far healthier relationship and the one that exists in athletics, music, and the trades, where American youth achievement is conspicuously excellent.

**The wager:** in a century where knowledge is ambient and instruction is nearly free, the genuinely scarce good is *trustworthy proof of capability*. Build that public good well, and the rest of the system reorganizes itself around real learning — because for the first time, faking it stops working.

**Flip the investment curve: make the first 2,000 days — not high school or college — the center of the American education system.**

We currently spend the least on children when their brains are most plastic and the most when they're least plastic, then spend decades running expensive remediation on gaps that were already fixed by kindergarten. If we want capable 22nd-century adults, the highest-leverage redesign is to treat education as beginning at conception and to build the system around the developmental window where returns compound for eighty years.

**What that means concretely:**

- **Universal, well-paid parental leave and a "birth-to-five" public system**, staffed by professionalized early educators paid on the K–12 scale rather than near minimum wage. Ratios small enough for responsive, back-and-forth adult–child conversation, which is the single best-documented driver of later language and reading ability.
- **Voluntary nurse and educator home visiting for every newborn**, as in the Netherlands and Denmark — coaching parents on serve-and-return interaction, sleep, nutrition, reading aloud, and stress reduction, and catching problems early instead of diagnosing them in third grade.
- **Universal developmental screening built into pediatric care**: vision, hearing, speech, dyslexia risk, and adverse-experience exposure, with automatic referral into treatment. Millions of American children are currently failing school for reasons an eye exam or a hearing aid would fix.
- **Attack the material preconditions of learning as education policy, not welfare policy**: child allowances, housing stability, prenatal care, lead abatement. Neurotoxins, hunger, eviction, and chronic stress are curriculum problems, because they physically constrain what a brain can later do.
- **Guarantee reading by nine.** Fund K–3 like an emergency: small classes, expert phonics-based instruction, intensive tutoring the moment a child falls behind rather than after they've failed. Literacy is the one skill on which every subsequent skill is parasitic, and it is the last thing we should let AI do for people.
- **Pay for it by rebalancing, not only by adding** — shifting some spending from late-stage remediation, credential inflation, and the fourteenth year of subsidized general-education coursework toward the years where a dollar buys ten times the outcome.

**The rest of the system reorganizes around this.** With foundations secure, later schooling can stop being a sorting-and-triage operation and become what it should be: apprenticeship, deep subject mastery, and real work. And parents become the system's primary partners rather than its customers — an education system that only begins when a child is five has already ceded the most important years to chance.

**The wager:** every ambitious vision of future schooling — AI tutors, project-based learning, lifelong credentials — quietly assumes a child who arrives able to focus, self-regulate, trust adults, and read. That child is manufactured in the first five years or not at all. Build the system that reliably produces them, and nearly everything downstream gets easier; fail to, and no amount of 22nd-century pedagogy will compensate.

**Stop redesigning the curriculum and redesign the *job*: rebuild American education around a small, elite, team-based teaching profession — because no school system has ever outperformed the quality of the adults standing in front of its students.**

We keep trying to reform education through content (new standards, new subjects, new technology) while leaving untouched the fact that we ask 3.2 million people — recruited from the middle of the college talent distribution, trained thinly, paid poorly, given no career ladder, and left alone in a room with 28 kids — to deliver it. Every high-performing system on earth (Finland, Singapore, Japan, Korea) got there by fixing that first. Whatever the 22nd century demands, it will be taught by *someone*, and the ceiling on any reform is the person implementing it.

**The redesign:**

- **Trade quantity for quality.** Deliberately employ meaningfully fewer classroom teachers and roughly double their pay, funding it by restructuring staffing rather than by new spending alone: team-based instruction, large-group direct instruction by the strongest teachers, AI tutors and paraprofessionals handling practice and feedback, and reversing decades of administrative and non-instructional staff growth (which has far outpaced student enrollment). A great teacher with 40 students, supported by a team, beats a mediocre one with 20.
- **Make entry genuinely selective, and training clinical.** Recruit from the top of the graduating class the way medicine and the military academies do — full tuition scholarships plus a service commitment. Replace the low-rigor education-school pipeline with a two-year paid residency under a master teacher, licensure by demonstrated classroom effectiveness, and a real washout rate. Selectivity is itself the recruiting tool: people want to join hard things.
- **Build a career worth staying in.** Today's teaching is the rare profession with no advancement except leaving the classroom. Create a public ladder — apprentice, professional, mentor, master — with master teachers earning near six figures for leading teams, designing curriculum, and coaching novices while still teaching. Expertise should compound and spread, not walk out the door in year five (as roughly half currently do).
- **Restructure the school day around teacher learning.** American teachers spend far more hours in front of students than international peers and almost none observing each other. Rebuild the schedule so 30–40% of paid time is collaborative preparation, joint lesson study, and peer observation — the Japanese practice that turns individual craft into institutional knowledge. This is the mechanism by which a system actually improves; without it, every good idea dies in isolated classrooms.
- **Give autonomy in exchange for standards.** A profession that is selective, trained, and evaluated by its own masters doesn't need scripted curricula and compliance mandates — it needs the freedom doctors and engineers have, paired with genuine accountability for results and real consequences for persistent failure.

**Why this prepares students for 2100 specifically:** as AI absorbs information delivery, explanation, and drill, the residual human work of teaching becomes the *hardest* part — diagnosing why a particular child is stuck, motivating the unmotivated, modeling intellectual seriousness, judging quality, forming character, holding a room of adolescents together. That is expert work, and it cannot be done by an underpaid, undertrained, exhausted workforce, no matter how good the software or the standards are. Fix the profession, and the system gains something no blueprint can supply: the capacity to keep improving itself long after our specific curricular guesses have expired.

**Fix the operating system, not the software: give American education a coherent national spine and insulate it from the electoral cycle.**

The deepest reason U.S. schooling underperforms isn't pedagogy or curriculum — it's governance. We run roughly 13,000 semi-independent districts across 50 regimes, funded largely by local property wealth, steered by three-year superintendents and two-year board majorities, with curricula chosen through political fights and textbook-adoption bidding wars. No coherent practice can accumulate in such a system. Every high-performing country has an architecture that lets improvements compound; we have 13,000 experiments that never talk to each other and reverse themselves every election. A century-long project needs an institution capable of thinking beyond four years.

**The redesign:**

- **A national, sovereign-fund-scale finance base.** Replace property-tax dependence with federal and state funding that follows the child at a guaranteed per-pupil floor, weighted for poverty and disability. A child's education should not be a function of the assessed value of the houses nearby — that single design flaw locks in inequality more effectively than any curriculum choice.
- **A common national core, deliberately small.** A specified, sequenced backbone in literacy, mathematics, science, and constitutional civics — perhaps 60% of instructional time — with the remaining 40% left entirely to local, school, and teacher discretion. Coherence where coherence pays (a child moving from Tulsa to Tacoma doesn't lose a year; teacher training can actually match what teachers teach), freedom where it matters (how it's taught, and everything beyond the core).
- **A public curriculum commons.** Publicly funded, openly licensed, continuously improved instructional materials — lessons, assessments, labs, AI tutoring tied to the actual sequence — free to every school. Today each district reinvents the same materials badly and pays publishers for the privilege. Build it once, well, and let every teacher in the country improve it.
- **A single longitudinal data spine.** Portable student records, common outcome definitions, and honest cross-state comparability, so the system can finally tell what works. Right now we can't even reliably compare states because everyone grades their own homework.
- **An independent stewardship body with a long clock.** A National Education Council on the model of the Federal Reserve or the Base Realignment Commission: members with staggered 10–14 year terms, statutory independence, control of the core standards and the assessment infrastructure, and a legal mandate to report on outcomes 20 and 50 years out. Elected officials retain the purse and the power to overhaul it; they lose the ability to churn it every two years. This is the only structural mechanism that makes multi-decade investments — early childhood, teacher pipelines, curriculum coherence — politically survivable.
- **Guardrails against centralization's failure mode.** Content limited to the demonstrable core, an explicit right of exit for families and charter/independent providers, and mandatory sunset review of every mandate. Coherence must not become sclerosis or ideological capture.

**Why this prepares students for 2100:** whatever the right answer about AI, skills, or content turns out to be, a fragmented, short-horizon, wealth-stratified system cannot adopt it at scale or sustain it long enough to matter. Institutions are the technology by which societies think across generations. Build one capable of holding a 75-year plan, and America finally gains the ability to implement its own good ideas — which, so far, has been the actual bottleneck.

**Redesign around motivation as the binding constraint: convert schooling from a compulsory obligation into a demand-driven system where students hold real power, real stakes, and real ownership of their work.**

The unspoken fact about American education is that most students are disengaged — by high school, large majorities report boredom, and roughly half say their schoolwork feels meaningless. We treat this as a discipline or delivery problem, but it's a design problem: we built an institution in which young people have essentially no authorship over what they do for thirteen years, and then we're puzzled that they don't want to do it. Every 22nd-century capability we care about — self-direction, initiative, creative judgment, lifelong relearning — is downstream of *wanting to*, and wanting to is the one thing AI tutors, better standards, and longer school days cannot manufacture.

**The redesign:**

- **Give students genuine jurisdiction.** Every school runs as a working republic: elected student governance with actual budget authority over a meaningful share of school funds, student-staffed judicial councils handling discipline restoratively, student participation in hiring committees and course design. Not "student voice" as decoration — real decisions with real consequences, including bad ones they must live with. Self-governance is learned the way a language is: by speaking it daily from age six, not by studying it in a civics unit at seventeen.

- **Make students producers rather than consumers.** Restructure the upper years so the central artifact is not a transcript but a body of *work* that exists in the world — a published paper, a working product, a business with customers, a documented experiment, a performed piece, a repaired building, a policy adopted by a town council. Students own what they make, including its intellectual property and revenue. Ownership converts effort from compliance into investment.

- **Widen choice radically after the foundations are secure.** Hold a tight, non-negotiable core through roughly age fourteen — literacy, numeracy, scientific and historical reasoning — because freedom without capability is a trap. After that, let students assemble their own path from a broad menu of academic tracks, apprenticeships, studios, labs, and outside providers, guided by a permanent advisor who stays with them for years. The system's job becomes helping each student find *the thing they'd stay up late for*, then building rigor around it, rather than distributing identical requirements and hoping.

- **Let failure be real, then recoverable.** Students choose projects that can genuinely fail, on public deadlines, before real audiences — and then get structured second attempts. Consequence-free environments teach that nothing they do matters; consequence-heavy environments without recovery teach fear. Preparation for a volatile century requires both edges: stakes that are real and failure that isn't fatal.

- **Redesign the incentive to point at the student, not at the school.** Fund a personal learning account each student partly directs; let a portion of it follow them into apprenticeships, courses, and mentors of their choosing. When providers must earn a young person's continued participation rather than assume it, the system's chronic indifference to whether students actually care becomes financially unsustainable.

- **Measure engagement as a primary outcome.** Track attendance, voluntary time-on-task, project completion, and self-reported interest with the same seriousness now given to test scores, and treat mass disengagement as a system failure rather than a youth failure.

**Why this prepares students for 2100:** in a century where instruction is nearly free, information is ambient, and machines will execute any well-specified task, the scarce human input is *the will to direct one's own effort at something worth doing.* Careers will be self-authored and repeatedly rebuilt; institutions will not carry people along. A system that spends thirteen years training compliance and then releases people into a world that rewards initiative has the wager exactly backwards. Give young people authority and ownership early enough that agency becomes a habit rather than a shock — and the rest of the curriculum, whatever it turns out to be, will be pulled rather than pushed.

**Redesign education around social cohesion: treat the school system's primary product not as skilled workers but as a *common citizenry* — people who can trust, deliberate with, and cooperate across difference.**

The 22nd-century risk that most worries me isn't a skills gap; it's a solvent society. A country whose citizens sort into sealed enclaves by class, ideology, and algorithmically curated reality cannot govern itself, absorb technological shocks, or agree on facts long enough to act — no matter how good its graduates' math scores are. Yet American schooling is currently one of the most powerful *sorting* machines we have: attendance zones drawn around housing prices, tracking that hardens by third grade, and a college pipeline that physically removes the ambitious from their hometowns. We are manufacturing the fragmentation we complain about.

**The redesign:**

- **Make integration a design requirement, not an aspiration.** Draw enrollment areas across, not within, income lines; use controlled-choice and weighted lotteries so every school's student body roughly mirrors its metro area's economic mix; fund inter-district transfer, transportation, and magnet programs that make crossing lines attractive rather than punitive. The best-documented finding in education is that socioeconomic mixing lifts disadvantaged students substantially without harming advantaged ones — and it is the only intervention that also builds the cross-class familiarity a democracy runs on.

- **Rebuild the classroom as the site of disagreement.** Teach argument as a discipline: structured deliberation, Socratic seminar, formal debate where students must argue positions they reject, and standing practice in steel-manning opponents. Grade the quality of reasoning, not the conclusion. Pair this with serious epistemics — source evaluation, statistical literacy, understanding of how recommendation systems and synthetic media manufacture consensus — because in a century of infinitely persuasive machine-generated content, the ability to reason with people who see a different world is a survival skill, not a soft one.

- **Restore a shared inheritance without imposing a single story.** A common core of American constitutional history, founding and dissenting documents, and the country's actual record — its achievements and its crimes — studied through primary sources and competing interpretations. Citizens need a shared body of reference to argue *about*; a nation with no common text has nothing to disagree over except identity.

- **Add a universal national service year between school and whatever comes next.** Paid, civilian or military, with placements deliberately mixing recruits by geography, class, and politics — disaster response, elder care, conservation, tutoring, infrastructure. Earned educational benefits on the GI Bill model make it attractive rather than coercive. This is the one institution that reliably produces friendships across the lines that otherwise never get crossed, and it gives every 18-year-old a year of real responsibility before locking in a path.

- **Root schools in place, then connect places.** Keep schools small and neighborhood-scaled so children are known, but build in structural exchange: sustained partnerships between urban, suburban, rural, and tribal schools; shared projects; residential exchanges within the U.S. treated as seriously as study abroad. Most Americans now grow up never having spent meaningful time with someone from a different kind of American community.

- **Measure it.** Track graduates' civic participation, cross-cutting friendships, institutional trust, and willingness to cooperate with people they disagree with — and hold schools accountable for these alongside academics.

**The wager:** the technologies arriving this century will amplify whatever social capacity a society already has. A cohesive nation gains enormous leverage from AI, biotechnology, and abundance; a fractured one gets faster, better-targeted ways to tear itself apart. Every other reform — better teachers, better curricula, better credentials — assumes a functioning polity capable of funding and sustaining it. Schools are the last institution nearly every American passes through. If they don't build the common ground, nothing else will.

**Decouple education from job training and rebuild it as an education for *living* — because the 22nd century's defining problem will not be a shortage of workers but a surplus of unstructured freedom, and Americans are almost completely unprepared for it.**

Every current reform proposal, including the futuristic ones, quietly assumes that the point of school is to produce an employable adult. But if machine intelligence and automation do even half of what they plausibly will, the economic value of the median person's labor falls, work becomes optional or intermittent for many, and the binding question shifts from *how do I earn a living* to *what is worth doing with a life?* That is a question our schools do not even attempt to answer — and the early evidence of what happens when people are released from structure without preparation (declining marriage and friendship, deaths of despair, ambient screen consumption, collapsing participation in civic and religious life) is not encouraging. A society of comfortable, purposeless people is a fragile and unhappy one.

**The redesign:**

- **Restore the liberal arts as vocational training for freedom.** Literature, history, philosophy, and theology are not decorative subjects for the leisured; they are the accumulated human record of how to bear mortality, choose commitments, handle desire, and live in company with others. Teach them as *practical* subjects — the ones you'll actually need — read seriously, in full, in discussion.

- **Teach the arts of the amateur.** Every student leaves fluent in at least one demanding, self-sustaining practice pursued for love rather than credential: an instrument, a sport, a craft, a language, a garden, a workshop skill, a form of making. These are the structures that hold a life together when a job doesn't. Schools currently treat them as electives to be cut; make them non-negotiable and hold them to real standards, because only competence produces durable enjoyment.

- **Train self-command explicitly.** In a century engineered to capture attention and supply frictionless pleasure, the scarce capacity is the ability to choose difficulty voluntarily. Build a curriculum of deliberate hardship and delayed reward — wilderness expeditions, long-form projects, physical training, fasting from devices, solitude — treated as seriously as algebra. Freedom without self-governance is just susceptibility.

- **Make relationships and care a taught competency.** Formal instruction and supervised practice in friendship, conflict repair, caregiving, elder companionship, and raising children — the domains AI will not take over and where American competence is visibly eroding. Pair every student with someone old and someone young throughout their schooling.

- **Teach economic literacy for a strange economy.** Not just budgeting, but how to live well on variable or partially unearned income, how to evaluate what work is genuinely worth doing, how status and consumption traps operate, and how to build value outside markets.

- **Keep rigor absolutely.** This is not softness — mastery of math, science, and writing remains the price of admission, because a person who can't reason has no real freedom either. But the *purpose* of that rigor changes from employability to capability for a self-directed life.

**The wager:** we are about to hand a generation more discretionary time, wealth, and capability than any humans in history, and we are training them exclusively for the one thing machines are most likely to take. The scarcity in 2100 will not be skills or knowledge — it will be people who know what to want, who can build a meaningful life without an employer to organize it, and who can find joy in effort that no one requires of them. Schools should be the place where that is learned, and right now it is the one thing they don't even try to teach.

**Cure the provincialism: rebuild American schooling on a planetary frame, so that graduates can operate as competent participants in a world where the United States is a minority stakeholder.**

The unexamined assumption in American education is that the relevant world ends at the border. Our history courses are national with a thin "world history" gesture; our geography instruction has largely vanished; our foreign-language study is a two-year requirement that produces almost no fluency; our science and math curricula are built and benchmarked in isolation. That was survivable in a century of American dominance. It is a serious liability in one where the U.S. will hold perhaps 4% of the world's people, where the decisive problems (pandemics, climate, AI governance, supply chains, migration, capital flows) are structurally transnational, and where most economic growth, scientific output, and cultural production will originate somewhere else. A generation educated to believe that America is the world, and everywhere else is a footnote, will consistently misjudge the century they live in.

**The redesign:**

- **Genuine bilingualism as a graduation standard.** Not four years of high-school Spanish, but dual-language immersion beginning in kindergarten, where half the school day is conducted in a second language — the model that already works in a minority of U.S. districts and in most of the developed world. Machine translation will handle transactions, but it will never give a person the second mental architecture that comes from thinking in another language, nor the trust that comes from speaking to someone in theirs. Bilingualism also converts the eight million American children who arrive speaking another language from a deficit to be remediated into a national asset to be cultivated.

- **Teach world history as the main story, and American history inside it.** Students should be able to explain the Song dynasty, the Islamic Golden Age, the Bantu expansion, the Meiji Restoration, and the partition of India with the same fluency they explain the Civil War — because the future's dominant actors will not be legible to anyone who learned that history began in Philadelphia. Add serious comparative religion, since roughly 80% of humanity is religious and Americans are increasingly unable to interpret the motivations of most of the species.

- **Restore geography and add geopolitical and economic literacy.** Where things are, where things are made, where the minerals and chips and food and water come from, how currencies and shipping lanes and treaties work. This is the substrate of adult judgment about news, war, trade, and migration, and we currently teach almost none of it.

- **Make international contact structural, not optional.** Every student engages in multi-year collaborative projects with a partnered classroom abroad — shared science investigations, translated correspondence, joint documentation of local conditions. Every student has a funded opportunity for extended time in another country before age twenty, publicly subsidized the way Germany and much of Europe subsidize exchange, so that living abroad stops being a marker of family wealth. Pair this with a serious effort to host: America's greatest soft-power asset is that the world's talent wants to come here.

- **Benchmark honestly and borrow shamelessly.** Institutionalize the practice of studying what actually works elsewhere — Singaporean mathematics sequencing, Japanese lesson study, Swiss apprenticeship, Finnish teacher selection, Estonian digital infrastructure — and adopting it, rather than treating every foreign result as inapplicable to American conditions. A country that believes it has nothing to learn has stopped being able to learn.

- **Locate American ideals in a comparative frame.** Study the Constitution alongside other constitutions, American liberty alongside other conceptions of freedom, American inequality alongside other distributions. Patriotism grounded in comparison is durable; patriotism grounded in ignorance shatters on first contact with the world.

**The wager:** the twenty-second century's decisive problems will not be solvable by any nation alone, and its opportunities will accrue to people who can move fluidly among cultures, capital markets, research communities, and languages. Whether the U.S. flourishes or declines in that world depends less on our students' test scores than on whether they can understand, negotiate with, learn from, and be trusted by the 96% of humanity that isn't American. Right now we are educating them as though those people don't exist.

**Redesign around *time*: treat the 13-year lockstep calendar as the system's biggest hidden waste, compress the academic core, and redistribute the years we recover across a whole life.**

American schooling is extraordinarily slack. The K–12 math sequence re-teaches fractions and linear equations for six consecutive years because it's "spiraled" rather than mastered. Roughly a quarter of the instructional year evaporates into summer learning loss and re-review each fall. Senior year is, for most students, an eight-month exit ramp. Then college adds two more years of general education that largely duplicates high school. A student can plausibly spend five of seventeen years relearning material they already met. No 22nd-century curriculum matters if it's delivered inside a container that leaks a third of its contents.

**The redesign:**

- **Compress the core and let students exit it by demonstration, not by birthday.** Define a rigorous common academic core — literacy, mathematics through statistics and calculus-readiness, science, history, civics — and let any student certify completion whenever they can, typically by 16, as the French *bac*, British A-levels, and IB already assume. Teach content once, to mastery, with cumulative retention, instead of eight diluted passes. Age-lockstep is an artifact of factory-era administration, not of how brains develop; a 13-year-old ready for real mathematics should get it, and a 17-year-old who isn't yet fluent in reading should get intensive time rather than a diploma.

- **Fix the calendar.** Move to year-round schooling with distributed breaks, ending the agricultural summer that costs the poorest students the most and forces every teacher to spend September rebuilding what August erased.

- **Convert the recovered years into a structured bridge from 16 to 20** — not more school, but real adult apprenticeship, paid work, national or community service, caregiving, deep specialization, travel, military service, or early university for those who want it. Adolescents are ready for consequence years before we allow them any; extending institutional childhood into the mid-twenties is a recent and costly invention, and much of the anxiety and aimlessness we see is what a capable young person does when given nothing serious to do.

- **Stop front-loading.** Instead of one continuous 17-year block that ends permanently at 22, distribute formal learning across a 100-year life: an intense compressed foundation, then deliberate re-entry points at 30, 45, and 60, when adults actually know what they need to learn and have the experience to make it stick. Make employers and universities architecturally expect returners rather than treat them as anomalies.

- **Give the time back to teachers too.** The hours freed by eliminating redundancy fund what American schools have almost none of: teacher preparation, collaboration, and tutoring for the students who genuinely need more time — because mastery-based progression means time becomes the variable and learning the constant, which is the exact inverse of today's design.

**The wager:** in a century of long lives, repeated technological displacement, and multiple careers, the most valuable thing we can hand a young person is not more schooling but *unspent years* — time to work, fail, and re-learn while still young enough to change direction, and the right to come back for more whenever the world changes under them. We currently spend that inheritance on repetition and calendar drift, and then wonder why graduates emerge at 22 exhausted, credentialed, and uncertain what they're for.

**Redesign around material competence and resilience: make every American graduate someone who can actually *do things in the physical world* — and make schools the civic infrastructure that holds communities together when systems fail.**

The blind spot in every futuristic education proposal is that it imagines a frictionless world of screens, symbols, and knowledge work, and trains children accordingly. But the 22nd century is likely to be a century of shocks — pandemics, extreme weather, grid and supply-chain failures, cyberattacks, displacement — arriving in a society whose members have become extraordinarily dependent and extraordinarily unhandy. We have produced a generation that can write code but cannot stop a leak, dress a wound, grow food, restart a generator, navigate without GPS, or organize thirty neighbors in a crisis. Meanwhile the jobs least vulnerable to automation are precisely the embodied ones — electricians, nurses, plumbers, linemen, HVAC techs, farmers, EMTs, elder caregivers — that we have spent forty years teaching children to look down on.

**The redesign:**

- **A required physical-competence core, held to real standards.** Every graduate certifies in wilderness-grade first aid and CPR, basic electrical and plumbing repair, small-engine and appliance maintenance, food growing and preservation, cooking from raw ingredients, sewing and repair, water purification, fire safety, navigation and orienteering, swimming and physical fitness, and safe tool use. Not a semester of "shop" for the non-college track — a graduation requirement for the valedictorian too, tested by demonstration. Competence in the physical world is not a lesser form of intelligence; it is the form that keeps people alive and free.

- **Make every school a working system that students run.** The building's solar array, greenhouse, kitchen, water and waste systems, workshop, and maintenance are visible, instrumented, and student-operated under staff supervision. Physics, biology, chemistry, and statistics are taught *on* these systems — real load calculations, real crop yields, real energy budgets, real failures with real consequences. A school that outsources its own functioning to invisible contractors teaches children that infrastructure is magic; a school that runs itself teaches them how a civilization is actually held up.

- **Rebuild the trades as a prestige path, not a consolation.** Swiss- and German-scale paid apprenticeships beginning at 16, in partnership with utilities, hospitals, builders, and manufacturers; credentials that stack toward engineering and business degrees so the track never becomes a dead end; and a deliberate cultural campaign — in counseling, in curriculum, in who gets honored at graduation — against the assumption that working with one's hands is what happens to people who failed at school.

- **Practice under real stress.** Regular multi-day expeditions, wilderness trips, extended physical challenges, and community-wide emergency exercises where students hold genuine roles. Capability under duress is not knowledge; it is a rehearsed habit of the body and nerves, and it cannot be acquired from a slide deck. This also delivers, as a side effect, the confidence and self-regulation that anxious, screen-saturated adolescents most conspicuously lack.

- **Make the school the community's resilience hub.** Design and fund every school building as a hardened node — backup power, water, medical supplies, food storage, shelter capacity, communications — that becomes the neighborhood's command center during disaster, staffed by trained faculty and older students. This gives schools a permanent, visible civic function beyond childcare, and gives every young person the experience of being *needed by adults* rather than merely processed by them.

- **Pair every technical skill with its systems context.** Students who wire a circuit also study the grid; students who grow food also study agricultural economics and soil science; students who provide first aid also study public health and triage ethics. The point is not survivalism or nostalgia for manual labor — it is the union of the hand and the head that produces people who can both understand a system and repair it.

**The wager:** as machine intelligence absorbs symbolic work, the durable human advantage moves toward the physical, the embodied, and the locally situated — the things that require a body in a place, judgment amid mess, and responsibility to actual neighbors. A century of accelerating capability will also be a century of accelerating fragility, and the societies that come through it well will be those whose ordinary citizens can fix, build, tend, and organize without waiting for someone else to arrive. We are currently educating an entire generation to be helpless the moment the screen goes dark. Reversing that would cost little, employ well, ground people in their own communities, and hedge against exactly the futures we cannot predict.

**Redesign around the tail: build a national talent-discovery and acceleration system, because the 22nd century will be shaped disproportionately by the small number of people who reach the frontier — and America currently loses most of them by accident.**

The premise almost every reform ignores: educational progress is not evenly distributed in its consequences. The vaccines, energy systems, and machine architectures that will define 2100 will come from a relatively tiny population of exceptional researchers, engineers, founders, and artists. Yet American schooling is built almost entirely around the median and the struggling — worthy goals — while treating exceptional ability as a private family matter to be purchased with tutors, test prep, and zip codes. The research on "lost Einsteins" is damning: a child from a top-1% family is roughly ten times as likely to become an inventor as an equally talented child from the bottom half. We are not short of ability. We are short of *detection and cultivation*.

**The redesign:**

- **Universal, repeated, free talent screening.** Every child in America is assessed for exceptional aptitude — quantitative, verbal, spatial, musical, mechanical — multiple times between ages 8 and 16, with above-level testing so ceilings don't hide outliers. Screening is automatic and universal, not by parent nomination or teacher referral, which is precisely how poor, rural, immigrant, and minority prodigies currently go unnoticed. Spatial and mechanical talent, ignored by nearly every existing pipeline, is screened seriously; it predicts engineering and invention better than the measures we actually use.

- **Then actually do something.** Detection without provision is cruelty. Guarantee every identified student a funded pathway: radical acceleration where appropriate (skipping grades and subjects is among the best-evidenced and least-used interventions in all of education), residential specialized academies in every state on the model of the North Carolina School of Science and Mathematics and Bronx Science, university coursework at 13, and — crucially — **relocation and boarding stipends**, so that a brilliant child in a county with no calculus teacher isn't sentenced to waste by geography.

- **Apprenticeship to working masters, early.** From roughly age 14, place these students in real research groups, labs, studios, startups, and design shops as junior contributors on live problems. Genius is not produced by coursework; it is produced by early, sustained proximity to people operating at the frontier — the pattern behind every historically productive cluster, from Cambridge's Cavendish to Hungary's math circles to Bell Labs.

- **Build the peer group.** The scarcest resource for an exceptional 15-year-old is not instruction — AI now supplies that — but *other exceptional 15-year-olds*. Fund national and regional olympiads, summer programs, research competitions, and residential cohorts aggressively, and make them free and actively recruited from, so the network effects that currently belong to a handful of wealthy suburbs become a public good.

- **Extend the same logic beyond STEM.** Conservatory-grade training in music, writing, and visual art; early entry into the trades' master tracks; identification of exceptional organizational and leadership talent through real responsibility. Excellence is domain-plural, and a culture that honors only one kind of exceptional will lose the rest.

- **Protect it from both failure modes.** Gifted programs historically became mechanisms for laundering privilege; universal screening and heavy weighting toward under-resourced students are the corrective, and the system should be judged on whether it *finds* talent where nobody was looking. Equally, acceleration must be paired with genuine care — these are children, and the pathology of hothousing is real. And none of this substitutes for excellent universal education; it runs alongside it, funded additionally.

**The wager:** every other reform is about raising the floor, which matters enormously and which I'd fund first. But a society also has to decide whether it will find its outliers. Right now America finds perhaps a fraction of them, and only those born to parents who knew what to ask for. In a century whose defining challenges — engineered pandemics, machine superintelligence, climate adaptation, energy transition — will be won or lost at the frontier of capability, the cheapest and most neglected investment available is simply to *look everywhere for the kids who could work there, and then let them go as fast as they can*. We already have the talent. We're just not looking.

**Redesign schooling around human–machine symbiosis, with a system of *graduated cognitive licensure*: students earn the right to use each cognitive tool only after proving they can do the thing without it.**

The 22nd-century student will spend their entire working life thinking alongside machines that are faster, cheaper, and often better than they are at any well-specified task. American schools are currently responding in the two worst possible ways — either banning AI and pretending it away, or letting it in wholesale and quietly outsourcing the very struggle that builds a mind. Both produce the same graduate: someone who cannot tell whether the machine is right, and has no independent standard against which to judge it. That person is not a user of AI; they are an appendage of it.

**The design principle — cognitive licensure.** Treat cognitive tools the way we treat driving, power tools, and prescription authority: as capabilities that require demonstrated underlying competence first. A student writes hundreds of pages unaided, in-person, before earning a license to draft with a model. A student computes, derives, and estimates by hand before earning a license to compute at scale. A student reads whole difficult books and defends them orally before earning a license to summarize. Every license is revocable and re-tested. The point is not nostalgia — it is that judgment about a tool's output is built only from having done the work yourself, and a generation that never built it will be unable to detect error, manipulation, or mediocrity for the rest of the century.

**The new core disciplines.** Once licensed, students study what actually becomes scarce:

- *Verification and epistemic security* — the systematic craft of checking claims: replication, sourcing, adversarial testing, calibration of one's own confidence, recognizing synthetic media and manufactured consensus. Make this a graded, four-year discipline as central as algebra. In a world of infinite persuasive content, the ability to say *how do I know this?* is the master skill.
- *Delegation judgment* — deciding what to hand to a machine, what to keep, and what must never be automated. Students run projects where they must justify every delegation decision and own every failure the machine introduced. Accountability cannot be delegated, and that must be taught explicitly.
- *Specification and taste* — the ability to state precisely what you want and to recognize excellent work when you see it. When execution is free, the bottleneck becomes knowing what is worth making and whether the result is any good. Taste is trained the old way: by long exposure to the best work humans have produced, and by criticism.
- *Human-only capacities, deliberately preserved* — extended unaided writing, mental arithmetic and estimation, memory for a real body of knowledge, live argument, and the ability to sit alone with a hard problem without reaching for help. Protected in the schedule as a matter of policy, because they will atrophy by default.

**The structural changes that follow.** Every student gets a publicly funded, privacy-protected, non-engagement-optimized AI tutor — built as public infrastructure, not by attention-economy vendors, since a tool that shapes a child's cognition should not be designed to maximize their time on it. Assessment moves almost entirely to in-person, real-time, unaided formats: oral defense, timed writing, lab practicals, public demonstration — because take-home work has permanently lost its evidentiary value. Teachers shift from explaining (which machines now do infinitely patiently) to the residual human work: diagnosing why a specific child is stuck, setting standards, modeling intellectual seriousness, and holding students to effort they'd rather avoid.

**The wager:** the difference between a 22nd century of augmented humans and one of dependent ones will be decided in classrooms, by whether we let children build minds of their own *before* handing them a machine that will happily think in their place. Every other capability we might teach — creativity, citizenship, judgment, resistance to manipulation — is downstream of a person who can still think unassisted, and therefore knows the difference between a tool and a substitute.

**Abolish the "average student": rebuild American schooling as a neurodiversity-first system, designed from the ground up for the full distribution of human brains rather than for a statistical fiction that describes almost no one.**

Our entire architecture — same age, same pace, same seat, same modality, same eight-hour day, same demand for stillness and silence and handwriting and eye contact — was engineered around an imagined average child. But roughly one in five American students is dyslexic, ADHD, autistic, anxious, sensory-atypical, gifted-and-struggling, or otherwise off-pattern, and a far larger share is atypical in at least one dimension. We handle this by building an enormous, adversarial, lawyer-mediated special-education apparatus bolted onto the side of a system that remains hostile by default — a system in which a child must first fail, then be diagnosed, then have parents who know how to fight, before receiving accommodations that should have been the design. The result is millions of capable people convinced they are stupid, plus the well-documented pipeline from undiagnosed learning difference to dropout, unemployment, addiction, and incarceration. That is not a fairness problem alone; it is a catastrophic waste of the exact cognitive variation a complicated century will need.

**The redesign:**

- **Make accommodation universal and unrequested.** Every classroom, by default, offers text with audio, adjustable typefaces and spacing, captions, speech-to-text, movement permission, noise-dampened and low-stimulus spaces, extended time on nearly everything, and multiple ways to demonstrate mastery (write it, build it, say it, film it, defend it orally). When the environment is designed for the edges, nobody needs a label to get what they need — and the stigma, the diagnostic bottleneck, and most of the legal machinery evaporate. Keep intensive services for those who need them; stop making ordinary flexibility a scarce entitlement.

- **Screen early and universally, treat immediately, label reluctantly.** Vision, hearing, speech, dyslexia risk, attention, and language development checked for every child by age six as routine care — then instant, no-gatekeeping intervention. Today we run a "wait to fail" model that costs a decade of a child's self-concept to obtain services that work best at five.

- **Separate the three things a grade currently conflates:** what a student knows, how fast they got there, and how they behave. Report mastery of specific competencies, allow uneven profiles to be normal (a fourteen-year-old doing college mathematics and third-grade spelling is a common human being, not an anomaly), and stop letting a single weak channel — usually handwriting speed or working memory under time pressure — mask everything else a mind can do.

- **Design for the sensory and emotional body.** Quiet rooms, natural light, acoustic treatment, outdoor classrooms, movement built into the day, predictable routines with visible structure, and school psychologists and counselors at ratios that permit actual relationships. A large fraction of what schools currently code as defiance is unmet sensory or regulatory need.

- **Retrain the profession around variation.** Every teacher — not just special educators — trained deeply in the science of reading, executive function, sensory processing, and differentiation, with co-teaching as the standard staffing model rather than pull-out segregation. Use AI tutors specifically for their one genuine superpower here: infinite patience and infinitely adjustable pacing, modality, and scaffolding for a child who needs the explanation eleven different ways.

- **Cultivate atypical strengths instead of merely remediating deficits.** Dyslexic spatial and narrative reasoning, autistic pattern detection and depth of focus, ADHD divergent search and crisis performance — identified and developed as assets with real pathways, rather than tolerated as the compensation for a disorder. Build placements, mentorships, and career routes around them.

**The wager:** the twenty-second century's hardest problems will be attacked by machines that are, cognitively, extraordinarily uniform — trained on the same data, converging on the same patterns, brilliant at the center of the distribution. What humans will uniquely contribute is *divergence*: the odd angle, the obsessive depth, the pattern nobody else saw. Those minds are being manufactured right now in American schools — and then systematically broken there, filtered out by an institution optimized for a child who does not exist. Designing for the whole distribution isn't charity toward the struggling; it is how a nation stops discarding its most differently powerful thinkers before they turn eighteen.

**Redesign the *container*: stop building schools as boxes of boxes and rebuild American education around place, land, and the outdoors — because the physical environment is a curriculum we are currently teaching badly.**

We debate content endlessly while ignoring that most American children spend 14,000 hours of childhood in a windowless-ish, fluorescent-lit, acoustically hostile building set behind a parking lot, moving between identical 900-square-foot cells at the sound of a bell, with 20 minutes of outdoor time and a fenced patch of asphalt. That architecture was designed for supervision and efficiency in 1910, and it silently teaches the lessons it was built to teach: that learning happens indoors, sitting still, apart from the world, on someone else's schedule, in a place you have no stake in and would never visit voluntarily.

**The redesign:**

- **Make the outdoors the default classroom, not the reward.** Follow the Scandinavian *friluftsliv* and forest-school model: a substantial share of instruction — science, math, art, writing, physical education — conducted outside year-round, in all weather, at every grade level, with the clothing and shelter to make it viable. The evidence on attention restoration, myopia prevention, stress hormones, motor development, and later academic performance is strong and almost entirely unacted on. A generation raised largely indoors and on screens has a nature deficit that shows up as anxiety, and the cheapest antidote is a door.

- **Give every school real land and let students be responsible for it.** Woodlots, wetlands, gardens, orchards, streams, prairie restorations, tidal flats, working plots — monitored, managed, and repaired by students over multiple years, with data that accumulates across cohorts into genuine long-term ecological records. Ecological literacy in a century of climate disruption cannot be taught from a textbook; it has to be acquired by tending something long enough to watch it change and to be accountable when it dies.

- **Build the building as the textbook.** Exposed structure, visible mechanical systems, instrumented energy and water flows, daylight and operable windows, workshops and kitchens and labs on display rather than hidden in basements. Children should be able to read their own building — where the heat comes from, where the water goes, why the beam is that shape — so that infrastructure becomes legible rather than magical.

- **Shrink and disperse the campus.** Replace the 2,500-student mega-high-school on the edge of town with small schools embedded in the fabric of neighborhoods and downtowns — above shops, inside libraries and civic buildings, within walking or biking distance — so that students are daily participants in a place rather than bused to a compound and released at 3 p.m. Walkable schools also restore the independent mobility that psychologists now identify as a major casualty of modern childhood.

- **Design for the nervous system.** Acoustic treatment, natural light, thermal comfort, air quality, green sightlines, varied room sizes and postures, quiet alcoves and gathering commons. These are not aesthetic luxuries; measured effects of daylight, ventilation, and noise on learning and absenteeism rival many instructional interventions and cost less to fix than another round of curriculum adoption. Meanwhile a huge share of American school stock is leaking, overheating, and mold-ridden — an infrastructure emergency we treat as a facilities line item rather than an education policy.

- **Root the curriculum in the actual place.** Local watershed, local geology, local economy, local history including whose land it was, local government, local elders. Universal knowledge is best entered through a particular door: students who have deeply studied one square mile understand how to study anywhere. This also gives young people a reason to stay, invest in, or knowingly leave their hometowns rather than drifting out by default.

**The wager:** the 22nd century's citizens will be the most screen-mediated, indoor, placeless humans in history, and the strongest counterweight available to a school system is simply *where it puts children and what it puts them in contact with.* Bodies in weather, hands in soil, feet on a walkable street, eyes on a building they understand, responsibility for a piece of ground that will outlast them — these produce the attention, health, ecological judgment, and attachment to real places that no reformed curriculum delivered inside the same fluorescent box ever will. We keep rewriting the script while leaving the stage untouched.

**End age segregation: rebuild American schools as intergenerational institutions where every student teaches, and where the country's fastest-growing resource — older adults — becomes the core instructional workforce.**

The strangest and least examined feature of modern schooling is that we sort children into cohorts by manufacturing date and seal them away from everyone else. No other human society has raised its young this way. The result is an institution that wastes two enormous assets simultaneously: the teaching capacity of students themselves, and the time, skill, and accumulated life of a population that by 2100 will include tens of millions of healthy, educated, underused retirees living decades past their careers.

**The redesign:**

- **Make teaching a daily student obligation.** Every child, from about age seven, spends a protected block each day instructing someone younger — reading, arithmetic, an instrument, a skill they've mastered — with real preparation, coaching, and accountability for their pupil's progress. The "protégé effect" is one of the best-replicated findings in learning science: you understand something only when you have to make someone else understand it. This also solves the tutoring bottleneck arithmetically. Individual tutoring is the single most powerful intervention we know and the one we can never afford; a school of 600 contains 600 potential tutors, currently used as none.

- **Bring the old inside the building.** Recruit, screen, train, and modestly stipend a national corps of older adults — a domestic teaching service on the scale of Medicare, not a volunteer program — embedded as tutors, mentors, shop and studio masters, reading partners, and apprenticeship supervisors. A retired machinist, nurse, accountant, farmer, or translator carries a curriculum no one else can deliver. Co-locate new schools with senior housing and adult day centers by default, so that contact is structural rather than an annual field trip. This addresses two epidemics of loneliness with one architectural decision, and it gives elders what longevity research says extends life: being needed.

- **Replace grade levels with mixed-age houses.** Students belong to a 4–6 year vertical family with the same lead teachers throughout, subdivided fluidly by *readiness* for each subject rather than by birthday. Mixed-age grouping makes mastery-based pacing socially possible — a child working two years ahead in math and behind in writing is unremarkable in a mixed room and humiliating in a graded one. It also generates the natural hierarchy of apprenticeship: you see who you will become, and who is watching you.

- **Teach care as a graded discipline.** Structured, supervised practice in caregiving — for young children, the elderly, the sick, the disabled — required of every student. In a century where the largest growth in human labor demand is care work, where AI will absorb the symbolic tasks and not the embodied ones, and where an aging America will need a generation genuinely competent at tending other people, this is vocational training, civic formation, and moral education at once.

- **Open the roll to adults.** Let a 55-year-old retraining, a grandparent finishing a diploma, or a mid-career returner take courses alongside sixteen-year-olds. Nothing raises the seriousness of a classroom faster than the presence of someone who chose to be there.

- **Credit and measure it.** Teaching hours, pupils' gains, and mentorship count on the transcript. Judge schools partly on whether their students can successfully teach what they claim to know.

**The wager:** every skill people say the 22nd century demands — explaining, coaching, judging quality, adapting to another mind, taking responsibility for someone weaker than you — is practiced automatically by anyone who teaches, and by almost no one who only studies. And every projection of that century shows the same demographic shape: fewer children, far more elders, and a shortage of the human attention that learning and caring both require. We are simultaneously starved for tutors and sitting on the largest pool of experienced adults in history, while confining children to rooms containing only same-aged peers and one exhausted adult. Undo the age segregation, and the system gains something no technology or curriculum can buy: an abundance of people who know things standing next to people who don't.

**Rewrite the academic core itself: retire the Cold War–era calculus-and-physics ladder and rebuild the STEM spine around probability, statistics, computation, and the life sciences.**

American math and science sequences were designed in the Sputnik era to produce rocket engineers. Every student still marches through arithmetic → algebra → geometry → algebra II → precalculus → calculus, and every student still meets biology as a vocabulary list of organelles and taxonomy. But the questions that will dominate the 22nd century — pandemics, engineered organisms, machine learning, climate risk, personalized medicine, longevity, ecological collapse — are almost entirely problems of *biology under uncertainty*, and the mathematics they require is not calculus. It is probability, statistics, computation, and modeling. We are teaching the wrong subjects extremely thoroughly.

**The redesign:**

- **Make probability and statistics the mathematical spine, taught from age six.** Children can reason about chance, sampling, variation, and evidence far earlier than we assume. By graduation every student should handle base rates, confidence intervals, correlation versus causation, regression to the mean, expected value, sensitivity and specificity of a test, and the arithmetic of exponential growth — the actual math of medical decisions, insurance, elections, pandemics, and investment. This is the single largest gap between what schools teach and what adult life demands.

- **Treat computation as literacy, not a vocational elective.** Not "learn to code" as a job program, but simulation and modeling as a way of thinking: build the model, run it, watch it fail, discover which assumptions mattered. Students should have built an epidemic model, an ecosystem model, a climate model, and a trained classifier before they leave school. Modeling is how humans will reason about complex systems in a century where no important system is simple.

- **Preserve calculus for those going deep, but stop making it the sole summit.** Keep a rigorous proof-based track for future physicists and engineers — do not water it down — but stop organizing eleven years of mathematics around a course most students will never use, at the cost of the ones they'd use weekly.

- **Rebuild biology as the flagship science, taught as an engineering and information discipline.** Genomics, molecular mechanism, evolution as a quantitative theory, immunology, neuroscience, and bioinformatics, with real wet-lab work — sequencing, PCR, CRISPR editing of bacteria — now cheap enough for high schools. Biology should come with its own hard math, not as the "easy science" for students avoiding physics. The century in which humans learn to read and write living systems will belong to people fluent in that language.

- **Teach the ethics and security of these tools inside the technical courses, not beside them.** Anyone who can edit a genome or train a model must also have studied biosecurity, dual-use risk, consent, and the history of scientific catastrophe — as a graded part of the discipline, because the students holding these capabilities will be ordinary citizens, not a licensed priesthood.

- **Add complex-systems reasoning explicitly:** feedback loops, tipping points, network effects, emergence, tail risk, and the limits of prediction. Most catastrophic adult misjudgments are failures to reason about nonlinear systems, and we currently teach that skill nowhere.

**The wager:** curriculum is the one thing schools unambiguously control, and ours is a fossil of the priorities of 1958. Whatever else we change about governance, teachers, or technology, students will still spend thousands of hours on *some* body of content. Spending those hours on uncertainty, computation, and life — rather than on manipulating symbols they will never manipulate again — is the cheapest available upgrade, and it equips a generation to make good decisions about exactly the technologies that will decide whether the 22nd century goes well.

**Redesign schooling around developmental reality rather than developmental fiction — and start by fixing the crisis we're most reluctant to name: the collapse of boys and young men in American education.**

Every reform debate treats "the student" as a single generic being. But the sharpest, most consequential gap in American schooling right now isn't between curricula or districts — it's that boys are roughly two-thirds of dropouts, disciplinary removals, and special-education placements; they trail girls by a full grade level in reading by eighth grade; they earn well under half of bachelor's degrees; and they account for nearly all the growth in young adults who are neither working nor in school. A society that fails to attach half its young people to institutions, work, and purpose does not get a skills problem in 2100. It gets an instability problem — disconnected, statusless young men are historically the most combustible input into any political system, and machine intelligence will hit exactly the entry-level rungs they currently climb.

**The redesign:**

- **Start boys later, on purpose.** Male brains mature roughly a year behind female brains in the prefrontal regions governing self-regulation and planning — meaning we routinely ask five-year-old boys to do what their nervous systems cannot yet do, then code the failure as defiance and hand them a decade of remedial identity. Make a later school-entry age the default for boys (as affluent families already choose informally), and decouple starting age from stigma by making mixed-age classrooms and mastery pacing normal.

- **Recruit men into teaching and care work at scale.** Fewer than one in four K–12 teachers and fewer than one in ten elementary teachers are men; most American boys pass through childhood without a single male teacher. Fund a national recruitment effort — scholarships, service commitments, targeted residencies — with an explicit push into early education, and treat men entering nursing, therapy, and elder care with the same deliberate cultivation used to get women into engineering. These are the fastest-growing and least automatable jobs in the economy, and men are almost entirely absent from them.

- **Build the applied path first, not last.** Boys respond disproportionately to work that has visible consequences, physical engagement, competition, and mastery you can demonstrate.
