Make paid apprenticeship, technical training, lab and shop work, and cooperative work-study a primary secondary pathway available at 16 — with credentials that stack toward degrees so it never becomes a dead end — rather than the residue for students who fail the academic track.

- **Restructure the day for bodies that cannot sit still.** Recess at every grade, daily physical training, movement built into instruction, hands-on and project-based delivery of reading and writing, sport and physical challenge as core rather than extracurricular. A large fraction of what we currently medicate and suspend is a mismatch between adolescent physiology and a schedule that demands six hours of stillness.

- **Give young men structured, named responsibility.** Mentorship pairings that persist for years, service and crisis roles where they are genuinely needed, and explicit instruction in what a life of contribution looks like — because purpose is what actually motivates young men, and we have largely stopped articulating any version of it that speaks to them, leaving the vacuum to be filled by online grifters and grievance entrepreneurs.

- **Do all of this without zero-sum framing, and disaggregate everything.** Girls' gains are one of the great achievements of the last half-century and must not be traded away; the point is that the system now visibly fails a different group and has no mechanism for noticing. So report every outcome — literacy, discipline, graduation, wellbeing, post-secondary attachment — broken out by sex as well as race and income, and hold schools accountable for both halves.

**The wager:** the 22nd century will need every mind it can get, and it will punish societies that leave large cohorts of young people unmoored, unskilled, and resentful. We built a system that inadvertently fit one developmental profile well and another badly, and then spent thirty years insisting the mismatch was a character flaw. Designing schooling around how boys actually develop — later starts, more male adults, more movement, earlier real work, explicit purpose — costs relatively little, harms no one, and reattaches millions of people to the institutions that make a self-governing society possible.

**Rebuild the system around the family, not the school: treat the household as the primary educational institution and make the state's job to equip and support it rather than to substitute for it.**

Every current reform argues about what happens in the building — but children spend roughly 85% of their waking hours from birth to eighteen outside it, and the best-established finding in all of education research is that the home learning environment predicts outcomes more powerfully than any school variable we can manipulate. We respond to this by treating parents as clients to be notified, volunteers to be scheduled, or problems to be worked around, and by designing an institution that structurally competes with family life: a schedule misaligned with work, homework that outsources teaching back to households without any support, and a professional culture that treats parental involvement as interference. A century of longer lives, remote and fragmented work, smaller families, and AI tutors that make instruction nearly free will make this design increasingly absurd — the marginal educational value will sit in the home, and we will still be pouring nearly all public money into the building.

**The redesign:**

- **Fund the household directly as an educational site.** A per-child learning allowance parents can spend on tutoring, instruments, sports, museum access, materials, camps, and enrichment — the informal curriculum that affluent families already buy and that accounts for a large share of the achievement gap. Add books to every home from birth, subsidized broadband, and quiet, well-lit study space as a housing-policy objective, because a child with no place to work has a curriculum problem no teacher can solve.

- **Teach parenting as an academic subject, seriously.** A required, rigorous course sequence in child development, language acquisition, attachment, nutrition, sleep, discipline, and how to read aloud and talk with a small child — because roughly 85% of students will become parents, it is the highest-stakes work most of them will ever do, and it is the only major human competence we currently leave entirely to folklore and improvisation. Every graduate should also have logged supervised hours with actual young children. This one change compounds across generations more than any curricular reform.

- **Coach parents continuously, from pregnancy onward.** Universal voluntary home visiting in the early years, then a permanent parent-support function attached to every school: workshops, coaching on the specific things that move outcomes (dialogic reading, math talk, screen boundaries, sleep, managing homework conflict), delivered at hours working parents can actually attend, with childcare provided. Not "parent engagement nights" — an actual service, staffed and funded.

- **Give families real authority and real information.** Parents choose pacing and pathway with a permanent advisor; they see honest, comprehensible data on what their child can and cannot do rather than a letter grade; they can assemble hybrid arrangements — three days in school, two in a co-op, an apprenticeship, an online course — without exiting the public system. Legitimize and support the millions of families already homeschooling or microschooling by giving them public resources, assessment access, and quality standards instead of pushing them outside the tent.

- **Redesign the calendar and building around family reality, not agrarian tradition.** Year-round schedules aligned with adult work, buildings open early to late as genuine community hubs with meals, health care, adult classes, and childcare for younger siblings. Stop forcing families to choose between a job and their child's schedule.

- **Build family where it's absent.** Not every child has functioning parents, so construct deliberate substitutes: long-term mentor assignment, kinship and foster support, residential options for children in chaos, and school staff who stay with the same family for years. The point is that every child needs a small number of adults durably committed to them — the family is simply the most efficient known technology for producing that, and where it fails, the state should replicate its function rather than pretend classroom staffing is sufficient.

- **Measure the home, and hold the system accountable for improving it.** Track reading at home, family stability, parental stress and health, and childcare access alongside test scores — because these are the actual inputs, and a system blind to them is optimizing a small fraction of the problem.

**The wager:** in a century when knowledge is ambient, instruction is nearly free, and a machine can explain anything to anyone at any hour, the scarce input becomes what only a committed adult provides — someone who knows a particular child, expects things of them, sits with them, and stays. Schools cannot manufacture that at a 25:1 ratio; families produce it naturally when they have the time, knowledge, money, and stability to do so. We have spent a century building an enormous institution to compensate for weak households while investing almost nothing in strengthening them. Reverse that priority, and every other reform gets a child who arrives ready to use it.

**Treat the school as the nation's preventive health system — and make the management of a 100-year body and mind the core curriculum, on the premise that health, not skills, is the binding constraint on everything else.**

The 22nd-century American will likely live past 100 in a body evolved for scarcity, inside an economy engineered to exploit it: hyper-palatable food, algorithmic slot machines in every pocket, legal gambling and cannabis on every phone, synthetic opioids, and increasingly persuasive machines competing for their nervous system. The early returns are already visible in the students we have — roughly 40% of American children are overweight or obese, a fifth of adolescents have a diagnosable anxiety or depressive disorder, teen sleep is an hour short of biological need, chronic absenteeism has become endemic, and a growing share of young adults are too unwell to work or serve. No curriculum reform survives contact with a generation that arrives sick, sleepless, and dysregulated. And in a century where machines can do the thinking, the one asset a person cannot delegate is the physical and psychological platform they think from.

**The redesign:**

- **Make health a graded, cumulative academic discipline — the fourth core subject alongside literacy, math, and science.** Not a semester of "health class," but twelve years of real content: metabolic and cardiovascular physiology, sleep architecture, nutrition and food science, strength and conditioning, the neuroscience of addiction and habit, mental-health first aid, reproductive and sexual health, how to read a lab result and a drug label, how to interpret a medical study and a relative-risk claim, how to navigate insurance and advocate for yourself with a doctor. Every graduate should leave able to run their own body the way an engineer runs a system — because in a century of personalized medicine, continuous biosensing, longevity interventions, and AI physicians, medical self-governance becomes a literacy, and the people who lack it will be the ones the century's health technologies leave behind or actively harm.

- **Teach resistance to engineered compulsion as an explicit skill.** Students should study, in detail, how food scientists design bliss points, how apps are built on variable-ratio reinforcement, how gambling and vaping and sports-betting products are optimized for the adolescent brain, and how recommendation systems exploit affect. Then practice countermeasures — environment design, friction, substitution, tolerance for boredom — with real accountability. The most valuable thing we can hand a child entering the most addictive environment in human history is an insider's understanding of how it is trying to capture them.

- **Rebuild the school day around the physiology it currently ignores.** Daily physical training for every student at every grade, held to real fitness standards, not an elective survived by the athletic. Later high-school start times matched to adolescent circadian biology. Genuine food service — cooked from raw ingredients on site, with students in the kitchen — instead of the reheated ultra-processed default. Outdoor light and movement built into the schedule. These are not wellness gestures; they are the highest-leverage cognitive interventions available, and the only ones that also lower lifetime disease burden by decades.

- **Put real clinical capacity inside the building.** A staffed school-based health center in every school — primary care, vision, hearing, dental, immunization, mental-health counseling, substance treatment — serving students and, where useful, their families. Schools are the one institution nearly every American child passes through, and for tens of millions they are the only reliable point of contact with the health system. Counselor and psychologist ratios that permit an actual relationship rather than triage. Universal early screening with immediate treatment, since a decade of school failure often traces to an uncorrected eye, ear, or mood disorder.

- **Teach psychological skill as practice, not exhortation.** Supervised, graded training in emotional regulation, sleep hygiene, exposure to feared things, cognitive reappraisal, grief, conflict repair, and knowing when and how to seek help — delivered by trained staff with fidelity, and evaluated. Pair it with structured, difficult, voluntary challenge — expeditions, competition, performance, physical hardship — because resilience is built by surviving graded stress, not by being protected from it.

- **Measure it and fund it as an outcome.** Report each school's fitness, sleep, mental-health, chronic-absence, and screening-and-treatment numbers alongside test scores, and hold the system accountable for them. What we don't measure, we quietly offload onto families and emergency rooms twenty years later.

**The wager:** we are about to hand a generation extraordinary technological power and simultaneously the most metabolically and psychologically hostile environment humans have ever inhabited. Every other vision of 22nd-century education — AI tutors, apprenticeship, lifelong relearning, self-authored careers — silently assumes an adult with the energy, attention, and emotional stability to use it. That adult is not a given anymore; they have to be built. Health is the substrate on which all human capability runs, it is the domain where prevention beats remediation by the largest margin of anything we know, and it is the one thing a machine cannot do on a person's behalf. A school system that produced graduates who could reliably keep themselves well for a hundred years would generate more human capacity — and more national wealth — than any curriculum we could write.

**Make imagination the core discipline: rebuild American schooling on the studio model, so that every student spends thirteen years learning to conceive of things that do not yet exist — and to judge whether they are any good.**

Schools are organized around convergent work: there is an answer, the teacher has it, your job is to arrive at it. That design made sense when the economy needed reliable executors. But machines are now excellent at convergence — they interpolate brilliantly within the distribution of everything humans have already made. What they cannot supply is the *goal*: the decision that this problem is worth solving, that this future is worth wanting, that this version is better than that one. In a century where execution is nearly free and the world is flooded with competent, derivative, machine-generated everything, the scarce human contributions become originality and taste. We currently treat both as the province of the art room, which we cut first.

**The redesign:**

- **Adopt the studio, not the lecture hall, as the master pedagogy — in every subject.** Architecture schools, conservatories, MFA workshops, and design programs have long used a model K–12 almost never touches: you make something, you present it publicly, a room of peers and a master critic take it apart, you rebuild it, repeat. Run history, science, engineering, and writing this way. The critique — rigorous, specific, unsentimental, and *about the work rather than the person* — is the single most powerful pedagogical technology we have, and it simultaneously trains the ability to give hard feedback and to receive it without collapse, which most American adults never learn.

- **Make "futures literacy" a required, examined discipline.** Students should be fluent in scenario construction, worldbuilding, forecasting with calibration and scoring, premortems, red-teaming, and speculative design — building detailed, internally consistent models of possible 2100s and then defending them. A generation that has practiced imagining many futures is far harder to stampede into the one that some vendor, ideology, or algorithm insists is inevitable. Right now we teach students to predict nothing and imagine less.

- **Require sustained production in a chosen medium, held to public standards.** Every student maintains a multi-year body of original work — a novel, an instrument, a film, a research program, a product line, a body of paintings, a piece of software with users — culminating in a public exhibition and defense, the way a thesis show works. Ten thousand hours are not available, but a thousand are, and a thousand hours of making anything to a real standard teaches what no survey course can: that quality is achieved by iteration, that the first version is always bad, and that finishing is a skill.

- **Teach taste explicitly, through long immersion in the best.** Taste is not innate and it is not decoration — it is the trained perception that lets someone recognize excellence, mediocrity, and fakery on sight. It is built by prolonged, guided exposure to the finest work humans have made, in every field, paired with practice in articulating *why* one thing is better than another. When AI can generate a thousand plausible options in a second, the person who can pick the right one is the whole value chain.

- **Design constraints, don't remove them.** Creativity is not produced by freedom; it is produced by interesting limits. Set hard constraints — this material, this budget, this deadline, this audience, this form — and require novelty inside them. Also, deliberately introduce *analog* constraints: draw before you CAD, build the physical prototype, write the first draft by hand. Friction is where original thought happens.

- **Own the output, and put it in the world.** Student work is published, sold, performed, patented, installed, submitted to real competitions and real clients. Work that only a teacher will ever see teaches that making things is a school-shaped ritual rather than a way of acting on reality.

- **Assess it the way the creative professions do:** portfolio, jury, defense, and the judgment of practicing masters — which is also, conveniently, the only form of assessment that AI cannot counterfeit.

**The wager:** the 22nd century will not be short of answers, competence, or content — it will drown in all three. It will be short of people who can *specify what is worth making*, recognize excellence when they see it, and hold a difficult creative vision through a hundred failed attempts. Those capacities are not mystical and not reserved for artists; they are teachable, and the studio has been teaching them for five hundred years. We have simply confined the method to the one wing of the school we consider optional, while training everyone else to produce exactly what a machine now produces better.

**Redesign around ownership: make every American graduate an *economic agent and capital owner*, not merely a trained worker.**

Every version of school we've built — vocational, academic, or "21st-century skills" — quietly assumes the same destiny: the student will sell labor to someone who owns something. That bargain has been the foundation of American middle-class life for a century, and it is precisely the thing most likely to weaken by 2100. If machine intelligence and automation keep pushing income from labor toward capital, then a generation trained only to be excellent employees will be excellently prepared for the shrinking half of the economy. The most consequential thing schools could teach is how to be on the *owning* side of the machines, and how to defend yourself economically when your labor is no longer scarce.

**The redesign:**

- **Give every student real capital, early, and make managing it part of the curriculum.** A publicly funded investment account opened at birth and progressively handed over to the student's own decision-making through adolescence — real money, real allocation choices, real gains and losses, with a mandatory long time horizon so they experience compounding personally rather than as a word problem. You cannot teach ownership to people who have never owned anything; asset-poor children grow into adults who treat markets as a casino run by other people. By graduation, every American should have a decade of lived experience as an investor and a durable stake in the productive economy.

- **Make economics, finance, and law a core examined discipline for twelve years, taught operationally.** Not "financial literacy" as a one-semester budgeting unit, but the working knowledge adults actually need and almost never get: how to read a contract, an employment agreement, a lease, a loan, a term sheet, a pay stub, a benefits election, and a tax return; how equity, debt, insurance, and interest actually function; how to negotiate compensation; how to form an LLC or a co-op; how intellectual property and licensing work; how monopoly, rent-seeking, and regulatory capture extract wealth from people who don't understand them. This is the literacy of self-defense in a market society, and we currently leave it to whoever a young person's parents happen to be.

- **Run real ventures with real stakes as a graduation requirement.** Every student, in teams, starts and operates something with actual customers and actual books — a business, a cooperative, a nonprofit, a licensed product — and keeps the proceeds and the intellectual property. The point is not to produce founders; it is that anyone who has once set a price, made payroll, priced risk, and read their own income statement understands the economy from the inside forever after, whether they later work for someone else or not.

- **Teach the specific economics of an AI century.** Where value accrues when execution becomes free; what data and creative work are worth and who currently captures that value; how to license rather than surrender your own output; how to build income that isn't a wage — royalties, equity, dividends, ownership of tools, small durable businesses; how to evaluate a job for what it teaches and what it accumulates rather than what it pays this year. Teach students to ask, about any technology, *who owns this, and how do I get on that side of it?*

- **Extend it collectively, not just individually.** Study and practice the institutions through which ordinary people have historically taken ownership stakes — cooperatives, credit unions, mutuals, employee stock ownership, unions, community land trusts, pension funds — so students understand that ownership can be built jointly and that economic power is organized, not merely earned. A generation that can only imagine individual hustle will lose to concentrated capital every time.

- **Fund the school system to reinforce it.** Judge schools partly on graduates' economic autonomy at 30 — assets, business formation, freedom from predatory debt, ability to leave a bad job — rather than only on college enrollment, which currently measures how well we prepared them to be sorted by someone else.

**The wager:** the 22nd century's central distributional question will be who owns the productive assets when human labor is no longer the main input, and the answer will be decided by millions of ordinary decisions made by people who were either taught to understand capital or taught to be indifferent to it. We spend thirteen years preparing children to compete for wages in an economy that may pay ever less for them, while teaching them essentially nothing about the mechanism that will actually determine their security. Producing graduates who own things, understand how ownership works, and know how to build more of it is the difference between a generation that inherits the machine economy and one that merely lives under it.

**Redesign schools as institutions of *character formation* — treat virtue, not skill, as the scarce output, and rebuild the school's structure (not just its curriculum) around the deliberate cultivation of honesty, courage, self-command, and responsibility.**

Almost every reform assumes the bottleneck is capability. But the 22nd century is the first in which ordinary people will hold extraordinary power — the ability to synthesize an organism, forge any voice or face, deploy autonomous agents, manipulate millions at near-zero cost. In that world, the marginal danger isn't that a graduate can't do something; it's that they can, and no one ever asked whether they should. Capability is becoming abundant and cheap; trustworthiness is becoming scarce and decisive. Yet American schooling, having decided that moral formation is either the family's business or a sectarian imposition, has quietly abandoned the thing that every serious educational tradition — Greek, monastic, Confucian, Jeffersonian — considered its primary purpose.

**The redesign:**

- **Make character the school's declared product, and design backward from it.** Name a small, defensible set of virtues nearly all Americans can endorse across their disagreements — honesty, courage, self-control, fairness, diligence, humility, care for others, keeping one's word — and treat their formation as the organizing purpose of the institution, the way athletic programs organize around competitive excellence. Not a values poster; the criterion by which the schedule, staffing, and discipline system are judged.

- **Virtue is a habit, not a subject, so build the *practices* that form it.** Real honor codes, drafted and enforced by student courts, where cheating carries genuine consequence and self-reporting is expected — the model that has worked for two centuries at places like West Point and the University of Virginia, and that becomes indispensable when AI makes dishonesty frictionless. Standing duties every student holds and can fail at: caring for younger children, maintaining the building, cooking and serving meals, tending a garden or animal, showing up when a team depends on them. Character is built by repeatedly doing hard, unglamorous things one has promised to do, in view of people who will notice if you don't.

- **Restore small, permanent moral communities.** Break schools into houses of 60–100 with a mentor who stays with each student for years and knows them well enough to say the true, uncomfortable thing at the right moment. Moral formation is transmitted through relationship and imitation, not instruction; it requires an adult who has earned the standing to hold you to something, which is impossible at 150 students a semester and four teachers a year.

- **Teach ethics as hard, contested reasoning — then make it costly.** Study the great moral traditions seriously and comparatively (including religious ones, taught rigorously and non-devotionally, since most of humanity reasons from them), work real dilemmas from medicine, war, business, and technology, and pair every technical capability with the ethics of its misuse. But grade the *conduct*, not the essay: students should face situations with actual temptation and actual cost — unsupervised responsibility, money they could take, credit they could steal, a friend they could betray — and be held to what they did.

- **Rebuild the moral imagination through story and exemplar.** Literature, biography, and history taught as case studies in how people behave under pressure — the whistleblower, the collaborator, the person who held the line, the one who didn't. Ceremony and ritual that mark commitments publicly, because vows made before a community bind in ways that private intentions do not.

- **Hold adults to it first.** Teachers and administrators are the actual curriculum; a school that tolerates dishonesty, favoritism, or cowardice among its staff teaches that lesson far more effectively than any unit. Hire and evaluate for it, and make faculty conduct visibly accountable to the same code.

- **Guard against the obvious failure mode.** This must be a floor, not an orthodoxy: a thin, publicly defensible core of virtues rather than an ideological program, with pluralism in how families and communities thicken it, strong exit rights, and honest teaching of the arguments rather than catechism. The goal is people who reason well about right and wrong and act on it — not people who recite our conclusions.

**The wager:** in a century where machines can execute anything and verify almost nothing about the person directing them, every institution — markets, science, law, democracy — will run on whether ordinary people can be trusted when no one is watching and defection is easy. That capacity is not innate and it is not automatic; it is grown by long practice in communities that expect it, and it is the one output no technology, curriculum, or credential can substitute for. We have built an education system exquisitely concerned with what young people can do and almost silent on who they are becoming — and we are about to hand that generation the most powerful tools in human history.

**Redesign by subtraction: make "less, but deeper" the organizing principle — cut the curriculum, the hours, the mandates, and the supervision, and give the recovered time back to children as slack.**

American schooling has grown by accretion. Every social anxiety of the last fifty years — drug abuse, bullying, obesity, financial illiteracy, internet safety, career readiness — has been solved by adding a mandate, and every academic worry has been solved by adding standards. The result is a curriculum "a mile wide and an inch deep," a school day stuffed to the edges, teachers legally obligated to cover more than can be taught, students moving through content too fast to retain any of it, and childhood itself scheduled from wake to sleep. Nothing in this system is protected from addition, so nothing in it goes deep. And the honest reading of the international evidence is that the highest-performing systems teach *fewer topics per year*, assign *less* homework, and keep *shorter* days than we do.

**What I would cut:**

- **Halve the number of topics per grade and teach the remainder to permanent mastery**, with cumulative review, few units, long dwell time, and the explicit expectation that a student still knows it three years later. Coverage is the enemy of retention; a graduate who deeply owns a third of the current curriculum is far more capable than one who has been exposed to all of it and kept none.
- **Cut the school day, not extend it.** Core academic instruction in a tight morning block, held to high standards, and an afternoon that is genuinely free — sport, making, reading, apprenticeship, or nothing at all. Most additional hours buy compliance, not learning.
- **Abolish most homework before high school**, which mainly transfers instructional failure into the household and converts family evenings into conflict.
- **Delete the mandate layer.** A statutory ceiling on required instructional content, automatic sunset on every curricular mandate, and a rule that nothing may be added without something being removed. Then strip the administrative and compliance load that consumes a large share of what schools spend and what teachers do.
- **Reduce adult supervision on purpose.** Restore recess, unstructured free play, mixed-age roaming, walking or biking to school, and unmonitored time — the conditions under which children have always developed judgment, negotiation, risk calibration, and a sense of their own competence. The collapse of independent childhood is one of the best candidate explanations for the collapse of adolescent mental health, and it is one of the cheapest things to reverse: it requires doing less, not more.
- **Protect boredom and unallocated time as a design requirement**, for students *and* teachers. Slack is what a system uses to absorb shocks, notice problems, and do anything unplanned. Ours has none, which is why nothing good survives contact with it.

**Why this prepares people for 2100:** the coming century will not be short of information, instruction, stimulation, or content — it will drown in all of it. The scarce goods will be depth, retained knowledge, self-direction, and the capacity to tolerate unstructured time without being captured by whatever is engineered to fill it. Those are grown in the empty spaces we have systematically eliminated. Every other reform proposal, including the good ones, wants to *put something more* into the child's day; the more radical and probably more correct move is to take things out, defend the vacancy, and trust that a young person with mastery of the essentials, an unhurried mind, and hours genuinely their own will build something better in that space than we could have assigned them.

**Redesign around *matching*: build a national vocation-discovery system, and treat helping each young person find the right path — and the right people — as the school's central function rather than an afterthought staffed by one overloaded counselor per 400 students.**

The largest waste in American education isn't bad teaching; it's misallocation. Students choose majors, careers, and training almost blind — on the basis of parental occupation, a friend's advice, TV depictions, and whatever the local labor market happens to look like. The result is enormous churn: a third of college students transfer or change fields, roughly 40% never finish, millions carry debt for credentials they don't use, employers can't fill skilled openings while graduates are underemployed, and huge numbers of adults spend decades in work they're neither good at nor suited to. Meanwhile, a talented mechanic's daughter never learns that computational biology exists. We have built a system extraordinarily good at *sorting* people and almost useless at *matching* them.

**The redesign:**

- **Guarantee every student a permanent advisor from age ten to twenty-five** — one adult, caseload capped near 40, who stays with them across school transitions, into the first job or program, and through the first failure. Continuity of one knowledgeable adult is the single most powerful predictor of good post-secondary decisions, and it is the thing we have systematically eliminated.

- **Make exposure structural and broad.** Before any student chooses, they should have spent real time — days, not assemblies — inside dozens of kinds of work: hospitals, machine shops, courtrooms, labs, farms, construction sites, studios, warehouses, server rooms, classrooms. You cannot choose from a menu you've never seen. Rotating short-term placements from age twelve, funded and treated as core curriculum, not enrichment.

- **Teach self-knowledge as a discipline.** Systematic, repeated aptitude and interest profiling (spatial, mechanical, verbal, quantitative, social, artistic), plus reflective practice: what work absorbs you, what conditions you thrive in, what you're actually good at versus what you wish you were. Most people reach thirty without an accurate model of themselves, and the century's careers will demand repeated self-reassessment.

- **Build the public information infrastructure that markets require.** Free, honest, program-level data: what graduates of *this* specific program at *this* specific institution earn, what fraction finish, what they do at 30, how the occupation is trending. Publish it, push it, and require it at the point of decision — as we require nutrition labels and mortgage disclosures. Today the biggest financial decision most Americans make is the least informed.

- **Run it as an actual matching market.** Regional clearinghouses that connect students to apprenticeships, employers, mentors, and training providers the way medical residency matching connects doctors to hospitals — with employers obligated to post real entry slots and paid placements, and with the system responsible for closing the loop, not just for advice-giving.

- **Design for re-matching, forever.** The same advisory and matching infrastructure stays open for life, so a 38-year-old displaced by automation re-enters a system that already knows how to assess, retrain, and place her — rather than facing the current void of expensive coaches, predatory bootcamps, and guesswork.

- **Hold schools accountable for fit, not just completion.** Measure whether graduates at 25 and 30 are in work they find meaningful and are good at, whether they finished what they started, and whether they avoided debt for abandoned paths — instead of counting college enrollments, which rewards pushing everyone through the same door.

**The wager:** in a century where instruction is nearly free and information is ambient, the binding constraint stops being *access to learning* and becomes *knowing what to learn, and who to learn it with*. Talent is distributed evenly and opportunity is not, but the gap is transmitted less by the quality of teaching than by whether a young person happens to know someone who knows how the world works. Building that knowledge as public infrastructure — an adult who stays, exposure to the full range of human work, honest data, and a real matching mechanism — would raise national output, cut the staggering waste of misdirected years and dollars, and give every child something currently reserved for the well-connected: a realistic map of the lives available to them.

**Fix the apex, and K–12 will fix itself: redesign the *selection system* at the top — how elite colleges and employers pick people — because that, not curriculum, is what actually governs American childhood.**

The overlooked truth is that no school controls its own incentives. What a suburban high school teaches, how it grades, which activities it funds, how much sleep its students get, and what a fourteen-year-old believes their life depends on are all set downstream of roughly a hundred selective colleges and their admissions criteria. As long as those institutions hold artificially fixed seat counts, admit by opaque "holistic" judgment, reward polished résumés, and confer enormous lifetime advantage, every reform we design gets bent into a credential-optimization strategy within a few years. Grade inflation, the AP arms race, the collapse of genuine intellectual risk-taking, teenage anxiety and sleeplessness, the industry of consultants and manufactured "passion projects," and the exclusion of talented kids whose parents didn't know the game — these aren't failures of pedagogy. They are rational responses to a selection tournament, and they will reappear under any curriculum we write.

**The redesign:**

- **Expand supply.** Selective American universities have barely grown their undergraduate classes in half a century while applications multiplied tenfold, manufacturing scarcity that they then trade on. Tie federal research funding and endowment tax treatment to enrollment growth, and build new public flagship campuses at scale — the way California once did. Most of the pathology dissolves if the acceptance rate is 40% rather than 4%.

- **Replace ranking with thresholds plus lotteries.** Above a defensible bar of academic preparation, admit by weighted random lottery rather than by micro-distinctions no one can measure reliably. The marginal difference between the 300th and 3,000th applicant is noise, and we are currently distorting the entire childhood of a generation to adjudicate it. A lottery ends the arms race overnight, is transparently fair, and eliminates the incentive to fake a self.

- **Strip out inherited advantage.** No legacy, donor, or early-decision preference; standardized measures used as a floor rather than a sorting device (they identify overlooked talent better than essays and activity lists, which are effectively income tests); and active recruitment from every high school in the country rather than the few hundred that feed the system now.

- **Make the qualifying signals ones that reward real learning.** Subject mastery examinations and oral or performance-based demonstrations — things a student improves by actually knowing more — rather than curated portfolios of leadership, service, and "voice," which reward whoever has the most sophisticated adults behind them.

- **Do the same on the employer side.** Break the practice of recruiting almost exclusively from a dozen campuses; require open, competency-based hiring for any employer taking public contracts. When prestige stops functioning as a labor-market shortcut, its grip on adolescence loosens.

- **Take the pressure off the single decision at seventeen.** Guaranteed transfer pathways, standing capacity for returning adults, and portable credits mean that a bad or unlucky choice at eighteen is recoverable — which is the real reason the current tournament feels existential to a teenager.

**Why this prepares students for 2100:** the capacities that century will actually demand — intellectual risk-taking, sustained obsession with something unfashionable, honest failure, curiosity pursued without an audience — are precisely the ones our selection system punishes, because they don't produce a legible résumé line by senior fall. We keep asking schools to cultivate originality while running a national competition that rewards conformity, and then blame teachers when they comply with the incentive rather than the exhortation. Change what the gate rewards, and thirteen years of American childhood reorganize around it without a single curricular mandate.

**Rebuild schooling around *practice environments*: make simulation, games, and rapid-feedback rehearsal the core instructional technology — because the way expertise is actually built is by doing a thing thousands of times in a world where mistakes are cheap, and school is the only serious human institution that has never adopted this method.**

Every field that must reliably produce competence under pressure abandoned the lecture long ago. Pilots log hundreds of hours in simulators before touching passengers. Surgeons train on cadavers, laparoscopic rigs, and virtual patients. Militaries run war games. Athletes and musicians live in a cycle of attempt → immediate correction → attempt. What these have in common is not technology but *architecture*: a realistic environment, a task with a clear outcome, feedback within seconds, difficulty tuned just above current ability, and permission to fail repeatedly without permanent cost. Ordinary schooling has almost none of these — a student attempts something once, gets feedback in a week, receives a grade rather than a correction, and never returns to it. We then blame motivation, phones, or parents for the result.

**The redesign:**

- **Make the simulator the default classroom for any complex system.** Students shouldn't read about epidemiology, monetary policy, ecology, supply chains, legislatures, or negotiation — they should *run* them, repeatedly, and watch their decisions produce consequences three turns later. Fund a national public library of open, non-commercial, research-validated simulations covering the systems a citizen must reason about, built to the standard of flight simulators rather than of educational software. The single most underdeveloped human skill is intuition for dynamic systems with delays and feedback, and it is learnable only by piloting one.

- **Adopt game design as pedagogy, not as decoration.** Not points and badges bolted onto worksheets — the actual mechanics that make people voluntarily do hard, repetitive, difficult things for thousands of hours: clear goals, visible progress, escalating challenge matched to skill, instant and non-punitive failure, mastery gates, and the freedom to retry until it clicks. Games are the most effective motivational technology humans have ever built, and every argument against using them in school ("it's not serious work") applies equally to the flight simulator.

- **Rebuild assessment as continuous, low-stakes, and diagnostic.** Feedback loops measured in seconds and minutes, not weeks; retakes as the norm; grades replaced by a live model of what each student can currently do and what they should attempt next. High-stakes single-shot testing is the exact inverse of how skill develops, and it teaches students that failure is a verdict rather than information.

- **Reserve reality for what only reality can teach — and use simulation to make reality affordable.** Simulate the parts that are dangerous, expensive, slow, or unrepeatable (running a business into bankruptcy, managing a pandemic, wiring a substation, delivering bad news to a patient), so that the scarce real-world time — apprenticeships, labs, live performance, patients, customers — is spent by students who already have reps and can benefit from it. This is precisely how aviation and medicine solved the same problem.

- **Train rehearsal of *human* situations too.** Difficult conversations, conflict repair, interviews, refusing a manipulative pitch, resisting social pressure, giving hard feedback, staying calm in an emergency — role-played and re-run under coaching until competent. These are performance skills, and we currently "teach" them by discussion, which is like teaching swimming by lecture.

- **Build it as public infrastructure, and evaluate it ruthlessly.** Publicly owned, openly licensed, engagement-neutral by design (no attention-optimized business model touching children's cognition), continuously A/B tested against real learning outcomes, with anything that doesn't demonstrably transfer to unaided real-world performance killed rather than defended.

- **Guard the failure modes.** Simulation is a model, not the world; every simulated unit must terminate in an unaided, real-world demonstration, and students must be taught explicitly what the model leaves out — since a generation that mistakes elegant simulations for reality is its own kind of danger.

**The wager:** the 22nd century will not reward people who have *heard about* complex systems; it will reward people whose judgment has been trained on them — who have felt exponential growth outrun their intuition, watched a second-order consequence arrive too late, and been wrong enough times to know the shape of their own error. That kind of judgment cannot be transmitted by explanation; it accretes only through cycles of consequential practice. We already know how to manufacture expertise reliably — aviation, medicine, athletics, and the military do it every day — and schooling is the one domain that has declined to use the recipe.

**Make industry a co-owner and co-financier of education: replace the school-to-work cliff with an employer-financed dual system, governed jointly by firms, unions, and the state — and fund it with a training levy that automatically grows as automation eliminates jobs.**

The peculiar American arrangement is that employers are the chief *beneficiaries* of education but bear almost none of its cost, risk, or governance. They complain that graduates aren't ready, poach trained workers rather than train any, and have steadily offloaded what used to be on-the-job apprenticeship onto families (as tuition) and taxpayers (as loans). Meanwhile the education system, cut off from the economy it feeds, guesses at what the world needs from inside a building and finds out it guessed wrong a decade later. That gap will widen violently in a century where the skill map is redrawn every few years — no ministry, no curriculum committee, and no professor can track it from the outside. The only actors who know what capability is becoming scarce are the ones using it, and they currently have no seat, no obligation, and no bill.

**The redesign:**

- **A national training levy.** Every employer above a modest size pays a percentage of payroll into a sectoral training fund, fully refundable against verified training they actually provide — apprentices hosted, instructors seconded, equipment donated, curricula co-developed. Firms that train pay nothing; firms that free-ride on others' trainees pay for the privilege. This is how Switzerland, Germany, Denmark, and Singapore solved the training-investment problem that markets chronically underprovide, and it converts poaching from a rational strategy into a taxed one.

- **Sectoral skills councils with real authority.** In each major industry — health, energy, construction, computing, logistics, manufacturing, care — a standing body of employers, unions, educators, and public officials sets occupational standards, writes and continuously revises the competency framework, and certifies training sites. Curriculum stops being a political artifact revised every decade by textbook adoption and becomes a living instrument revised annually by people whose own operations depend on getting it right. Crucially, labor sits at the table too, so standards serve worker mobility and broad transferable skill rather than firm-specific lock-in.

- **Paid employment as a normal part of secondary education.** From roughly 16, a majority pathway in which students are legally apprentices — wages, contracts, supervisors, real accountability — spending several days a week at a certified firm and the rest in academic instruction that is explicitly tied to what they're doing. Not a track for those who fail, but the default route for most, with credentials that stack all the way to engineering and management degrees so no door closes. A teenager who is paid, supervised by adults who need them, and responsible for real output is a fundamentally different person at 20 than one who has spent four more years in a classroom performing for a transcript.

- **A legal duty to train, and a legal duty when you don't need people anymore.** Extend the levy into an automation clause: firms that eliminate roles through automation contribute proportionally to a national retraining account owned by displaced workers, drawable for however long re-education takes. The company that captures the productivity gain pays a defined share of the human transition it caused. This makes the system self-funding precisely as displacement accelerates — the more the 22nd-century economy replaces labor, the more resources flow automatically into re-equipping people, without requiring Congress to notice in time.

- **Make the training relationship enforceable and portable.** Public certification and inspection of every training firm, so apprenticeship means instruction rather than cheap labor; credentials owned by the worker and recognized nationwide; and a duty of care that keeps a young person from being used up and discarded at 19.

- **Let public education specialize in what firms can't provide.** Freed of the impossible task of predicting labor demand, schools concentrate on the durable foundations — literacy, mathematics, science, history, civics, ethics, and the capacity to keep learning — precisely because industry now supplies the applied, current, expensive-to-simulate part directly. Each side does what only it can, instead of both doing the other's job badly.

**The wager:** for a century, America has treated preparation for work as something schools should somehow accomplish alone, and displacement as something workers should somehow absorb alone. Both assumptions fail in a century of repeated technological upheaval. Bind the institutions that create the demand for skill — and that profit from destroying it — into permanent financial and governance responsibility for producing it, and education gains something no reform designed inside the schoolhouse can supply: a continuous, self-correcting connection to the actual economy, and a funding mechanism that grows stronger exactly when the disruption is worst.

**Turn schools into producing members of the knowledge commons: make every student's core requirement a *verified, accepted contribution to real public knowledge* — and treat America's 50 million students as the largest untapped research and civic-infrastructure workforce in the world.**

Schools currently consume knowledge and produce nothing but transcripts. Every lab is a re-enactment of an experiment whose answer is in the back of the book; every essay is written for an audience of one and thrown away. That single fact — that student work is fake — is the source of most disengagement, most cheating, and most of the reason AI has destabilized schooling overnight (a machine can trivially counterfeit fake work; it cannot counterfeit a genuine accepted contribution to a real body of knowledge).

**The redesign:**

- **Graduation requires a portfolio of *accepted* contributions**, each validated by an authority outside the school: a merged pull request in an open-source project, a Wikipedia article that survives editorial review, a verified species observation or archival transcription, a replication of a published study submitted to a registry, a translated public document, a municipal dataset collected to standard, an air-quality or water or soil monitoring series added to a state record. The bar isn't "you tried" — it's "someone who didn't know you accepted it."

- **Build the matching infrastructure that makes this possible at scale.** A national clearinghouse that brokers between real institutions with genuine unmet labor needs — universities, agencies, museums, herbaria, hospitals, land trusts, open-source foundations, local governments — and classrooms with a teacher, a subject, and 180 days. Research groups get contributors; students get real problems with real supervisors and real rejection.

- **Design curriculum backward from the contribution.** Statistics is taught because your dataset needs it; writing is taught because your article will be reverted by strangers if it's sloppy; chemistry is taught on the actual water samples. Rigor arrives as a *constraint of the work* rather than as an arbitrary demand from an adult, which is the only form of rigor adolescents reliably accept.

- **Let the aggregate matter.** A hundred thousand students taking standardized measurements is a national sensor network; a million students transcribing archives digitizes American history in a decade; ten thousand student teams attempting replications addresses a scientific crisis no professional system has the labor to fix. Students should be able to see the national dataset their line is in — which is the experience of being *counted on* that almost no young American currently has.

- **Assess it the way professions do:** external acceptance, contribution logs, oral defense of methodology, and responsibility for errors that propagate. Falsifying data becomes a real offense with real consequences, which teaches research ethics far more durably than a unit on it.

- **Keep the foundations sacred.** This runs *after* and *alongside* a demanding academic core — you cannot contribute to knowledge you don't possess. But from roughly age twelve, an increasing share of school time shifts from rehearsal to participation.

**The wager:** in a century where explanation is free and simulated work is indistinguishable from real work, the scarce and unfalsifiable thing is *provenance* — evidence that a particular person actually did something that entered the world and held up. Schools that graduate students with a public record of accepted contributions produce three things at once: young people who have experienced being useful (the strongest known antidote to the aimlessness and disengagement now epidemic among them), a citizenry that understands how knowledge is actually made and therefore how it can be corrupted, and an enormous new national capacity for the patient, distributed, human-scale observation and verification work that the 22nd century will need far more of, not less.

**Give the diploma a warranty: make schools legally and financially liable for whether their graduates can actually do what the credential claims — and keep them on the hook for decades.**

Every proposal for the 22nd century argues about *what* schools should teach. The deeper problem is that no American educational institution bears any consequence for whether its graduates can do anything. A district hands a diploma to a student reading at a fifth-grade level and faces no cost; a university awards a degree that leaves a graduate unemployable and carrying $80,000 in federally guaranteed debt, and the bill lands entirely on the student and the taxpayer. In every other sector where the customer can't evaluate the product — medicine, engineering, construction, aviation — we solve this with warranties, liability, and professional standards of care. Education is the one field allowed to sell a lifelong-consequence product with no guarantee attached and no refund possible.

**The redesign:**

- **A diploma warranty.** A high school credential becomes a legally enforceable claim that its holder possesses specified competencies. If any graduate is later found deficient in the core — reading, writing, mathematics — the issuing district must provide remediation to standard, free, at its own expense, at any age. Where colleges must place a graduate into remedial coursework, they invoice the district that certified them. This one change immediately kills social promotion and grade inflation, because the institution now eats the cost of its own dishonesty rather than exporting it to employers, colleges, and the graduate's whole adult life.

- **A reading guarantee with a funded right of exit.** Any child with no disabling condition who is not reading fluently by age nine triggers an automatic, portable entitlement — publicly funded intensive tutoring the family may spend anywhere, charged against the school's budget. Failure to teach reading stops being a sad statistic and becomes a line item the institution feels.

- **Outcome-contingent funding on a long clock.** Shift a meaningful minority of school and college funding from enrollment-based payment to payment released over ten to twenty years, contingent on longitudinal graduate outcomes — earnings, employment, credential completion, debt avoidance, health, civic participation, self-reported flourishing at thirty. Crucially, pay on *value added against demographically matched intake*, not raw outcomes, so that schools serving poor children are rewarded, not destroyed, and every student who ever enrolls counts, so pushing out the difficult becomes financially suicidal. Institutions that produce durable capability get paid; institutions that produce transcripts do not.

- **Real skin in the game for higher education.** Colleges co-sign a share of their students' loan default risk. An institution that enrolls someone, takes four years of tuition, and delivers no capability should absorb part of the loss it created — which would end the enrollment of unprepared students into programs the institution knows will fail them faster than any accreditation regime ever has.

- **A standard of care, enforceable like malpractice.** Teaching is licensed on the condition of using methods with evidentiary support, and knowingly using discredited ones — three-cueing reading instruction being the notorious case that cost millions of American children their literacy — is a professional violation, not a curricular preference. Districts carry the liability; teachers get, in exchange, what doctors have: real training, real authority, and protection when they follow the evidence.

- **A lifetime right of return, honored by the institution that certified you.** Every graduate holds a permanent, funded claim on their school system for re-education whenever the world moves under them — at thirty, at forty-five, at sixty. Schools that must serve their alumni for sixty years stop optimizing for the exit exam and start optimizing for what survives: literacy, numeracy, learning capacity, health, judgment.

- **Build the measurement honestly, and audit it.** None of this works without a trustworthy longitudinal data spine and independent auditors — the equivalent of financial statement audits — because self-reported outcomes will be gamed within a year. Publish everything at the institution level; make manipulation a fraud offense.

**The wager:** the twenty-second century will demand constant re-skilling, and its schools will be judged not by what a graduate knew at eighteen but by what they could still do at fifty. No curriculum reform, technology, or teacher-quality initiative survives inside an institution that is paid the same whether it succeeds or fails and never hears from its students again. Attach genuine, durable, financial consequence to the promises education makes — the way we do for every other product that can ruin a life — and the system will discover, on its own, the pedagogy, the pacing, and the human attention it takes to keep them. We have spent a century exhorting schools to care about outcomes. It would be simpler, and far more effective, to make them liable for them.

**Copy the one part of American education that already works: transplant the *extracurricular* model into the academic core.**

The strange fact about American schooling is that the same institution that produces mediocre math scores also produces the best high school athletics, debate teams, robotics squads, marching bands, and theater programs in the world — and it does so with the *same kids*, often the ones failing third period. Whatever is wrong with American education is clearly not the students, the culture, or the capacity for effort. It's that the academic side is organized on a fundamentally worse model than the after-school side, and we have never asked why.

**What the after-school model actually does differently:**

- A **coach**, not a lecturer — someone whose job is your improvement, who stays with you for four years, who knows your ceiling and pushes you toward it, and who is judged by what you can do in public rather than by whether you covered the material.
- A **team** with mixed ages, in which seniors teach freshmen as a matter of course and belonging is contingent on contribution.
- A **season** — a defined arc of daily practice building toward a real, public, high-stakes culminating event with an outcome nobody controls.
- **Practice structure**: repeated attempts, immediate correction, film review, drilling of weak components in isolation, difficulty tuned to current ability.
- **Honest evaluation without cruelty**: everyone knows who the best pitcher is, playing time is earned, and being cut or losing is survivable and recoverable rather than shameful.
- **Real failure in front of people who matter**, followed by practice on Monday.

**The redesign:** run mathematics, writing, science, and history on exactly this architecture. Every academic subject becomes a *team with a season*. Teachers are retrained and re-titled as coaches with multi-year rosters of forty students they follow across grades, evaluated on growth in demonstrated performance. Class time becomes practice time — short instruction, then drills, scrimmages, and correction, with the coach circulating rather than presenting. Every season ends in a genuine public contest or performance: a mathematics competition, an oral defense before outside judges, a research symposium, a debate tournament, a published investigation, a build that must work in front of an audience. Build the leagues to support it — regional and national academic competition infrastructure funded at the scale we currently fund high school football, with rankings, letters, banners, local newspaper coverage, and the same community attention. Fold the existing extracurriculars into the school day rather than exiling them to 4 p.m., and let older students coach younger ones as a graduation requirement.

**Why this is more than a gimmick:** it fixes the incentive problem, the motivation problem, and the assessment problem simultaneously and without asking anyone to be better than they already are. Students work harder for a team than for a grade, because someone is counting on them. Public performance is inherently AI-proof — you cannot outsource a live oral defense or a robot that has to drive. Multi-year coaching relationships supply the durable adult attachment that 25:1 semester-long classes structurally cannot. Mixed-age teams make mastery-based pacing socially normal. And competition, properly bounded, gives adolescents the status, belonging, and legible progress they are neurologically starved for and that we currently make them find on their phones.

**The guardrails:** every student is on a team — no benchwarmers, no cutting from the academic core; team performance is measured as *growth*, so the strongest programs aren't just the ones that recruited the best intake; and the seasons must be capped and staggered so this restores structure rather than adding another arms race to a schedule already full.

**The wager:** we keep importing designs from Finland and Singapore while ignoring an indigenous American model that reliably extracts obsessive, voluntary, disciplined effort from ordinary teenagers, teaches them to lose and come back, and makes them love the institution that demanded it. The 22nd century will reward people who can practice deliberately, perform under pressure, work inside a team, and keep showing up after failure — and American high schools already manufacture exactly those people, every fall, in the gym and the auditorium, and then send them to sit passively in Algebra II. Run the whole school the way we run the season.

**Rebuild American schooling as a ladder of *initiations*: replace the featureless thirteen-year drift with a sequence of public thresholds that a young person must actually pass, each one conferring real, expanded rights in the adult world.**

The overlooked defect in our system is that nothing in it ever *happens*. A child moves from grade to grade by birthday, receives a diploma for attendance, and turns eighteen into a legal adulthood that arrived by calendar rather than by achievement. Every society that has successfully made adults out of children — and there is no exception — did it through marked, difficult, publicly witnessed passages: you are tested, the community watches, and afterward you are treated differently and you know it. We deleted that entire technology and replaced it with a slow gradient of supervision, then wondered why adolescence stretched into the late twenties, why status-hunger gets discharged online instead of in the world, and why so many young Americans report not knowing whether they have become adults or what would prove it.

**The redesign:**

- **Define six or seven thresholds between roughly age 10 and 20, each with an explicit standard, a real test, and a real reward.** Not grades and not credits — passages. A literacy-and-numeracy threshold that certifies you can read anything and reason with numbers. A wilderness/physical threshold: a solo, a long expedition, a demonstrated capacity to keep yourself and others alive. A craft threshold: you make something to a master's standard and it is judged by that master. A knowledge threshold: an oral defense before adults from outside the school who are free to fail you. A service threshold: a year of real labor for the community, where people depended on you. A civic threshold at the end: an examined, sworn entry into full citizenship, held as a public ceremony with the same weight as a wedding or a naturalization.

- **Attach genuine rights to each passage, so the ladder is not symbolic.** This is the crucial mechanism, and the one modern schooling has abandoned: passage must *purchase* something. Unsupervised mobility around the town. The right to work and be paid. Control of your own money and time. Access to dangerous tools, vehicles, labs, and workshops. Standing on committees that govern the school. Progressive legal emancipation and the ability to sign for yourself. Rights that are earned and can be lost teach responsibility in a way that rights automatically conferred by birthday never can — and rights that arrive all at once at eighteen teach nothing at all.

- **Make the tests real, fail-able, and retakeable.** A threshold no one fails is not a threshold; a threshold you can only attempt once is a cruelty. Standards published, examiners external to the school, honest verdicts, and unlimited returns. What we currently give adolescents is the exact inverse: constant low-stakes evaluation they cannot really fail and cannot really pass, which produces anxiety without meaning.

- **Require witnesses.** Every passage is attested by adults who are not paid to be kind — a master craftsman, a nurse, a farmer, a judge, an elder, a neighbor — and marked publicly, with the family and community present. The point is not ceremony for its own sake; it is that adult identity is conferred socially. A young person needs to be *recognized* by people who count, and today almost none are.

- **Let the ladder, not the calendar, govern progression.** A fourteen-year-old who has passed four thresholds should have more freedom and more responsibility than an eighteen-year-old who has passed none. This makes mastery pacing socially legible, restores the incentive that grade inflation destroyed, and finally gives American adolescents a real answer to the question they are actually asking, which is not *what will this be on the test* but *when do I get to count?*

- **Keep it plural and non-coercive.** Communities, tribes, religious traditions, and families should be able to add their own thresholds and shape the form; the state defines only a thin common core of them and guarantees every child access, funding, mentors, and the equipment to attempt them, so that initiation isn't another privilege of the well-connected.

**The wager:** the 22nd century will hand young people enormous power and almost no structure — self-authored careers, dissolving institutions, infinite optionality, and machines happy to do their thinking. What such a world demands is not more instruction but formed adults: people who have been genuinely tested, who know what they can withstand, who have been publicly entrusted with something and did not drop it. Our current system produces credentialed people who have never once been told, by anyone whose judgment they respect, that they had passed. Build the thresholds back in, and adolescence stops being a holding pen and becomes what every other human society understood it to be — a series of doors, each one difficult, each one opening.

**Make oracy the core discipline: rebuild American schooling around the spoken word — speaking, listening, memory, and live argument — as the central medium of instruction and assessment.**

American schools are almost entirely a *literate* institution: children read silently, write alone, and are graded on paper. Yet the typed page is precisely the medium machines have just mastered and counterfeited. Meanwhile the things adults actually do — persuade a room, run a meeting, calm an angry customer, interview, negotiate a raise, testify, teach, comfort, lead — are done aloud, in real time, in front of other people, and we teach almost none of it. Most American students go thirteen years without ever being required to speak at length before an audience, and graduate unable to hold a disagreement without either capitulating or detonating.

**The redesign:**

- **Make speech a graded, cumulative subject from kindergarten through graduation**, sequenced like mathematics: recitation and storytelling in the early years; explanation and questioning in the middle years; formal rhetoric, debate, interviewing, negotiation, and extemporaneous argument in the upper years. Every student leaves able to speak for twenty minutes on something they know, without notes, and to think clearly while being challenged.
- **Convert assessment to the oral defense.** The default demonstration of learning becomes a live viva before teachers and outside examiners who may probe anywhere. This is unforgeable — no model can sit in the chair for you — and it exposes instantly the difference between understanding and retrieval. It also ends the assessment crisis AI created, without banning anything.
- **Teach listening as a trained skill, not a courtesy.** Structured practice in accurate paraphrase (you may not reply until you can restate the other person's position to their satisfaction), in interviewing strangers, in eliciting rather than asserting, in detecting evasion. Listening is the scarcer half of dialogue and the one almost never taught; it is also the foundation of every care profession, every negotiation, and every functioning democracy.
- **Restore memorization and performance.** Poems, speeches, scripture and secular equivalents, monologues, songs — held in the body and spoken aloud. Committing great language to memory furnishes a mind with rhythm, cadence, and moral vocabulary that surfaces decades later, and public performance builds the nerve to stand up and be judged.
- **Teach the dark side of speech explicitly**: rhetoric's manipulative machinery, propaganda technique, synthetic voice and video, high-pressure sales, cult and grievance recruitment scripts, and the specific ways persuasion will be industrialized by machines optimized to move you. A student who has *practiced* constructing a manipulative argument recognizes one instantly for life.
- **Restructure classrooms as seminars and disputations.** Fewer lectures and worksheets; more circles where every student speaks daily, argues assigned positions they reject, and is graded on the quality of reasoning offered aloud. Track speaking time so the quiet are drawn out and the dominant learn restraint.
- **Give it public stakes.** Regular town-hall style presentations to real community audiences, school-wide oratory and debate competitions with the standing of athletics, and a capstone: an hour-long public defense of a body of work before family, faculty, and outside judges before anyone graduates.

**The wager:** the twenty-second century will be flooded with fluent, plausible, machine-generated text, and the value of unattributable writing will collapse. What will remain unfalsifiable — and what no one can outsource — is a human being standing in a room, thinking under pressure, answering the unexpected question, and being trusted or not by the people watching. That is how leadership, teaching, care, diplomacy, sales, law, medicine, and self-government have always actually operated, and it is the one competence we have left almost entirely to chance.

**Design the system for the demographic reality nobody is planning for: American cohorts are shrinking, and the 22nd century's schools should be built to convert that decline into per-child abundance rather than into budget cuts.**

Every reform debate implicitly assumes a steady stream of children. But U.S. births have fallen for fifteen years, K–12 enrollment has already peaked, and by mid-century most districts will be educating substantially fewer students — with the shrinkage concentrated in rural counties and older cities. The automatic institutional reflex is to treat this as a fiscal problem: close schools, consolidate onto longer bus rides, lay off teachers, and shrink budgets in proportion to enrollment. That would be the single largest missed opportunity in American education, because a smaller generation is the first chance in history to afford the one thing we know works and have never been able to buy — sustained, individual adult attention for every child.

**The redesign:**

- **Lock per-pupil funding in real terms as enrollment falls.** Hold total spending flat while cohorts shrink and the ratio collapses on its own: 25:1 becomes 15:1, then 10:1, and every student gets genuine one-on-one instructional time each week. Tutoring is the best-evidenced intervention we have (roughly two standard deviations in Bloom's classic result) and has always been dismissed as unaffordable. Demography is about to make it affordable, if we simply decline to bank the savings.

- **Retain and repurpose the workforce rather than shedding it.** Convert surplus teaching positions into tutors, advisors, and mentors with small permanent caseloads who follow students for years, instead of firing them and calling it efficiency. The same demographic wave that empties classrooms also produces tens of millions of healthy retirees who can be recruited into that corps.

- **Build for graceful shrinkage.** Modular, multi-use, right-sized buildings; small distributed campuses instead of consolidating a county into one remote megaschool; and a shared national faculty for low-enrollment subjects — so that a rural student in a district of 200 children still gets organic chemistry, Mandarin, or music theory from a specialist, paired with a local coach who knows them. Excess capacity goes to birth-to-five programs, adult re-entry, and community health and civic functions, not to demolition.

- **Treat every child as irreplaceable, because arithmetically they now are.** Each young American will support more elderly dependents than any generation before them, which means dropouts, undiagnosed disabilities, and disengagement stop being tolerable losses. Universal screening, active case management, and a legal obligation to keep every enrolled child attached to the system until they leave with real competence.

- **Make schools family-formation infrastructure.** On-site infant and toddler care, schedules aligned to adult work, school-adjacent housing, and services for siblings — because the decisive variable in what American classrooms look like in 2100 is whether people can afford, in time and money, to have the children they say they want. An education system that makes parenting harder is quietly determining its own future enrollment.

- **Make integration a permanent core function, not an emergency response.** America's demographic advantage over aging peers is immigration, and schools are the country's primary integration machine. Build standing capacity for rapid language acquisition, credential recognition, and adult education as ordinary infrastructure — designed for high volume in perpetuity rather than improvised each time a bus arrives.

- **Prepare students for an old society.** Fluency in care work, geriatric health, automation that complements a shrinking labor force, and the fiscal and political literacy of a democracy in which the median voter is elderly and the young are outnumbered — the defining distributional conflict they will inherit.

- **Change the headline metric.** Report *adult contact hours per child per week* alongside test scores. It is the input that actually varies, the one wealthy families buy privately, and the one a shrinking cohort finally lets us provide publicly.

**The wager:** we are about to receive, unasked, the resource education has always lacked — a favorable ratio of adults to children — and our institutional defaults will spend it on closures and cost savings before anyone notices. A smaller generation that each received a decade of near-tutorial attention, and grew up in a system built to support the formation of families rather than to compete with it, would be far more capable than a larger one processed in batches. The 22nd century will have fewer American children in it than the 21st. The only question is whether each of them gets more, or the system simply gets smaller.

**Teach Americans how to *build and finish things at scale*: make execution — project management, systems engineering, and the practical craft of getting a large collective effort done — a core discipline from middle school onward.**

The bottleneck in 21st-century America is not ideas, talent, or capital; it is the collapsed ability to convert intention into completed reality. We take decades to build a rail line, years to permit a transmission tower, and routinely blow schedules and budgets on projects our great-grandparents finished in months. That is not a technology problem — it is a *competence and institutional* problem, and it will be far worse in a century whose defining tasks (rebuilding the grid, adapting coastlines, deploying new energy and medical systems, governing machine intelligence) are all enormous, multi-decade, multi-party undertakings. Yet no American student is ever taught how a big thing actually gets done. We teach them to have opinions about projects and never to run one.

**The redesign:**
