- **Guarantee continuity for the mobile.** A portable, learner-owned record and instant enrollment rights so that a child who changes schools four times, a family displaced by a hurricane, or a teenager entering foster care never restarts from zero. Assign one advisor who follows the *person*, not the building, across every institutional boundary — school, shelter, hospital, jail, job.

- **Recognize what people already know.** A national system of prior-learning assessment and foreign-credential recognition, so that the immigrant physician driving a taxi, the veteran with a decade of technical experience, and the self-taught programmer can convert existing competence into usable certification in weeks rather than repeating four years they don't need.

- **Design against stigma.** Mixed-age classrooms where a 17-year-old, a 34-year-old retraining, and a 60-year-old learning to read are ordinary co-students; buildings that look like campuses rather than remedial annexes; and language that treats re-entry as normal maintenance of a long life rather than as evidence of failure.

**The wager:** we have built an education system on the assumption that a person's trajectory is set between ages five and twenty-two, and that anyone who falls off it is a residual cost to be absorbed by prisons, disability rolls, and emergency rooms. That assumption was always cruel and is about to become economically absurd: in the 22nd century, careers will end unexpectedly, industries will vanish inside a decade, lives will run past a hundred, and there will be far fewer young people to carry those who were discarded. The most valuable thing a country could own is not a better kindergarten curriculum but the demonstrated institutional capacity to take a 35-year-old — displaced, incarcerated, illiterate, or simply lost — and reliably make them capable again. Build that, and the front end of the system gets safer to reform, because failure stops being permanent.

**Fix what's actually in front of the child: treat *instructional materials* as national public infrastructure, built and maintained like open-source software rather than bought from publishers or improvised weekly by exhausted teachers.**

The overlooked fact is that American teachers largely don't have a curriculum. Surveys find they spend seven-plus hours a week hunting for and cobbling together lessons — from Pinterest, Teachers Pay Teachers, a shared drive, a twenty-year-old binder — because the adopted textbook is unusable and no one has given them anything better. The result is that two children in the same building, in the same grade, receive wildly different content of wildly different quality, and no child receives a coherent sequence in which each year's work builds on the last. Meanwhile the research is unusually clear that swapping in genuinely well-designed materials produces gains comparable to a much better teacher, at a marginal cost near zero — the cheapest known lever in education, and the one we've handed to a three-firm publishing oligopoly and a gig marketplace.

**The redesign:**

- **Build a national open curriculum commons.** Publicly funded, openly licensed, free to every school forever: full K–12 sequences in every subject — daily lesson plans, texts, problem sets, labs, assessments, rubrics, remediation branches, translations, accessible formats — designed by the best curriculum designers, cognitive scientists, and classroom teachers the country can hire, at the scale we'd fund a weapons program. Not standards (which describe outcomes and teach no one), and not a mandate: an *offer* so good that adopting it is the obvious choice.

- **Govern it like Linux, not like a textbook adoption.** Version-controlled, forkable, publicly issue-tracked. Any teacher can propose an improvement to Lesson 47 because it failed in her room on Tuesday; maintainers review, test, and merge; the fix propagates to three million classrooms in the next release. Today the same lesson fails in fifty thousand rooms and each teacher patches it alone, and the knowledge dies with them. This gives American education something it has never possessed: a mechanism by which craft accumulates instead of evaporating.

- **Make it an evidence engine.** Because usage and outcomes are instrumented, individual units can be A/B tested at national scale and revised continuously against what actually produces durable learning — versioning curriculum the way software is versioned, rather than rewriting it every seven years by political fight and sales pitch.

- **Bind teacher training, tutoring, and AI to it.** Preparation programs, coaching, and professional development teach *the actual materials teachers will use*, which is how Japan and Singapore train teachers and the opposite of our abstract methods coursework. AI tutors and homework helpers are built on top of the commons — aligned to today's lesson, transparent, publicly owned, and not attention-optimized — instead of being a separate parallel curriculum nobody controls.

- **Buy back teachers' time and spend it on children.** Eliminating lesson-hunting returns something like a full workday per week per teacher, redirected to small-group instruction, tutoring the stuck, and observing colleagues — an enormous capacity gain with no new hiring.

- **Guard against monoculture.** Multiple competing forks and pluralism in contested content; local adoption remains voluntary; independent audits for quality and bias; nothing prevents a district or a teacher from teaching their own material. Coherence is offered, not imposed.

**The wager:** most reform proposals require heroic changes in people, politics, or money — better teachers, braver governance, more funding. Materials are the rare lever that is cheap, fast, invisible to the culture war when done carefully, and effective the day it lands on a desk. And in a century when instruction will be delivered by tutors, screens, machines, and half a dozen providers per child, the one thing that must be excellent, coherent, and commonly owned is the *substance* being taught. We currently let it be the least designed thing in the entire system. Build it once, superbly, in the open — and every teacher, tutor, parent, and machine in America is suddenly working from the best version of the lesson rather than the nearest one.

**Fix the last five years, not just the first thirteen: redesign the *university* itself — because American higher education is the one tier where nobody whose job is teaching was ever trained to teach, and no institution is rewarded for whether students learn.**

We spend enormous energy debating K–12 while the credential that actually governs American life is produced by institutions with a structural problem nobody names: undergraduate tuition subsidizes research, prestige is earned by discovery and exclusivity rather than by instruction, and the person standing in front of a 300-seat lecture hall was hired, promoted, and tenured on the basis of publications, with zero preparation in pedagogy and no consequence for teaching badly. Meanwhile the actual teaching has been quietly offloaded onto adjuncts paid per course with no office, no continuity, and no stake. We have built the only professional-scale teaching enterprise in the world in which teaching ability is neither trained, measured, nor rewarded — and then we hand it four years of every young person's life and a hundred thousand dollars.

**The redesign:**

- **Unbundle research from undergraduate instruction, and fund each honestly.** Pay for research directly through public research funding and dedicated institutes rather than through an opaque cross-subsidy from nineteen-year-olds' tuition and federal loans. Some universities remain research-intensive; most should become explicitly *teaching* institutions with that as their declared, funded, and evaluated mission — which is what the overwhelming majority of students actually need and are currently charged research prices for.

- **Create a real teaching professorate with real preparation.** Anyone who teaches undergraduates completes genuine training in instructional design, assessment, and cognitive science — a licensure requirement as normal as it is for a third-grade teacher — with permanent, well-paid, promotable teaching-track positions replacing the adjunct underclass. Promotion depends on observed instruction, peer review of course design, and measured student learning gains, not on student-satisfaction surveys (which mostly measure charisma and grade generosity) and not on citations.

- **Measure learning, not inputs, and publish it.** Standardized, discipline-specific assessments of what students can actually do at entry and exit, reported as *value added* per program, per institution — alongside completion, debt, and outcomes at 30. Right now the entire sector is ranked by the quality of the students it turns away, which is an incentive to teach nobody well. Rank by how much students grew, and the whole prestige machine inverts.

- **Compress the degree and make it modular.** Three-year degrees as the norm (as in most of the world), with the redundant general-education year eliminated by honest credit for secondary work, and competency-based completion for those who can demonstrate mastery sooner. The recovered year is returned to students as money and time — the two things a person needs most at twenty-two.

- **Rebuild doctoral training for the jobs that exist.** Stop producing PhDs almost exclusively for a professoriate that hires a fraction of them, and stop using them as cheap instructional labor. Train them in teaching, industry practice, public service, and communication — and shrink cohorts to honesty.

- **Restrain the cost drivers deliberately.** Cap administrative growth, unbundle the amenities arms race from the academic price, tie federal aid eligibility to instructional spending share, and make institutions bear part of the loan losses they generate.

**Why this prepares students for 2100:** every vision of the coming century assumes adults who return to formal learning repeatedly across sixty-year lives — at thirty, forty-five, sixty. That entire architecture rests on universities being *good at teaching adults*, which is precisely the capability we have never built, measured, or paid for. We have world-leading research institutions and mediocre teaching ones wearing the same name, and we charge families for the former while delivering the latter. Separate them, professionalize college teaching the way we professionalize everything else that matters, and America gains the one institution a century of continuous re-education actually requires.

**Build the missing institution: give American education its own version of the teaching hospital — a national network of university-affiliated clinical schools where training, practice, and research happen in the same building, on the same children, at the same time.**

Medicine in 1900 looked like education today: apprenticeship without evidence, proprietary schools of wildly varying quality, practitioners doing whatever their mentor did, and no reliable path from discovery to bedside. What transformed it wasn't a new curriculum for medical students — it was an *institutional form*. The academic medical center fused three functions that had been scattered: caring for patients, training new clinicians on real cases under supervision, and generating and testing knowledge where the work actually occurs. Education has all three functions too, and we have deliberately kept them apart. Ed schools train teachers in buildings with no children. Researchers study classrooms they don't work in and publish for other researchers. Schools practice without evidence and generate none. Nothing anyone learns anywhere reaches anyone else, which is why the same debates recur every twenty years and why "what works" and "what is done" have almost no relationship.

**The redesign:**

- **Establish several hundred clinical teaching schools**, ordinary public schools serving ordinary neighborhood children, jointly governed by a university and the district, deliberately sited in the communities with the hardest problems — because that is where a teaching hospital belongs. Every one is simultaneously a school, a training site, and a research site, funded for all three rather than asked to do two of them for free.

- **Make clinical residency the only route into teaching.** No one is licensed without two paid years on a teaching-school floor under a master clinician, carrying a gradually increasing caseload, observed daily, with a real washout rate. This ends the absurdity of preparing teachers through coursework about teaching, and it makes the profession's standards visible and enforceable by its own experts rather than by state seat-hour rules.

- **Import the clinical apparatus wholesale, because it is the actual technology.** Rounds: teams of teachers walking through real cases together every week. Case conferences on a specific stuck child, with the specialists — reading, language, behavior, psychology — in the room. Morbidity and mortality conferences: honest, blame-free examination of the students who failed and why, which is how medicine converts disaster into institutional memory and which education does nowhere. Attending physicians, residents, and interns as an explicit hierarchy of expertise, so novices are never left alone with 28 children and masters never leave the classroom to get promoted.

- **Run the research where the patients are.** Trials, replications, and instrument development conducted inside working schools by people who also teach, on questions practitioners actually asked — with the results owed back to the field in usable form. This is the missing translational layer: not more studies, but a standing institution whose job is to move a finding from a journal into three million classrooms and to kill the findings that don't survive contact with real children.

- **Give the network a diffusion mandate and a budget.** Every teaching school is responsible for a ring of ordinary schools — placing residents, sending master teachers out on rotation, running regional case conferences, hosting observation. Diffusion is a staffed, funded function, not a hope. Medicine spreads a new technique in a few years through exactly this mechanism; education takes a generation because no one owns the job.

- **Establish specialties and referral.** Reading disability, mathematics remediation, English acquisition, behavior and trauma, gifted acceleration — genuine specialist credentials, real consultation, and referral pathways, so a struggling child in any school can reach the country's best-trained person for their specific problem instead of whoever happens to be down the hall.

- **Guard the failure modes.** Teaching hospitals can become detached elite enclaves or exploit the poor communities that host them, so: neighborhood enrollment with no selection, community boards with real power, published outcomes for the children served, and accountability first for the school's own students and only second for its research output. Care comes before the study, always.

**The wager:** every other proposal — better curricula, AI tutors, apprenticeships, mastery pacing, whatever the 22nd century turns out to need — will be discovered, tested, and implemented by *someone standing in a room with children*, or it will not happen at all. America has no institution whose job is to connect the knowing to the doing, so our good ideas die in journals and our bad practices survive for decades. We built the teaching hospital once, and it converted medicine from folklore into a self-improving profession within a single generation. Building the same thing for education would not tell us what to teach in 2100 — it would give us, at last, a system capable of finding out and then actually doing it.

**Make American education a *global* institution: redesign it as the world's premier talent magnet, so that our own students grow up learning alongside the best people on earth rather than in a sealed national bubble.**

The 22nd century's decisive question for the United States is not what its schools teach but *who is in them*. America's single most durable competitive advantage has never been its pedagogy — by international measures our K–12 results are mediocre — it has been that ambitious, capable people from everywhere wanted to come here, and that our universities were the funnel. That advantage is eroding: other countries are building world-class systems, our visa architecture actively expels the graduate students we just trained, and our K–12 system is almost entirely closed to the world. Meanwhile the domestic cohort is shrinking, the tax base that will pay for schools is shrinking with it, and the frontier of every field is becoming irreducibly international. A country that educates only its own dwindling supply of children, inside its own borders, in its own language, is choosing to compete in 2100 with a fraction of the talent it could have had — and is raising its own children with no idea what world-class actually looks like.

**The redesign:**

- **Staple green cards to serious credentials, and design the whole education pipeline around retention.** Any student who completes a rigorous degree or advanced technical credential at an accredited American institution receives permanent residency automatically, on the day of graduation. We currently spend years and enormous public subsidy training the world's best engineers, physicians, and researchers and then deport them to compete against us — the most expensive unforced error in American policy. Fix that, and every downstream problem of teacher shortage, research capacity, and demographic decline gets easier at once.

- **Open secondary education to the world, deliberately and at scale.** Publicly funded international scholarship places in American high schools, residential academies, and community colleges — recruited by competitive examination from every country, the way France runs its lycées abroad and Singapore recruits regional talent. The point is not charity; it is that a sixteen-year-old in Ohio who spends four years with a classmate from Lagos and a lab partner from Seoul acquires a calibration of the world, and a network in it, that no curriculum can supply. Today that experience is a purchased privilege of a few boarding schools; make it ordinary.

- **Export the system as infrastructure and influence.** A national network of American-standard schools, community colleges, and university branch campuses abroad — publicly supported rather than left to private franchising — offering American curricula, credentials, and pathways to millions who will never emigrate. This does three things simultaneously: it creates a permanent global constituency educated in American institutions and habits of mind, it opens reciprocal placements so our students can spend a year in Nairobi or Jakarta at public expense, and it gives American teachers international careers rather than a single classroom for forty years.

- **Build the reciprocal machinery that makes talent flow both ways.** Automatic recognition of foreign credentials with fast bridging exams, so the immigrant physician isn't driving a taxi and can instead be teaching in a clinical school. Portable, internationally legible competency records. Standing partnerships that let American students earn credit anywhere and foreign students earn credit here without institutional friction.

- **Make the classroom itself internationally benchmarked.** Every American student's work compared not to the district average but to the international standard in that subject — with the recruitment of foreign teaching talent, foreign materials, and foreign methods treated as normal rather than exotic. A country that measures itself only against itself cannot tell that it is falling behind, which is precisely our current condition.

- **Fund it as national strategy, and defend it honestly.** This must be built so that it visibly benefits the American-born child in the ordinary school — funded seats, funded travel, funded language instruction, and enforceable guarantees that international enrollment expands capacity rather than displacing domestic students. Otherwise it will be, and should be, politically destroyed.

**The wager:** by 2100, roughly 96% of humanity will be non-American, most scientific and economic output will originate outside the United States, and the fundamental input to national capability will be talent — which, unlike land, minerals, or manufacturing capacity, is mobile and chooses where to go. Every other reform we might attempt improves the education of the people who happen to be born here. This one changes *who is here*, deepens the pool our own children are formed in, competed with, and married into, and turns education from a domestic service into the country's principal instrument of renewal. We already run the institution the world most wants to join. We are simply declining to let it in — and thereby educating our own children as though the other 96% were a rumor.

**Reorganize schooling around *tacit* knowledge — the kind that cannot be written down — because everything that can be written down has already been absorbed by machines.**

The premise: AI was trained on humanity's explicit knowledge, the codified stuff that fits in text. It is now better than almost anyone at reciting, explaining, and recombining it. What it has no access to, and no way to acquire, is the enormous body of human competence that was never verbalized in the first place: how a surgeon knows the tissue is wrong before any instrument says so, how a machinist hears a bad cut, how a good teacher senses that a room has stopped following, how an experienced negotiator reads the moment to stop talking, how a nurse knows a patient is deteriorating an hour before the monitors do. Polanyi's point — that we know more than we can tell — is now the entire competitive question. And American schooling is built almost exclusively to transmit the explicit half: it verbalizes, prints, lectures, and tests recall, which is precisely the function that has just been commoditized.

**The redesign — trade explanation for proximity.**

- **Make sustained apprenticeship-by-observation the default pedagogy.** Tacit knowledge transmits only one way: prolonged closeness to someone doing the real thing, watching, imitating badly, being corrected in the moment, and doing it again. So restructure the upper years so students spend long, continuous stretches beside working practitioners — clinicians, machinists, farmers, litigators, researchers, chefs, electricians, engineers — not on tours, but embedded long enough to absorb what nobody in that workplace could articulate if asked.

- **Require teachers to work in front of students, not just talk in front of them.** A mathematician should solve an unfamiliar problem live, including the false starts; a writer should revise a real draft on the board; a scientist should design an experiment aloud and get it wrong. Students almost never see expert cognition in motion — only its polished output, which is exactly what a model can produce. The mess is the curriculum.

- **Train perception, not just procedure.** Deliberate practice at *noticing*: thousands of cases, guessed and corrected — radiographs, soil samples, weld beads, bird calls, financial statements, student essays, faces. Expertise is largely trained pattern recognition, it takes volume and immediate feedback, and it is teachable at fifteen.

- **Preserve what is being lost.** A national effort to capture endangered craft and clinical knowledge before its holders die — long-form video, master-apprentice residencies, funded transmission of skills that exist in perhaps a few hundred pairs of hands.

- **Assess in situ.** Performance under real conditions, judged by masters — the only evaluation a language model cannot sit for.

**The wager:** in 2100, articulate knowledge will be free and infinitely available, so the scarce human capital will be the inarticulate kind — feel, judgment, touch, timing, taste — which passes from person to person only through time spent together doing real work. We have built an education system optimized to transmit the half machines already own, and we transmit the other half by accident, if at all.

**Teach digital sovereignty: make every American graduate a competent operator, defender, and auditor of the computational systems they will live inside — not merely a user of someone else's.**

The 22nd-century citizen will conduct their finances, medicine, identity, work, relationships, and politics through software they did not write, cannot inspect, and do not control, increasingly mediated by autonomous agents acting in their name. We currently prepare them for this by teaching "digital citizenship" (don't be mean online), a keyboarding unit, and an optional coding elective. That is the equivalent of teaching a maritime nation to admire boats. A population that cannot read, secure, verify, or replace its own infrastructure is not a citizenry; it is a user base, and it will be governed by whoever owns the stack.

**The redesign:**

- **Make the security mindset a core, examined discipline from middle school.** Threat modeling as a habit: who wants what from me, what are they capable of, where is the weakest link, what happens when this fails? Students learn adversarially — they are required to *attack* systems in sanctioned ranges (phish each other, break their own school's test network, defeat a poorly built authentication scheme, red-team a classmate's project) before they are asked to defend anything. Nothing else produces the permanent, healthy paranoia that a century of industrialized fraud, deepfaked voices, and automated social engineering will demand. Pair it with the ethics and law of the same skills, taught as a professional code, with real consequences.

- **Teach cryptography as ordinary civic literacy, not as advanced computer science.** Keys, signatures, hashing, encryption, provenance, and identity — enough that every graduate can manage their own keys, verify that a document or a video is signed by who it claims, communicate privately when it matters, and understand why "trust me" is not a security model. In a world where any face, voice, or document can be synthesized on demand, cryptographic verification becomes the only durable basis for knowing anything came from anyone — and it should be as universal a skill as reading a contract.

- **Require every student to build, run, and maintain real infrastructure.** Not toy exercises: a server they administer, a network they configure, a database they back up (and restore, after the teacher deletes it), a site with real users, a local model they run on their own hardware. Maintenance is the lesson — updates, outages, logs, breaches, and the discovery that systems rot unless someone tends them. A generation that has personally kept something running understands both how fragile the digital world is and that it is made by people, not delivered by magic.

- **Teach the supervision of autonomous agents as a discipline of delegation and liability.** Students will spend their lives directing software that acts on their behalf. So they should learn, formally and with real stakes, how to scope an agent's permissions, sandbox it, log and audit its actions, set spending and authority limits, detect when it has been manipulated, and take responsibility for what it does. Every student runs agents on genuine tasks with genuine consequences and must answer for the outcomes — because the central legal and moral question of the coming century is who is accountable when a machine acting for a person causes harm.

- **Make schools model the thing they teach.** The school runs on open, auditable, publicly owned software; students can read the code that grades them, see the data held about them, and file issues against it. No black-box vendor decides anything consequential about a child that the child cannot inspect. An institution that teaches transparency while operating as an opaque data extractor teaches only the second lesson.

- **Teach the political economy of the stack.** Who owns the chips, cables, models, standards, app stores, and payment rails; how protocols become power; how lock-in, interoperability, monopoly, and open standards actually determine what freedoms exist. Study the internet's founding decisions as constitutional history, because they function that way. Citizens who cannot see the infrastructure cannot regulate it, and by 2100 the most consequential legislation will be about systems the public does not remotely understand.

- **Assess by demonstration.** Capture-the-flag competitions with the standing of athletics, live incident response under time pressure, audits of real code, oral defense of a security design. All of it unforgeable and all of it AI-resistant, since a model can write the code but cannot sit in the chair while a system is failing.

**The wager:** every other reform assumes a person who can act freely in the world their instruction prepared them for. But the 22nd-century world is a computational one, and the default trajectory is a population living entirely inside systems owned by a handful of firms and states, unable to verify a single claim, secure a single account, or replace a single dependency — which is not a skills problem but a sovereignty problem, individual and national. We already know what happens to societies that cannot maintain their own critical infrastructure. Educate a generation that can read the machine, defend itself inside it, and build an alternative when the one on offer is unacceptable, and everything else we want from them — privacy, trust, honest information, self-government, the ability to hold power accountable — becomes technically possible rather than merely aspirational.

**Educate for optionality: stop trying to guess the 22nd century's demands and instead build deliberate *redundancy* into every graduate — and into the system itself — so that no person and no institution is a single point of failure.**

Every reform proposal, including the futuristic ones, is a bet on a forecast: AI will do this, jobs will look like that, these skills will matter. The historical record of such forecasts is terrible — we trained a generation for manufacturing that left, then for coding that AI now does, then for "21st-century skills" nobody can define. The honest response to deep uncertainty isn't a better prediction; it's a portfolio. Finance, ecology, and engineering all solved this problem the same way: you don't optimize for the expected case, you build redundancy, you keep uncorrelated assets, and you make small reversible bets instead of one large irreversible one. American education does the exact opposite — it makes every child place a single, enormous, irreversible bet on one narrow specialization by age twenty, in an economy that will be redrawn five times in their life.

**The redesign:**

- **A "barbell" graduation requirement: every student leaves with at least three *uncorrelated* competencies.** One embodied trade that can generate income anywhere and cannot be offshored or automated cheaply (electrical, plumbing, welding, culinary, EMT, phlebotomy, machining, agriculture). One deep academic or technical specialty pursued to genuine frontier-adjacent depth, because shallow breadth teaches nothing about what mastery costs. One competency in care or human service — childcare, eldercare, nursing basics, teaching, counseling — the domain of guaranteed and growing demand. Plus mobility assets: a second language and a driver's/operator's license. The requirement is *uncorrelation*: a graduate whose three skills all die in the same technological shock has no portfolio at all, and today's system produces almost nothing else.

- **Teach small bets, not big ones.** Replace the single high-stakes life decision at eighteen with a decade of cheap, reversible experiments: short apprenticeships, sampled trades, semester-length ventures, tried-and-abandoned specialties. Grade students on the quality of their experimental design and what they learned from the ones that failed, not on picking correctly the first time. Make dropping a path costless and re-entering it costless, so exploration stops being punished by sunk tuition and lost credits.

- **Teach the mathematics of uncertainty as the discipline that governs all of this** — convexity, tail risk, ruin versus loss, ergodicity, the difference between an outcome that can be recovered from and one that cannot, why survival dominates optimization. A generation that intuitively distinguishes "bad but survivable" from "unrecoverable" will make better decisions about their careers, their debts, their health, and their country's technologies than one drilled in whatever content we currently think matters.

- **Build slack into the graduate, not just the curriculum.** Skills held in reserve that may never be used, savings, a fallback trade, a second place they could live, a network outside their industry. We currently teach children to be maximally optimized assets — thin, specialized, leveraged, and fragile — which is precisely the profile that gets destroyed by shocks. Teach reserve capacity as a life discipline, the way a good engineer specifies a safety factor.

- **Make the institution itself redundant.** No child's education should depend on one school, one teacher, one district, one funding stream, one vendor, one internet connection, or one uninterrupted year. Multiple concurrent providers per student, portable records, offline-capable materials, distributed small campuses instead of consolidated megaschools, and demonstrated continuity through disruption — pandemics, disasters, family moves, illness, displacement — as an audited requirement rather than an improvisation. The last five years should have taught us that a system with no failover isn't a system; it's a bet.

- **Preserve variety at the population level.** Resist national convergence on one curriculum, one pedagogy, one definition of success — not because any given alternative is better, but because a monoculture is optimized for a world that hasn't arrived yet. A country whose young people are all trained the same way has staked everything on one forecast being right.

**The wager:** we are being asked to prepare people for a century we cannot describe, and the standard move is to pick our favorite future and train for it — which is how we produced a generation of coal towns, a generation of coders, and a mountain of unusable degrees. The alternative is to accept that we will be wrong, and to build people and institutions that survive being wrong: multiply capable, cheaply adaptable, holding reserves, able to lose a bet without losing a life. Optionality is not indecision; it is the only rational strategy under genuine uncertainty, and it is the one thing an education system can guarantee its students regardless of which future actually shows up.

**Make biology the unit of personalization: build a "precision education" system that treats each child as a distinct physiological and cognitive system to be understood and tuned — the way medicine moved from standard protocols to individualized care.**

Education's deepest inefficiency is that we deliver an identical intervention — same content, same pace, same hour of day, same modality, same room temperature, same nutrition, same expectation of stillness — to thirty organisms that differ enormously in chronotype, sensory thresholds, working-memory span, processing speed, arousal regulation, developmental tempo, blood sugar stability, and rate of consolidation. Then we call the resulting variance in outcomes "ability" and grade it. Medicine made its largest gains not by inventing new drugs but by learning *who* a treatment works for; education has never even asked the question.

**The redesign:**

- **A longitudinal developmental profile for every child, built from real measurement rather than teacher impression.** Vision, hearing, sleep timing and duration, iron and vitamin D status, lead exposure, allergy and asthma burden, language exposure, executive function, processing speed, reading substrate skills — assessed early, repeatedly, and acted on within days. An enormous share of what we currently classify as low ability, laziness, or behavior problems is an uncorrected sensory deficit, a chronic sleep deficit, an untreated deficiency, or a mismatch between task demand and working-memory capacity — all measurable, all fixable, and almost none currently measured.

- **Schedule instruction to individual chronobiology.** Adolescents differ by hours in circadian phase; late chronotypes lose a full grade level to a schedule built for early ones. Offer staggered start times, let students take their hardest cognitive work at their own peak, and treat sleep timing as an instructional variable rather than a family failing.

- **Tune load, not content.** The same rigorous material delivered with individually calibrated chunk size, pacing, rehearsal spacing, and modality — driven by continuous diagnostics and AI tutors whose actual comparative advantage is running a different instructional schedule for each of thirty children simultaneously. Spacing intervals set by each student's measured forgetting curve rather than by a unit calendar.

- **Treat the body as instructional infrastructure.** Individually prescribed movement, light exposure, food timing, and recovery — not as wellness programming but as dosed inputs to attention and consolidation, with effects measured per student rather than asserted in the aggregate.

- **Run it as continuous n-of-1 experimentation, with the student as co-investigator.** Each child periodically tests interventions on themselves under supervision, keeps the data, and learns to read their own system — producing adults who can manage their own cognition for eighty years and who understand, from the inside, what evidence about a single person can and cannot show.

- **Build the ethical guardrails first, because the failure modes are severe.** No genetic or predictive scoring used to sort, track, or set expectations; the data is the student's property under fiduciary law, never a district asset, vendor corpus, or insurer's input; profiles describe *how to teach this person*, never *how far this person can go*; and every intervention must be shown to raise attainment, never to justify lowering it. Precision without this becomes phrenology with better instruments — the single most dangerous version of any 22nd-century education reform.

**The wager:** every other proposal argues about *what* to deliver; this one addresses the fact that we deliver everything as if variation between children were noise rather than the central fact. The tools to do otherwise — cheap continuous diagnostics, wearables, adaptive tutors, screening at scale — are arriving now and will be ordinary by 2100. A system that used them to find, for each individual child, the conditions under which that child's brain actually works well would recover an immense amount of capability we currently discard as innate difference — and would graduate people who know how to run their own minds, which is the one form of expertise no machine can hold on their behalf.

**Train every American as *crew*: rebuild secondary education on the expeditionary model used by space agencies, polar stations, submarines, and research vessels — small interdependent teams operating with real autonomy, far from help, inside closed systems they must understand and repair.**

The 22nd century's defining human situations will look less like the office and more like the mission: small groups holding responsibility for complex technical systems, far from supervision, with communication delays and no one coming to rescue them — whether that is a Mars habitat, an Antarctic or seafloor station, a wildfire crew, a disaster zone, a remote clinic, an isolated grid node, or simply a self-directed life in institutions too thin to carry anyone along. Every organization that must reliably produce competence for those conditions long ago converged on the same training architecture, and American schooling uses none of it.

**The redesign:**

- **Make the crew, not the class, the organizational unit.** Students are assigned to standing teams of six to ten for years, cross-trained so every member can cover every role, rotating command, and evaluated primarily on the crew's performance. You cannot choose your crewmates and you cannot leave them — which is precisely the condition under which people learn to work with those they don't like, the single most-cited failure mode in real isolated-team research and the one American schools, organized around individual grades and self-selected friends, never impose.

- **Deploy them.** Several times before graduation, every crew undertakes a genuine expedition of two to six weeks — a remote field station, a research vessel, a wilderness traverse, a farm season, an infrastructure build, a rural clinic, a simulated habitat with sealed resource budgets. Real logistics, real weather, real consequences, minimal adult intervention, and a formal debrief afterward. Deployment is the curriculum, not an enrichment trip: physics, biology, chemistry, statistics, writing, and ethics are taught in preparation for it and assessed by performance during it.

- **Teach the closed loop.** Air, water, food, energy, waste, and materials as a single accountable budget the crew must actually balance — because that is both the literal condition of a spacecraft and the honest description of a planet. A generation that has personally run a closed system for three weeks has an intuition about sustainability that no amount of climate curriculum produces.

- **Teach autonomy under delay.** Exercises deliberately structured so help is minutes, hours, or days away: no instructor to ask, no instant answer, sometimes no connectivity. Students must decide with incomplete information, document their reasoning, and live with the outcome. This is the exact inverse of a schooling environment in which an adult or a model is always one question away, and it is the only way to build the judgment a century of self-directed, machine-augmented work will demand.

- **Adopt the operational disciplines wholesale:** checklists and standard procedures, pre-mission briefs and after-action reviews, redundancy and single-point-of-failure analysis, medical and psychological first response, communication protocols under stress, and blameless incident investigation. These are teachable, examinable, transferable to every adult domain, and taught almost nowhere in general education.

- **Select and train for the human factors, honestly.** Confinement, monotony, conflict in tight quarters, sleep discipline, boredom tolerance, morale, and the discovery of one's own behavior under fatigue and fear — coached explicitly, with graded practice, the way agencies train crews and unlike anything a school currently attempts. Students learn what they are actually like when things go wrong, which most Americans never find out until it matters.

- **Have them found something.** Each crew's capstone is designing and briefly living under the governance of a small community they wrote the rules for: resource allocation, decision procedure, dispute resolution, obligations to newcomers and to those who can't contribute equally. Founding rather than inheriting institutions is the political skill a century of new settlements, new platforms, and reconstituted communities will require.

**The wager:** we keep debating what content to load into individual students, when the durable unit of human capability has always been the small, trained, interdependent team that can keep itself and its systems alive far from support. Machines will supply the knowledge and much of the execution; what they cannot supply is a group of people who have been tested together, know each other's failure modes, can hold a complex system in their collective head, and will not abandon the mission or each other when it gets hard. Train every American as crew, and you produce citizens fit for a century of frontiers — planetary, technological, and civic — instead of passengers waiting for instructions.

**Redesign around *tools for thought*: make the invention and mastery of external representations — notation, diagrams, models, maps, formalisms — the spine of the curriculum, because human intelligence has always been prosthetic, and the 22nd century will belong to people who can build new instruments for thinking rather than merely operate someone else's interface.**

The unexamined assumption in every reform debate is that thinking happens inside a head, so education should load the head. But almost every leap in human capability came from a *representation*, not from smarter brains: Arabic numerals made arithmetic ordinary; algebraic notation made physics possible; double-entry bookkeeping made the modern firm possible; musical notation let a composer coordinate a hundred strangers across centuries; Cartesian coordinates fused geometry and algebra; the map, the graph, the periodic table, the flowchart, the spreadsheet each converted a class of problems from impossible to routine. Yet we teach these as inherited furniture — "just how math is written" — and never as inventions, never as things a student might critique, redesign, or create. The result is graduates who can fill in a representation handed to them and are helpless the moment a problem doesn't arrive pre-formatted.

**The redesign:**

- **Teach notation as history and as engineering.** Every symbolic system students use gets taught with its origin, its predecessors, and its costs: why Roman numerals strangled European arithmetic, what Leibniz's notation could do that Newton's couldn't, what a mercator projection distorts, what a p-value hides, what a résumé or a GPA compresses away. A student who has seen notation *chosen* understands that every representation is an argument about what matters, and can therefore ask the most valuable question in any field: what is this framing making invisible?

- **Require students to invent representations, repeatedly and under critique.** Given a messy real situation — a school's energy use, a neighborhood's traffic, a novel's character relations, a chemical pathway, a legislative process — invent a notation, diagram, or model that makes it thinkable, then defend it against a room trying to break it, then use it to answer a question no one could answer before. Grade the *representation*, not the answer. This is the one intellectual act machines are worst at: they interpolate brilliantly within existing formalisms and rarely propose a better one.

- **Make fluency in a small set of universal thinking instruments a graduation standard**, held to real proficiency: sketching and diagramming by hand; the spreadsheet as a modeling language; a programming language used for simulation rather than employment; formal logic and proof; statistical graphics and their deceptions; maps and spatial data; systems and causal diagrams; and disciplined written argument. These are not "tech skills" — they are the general-purpose lenses through which every complex adult problem becomes tractable, and we currently teach most of them to almost no one.

- **Train the hand and the whiteboard, not just the interface.** Protected daily practice thinking on paper and at a board — because externalizing a half-formed idea where you and others can see and revise it is the actual mechanism of collaborative reasoning, and it is being replaced by tools that hand you a finished output before you have formed a thought. Friction is where representation gets built.

- **Teach interface criticism as a discipline.** Every tool a student uses is examined for what it makes easy, what it makes hard, whose interests it encodes, and what it does to the user's mind: the search bar, the feed, the dashboard, the LLM chat window, the grading portal, the recommendation engine. Then have them build a better one. In a century where nearly all cognition is mediated by designed interfaces, a population that cannot see the medium is a population that thinks whatever the medium permits.

- **Reorganize subjects around their instruments rather than their content lists.** Mathematics becomes the study of what happens when you invent a good symbol system and follow it; science becomes the study of instruments and models; history becomes the study of sources, archives, and how the past is encoded and lost; art and music become the study of how meaning is stored in a form and released in a performance. Content is still rigorous and cumulative — but organized so that students perpetually see the tool, not only the result.

**The wager:** machines now execute superbly inside any representation we hand them, and they were trained on the ones humanity already invented. What remains scarce — and what compounds — is the ability to look at an unformed mess and construct the framework that makes it thinkable, then hand that framework to others and to machines. That skill has produced nearly every jump in human capability, it is teachable, and American schooling treats it as an accident that occasionally happens to geniuses. Teach every child to build instruments for their own mind, and you have given them the one thing that keeps paying off in a century whose problems will not arrive in any format we have seen before.

**Give ordinary public schools what only elite institutions currently have: permanence, identity, endowment, and alumni — so that a school is something you *belong to for life* rather than a facility you pass through and forget.**

The overlooked asymmetry in American education is that the wealthiest 2% of students attend institutions with 200-year charters, endowments, crests, traditions, and — decisively — a lifelong alumni network of adults obligated to help them. Everyone else attends a municipally administered building that may be renamed, reconstituted, reconstituted again, or closed by a board vote, staffed by adults who rotate through in five-year cycles, and which they exit at eighteen with no further relationship of any kind. We have systematically stripped public schools of institutional identity in the name of administrative efficiency, and in doing so we removed the two things that actually convert schooling into lifelong advantage: durable membership and social capital.

**The redesign:**

- **Charter every public school as a permanent institution with a long clock.** A named, self-governing body with a founding document, a 100-year charter, its own board including alumni and teachers, and legal protection against arbitrary closure, renaming, or consolidation. Institutions that expect to exist in 2150 make different decisions than facilities managed on a three-year superintendent's horizon.

- **Endow them, and equalize the endowments deliberately.** Public seed capital for every school's permanent fund, with federal matching weighted *inversely* to community wealth — so a rural or high-poverty school's dollar raised is matched five-to-one and an affluent suburb's is matched not at all. Endowment income funds what line budgets never survive: tutors, instruments, expeditions, emergency help for families, a teacher's sabbatical. This is the mechanism that lets an institution accumulate rather than merely be appropriated to each year.

- **Make alumni a permanent, organized constituency with real obligations.** Every graduate is enrolled for life: they return to mentor, host apprentices, teach a unit in their trade, hire, tutor, sit on the board, and give. Not sentiment — a structured pipeline in which the school's own graduates are the primary source of the internships, connections, references, and adult guidance that currently reach only children whose parents already have them. The single greatest thing an elite school confers is not instruction but a network; there is no reason a public high school in Youngstown cannot build the same one out of its own graduates, and every reason it should.

- **Keep the doors open for eighty years.** Membership includes standing rights of return — evening courses, the library and shop and labs, career help, retraining at 35 and 55 and 70, a place to bring your own children. A century of hundred-year lives and repeated technological displacement needs an institution a person can walk back into as a member rather than reapply to as a stranger.

- **Build the culture that makes belonging real.** Names, houses, colors, songs, honors read aloud, a hall of graduates, ceremonies of entrance and departure, older students formally responsible for younger ones, and physical buildings worth caring about rather than fungible boxes. This is not nostalgia; it is the low-cost technology by which institutions generate loyalty, and loyalty is what makes people show up for it forty years later.

- **Guard the obvious failure mode.** Institutional identity easily becomes hereditary caste, so: no legacy preference, open or lottery enrollment, publicly equalized operating funding independent of endowment size, caps on how much endowment wealth may exceed the national median, and public reporting of graduate outcomes at 30 as the institution's actual reputational currency — not selectivity, which is how prestige is measured now and precisely the incentive that must be broken.

**The wager:** everything the 22nd century will demand of a person — lifelong relearning, obligation to people not yet born, adult mentors outside the family, the ability to rebuild a career at fifty, a stake in some community larger and older than oneself — requires an *institution that lasts*, and American public education has almost deliberately built the opposite: transient, interchangeable, relationship-free, and dissolved the day the diploma is handed over. Wealthy Americans have always understood that the durable asset is membership, and they buy it for their own children. Build it into every public school, endow it, and hand it to everyone, and each child inherits not just thirteen years of instruction but a permanent institutional home, a network of adults who owe them something, and a place to return to every time the world changes under them.

**Make *law and rule-making* the core civic discipline: graduate every American able to read a statute, draft a contract, argue both sides of a case, run a hearing, and change a rule — because in the 22nd century, power will be exercised almost entirely through instruments ordinary people currently cannot read.**

We teach "civics" as a description of institutions — three branches, how a bill becomes a law — and then release citizens into a world governed by documents they sign without reading and processes they don't know how to enter. Americans encounter law constantly and competently almost never: leases, employment agreements, terms of service, arbitration clauses, medical consents, custody arrangements, zoning hearings, licensing boards, insurance policies, permits, HOA covenants, algorithmic decisions with no visible appeal. The result is a population that experiences rules as weather — arbitrary, unappealable, arriving from somewhere else — which is precisely the disposition that lets rules be written by whoever bothers to show up. And the century ahead will be *more* law-saturated, not less: machine agents acting under delegated authority, liability for autonomous systems, biotechnology licensing, data and identity rights, model governance, standards bodies whose technical choices function as legislation. Whoever can read and write the rules will govern the century; everyone else will click "agree."

**The redesign:**

- **Twelve years of law as a practiced craft, not a survey.** Sequenced like mathematics: fairness and rule-making in the early grades (children are natural jurisprudes about what's fair and why); contracts, evidence, and procedure in middle years; statutory interpretation, constitutional reasoning, administrative process, and comparative legal systems in the upper years. Every graduate can read a statute and a contract with actual comprehension — find the definitions section, spot the exceptions, identify who bears the risk, and notice what the drafter buried.

- **Adversarial practice as a standard classroom form.** Moot courts, mock legislatures, real arbitration of school disputes, and the requirement to argue positions you reject and lose gracefully. The adversarial method is the most powerful engine for exposing weak reasoning humans have built, and it is the only reliable inoculation against a century of fluent, one-sided, machine-generated persuasion.

- **Require every student to actually change a rule.** Not simulate it — do it: petition a school board, testify at a zoning or utility hearing, draft an ordinance a town council considers, file a public-records request and pursue it, organize a comment campaign on a real proposed regulation. Graduation requires demonstrated evidence that you moved an institution, or a documented account of exactly why you failed. Nothing else teaches so quickly that rules are made by people and can be unmade by people.

- **Teach the administrative state, where most law actually lives.** Agencies, rulemaking, comment periods, licensing boards, permits, appeals. The decisions that shape a life — whether a clinic opens, a home gets built, a drug is approved, a benefit is denied — happen in procedures no one is taught to enter and almost nobody attends.

- **Teach self-defense against the fine print.** Practical, examined competence in the contracts every adult signs: leases, employment and non-compete clauses, arbitration waivers, loans, insurance, medical consent, EULAs and data licenses. Then teach the countermeasures — negotiation, small claims court, regulatory complaint, collective action, refusal.

- **Teach law and code as converging systems.** Students should analyze a terms-of-service agreement, a licensing regime, a technical standard, and an algorithmic decision rule as the same kind of object: a set of enforceable constraints on human behavior, written by someone with interests. Then require them to draft governance for something they built — an agent's permissions, a shared project's dispute rules, a data-use policy — and defend it against people trying to exploit it. Delegating authority to machines is a *legal* act, and the century's central question is who answers for what an agent does.

- **Practice sitting in judgment.** Real jury service in student courts, with real facts, real stakes, and the discipline of deciding under uncertainty according to a standard rather than a feeling. Judging is a civic skill Americans are randomly conscripted into and never trained for.

- **Cheap access as the point of the exercise.** Pair this with public legal infrastructure — plain-language statutes, free public tools, community legal clinics attached to schools — so that competence has somewhere to go.

**The wager:** every other reform assumes a citizenry capable of defending the reforms once they exist. The 22nd century's real distributional fights will be fought in licensing regimes, standards committees, liability rules, and contract boilerplate, at a level of technicality designed to exclude the public — and machine intelligence will make the drafting of one-sided rules effectively free while leaving comprehension of them expensive. A society whose ordinary members can read the rules, contest them, and write better ones is self-governing; one whose members can only comply is administered, however good its schools' test scores are. We currently teach the *shape* of a legal system to people who will never once use it, and leave the operating manual to a professional class that charges $400 an hour. Teach every child to work the machinery, and the machinery starts working for more people.

**Make the tutorial the atomic unit of American education: every student, every week, sits down alone (or two or three at a time) with an expert adult, presents work they made, and defends it — and we restructure everything else in the system to pay for that hour.**

The single best-evidenced fact in education is also the one we've decided to ignore: individual and very-small-group instruction produces gains no classroom method approaches. We treat it as unaffordable and then spend enormous sums on things that don't work — batch lecturing to thirty students at one pace, grading stacks of homework nobody reads carefully, administrative layers, remediation of failures the batch model created. Oxford and Cambridge have run on the opposite principle for centuries, and it is not a mystery why it works: nowhere to hide, nowhere to coast, no possibility of being anonymous or fake, and a weekly obligation to produce something and answer for it in front of someone who knows exactly what you're capable of.

**The redesign:**

- **Split the week deliberately.** Content transmission — lectures, readings, drills, problem sets, practice, feedback on routine work — is delivered asynchronously and at scale, by the best materials and instructors in the country plus AI tutors, at whatever pace each student needs. This is the part machines and recordings genuinely do well, and it is currently the part we spend nearly all our human labor on.
- **Reserve every hour of adult contact for tutorial.** The student arrives with an essay, a proof, a translation, a lab write-up, a design, a piece of code, or a performance. The tutor takes it apart with them, live, for an hour. The student defends it, revises, and returns the next week. That is the entire architecture: produce, defend, revise, repeat, for thirteen years.
- **Fund it by stopping the things it replaces.** Larger asynchronous cohorts for content, elimination of the mass-lecture format and most take-home grading, sharp cuts to administrative and compliance layers, and a tutoring workforce that includes not only teachers but trained older students, retirees, subject-matter professionals working a few hours a week, and graduate students. A weekly hour per student per subject is arithmetically reachable if we stop paying our most expensive people to talk at rooms.
- **Assign each student a permanent tutor who follows them for years** — someone who has read everything they've written and can therefore say the specific true thing: *you always dodge the hard step*, *this is better than what you did in October*, *you're capable of more and we both know it*. Accountability to a person who knows your work is a fundamentally different motivational force than accountability to a grade.
- **Make the tutorial the assessment.** No proctoring crisis, no cheating crisis: a student who used AI to write the essay is discovered within ninety seconds of being asked why they chose that argument. Transcripts become tutor reports plus periodic external oral examinations. This is the only assessment design that is both rigorous and structurally immune to synthetic work.
- **Train tutors as a distinct craft** — Socratic questioning, diagnosing the missing prerequisite, giving hard criticism without crushing, knowing when to shut up. It is not the same skill as lecturing, and we currently train nobody in it.

**The wager:** almost every capacity people say the 22nd century demands — thinking under live questioning, producing original work, taking criticism, self-direction, judging quality, being known by a mentor — is trained automatically by the tutorial and by almost nothing else in a modern school. We have long known the most effective instructional format ever devised, have reserved it for the children of the wealthy and for a handful of ancient universities, and have organized public education around the mass-delivery format precisely because delivery was expensive. Delivery is now nearly free. The only defensible use of scarce human attention is the hour in which one adult makes one young person account for their own thinking — and for the first time in history, we can afford to give that hour to everyone.

**Rebuild the American school around the farm, the kitchen, and above all the table — make the shared daily meal, and the food system that produces it, the organizing spine of the institution.**

This sounds like a lifestyle preference and is actually a structural claim. Food is the one subject that is simultaneously biology, chemistry, ecology, economics, history, health, craft, and ritual — and the one daily event in which every human being participates regardless of aptitude. American schools currently treat it as a logistical nuisance: twenty rushed minutes, reheated ultra-processed trays, a cafeteria designed for throughput, kitchens converted to storage, and agriculture taught nowhere. Meanwhile we have a generation that cannot cook, is metabolically sick before adulthood, has no idea where anything it eats comes from, and — most consequentially — has almost no experience of the unhurried shared meal, which for all of human history was where children learned to converse, to wait, to serve others, to disagree without leaving, and to belong to a group.

**The redesign:**

- **Every school grows, cooks, and serves its own food, and students do the work.** A farm or garden, greenhouse, orchard, chickens or fish where feasible; a real production kitchen; students on rotating crews in planting, harvest, prep, service, and cleanup as an ordinary graduation obligation, not an elective. The school buys the rest from farms within its own region, making the institution an anchor customer for local agriculture rather than a purchaser of the cheapest commodity calories in the world.

- **Teach the sciences on the food system, where they become unavoidable and real.** Soil chemistry and nitrogen cycling; photosynthesis and yield; genetics through seed selection and breeding; microbiology through fermentation, food safety, and the gut; thermodynamics and reaction kinetics through cooking; statistics through crop trials and harvest data; ecology through pollinators, pests, and water; and — critically for the coming century — the whole contested frontier of cellular agriculture, gene-edited crops, precision fermentation, synthetic proteins, and climate-driven agricultural collapse. Nine billion people will need to be fed on a hotter planet with fewer farmers; that is not a niche topic, it is one of the defining engineering and political problems of the 22nd century, and we teach it to essentially no one.

- **Teach the economics and politics of eating.** Commodity markets, subsidies, water rights, labor and immigration, shipping and cold chains, monopoly in meatpacking and seed, food deserts, marketing to children, and the design of hyper-palatable products engineered to defeat satiety. A citizen who can trace a chicken nugget backward through the entire system understands supply chains, externalities, lobbying, and industrial food science better than any economics unit could teach them.

- **Make the long, seated, shared meal a protected daily institution** — cooked on site, eaten together at tables with adults present, with time to actually talk, and with students serving and clearing for one another. This is the French, Japanese, and Italian practice, and it is closer to being the load-bearing wall of the school than anything on the schedule. It supplies, cheaply and daily, exactly what American adolescence most lacks: unhurried face-to-face conversation, cross-class and cross-clique contact under a shared obligation, adults modeling how to hold a disagreement, and the experience of being fed by someone who cares whether you eat. Hospitality — feeding a guest well — is also the oldest and most universal form of moral instruction humans have.

- **Guarantee that every child leaves able to feed themselves and others well for eighty years.** Cooking from raw ingredients to a real standard, preserving, budgeting and shopping, nutrition sufficient to resist both marketing and wellness quackery, and the ability to host a meal. This is the single highest-return health intervention available — cardiovascular and metabolic disease is largely diet-built over decades — and it is the one skill that both machines cannot do for you and the food industry profits enormously from you never acquiring.

- **Universal free meals, no exceptions and no lunch debt**, because a hungry child is a curriculum problem, and because the moment eating together is means-tested it stops being a shared ritual and becomes a mark of who's poor.

**The wager:** every ambitious vision of 22nd-century education assumes a student with a working body, a regulated nervous system, people they belong to, and daily practice at being with other humans — and all four are supplied, almost incidentally, by growing food, cooking it, and eating it together at a table. We have taken the one universal human ritual, industrialized it into a twenty-minute transaction, removed the adults, removed the cooking, removed the growing, and then spent enormous sums trying to buy back health, community, and attention through programs. Put the farm, the kitchen, and the table back at the center, and a school stops being a place children are processed and becomes a household — which is the institution that actually raises people.

**Rebuild the school on the model of the *research library*: make provenance, curation, and preservation the core disciplines, and graduate every American as a keeper of the record.**

The classroom and the library are two different theories of learning that have coexisted in the same building for a century, and we chose the wrong one to build around. The classroom assumes knowledge is scarce and must be dispensed on a schedule to a captive cohort. The library assumes knowledge is abundant and the hard problems are *finding, judging, organizing, and keeping* it — which is exactly the situation the 22nd century will present, at a scale no previous generation has faced: infinite synthetic text, collapsing provenance, link rot, decaying formats, and archives owned by firms that may not outlive the decade.

**The redesign:**

- **Make the library the center of the building and the librarian a core member of the faculty**, staffed at the density of English departments. Students work in a great reading room with expert help available on demand, rather than sitting in rows waiting to be addressed. The default posture becomes inquiry with a reference desk behind it — the posture of every serious adult intellectual life, and the one we currently reserve for graduate school.

- **Teach information science as a twelve-year examined discipline**: how a claim is sourced and traced to its origin; how documents are authenticated, dated, and forged; what a citation actually promises; how cataloging and classification encode judgments about what exists; how search ranking, retrieval, and model training corpora silently determine what a society can even find. In a century where any text, voice, or image can be manufactured, provenance is the master literacy, and it is a real craft with centuries of accumulated technique that we teach to almost no one.

- **Require every student to build and defend a collection.** Over years, each student curates a body of sources on a subject they care about — acquiring, annotating, cataloging, cross-checking, discarding — and is examined on their selection decisions, not their essay. Curation under scarcity of attention is the skill that replaces retrieval, and it can only be graded by asking someone why they kept this and threw out that.

- **Make preservation a graduation requirement and a civic service.** Students digitize, transcribe, and properly archive real endangered material — local newspapers, oral histories, court and land records, family papers, dying software, community photographs — deposited to standards in institutions that will outlast them. They learn firsthand that memory is not automatic, that formats die, that the "digital dark age" is a real engineering problem, and that someone must do the unglamorous work of carrying the record forward.

- **Adopt the library's ethics as the school's constitution**: free access without means-testing, patron privacy against surveillance, service to every age from toddlers to retirees, no compulsion, and the obligation to preserve what one generation finds inconvenient.

**The wager:** machines will supply answers in unlimited quantity; what they cannot supply is a society that knows where its knowledge came from, what it has already lost, and who is responsible for keeping the rest. Build schooling around the institution designed to do precisely that, and we graduate not consumers of information but custodians of it — which is the only defense a self-governing people has when the record itself becomes contestable.

**Make the *question* the unit of American education: build schools that train students to find, sharpen, and own good questions — and grade them on the questions they pose rather than the answers they produce.**

Our entire system runs backwards for the century ahead. An adult hands a child a question whose answer is already known, the child produces it, and the child is ranked on the match. That was defensible when answers were scarce and expensive. It is nearly worthless now: any answer to any well-posed question is instantly and freely available, and getting better every year. What remains scarce — and what no machine generates on its own, because a model has no stake, no confusion, and nothing it needs to know — is a human being who notices that something doesn't add up, cares enough to pursue it, and can formulate the version of the question that is actually answerable. We spend thirteen years systematically extinguishing exactly that capacity: four-year-olds ask hundreds of questions a day, and by high school most students ask essentially none, having correctly learned that questions signal ignorance and slow the class down.

**The redesign:**

- **Make question formulation a taught, sequenced, examined discipline from kindergarten.** It is a real craft with real technique: turning a vague irritation into a testable claim; distinguishing empirical, definitional, and normative questions; decomposing a big question into tractable sub-questions; recognizing when a question is unanswerable, badly framed, or presupposes something false; knowing what evidence would settle it and what it would cost to get. Teach it explicitly, drill it, and hold it to standards.

- **Invert the assessment.** Give students the answer and ask what question it answers. Grade the quality of a research question before any research is done. Run oral examinations in which the student is judged on the questions they put to a text, a dataset, a witness, or an expert — including questions put to an AI, since the sole determinant of whether these tools make someone smarter or stupider is the quality of the interrogation. A capstone becomes: here is a question nobody I could find has answered, here is why it matters, here is how I attacked it, here is where I got stuck.

- **Teach the map of what isn't known.** Every discipline should be introduced through its open problems and its live disagreements, not as a settled body of results — the unsolved questions in biology, the contested interpretations in history, the things economists genuinely don't agree on, the places where the textbook is a simplification and everyone in the field knows it. Students currently graduate believing knowledge is a finished object, which makes them both credulous and incurious. Show them the frontier from age eight and the subject becomes something they could join rather than something they must absorb.

- **Protect and reward the dumb question.** Structurally: a daily period where the only acceptable output is questions, no answers permitted; a public "question wall" of what the school is currently wondering about; recognition and honors for the best question of the term, not only the best essay. Teachers trained — and evaluated — on how they respond to being asked something they can't answer, since a single dismissive reply teaches a child to stop for years. Adults model it by working visibly on things they don't know.

- **Build the school's calendar around pursued questions rather than covered units.** A defined core of foundational knowledge remains non-negotiable, because you cannot ask a good question about a field you know nothing about — ignorance produces vague questions, expertise produces sharp ones. But beyond that core, an increasing share of each year is spent on questions the student generated, refined with a mentor, and pursued to a real result or an honest account of failure.

- **Teach the ethics and politics of questioning.** Which questions get funded and which don't; how framing a question determines the range of possible answers; how institutions and algorithms quietly foreclose inquiry; how to ask something dangerous or unwelcome well, and how to know when a question shouldn't be pursued at all. Also its cousin: how to interrogate a person — a doctor, a landlord, a salesperson, a candidate — which is the everyday form of the same skill and one Americans conspicuously lack.

**The wager:** the 22nd century will be drowning in answers, most of them fluent, most of them plausible, many of them synthetic and unattributable. The bottleneck moves entirely upstream, to the person who decides what is worth asking — which is also where curiosity, originality, scientific progress, and resistance to manipulation all actually originate. We have built the world's largest apparatus for teaching children to supply answers to questions they didn't ask, at precisely the moment that skill became free. Reverse the direction of the arrow — reward the question, teach it as a craft, organize the school around the pursuit of things nobody yet knows — and we produce people who can still learn something new when there is no one left to assign it.

**Make the study of catastrophe and complicity the spine of the humanities — and train every American in the concrete skill of refusing an order.**

The 22nd century's characteristic disaster will not be committed by monsters. It will be committed by competent, credentialed, well-meaning employees doing their assigned piece of work: the technician who runs the assay, the engineer who signs off on the deployment, the analyst who builds the targeting dataset, the clerk who processes the list. Every atrocity and every engineered catastrophe of the last hundred years ran on exactly that machinery — division of labor, deference to expertise, career pressure, ambiguity about who was responsible, and the near-total absence of anyone willing to be the one person who says *no, and I'm putting my name on it.* Meanwhile the century ahead will hand ordinary mid-level people access to synthetic biology, autonomous weapons, population-scale surveillance, and persuasion systems of unprecedented power. The decisive safety mechanism in that world is not a regulation. It is a human being inside the institution who recognizes what is happening early and stops.
