Released out of a declared apparatus element — a hoop rotation passed under the trailing leg (1.4), a toss‑and‑recatch‑and‑throw (1.8), a full‑body illusion turn on the outside edge (2.2), a blind over‑the‑shoulder release out of a spin (2.5) — the Peg's value is multiplied by the tariff. **No element may be repeated by the same skater in a period**, so a deep 5 taken with a 2.5 is worth 12.5 and can only be pulled off once.
5. **Land it or lose it.** If the thrower stumbles, dabs a hand, or leaves the racing line during the element, the multiplier is voided *and* the throw scores nothing, however sweetly the Halo lands. Ambition is always a wager.
6. **The Push (the relay rule).** Only a skater who entered the ice during that lap via a **Push** — a teammate physically hurling them out of the Pit gate into the pack, short‑track relay style — may throw at a **5‑Peg**. Deep points therefore cost a full changeover, fresh legs bought at the price of a body coming off the ice.
7. **Lane discipline, not contact.** You may take the inside line, close the door and force a rival wide; you may not impede, block with hands, or cross a skater's blades. Fouls cost a **penalty lap** in the outside lane, skated immediately, and any Halo you were carrying is forfeited to the opposition.
8. **Nothing is safe (the quoits rule).** A later Halo may knock an opponent's ring off its Peg — the displaced ring's points are struck from the board and the ring lies live on the ice. Teams have won matches in the final thirty seconds with one flat, cheap, unmultiplied throw aimed at somebody else's 5.
9. **Ammunition discipline.** Six Halos each per period. Spray them at the deep Pegs early and you finish the period with empty hands, skating laps while the other team rearranges the infield.

**Positions:** the *Pacer* (front‑of‑pack workhorse who controls tempo and shelters the throwers in her draft), the *Artist* (the ex‑gymnast — the only skater who can hold a 2.5 tariff through a corner, and the one everybody drafts off and nobody can catch on the exit), the *Lancer* (the arm, pushed in fresh for the 5‑Pegs), and the *Sweeper* — the coldest hands on the team, deliberately rested, kept back for the last two Halos, whose entire job is knocking rings off pegs.

**Why it works:** short track supplies a continuous, wildly legible race in which position, drafting and one clean pass on the apex decide everything, and it does it in a 111 m loop where the crowd sees the whole sport at once; rhythmic gymnastics grafts on an unfakeable technical skill — an apparatus that must never stop moving — and its tariff system solves the judged‑sport problem, because the ring either lands on the peg or it doesn't, and the judges only decide *how much* the landing was worth; and quoits is the masterstroke, because points sit out on the ice all period long, exposed, waiting to be knocked off by an opponent, so the fastest, most spectacular team on the oval can still lose to four people who simply threw last and aimed better. It needs one ice rink, nine pegs and a crate of hoops, involves no collision at all, and demands an athlete nobody currently trains: a short‑track skater with a gymnast's hands who can throw a spinning hoop seven metres, blind, out of an illusion turn, on the exit of a corner.

**SALVO** — a fusion of **padel** (an enclosed glass court where the walls are live and the ball is played with solid paddles), **Battleship** (a hidden fleet placed on a coordinate grid, hunted by called shots and pure deduction), and **CrossFit‑style fitness racing** (a work pit where ammunition must be physically earned before it can be spent).

**The Court:** A 20 m × 10 m glass box split by a 0.9 m net. The **back wall of each half is a 6 × 6 grid** of one‑metre padded panels, lettered A–F across and numbered 1–6 up, each wired to a light. Behind the glass, at the side of the court, sits the **Work Pit**: a rowing erg, a 40 kg sandbag and a pull‑up rig.

**Teams:** Four a side — two on court, one in the Pit, one at the plotting board. Substitution through a gate is free and constant. Two 20‑minute halves.

**The Fleet:** Before the match each team secretly places its fleet on **its own** grid and lodges the chart with the referee: one 4‑panel **Carrier**, two 3‑panel **Cruisers**, three 2‑panel **Frigates**. Fourteen of thirty‑six panels are loaded; the panels stay dark until they are struck, so nobody can see where a ship lies — you find it by hunting.

**Core Rules:**
1. **The rally is padel.** Serve underarm, one bounce, walls live, two touches per side, no catching. Rallies are fast, angled and long, and everyone on court is trying to manufacture one clean look at the far wall.
2. **Call your shot.** A strike at the opposing grid only counts if the **Plotter** has called the coordinate aloud — "**D‑four**" — before the paddle meets the ball. Hit the called panel: a **Salvo**. Hit any other panel, or the glass: a miss, and possession turns over.
3. **Hit or water.** A called panel that holds fleet lights **red — 2 points**, and your team keeps the serve, which is how a hot streak becomes a sinking. An empty panel lights **white** for the rest of the match: nothing scored, but the information is permanent and public, painted up on boards both teams and the crowd can read.
4. **Sinking.** Cover every panel of a ship and it is sunk — **5 points per panel** (a Carrier is worth 20) and the referee announces the class, which tells the enemy Plotter exactly how much of the grid is now impossible. **Sink the whole fleet and you win outright, whatever the score.**
5. **Ammunition is earned, not issued (the fitness element).** A shot may only be called if your team holds a **Shell**, and Shells come solely out of the Work Pit: 500 m on the erg, ten sandbag ground‑to‑shoulders, or fifteen strict pull‑ups, each buys one. Shells are announced as they land. The Engine in the Pit is a body **not** on the court, so a team building a magazine is playing one‑on‑two while it does so — and a team that squanders Shells on wild coordinates finds itself rallying beautifully with nothing to shoot.
6. **Screening is legal, blocking is not.** A defender may stand in front of a panel and take the ball on the paddle, but may not touch the wall or use their body as a shield. There is no contact between opponents at all.
7. **The 30‑second gun.** Hold possession longer and the Shell is forfeit. Nobody stalls a lead.
8. **The Broadside bonus:** land **three called Salvos in a single rally without the ball touching the floor** and the whole rally's value triples. It requires three Shells in the magazine, three coordinates worth calling, and legs that have not been in the Pit for four minutes.

**Positions:** the *Gunner* (millimetre paddle accuracy, the only player trusted with a Shell late), the *Wall* (a retriever who keeps rallies alive and screens the enemy's best coordinates), the *Engine* (the aerobic monster who converts sweat into ammunition and rotates in and out gasping), and the *Plotter* — a non‑striking captain at the board whose entire job is deduction: reading the white lights, eliminating geometry, and deciding whether the team can afford the shot at all.

**Why it works:** padel supplies a rally structure that a first‑time spectator understands in ten seconds, played in a glass box where nothing is ever out and the ball comes back off three surfaces; Battleship is the masterstroke, because the scoreboard is only half the story — the grid of red and white lights is a second, visible, purely intellectual contest in which a team can be outplayed physically all match and still win by guessing better; and the Work Pit makes every guess expensive, since a coordinate costs 500 metres of somebody's lungs, so hunches are rationed and the last five minutes are shot by exhausted athletes who cannot afford to be wrong. It needs one enclosed court, seventy‑two lit panels and a rack of gym kit, involves no contact whatsoever, and demands an athlete nobody currently trains: a paddle sniper with an ergometer engine, aimed by a captain who plays coordinates the way a codebreaker plays odds.

**TOTTER** — a fusion of **Ninja‑style obstacle course racing** (a timed rig of warped wall, salmon ladder, ring traverse and balance plank), **Jenga** (a shared, growing block tower where pulling from below to build the top is the only way up), and **blackjack** (press‑your‑luck: hit for more, or stand and bank before you bust).

**The Arena:** A 25 m × 15 m hall. On two raised daises stand the **Towers** — one per team, built of 30 cm foam‑cored blocks stacked three per layer, starting at 18 layers. Encircling them is the **Rig**, a 60 m obstacle loop that begins at each team's gate and finishes on a narrow plank delivering the athlete onto their dais. There is no other way to touch a Tower.

**Teams:** Six a side. Three 8‑minute rounds.

**Core Rules:**
1. **Blocks are earned, not issued.** A block may only be moved by an athlete who has just completed a clean lap of the Rig. Fall off an obstacle and you return to the gate — no block that lap.
2. **Jenga's law.** On the dais you pull a block from any layer *below the top three* and place it on top. Height is score: layers 1–20 are worth 1 point each, 21–30 worth 2, layer 31 upward worth 3. So the tower gets taller, thinner and more valuable at exactly the same rate.
3. **Hit or stand (the blackjack heart).** Each visit, the runner may take *one* block and walk off — or keep going, pulling a second, third, fourth, building height in a single trembling visit. Every extra pull weakens the structure. Height is only converted to points when a runner **stands**, leaving the dais cleanly; unbanked layers are worth nothing.
4. **Bust.** If the Tower falls, everything above the last banked line is gone, and must be rebuilt at one block per lap of the Rig by athletes whose forearms are already finished. A team can lead all match and end the round with a pile of blocks on the floor.
5. **The Raid.** A runner may instead run the Rig to the *opponent's* dais, where they may pull exactly one block and carry it home for their own Tower next lap. You may never add to an enemy Tower — the only thing you can do to an opponent is make them thinner and hope they hit again.
6. **No contact anywhere.** Passing on the Rig is legal; obstruction costs a full penalty lap. The tower is protected by geometry and nerve, never by a body.
7. **The Spire:** stand and bank a Tower of 40 layers or more, and its whole value doubles. It has to be pulled off by someone with shaking hands who has just run an obstacle course, in front of a silent hall.

**Positions:** three *Runners* (obstacle athletes, the engine of block supply), the *Hand* (the steadiest fingers on the team, deliberately rested and sent only for the dangerous low pulls), the *Raider* (fast, light, lives on the enemy dais), and the *Caller* — a non‑playing captain who watches the lean of both Towers and decides, every single lap, hit or stand.

**Why it works:** obstacle racing makes every point physically expensive and produces visible, unfakeable failure; Jenga guarantees that success *builds its own fragility*, so the leading team is always the most precarious one; and blackjack's hit‑or‑stand converts greed into an explicit, public decision, meaning the fittest team in the hall can lose to six people who simply knew when to stop. It needs one gym, one rig and a crate of blocks, involves no contact at all, and demands an athlete nobody currently trains: a ninja racer with a surgeon's hands and the discipline to walk away from a tower that is still standing.

**COURSER** — a fusion of **kitesurfing** (riders powered across open water by traction kites, working wind angles and apparent wind), **croquet** (a numbered sequence of hoops that must be run in order, plus the *roquet* — using contact with an opponent to send them where you want), and **backgammon** (the doubling cube: either side may raise the stakes of the current leg, and the other must accept or concede).

**The Venue:** A 1 km × 600 m bay laid out on the wind axis. Six inflatable **Hoops** — 6 m arches floating on pontoon feet — are anchored around it, numbered 1 to 6 and deliberately set so the sequence zig-zags: 1, 3 and 5 lie downwind (fast, easy reaches), while 2, 4 and 6 sit high upwind, reachable only by long tacking beats. In the centre floats the **Peg**, a tall orange buoy.

**Equipment:** Twin-tip boards and 8–12 m kites (riders choose their own size at the start of each leg and cannot change mid-leg — a wager on the day's breeze). Impact vests, helmets, and a wrist transponder that logs hoop passes.

**Teams & Format:** Four riders a side. A match is played to **12 points** across a series of **legs**, each leg lasting until one team completes the sequence or the 15-minute gun sounds.

**Core Rules:**

1. **Run the hoops in order.** Every rider must pass through Hoop 1, then 2, then 3, and so on — in the correct direction, marked by a coloured face on each arch. Passing a hoop out of sequence scores nothing and costs nothing; passing the *right* hoop advances that rider one place along the sequence, publicly displayed on the beach board.
2. **Peg out to win the leg.** A leg is won when **all four** riders of one team have cleared Hoop 6 and touched the Peg. So a team is paced by its weakest rider, and the strongest kiter's job is usually not to be first but to go back for the last.
3. **The Blanket (croquet's roquet, rewritten by the wind).** There is no contact — but a rider who establishes position directly upwind of an opponent, within two board lengths, and holds it for **three seconds**, **blankets** them: steals their wind, drops them off the plane, and sends them **back one hoop in the sequence**. The blanketed rider must re-run that hoop. Blanketing is the only defence in the sport, it costs you your own speed and line to execute, and a rider who mistimes it ends up parked in a lull themselves.
4. **Cover, don't chase.** A rider may not be blanketed twice by the same opponent inside 60 seconds — so a team cannot simply assign one athlete to bully one victim all afternoon.
5. **Right of way is absolute.** Starboard over port; the downwind rider has the water; the rider going upwind gives way to the one coming down; kite lines are never crossed. A breach is a **penalty gybe** — stop, turn a full circle downwind and restart from the last hoop cleared. On loaded lines, the rulebook is the only thing between a sport and an accident.
6. **The Cube (the backgammon heart).** Each leg begins worth **1 point**. At any moment, a team that believes it is winning may **double** — hoisting a yellow flag on its coach boat. The opponents must immediately either **concede the leg at its current value**, or **take**, doubling it to 2 and seizing sole ownership of the cube, meaning only they may double next (to 4, then 8). A leg can therefore be worth more than the rest of the match combined.
7. **Doubling is a claim about bodies, not boats.** Because the leg is won by the *last* rider home, the honest question behind every double is: *can our slowest athlete still beat their slowest athlete in this breeze, on this tide, with those arms?* Doubling into a team whose weakest rider is quietly recovering downwind has lost more matches than any wipeout.
8. **The Gybe-out:** if a team pegs out with all four riders while **never having been blanketed once** during the leg, the leg's cube value is **tripled**. It is the only reason a team will ever sail the long, cautious, defensive line.

**Positions:** the *Pathfinder* (best upwind rider, first through the hard even-numbered hoops, and the team's eyes on the gusts), two *Coursers* (the engines, who run the sequence and blanket), the *Anchor* (the slowest rider, whose progress is the team's true clock and who is escorted the whole way), and the *Caller* — a non-riding captain on the coach boat with binoculars and the cube, whose only job is to decide, twice a leg, how much of the match to bet on the next four minutes.

**Why it works:** kitesurfing supplies a playing field that is invisible, unequal and constantly rewriting itself, so tactics are about reading air rather than reading a defence, and it is fast, colourful and legible from any beach; croquet's ordered hoops turn the bay into a *sequence*, which means being fastest is worthless if you are on the wrong number, and its roquet — reimagined as stealing an opponent's wind — gives the sport a defensive weapon that requires zero contact and pure positional cunning; and backgammon's doubling cube is the masterstroke, because it means the better team can lose without ever being beaten on the water. It needs a bay, six inflatable arches and a flag, involves no physical contact whatsoever, and demands an athlete nobody currently trains: a kiter with a croquet player's sense of sequence, sailing for a captain who is playing the wind the way a backgammon player plays the cube.

**BONEYARD** — a turn‑based aerial sport fusing **flying trapeze** (pedestal boards, swinging bars, catchers hanging in lock, and a mid‑air hand‑off over a net), the **firefighter combat challenge** (a ladder‑and‑hose circuit in full kit that must be completed to earn every new piece), and **dominoes — "fives and threes"** (a shared chain of tiles laid end‑to‑end, scoring whenever the open ends total a multiple of five).

**The Rig:** A 20 m × 12 m hall. At each end an 8 m **pedestal board** faces a shared central **catch zone**, where two catchers hang in lock from swinging trapezes above a full‑width net. Directly beneath the net, angled toward the crowd, is the **Board**: a single shared magnetic wall on which the domino chain grows, its two open ends lit up on a scoreboard so every spectator can do the arithmetic. Off to one side runs the **Circuit**: a 6 m ladder climb, a 25 m charged‑hose drag and a 40 kg dummy carry.

**Equipment:** Chalk, safety belts, lycra — and **Tiles**: 28 foam dominoes with a wrist strap, pips 1 m tall so the crowd reads them from the back row.

**Teams:** Six a side — two Flyers, two Catchers, two Groundworkers. Each team starts holding **seven tiles**, concealed; the remainder sit in the **Boneyard**.

**Core Rules:**
1. **Turns alternate**, dominoes‑style, with a 90‑second shot clock. Two teams are never in the air at once — this is a duel of nerve, not a scramble.
2. **A tile must fly.** To play a tile it is strapped to a Flyer, who launches from the board, is **caught by the opposing team's own catcher** (the catchers are neutral, shared, and hang for both sides — trapeze's oldest rule: you catch whoever is thrown to you), passes the tile hand‑to‑hand in the air, and returns to their bar. Only then may a Groundworker place it. A dropped tile falls to the net and goes back to the Boneyard, and the turn is lost.
3. **Dominoes law.** The tile must match an open end of the chain. Play a tile that leaves the two open ends summing to a **multiple of five** and you score that sum — ends of 5 and 5 score **10**; doubles are counted crosswise on both pips. The chain is shared, so half of every placement is a calculation about what you are handing your opponent.
4. **The Difficulty Multiplier (the trapeze heart).** A tile delivered on a **plain pass** scores face value. Delivered out of a declared aerial element — half‑turn 1.3, forward somersault 1.7, double 2.2, layout full 2.5 — the whole scoring play is multiplied. **No element may be repeated by the same Flyer in a set**, so a champion needs a repertoire, and a miss on an ambitious trick costs the tile, the turn and the points.
5. **The Circuit (the fatigue tax).** You may only draw from the Boneyard by sending an athlete through ladder, hose and dummy in full kit — roughly 70 seconds of pure lactic misery — and that athlete may not fly on the next turn. A team that hoards tiles it cannot play must send its Flyers to do heavy labour, then ask them to somersault.
6. **Knocking.** If you cannot match either end and the Boneyard is empty, you knock and forfeit the turn. Two consecutive knocks by both sides ends the set: the team holding the fewer total pips scores the difference.
7. **Going out.** Play your last tile and the set ends immediately with a **25‑point bonus** — the reason teams will sometimes decline an obvious 15 to keep a matching tile in hand.
8. **No contact of any kind, ever**, between opponents. Interference with a Flyer, a catcher or a bar is disqualification. The only opponent in the air is gravity.

**Positions:** two *Flyers* (the tariff carriers — light, brave, and the only people who can turn a 5 into a 12.5), two *Catchers* (the calmest hands in the building, who catch friend and enemy alike), a *Groundworker/Engine* (the hose‑and‑ladder body who buys the team its tiles), and the *Caller* — a non‑flying captain who reads the chain, counts the unseen pips, and decides whether the next flight is a safe three or a double somersault for eighteen.

**Why it works:** flying trapeze gives the sport a scoring act that is spectacular, unfakeable and self‑limiting — you cannot bluff a catch — and its turn‑based rhythm makes every attempt a solo moment the whole hall watches in silence; the combat‑challenge circuit means ammunition is bought in lungs, so late in a set the tiles are flown by people who have just carried a dummy up a ladder; and dominoes is the masterstroke, because the chain is *shared* — the bravest, most beautiful flyers in the world can lose to a team that simply knew which pip to leave hanging.

**CLINCH** — a fusion of **boxing** (gloved, scored rounds fought in a ring), **rope climbing** (a 6 m gymnastic rope, legless ascent, the only way to reach the scoreboard), and **Connect Four** (a vertical grid in which tokens fall to the lowest free slot, and four in a row ends everything).

**The Arena:** A standard 6 m ring at the centre of the hall. Behind it, mounted on the back wall at a height of 6 m, hangs **the Grid** — seven columns, six rows, open-faced so the crowd reads it like a scoreboard. Three gymnastic ropes hang from the gantry in front of it: the **left rope** serves columns 1–3, the **centre rope** columns 3–5, the **right rope** columns 5–7. Column 3 and column 5 are the only shared ones, which is why every match is fought over them.

**Equipment:** 12 oz gloves and headguards with sensor pads on head, torso and flanks; chalk; and **tokens** — 2 kg discs carried up in a chest sling.

**Teams:** Five per side, alternating rounds. No boxer may fight twice in a row, and none may fight more than four rounds in a match.

**Core Rules:**

1. **The Round.** Each round is a **90-second bout** between one athlete from each side. Clean sensor-scored contacts decide it. The winner earns **one token**; a winner who takes the round without conceding a single scoring contact earns **two**.
2. **You must climb what you win.** A token is only placed by the boxer who earned it, and only by ascending a rope **legs-free, arms only**, and reaching across to drop the token into a column. This is the joke at the heart of the sport: three rounds of punching leaves an athlete with forearms of concrete, and the grid is six metres up. Fail the climb — slip, or need your legs — and the token is forfeit.
3. **Rope choice is decided in the ring, not on the board.** A winner may only use the rope in front of **their own corner**, and corners swap every three rounds. So a team that needs column 7 must win rounds from the right-hand corner, which the schedule gives them only twice a half. The Caller is forever choosing between the fighter who can win and the fighter who can win *from the correct side*.
4. **Gravity, not placement.** As in Connect Four, a token falls to the lowest free slot in its column. Nobody chooses a row; you can only choose to build, or to block.
5. **The Pop-Out (the knockdown rule).** A bout won by a **standing count** lets the winner, on their climb, instead pull a token from the **bottom** of any reachable column — the whole stack slides down one, rearranging both teams' patterns at once. Nothing on the Grid is ever safe, and a beautifully built diagonal can be dismantled by one clean left hook eleven rounds later.
6. **Winning.** Four of your tokens in a line — vertical, horizontal or diagonal — ends the match instantly, whatever the round score. If nobody connects in 14 rounds, the team with the most tokens on the Grid wins; if that too is level, the team that conceded fewer scoring contacts.
7. **Safety is absolute.** Headguards mandatory, standing counts end the bout immediately, and any boxer who takes two counts in a match is finished for the night — their tokens stand, but their team is a body short and must fight its remaining four on rotation. No climbing without a spotter mat and a chalked grip check.

**Positions:** two *Punchers* (the token earners — busy, points-scoring boxers with light hands and heavy lungs), a *Wrecker* (the heaviest hitter, kept on the bench and spent only when the team needs a Pop-Out to break an enemy line), a *Monkey* (a mediocre boxer with a phenomenal rope — sent out purely to survive 90 seconds, win narrowly, and get the token up), and the **Caller**, a non-fighting captain who holds the board in their head and decides which corner, which rope, and which column.

**Why it works:** boxing supplies a duel that needs no explanation and produces a clear, earned reward every 90 seconds; rope climbing taxes exactly the muscles boxing has just destroyed, so the currency of the sport must be carried upward by someone who has just spent everything, and the crowd watches an exhausted athlete hang one-armed six metres up trying to reach column five; and Connect Four is the masterstroke, because the strongest team in the ring can lose to four people who simply arranged their tokens better — and because a single knockdown can pull the floor out from under a pattern built all night. It needs one ring, three ropes and a wall-mounted grid, and it demands an athlete nobody currently trains: a boxer with a climber's grip, fighting for a captain who is playing a board game with other people's arms.

**RONDO** — a fusion of **unicycling** (every athlete plays while riding a 24‑inch unicycle; a foot on the floor is a penalty), **club‑passing juggling** (the "ball" is a set of clubs that must stay in continuous flight and are passed between riders in patterns), and **Uno** (each club carries a colour and a number, and may only be played onto the central stack if it matches one of them — with Wilds, Skips, Reverses and Draw‑Twos).

**The Arena:** A 30 m × 20 m sprung wooden floor with a marked **Ring Lane** around the outside (the penalty circuit). At the centre stands the **Chute** — a funnel mouth 2.5 m up on a padded post, with a lit display above it showing the **Face**: the colour and number of the last club played. Each team has a **Rack** on its own baseline, holding its undealt clubs.

**Equipment:** Unicycles, helmets, gloves, and 60 juggling clubs in four colours numbered 0–9, plus black **Wilds**, orange **Skips**, blue **Reverses** and red **Draw‑Twos**.

**Teams & Format:** Five riders a side. A match is best of five **Hands**; each Hand begins with seven clubs per team and ends when someone goes out.

**Core Rules:**
1. **Wheels only.** Dabbing a foot, dismounting, or stopping dead costs a **Lap** of the Ring Lane before you may rejoin. Everyone in Rondo is permanently, visibly fighting for balance while doing something else with their hands.
2. **Clubs live in the air.** A team's clubs must be in motion — juggled, passed, or in flight. Any club that hits the floor is **dead litter**: it lies there as an obstacle and a hazard, and can only be recovered by a rider who scoops it up without dismounting.
3. **Play the Face.** To score you throw a club into the Chute, and it only counts if it matches the **colour or the number** currently showing. A club that goes in unmatched is a **Misplay**: it comes back to your Rack, and the referee adds **two more clubs** to your Hand. Nothing punishes greed like being handed two extra objects to keep aloft.
4. **Two hands minimum.** A club may not be thrown at the Chute by the rider who last received it from the Rack — it must be **passed between at least two teammates in flight** first. Rondo cannot be played by one brilliant juggler; the pattern is the team.
5. **Action clubs.** A **Skip** sends the nominated opponent on a Lap. A **Reverse** flips the compulsory direction of travel for every rider on the floor — five people turning a unicycle at once, mid‑pattern, is the sport's most reliable source of chaos. A **Draw‑Two** adds two clubs to the opposing Rack. A **Wild** matches anything and lets you declare the new colour, which is how you strand an opponent holding six reds.
6. **Going out.** Empty your Rack and hold no clubs in flight and the Hand ends: your team scores the **pip total of every club the opposition still holds**, action clubs counting 20. So a team can dominate the floor all Hand and lose 60 points because it never dumped its Wilds.
7. **The Rondo bonus.** A club played into the Chute **straight out of a live three‑person passing pattern**, never having been held still, scores **double** — and if it also matched on both colour *and* number, it triples.
8. **No contact whatsoever.** Screening the Chute, riding a lane and stealing dead litter are legal; touching an opponent, their wheel, or a club in flight is a Lap and a Draw‑Two against you.

**Positions:** two *Feeders* (metronomic passers who keep the pattern alive and never throw at the Chute), a *Runner* (the fast rider who hunts dead litter and delivers from the Rack), the *Sniper* (the accurate arm, the only one trusted with a Wild), and the *Caller* — a non‑riding captain who tracks which colours the opposition is drowning in and decides whether to play the match‑winning number or sit on it.

**Why it works:** unicycling makes balance a tax paid on every single action, so nothing is ever done from a stable base; club juggling turns possession into something that is literally always in the air, where a drop is instant, visible and expensive; and Uno's matching rule is the twist that makes it a genuine game rather than a circus act — the finest jugglers in the world can lose to five riders who simply hoarded the right colour and made them draw.

# HIGH HAND

**A fusion of *pickleball* (paddle rallies over a low net, with a no‑volley "kitchen" zone), *speed climbing* (a standardised race up a 12 m wall against a rival, on a buzzer), and *mahjong* (drawing, discarding and claiming suited tiles to complete a declared hand).**

### The Arena
A hall containing a single 14 m × 7 m pickleball court with a 0.86 m net and a 2 m kitchen either side. Behind each baseline, six metres back, stands a **12 m speed wall** — two mirrored routes, IFSC‑standard holds, auto‑belays, buzzer at the top. Bolted beside each buzzer is the **Wall Rack**: a tray of face‑down tiles. Between the two walls, facing the crowd, hangs the **Table** — a lit board showing each team's exposed tiles and the growing **Discard River** running down the middle.

### Equipment
Paddles, a perforated plastic ball, chalk, harnesses, and 108 foam **tiles** in three suits (Bamboo, Circle, Stone), numbered 1–9, four of each, plus eight **Winds** (wild).

### Teams & Format
Four per side. No clock. The match ends the instant somebody declares a complete hand.

### Core Rules

1. **Rallies buy climbs.** Play is doubles pickleball — underhand serve, double bounce, no volleying from the kitchen. Rallies score nothing. The team that wins the rally earns **the right to race**.

2. **The Race.** Both teams send one climber (never the same athlete twice in a row). The rally winners start on the wall; the losers start **1.5 seconds later**, a handicap that keeps the race honest rather than ceremonial. First to the buzzer **draws two tiles** from the Wall Rack and carries them down; the loser draws **one**. Fall, and you draw nothing and climb back down the hard way.

3. **Mahjong's law.** A team wins by holding a **declared hand of nine tiles: three sets** — three‑in‑a‑row of one suit, or three identical — with at most one Wind standing in. Hands are held concealed on a team's rack at the baseline; a team may hold no more than eleven tiles, so every draw forces a **discard**, thrown face‑up into the River where everyone, including the crowd, can read it.

4. **The Claim (the game's coldest weapon).** Any team may claim the tile just discarded, out of turn, if it completes a set — but claiming **forfeits the next rally**, handing the opposition a free climb with no race. Taking a tile you need while giving away a free draw is the entire strategic argument of the sport, repeated forty times a match.

5. **Exposure.** A claimed set must be laid face‑up on the Table forever. Speed is bought with information: everyone can now see two‑thirds of what you're building, and will discard accordingly to starve you.

6. **Forearms are the currency.** Speed climbing destroys exactly the grip a paddle needs, so a team that keeps sending its best climber will find that athlete shanking dinks four rallies later. No substitutions; the bench is the same four people, and fatigue is public — every climb is chalked on a board.

7. **The Declaration.** A team may only declare a winning hand from the **top of the wall** — the declaring athlete must win a race, hit the buzzer, and call the hand aloud from twelve metres up. If the hand is invalid, the team loses two tiles of the referee's choosing and the opposition climbs unopposed twice.

8. **The High Hand bonus:** a hand completed **entirely from tiles drawn, never claimed** — no exposures, nothing shown all match — is worth the win *and* the record book. It requires a team that never once took the fast, cheap, visible route.

### Positions
Two *Rallyers* (touch players who live at the kitchen line and never climb), a *Sprinter* (the wall specialist, hopeless with a paddle, deliberately hidden at the back of the court), a *Closer* (competent at both, saved for the declaration climb with fresh arms), and the *Reader* — the non‑playing captain who tracks the River, counts which tiles are dead, and decides whether a claim is worth a free enemy draw.

### Why it works
Pickleball supplies a rally structure a first‑timer understands in ten seconds and a soft‑hands skill that punishes brute force; speed climbing turns each won rally into a five‑second, head‑to‑head, buzzer‑decided spectacle where the crowd can see the whole sport at once; and mahjong is the masterstroke — the fastest climbers and the best paddles in the hall can still lose to four people who simply read the River better and knew which tile to let go. It needs one court, two walls and a bag of tiles, involves no contact whatsoever, and demands an athlete nobody currently trains: a soft‑handed paddle player with a speed climber's forearms and a card counter's memory.

# CUCKOO

**A fusion of *rugby sevens* (a continuous handling game in which the ball may never be passed forward), *kubb* (underarm throws that topple wooden blocks, with felled blocks re-planted in enemy ground, and a King that must fall last), and *Werewolf/Mafia* (one secretly disloyal player per side, and formal councils in which a team may accuse its own).**

### The Field
60 m × 30 m of grass, split by a halfway line. On each baseline stand five padded 60 cm **Kubbs**. On the centre spot stands the **King** — a 1.2 m block, taller than everything else on the field and visible from every seat.

### Equipment
A dense, soft-cored ball the size of a melon — heavy enough to topple a block, safe enough to be caught one-handed at a sprint. No pads, no boots with studs longer than 8 mm. And, before the whistle, a sealed card dealt to every player.

### Teams & Format
Seven a side. Two 20-minute halves. There is no points target: the match ends when a King falls.

### Core Rules

1. **Rugby's law of direction.** The ball is carried and passed **backwards or sideways only**, and tackles are wrap-and-hold to ground, with a two-second release and no rucking. The only way the ball ever travels forward is a **Cast** — a throw at a Kubb.
2. **Kubb's law of the throw.** Every Cast must be **underarm, from a standing position, with the ball swinging along the vertical plane** — no sidearm, no spin, no run-up. Arm strength is worthless; a 60 kg scrum-half out-casts a shot-putter every time. A missed Cast leaves the ball live in enemy ground, which is how most matches are lost.
3. **Felling and replanting.** Topple a baseline Kubb and you score **3 points** — and the opposition immediately **casts that Kubb back into your half**, where it is stood up where it lands, becoming a **Field Kubb**. Field Kubbs must be cleared before you may Cast at their baseline again. So every success plants an obstacle in your own territory, and a team that scores fast finds its own half forested with blocks.
4. **The King falls last.** Fell all five enemy baseline Kubbs plus every Field Kubb they own, and you may Cast at the King. Topple it and you win outright, whatever the score. **Topple the King early — even accidentally, even off a deflection — and you lose instantly.** The King stands in the middle of the pitch all match, ten metres from every ruck, and it cannot be defended, only avoided.
5. **The Cuckoo.** Exactly one card per team reads CUCKOO. That player is bound by every rule and may never foul, feign injury or hand the ball over — their only weapons are *choices*: the pass not thrown, the tackle arriving a beat late, the Cast that drifts a hand's width wide. The Cuckoo's personal result is recorded as a win only if **their own team loses**, and they play a full season of matches on both sides of that card.
6. **The Council.** Twice per half either captain may stop play for a 60-second **Council**. The team huddles in public view, microphones live for the broadcast, and may name one of its own. **Correct:** the Cuckoo is banished for the remainder of the match — the team plays a body short but is awarded an **uncontested Cast** from the 15 m line, unopposed and unrushed. **Wrong:** the accused sits out five minutes, the team plays six against seven, and the real Cuckoo helps defend the shortfall with visible enthusiasm.
7. **Nothing is proof.** Referees rule only on rugby and kubb; suspicion is never a foul and a bad game is never an offence. The card is revealed at the final whistle regardless of the result.

### Positions
Two *Carriers* (rugby engines who never Cast), two *Hands* (the underarm specialists, deliberately spared contact so their throw stays soft), a *Forester* (whose entire job is clearing the Field Kubbs choking their own half), a *Sweeper* (the last body between the ball and the King), and the *Reader* — a captain who plays, calls Councils, and spends the whole match watching their own teammates.

### Why It Works
Rugby supplies a fast, legible, continuous contest in which the ball can only go forward by an act of deliberate precision; kubb is the masterstroke of geometry, because scoring literally builds your own obstacle course and the winning shot is also the shot that can lose you the match on a ricochet; and the hidden role turns a sport into a drama, because for eighty minutes the crowd, the commentators and the other six players are all trying to answer the same question — *was that a mistake?* It needs a field, eleven blocks and a ball, and it demands an athlete nobody currently trains: a tackler with a lawn-bowler's touch and a poker player's face.

**RIFFLE** — a river sport fusing **competitive fly casting** (accuracy casting to distant targets with a fly rod), **log rolling / birling** (barefoot duels spinning a floating log until one competitor falls in), and **Othello/Reversi** (two‑sided discs that flip whenever they are flanked, so nothing on the board is ever permanently yours).

**The Venue:** A slow log‑pond or river pool, 60 m × 40 m. Anchored in the middle floats **the Grid** — an 8 × 8 array of 64 buoyant discs, 40 cm across, spaced 1.5 m apart, each white on one face and red on the other, weighted so a landing fly rolls them over. The four centre discs start in the standard Othello opening, two red and two white. Ringing the Grid at 12–25 m is **the Boom**: sixteen free‑floating cedar logs, the *only* legal casting platforms. A cast made from the bank, from a boat, or while wading scores nothing.

**Equipment:** 9 ft rods with a yarn fly — no hook, no point; calk boots; buoyancy vests. Nothing else.

**Teams & Format:** Five a side, two 20‑minute halves, free rotation through a beach gate.

**Core Rules:**

1. **You must own a log to cast.** Only one athlete may stand on a log at a time. A rival may board the far end at any moment, and the two then **birl** — feet only, no hands, no contact of any kind, spinning and checking the log until one goes in the water. The dunked player swims to the beach and re‑enters after 30 seconds. Every metre of casting range in this sport is bought with somebody's ankles.
2. **Othello's law is the scoring law.** A fly that lands and holds on a disc for two seconds flips it — **but only if the flip flanks**: the claimed disc must sit at the end of an unbroken line of enemy discs (row, column or diagonal) closed by a disc already yours. Every disc between them turns. A cast to any square that does not flank is a **dry cast**: nothing flips, and the log's casting turn passes to whoever is standing on it next.
3. **Distance is difficulty.** The near squares are a 12 m lob; the far side of the Grid is a 25 m double‑haul across moving air, thrown from a platform that another human being is deliberately rolling under your feet.
4. **Corners are forever.** The four corner discs can never be flanked, so once claimed they are permanent — and each is worth **3 points** at the count instead of 1. The whole match is a slow war over four squares that a team can only reach from the two most exposed, most contested logs on the Boom.
5. **Nothing is banked.** A team can hold fifty discs at minute thirty and lose. The board is counted only at the final whistle, and one long diagonal in the last ten seconds has decided finals.
6. **The Riffle bonus:** flip **six or more discs with a single cast** and the whole line counts **double**. Setting one up takes three earlier casts that appeared to give the opposition free ground.
7. **Fouls:** touching an opponent, touching their log with a hand, hooking a rod over a rival, or casting across another athlete's line — 60 seconds on the beach, and the offender's team forfeits its next flip.
8. **The Sweep:** flip every disc on the Grid to one colour and the match ends instantly, whatever the clock says.

**Positions:** two *Rollers* (birling specialists — heavy calves, no casting arm to speak of, whose job is simply to own the corner logs), two *Casters* (the arms, deliberately kept off the contested logs so their loops stay tight), and the *Reader* — a non‑playing captain on the bank with an elevated view of the board, who calls every square and decides when to hand the opposition a cheap edge in order to open a diagonal four minutes later.

**Why it works:** fly casting gives the sport a scoring act of pure, unfakeable finesse — a 25 m loop laid down on a dinner‑plate target, done with a heart rate of 170 and wet feet; log rolling turns *position itself* into a contest, non‑contact but brutally physical, so the best caster in the world is useless if he cannot stay dry; and Othello is the masterstroke, because possession is inherently unstable — every disc you take advertises the line that will take it back, and a team that scores greedily all match hands its opponent one final, match‑winning cast. It needs a pond, sixteen logs, sixty‑four discs and five rods, involves no contact whatsoever, and demands an athlete nobody currently trains: a caster with a river driver's balance and a board player's patience.

# BELLWATER

**A fusion of *deep-water soloing / psicobloc* (ropeless climbing above the sea), *stand-up paddleboard racing* (all transit between walls is paddled), and *high diving* (the way you come down is judged, and it decides whether the climb counted at all).**

### The Venue
A sheltered sea cove with 400 m of limestone cliff dropping straight into deep water. Three walls — the **Near Wall**, the **Spur** and the far **Cathedral** — are separated by 200–600 m of open water. Bolted flush to the rock are **Bells**, brass and loud: at 6 m (**1 point**), 10 m (**2**), 14 m (**3**) and, on the Cathedral only, 20 m (**5**). A floating **Pontoon** by the beach is the start, the finish and the only place an athlete may rest.

### Equipment
Boards, paddles, climbing shoes worn on a neck cord, chalk, and nothing else. **No ropes, no harnesses, no buoyancy aids on the wall.** Two safety craft and two divers are in the water at all times; a green/red **Depth Flag** on each wall is controlled by the tide marshal.

### Teams & Format
Four athletes a side. One **75-minute tide window**, from mid-flood to slack high water. Both teams are on the water at once; each Bell may be scored **only once per team**, so the cove is steadily used up and the far, deeper, higher walls become the only ground left.

### Core Rules

1. **Everything is paddled.** No swimming between walls, no towing, no boat assistance. A team moves as four boards; the whole squad must be within one board-length of the wall before anyone climbs.
2. **The wall is entered off the board.** A climber must start from a floating, unheld SUP — standing up on moving water and committing to the rock is the signature move of the sport, and the reason the first three metres end more attempts than the last ten.
3. **Ring it and you own the height.** Sounding a Bell banks nothing yet: it simply sets the height you must now come down from.
4. **The Descent decides (the diving element).** You must leave the wall by diving or entering the water **at or above the Bell you rang**, and two judges score the entry 0–10 for line, control and splash. **Score 5.0 or better and the Bell's points are banked; score below 5.0 — a flail, a back-slap, a scrabbling let-go — and the Bell is void and cannot be re-attempted by your team.** Climbing brilliantly and falling badly is worth precisely nothing, which is the whole sport in one sentence.
5. **Safety is written into the scoring.** Bells at 14 m and above must be entered **feet-first, arms crossed**, and judged on that standard; a head-first entry from those heights is an instant void and a five-minute stand-down. No Bell may be attempted under a **red Depth Flag**, and never with another athlete on the wall beneath you.
6. **Nobody climbs twice in a row.** Forearms recover in ten minutes and lungs don't recover at all, so the paddling legs and the climbing arms have to be spread across four bodies. The team that sends its best climber three times will watch that athlete fail a 6 m Bell in the last ten minutes.
7. **The Traverse.** Ring two Bells on the same route without downclimbing or touching the water, then take a single dive from the higher — the two values are added **plus 3**. Doing it means hanging on chalkless, over the sea, for an extra ninety seconds, and then still owing the judges a clean entry.
8. **The tide is the referee no one argues with.** The 20 m Cathedral Bells go green only in the last twenty minutes of the flood. A team that spends its energy early on cheap Near Wall points arrives at the Cathedral with a full green flag and no arms left; a team that saves itself arrives fresh but may find the window shut by weather.
9. **No contact whatsoever.** Blocking a start position with your board, crowding a landing zone, or paddling wash across a launching climber costs a **beach hold**: two minutes sitting on the Pontoon while the tide runs on.

### Positions
The *Engine* (the fastest paddler, who ferries the squad between walls and never climbs high), the *Spider* (the pure climber — reads the rock, takes the hard traverses, and is honestly mediocre in the air), the *Swan* (an ex-diver with modest climbing but immaculate entries, saved exclusively for the 20 m Bells where a bad descent would void five points), and the *Reader* — the captain, who watches the flag, the swell period and the opposition's arms, and decides which wall the team is paddling to next.

### Why It Works
Deep-water soloing supplies a scoring act that cannot be faked or protected — there is no rope, so every metre gained is honest, and the crowd on the clifftop reads the height instantly. Paddleboarding turns the cove into a course rather than a venue, so the best climbers must also be the ones who arrive first and arrive rested. And high diving is the masterstroke: in every other climbing sport the way down is an afterthought, but here it is the audit — a team can out-climb everyone in the bay all afternoon and bank nothing, because points are only paid to athletes who can finish twenty metres of exhaustion with a clean, quiet entry into the sea. It needs one cove, sixteen brass bells and a tide table, involves no contact at all, and demands an athlete nobody currently trains: a soloist with a paddler's shoulders who has to fall beautifully for a living.

# TRIAD

**A fusion of *soccer* (feet‑only ground play into a low net), *team handball* (a hands‑only game with limited steps and a shot clock), and *rugby* (a carried oval ball, backward passes only, and the game's only legal tackling) — all three played simultaneously, on the same pitch, by the same eighteen people.**

### The Pitch
An 80 m × 50 m grass field. At each end stands a triple goal built as one structure: a **low net** (2 m × 5 m) at ground level, a **raised ring** 3 m up and 1.2 m across mounted above it, and, behind the whole thing, a 6 m **try zone** with a painted grounding line. One keeper per end defends the net and the ring; nobody defends the try zone but bodies.

### The Three Balls
All three are live at once, from first whistle to last.
- **The Ground** (a size‑5 football): played with feet, knees, chest and head only. Into the low net = **2 points**.
- **The Air** (a handball): hands only, three steps, three seconds, and a 20‑second shot clock. Through the raised ring = **3 points**.
- **The Oval** (a rugby ball): carried, passed backwards or sideways only. Grounded in the try zone = **5 points**.

### Teams & Codes
Nine a side, plus a keeper. Every outfield player wears a **cuff** in one of three colours, and may only touch the ball matching their cuff — touching any other ball is a turnover of that ball and a 30‑second suspension. **A player changes code by running back and slapping their own goal frame**, swapping cuffs at the post rack. So a captain is not choosing a formation but an *allocation*: how many bodies do we put into the foot game, the hand game and the carry game, right now, and who do we pull out of one to swamp another?

### Core Rules
1. **Contact belongs to the Oval alone.** Rugby‑code players may tackle and be tackled — wrap and hold, below the shoulders, ball released within two seconds. Tackling, blocking or obstructing a player wearing a different cuff is a **penalty**: the offending team loses that code entirely for 60 seconds (all its cuff‑holders in that colour must stand behind their own line), and the pitch is suddenly wide open for two of the three games.
2. **The Ground and the Air never stop.** No throw‑ins and no restarts for the light balls: if either goes out, the nearest player of the correct cuff restarts it on the spot within five seconds. Only the Oval has set pieces.
3. **Traffic is legal.** A rugby maul stumbling through a soccer passing lane is nobody's foul — the three games are entitled to occupy the same square metre, and reading the field means reading two contests you are not allowed to touch.
4. **The keeper is one person with three problems.** They may use hands anywhere in their 8 m arc, but every save leaves two other targets naked.
5. **The Treble.** Score with all three balls inside a single rolling three‑minute window and the team banks a **10‑point bonus** — the reason a side leading comfortably on tries will still burn bodies chasing a cheap two.
6. **Fatigue and the cuff.** Only two code changes per player per half, publicly chalked on a board. Late on, both captains know exactly which of your athletes are locked into which game, and attack the one you can no longer reinforce.
7. **Format:** four 15‑minute quarters, running clock, free substitution — but a substitute inherits the cuff of the player they replace.

### Positions
Two *Anchors* (rugby engines who never change code and simply grind the Oval forward), two *Shooters* (handball specialists working the ring and the shot clock), three *Footers* (the soccer game's technicians), two *Floaters* (multi‑code athletes deliberately held on their change quota, spent like substitutions to overload whichever game is turning), and the *Keeper* — plus a non‑playing **Marshal** on the touchline whose only job is watching all three balls at once and calling the reallocations.

### Why It Works
Soccer supplies the game everybody already reads and a scoring act that requires patience and geometry; handball adds a fast, shot‑clocked contest played entirely above the waist, so the pitch has a second, higher layer with its own tempo; and rugby supplies the sport's only violence and its biggest prize, so the try is expensive in exactly the bodies the other two games need. The masterstroke is that the three games share one field and one squad but never touch each other legally — meaning Triad is not really three sports at once, it is a continuous resource problem played at a sprint, where a team can be the best footballing, throwing and tackling side on the park and still lose because it had four people in the wrong colour cuff when the last two minutes arrived.

# TEMPO

**A fusion of *breaking / b-boying* (crews battling in judged rounds on a circular floor, to a live DJ), *taekwondo board-breaking* (rigid boards that must be struck with clean, powerful technique to score), and *Simon / memory sequencing* (a called sequence that must be reproduced exactly, growing one step longer every round).**

### The Arena
A 12 m sprung circle — **the Floor** — with a DJ booth on the rim and two crew corners opposite each other. Ringed around the Floor are **eight numbered Tiles**, each a padded post holding a replaceable break-board at a set height: four **Low** boards at ankle/shin (**1 point**), two **Mid** at waist (**2**), one **High** at head height (**3**), and one **Crown** at 2.4 m, reachable only from a jump or an inverted push (**5**). Each Tile lights when it is called.

### Teams & Format
Five per crew. A match is a series of **Passes**, alternating crews, until one side fails. The DJ starts at 90 bpm and raises the tempo by 6 bpm every second Pass — the music, not a referee, is the thing that eventually beats everybody.

### Core Rules

1. **The Call.** Before each Pass, the Tiles flash a sequence — Round 1 is two Tiles, Round 2 is three, and so on. The whole crew sees it once, for two seconds. There is no repeat, no screen, no coach shouting numbers: the sequence lives in the dancers' heads.
2. **One phrase, no stopping.** A Pass is a single continuous danced passage. Every board in the sequence must be broken **in order**, and each break must land **on a downbeat** within a 100 ms window, judged by the timing rig. Walking between Tiles, pausing, or breaking off the beat voids the Pass.
3. **Any body, any order of bodies.** All five dancers are on the Floor; any of them may take any board, so a sequence of six is shared out mid-phrase, on the fly, with no talking. The crew that spends its practice hours on silent hand-offs beats the crew with the better individual.
4. **The Difficulty Multiplier (the breaking heart).** Three judges tariff the *technique that delivers the break*: a standing kick or punch = **1.0**; a break out of a power move — windmill into a hook kick, flare into a back kick — = **1.6**; a break taken from a **freeze or inverted position**, hands on the floor and feet above the hips, = **2.2**. The board's value is multiplied by the tariff, so the Crown taken out of an air-flare is worth 11.
5. **No repeats.** A dancer may not score with the same tariffed element twice in a match. Crews need a repertoire, not a signature trick — and by round nine the best mover on the Floor is out of ideas and reduced to 1.0 kicks.
6. **Fail and it's a Break-Out.** Wrong board, wrong order, a board that doesn't fully break, or a miss off the beat ends the Pass instantly: the opposing crew banks the whole Pass value and the sequence resets one step shorter. Boards are re-set by marshals between Passes; there is no time-out.
7. **The Steal.** A crew may, once per match, decline to dance and instead **call the sequence back** — reciting the numbers aloud to the judges. Correct, and the opponents must dance a sequence **one longer** than the one they set. Wrong, and the opponents score double. It is the moment every match hinges on: do you trust your memory more than your legs?
8. **No contact whatsoever** between crews, and none with an opponent's Tile. Screening, mirroring and cyphering around the other crew are legal and encouraged; touching anyone costs the Pass.

### Positions
The *Head* (a low-tariff, ice-cold specialist who never misses a sequence and farms safe Low boards), two *Powers* (windmills and flares — the tariff engines), the *Crown* (a tall, explosive dancer kept fresh all match for the one 5-point board nobody else can reach), and the *Ear* — the crew's memory, who takes no boards at all in long sequences and simply positions herself so that every teammate can read the next Tile off her body language.

### Why It Works
Breaking supplies a scoring act that is beautiful, exhausting and impossible to fake, plus a battle format the crowd already understands — you go, then I go. Taekwondo's boards solve the oldest problem in judged sport: the board either breaks or it doesn't, so the judges never decide *who* won, only *how much* a win was worth. And the memory sequence is the masterstroke, because it makes the sport get harder in exactly the dimension that fatigue attacks first — by the twelfth Pass the athletes are asked to hold nine numbers in their heads at 140 bpm, upside down, having just thrown themselves at a board 2.4 m in the air. It needs one sprung circle, eight posts, a crate of boards and a DJ, involves no contact at all, and demands an athlete nobody currently trains: a b-boy with a black belt's foot and a card counter's short-term memory.

# DRAUGHT

**A fusion of *ice climbing / dry‑tooling* (axes and crampons up a vertical ice tower), *snowshoe racing* (every action must first be earned on foot across a snowfield), and *draughts/checkers* (diagonal‑only movement, capture by jumping, and crowning on the far row).**

### The Venue
A 12 m artificial ice tower standing in the middle of a snowfield. Its face is screwed with an **8 × 8 grid** of anchor points, painted alternately dark and pale like a draughts board — only the dark squares take a marker. Each team's home row is the bottom row of its own half of the tower. Encircling the tower is the **Loop**, a 300 m packed snowshoe circuit with a **Cache** at the far end holding that team's twelve **Markers** (coloured aluminium discs that clip into an anchor).

### Equipment
Ice tools, crampons, helmets, auto‑belays on every column, snowshoes. Nothing else. Twelve markers per team for the whole match, no resupply.

### Teams & Format
Five a side. Forty minutes, running clock, free rotation. The match ends at the horn — or instantly if one team removes every enemy marker from the tower.

### Core Rules
1. **Nothing is free.** A climber may only touch the ice holding a **Move Token**, and a token is bought by a teammate completing one full snowshoe lap of the Loop. Ten laps a match is a hard afternoon; the scoreboard is paid for in quadriceps.
2. **Diagonal only, one square, upward.** A marker is moved by climbing to it, unclipping it, and re‑clipping it one dark square diagonally higher. There is no vertical movement, no sideways movement, and no shortcuts — the geometry of the board dictates the route your tools have to follow.
3. **The Jump (capture).** If an enemy marker sits on the diagonal square above you and the square beyond it is empty, you may traverse over it: the enemy marker is stripped and handed to the marshals (**3 points**) and yours is clipped beyond. **A chain of two or more captures made without your feet touching the snow scores double** — it is also the fastest way to fall.
4. **Crowning.** A marker clipped into the opponents' top row is **Crowned** (**5 points**) and thereafter may move diagonally *downward* as well, hunting back through the board. Crowned markers are also the ones everybody now climbs to kill.
5. **Falling is expensive.** A climber who comes off the ice with a marker in hand returns it to the square it left, forfeits the token, and owes an immediate penalty lap of the Loop. Ice is honest: it fails the tired long before it fails the weak.
6. **Ammunition discipline.** Twelve markers, no resupply. A team that pushes everything forward early ends the match defending a thin, jumpable line with nothing in the Cache.
7. **No contact whatsoever.** One climber per column, and no ascent beneath another athlete. Screening a route on the snow is legal; touching an opponent, their tools or their marker is a two‑minute stand‑down.
8. **The Draught bonus:** crown a marker in a possession in which no member of your team touched the snow between the first anchor and the top row — the crown counts **triple**.

### Positions
Two *Engines* (pure snowshoe athletes who never climb and simply manufacture tokens), a *Tool* (the technical climber who owns the mid‑board and the awkward captures), a *Crowner* (light, explosive, deliberately rested for the top three rows), and the *Reader* — a non‑climbing captain on a tower platform with a live board display, who decides which square is worth somebody's legs.

### Why It Works
Ice climbing supplies a scoring act that cannot be faked and gets visibly harder as forearms die; snowshoe racing makes every single move on the board cost 300 metres of somebody's lungs, so a team is rationing effort rather than spending it; and draughts is the masterstroke, because the diagonal‑only law means the strongest climbers in the field can be forced to attack exactly where they are weakest — and one greedy advance in minute six leaves a jump chain waiting in minute thirty‑eight. It needs an ice tower, a snow loop and twenty‑four discs, involves no contact at all, and demands an athlete nobody currently trains: a dry‑tooler with a distance runner's engine, playing a board game with axes.

# HARROW

**A fusion of *fell running* (steep, pathless hill racing), *Highland heavy events* (stones and weights thrown for distance from a standing mark), and *mancala* (seeds sown one-per-pit around a circuit, with captures triggered by where your last seed lands).**

### The Venue
A rough hillside with a **Ring** of fourteen stone-lined **Pits** set out in a 1.2 km loop that climbs 180 m: seven "low" pits on the easy lower arc, seven "high" pits strung along a steep scree band. Each pit has a lit counter post so spectators (and both teams) always see how many stones it holds. At the base sits each team's **Byre** — its store and its scorebox.

### Equipment
Sixty **stones** (4 kg, hand-sized, colour-blind neutral — stones belong to the pit they sit in, not to a team), fell shoes, and nothing else. No poles, no packs, no resupply beyond what is in the pits.

### Teams & Format
Five a side, 60 minutes, running clock, free rotation through the Byre. The final count decides it.

### Core Rules

1. **Sowing.** A runner lifts **every stone from a single pit** and runs anticlockwise round the Ring, dropping exactly one stone into each pit in turn. You may not skip a pit, split the load, or hand stones to a teammate mid-sow. Lift eight stones and you have just committed yourself to 32 kg and eight pits of climbing.
2. **The capture.** If your **last** stone lands in a pit that thereby holds exactly **four**, you carry all four to your Byre — **1 point each**. If it lands in a pit holding anything else, the sow simply ends and the ground stays as you left it, arranged for whoever runs next.
3. **The relay sow.** If your last stone lands in a pit that already held stones and does *not* make four, you may **choose** to pick that whole pit up and keep sowing. Chains of three or four continuations have decided finals, and have also emptied a runner completely at the top of the scree.
4. **The scree band (the Highland element).** The steep arc is closed ground: you may not run through it carrying stones. The four pits inside it can only be fed by **putting a stone from the marked trig**, standing, one-handed, shot-put style, at 12–18 m. A put that misses the pit lies where it falls and is dead ground for the rest of the match. Because those pits fill slowly and by hand, they are where fours accumulate — and where the biggest captures live.
5. **No contact, no interference.** Runners may take any line, shadow an opponent, and read their load; touching a person, a pit or a stone in flight costs a full penalty lap of the Ring, unloaded.
6. **You cannot hoard.** A pit may never hold more than eight stones; a sow that would make nine forces the sower to keep going with the whole pit in hand.
7. **The Harrow.** Empty **four consecutive pits** in a single unbroken sow and the captured stones count double.

### Positions
Two *Engines* (pure fell runners who carry the big loads uphill), a *Thrower* (the heavy athlete kept off the long sows so their arm is fresh for the trig), a *Counter* (light and quick, sent for one- and two-stone tactical sows that set up a four), and the *Reader* — a non-running captain with a view of every pit counter, who decides which pit is worth someone's legs and which four to leave sitting as bait.

### Why It Works
Fell running makes every stone honestly expensive — the scoreboard is paid for in vertical metres — and produces a race with no lanes, no referees and no hiding. The Highland put grafts on a moment of pure standing power in a sport otherwise made of endurance, and it does it exactly where the athletes are most wrecked. And mancala is the masterstroke: because the stones belong to the hill rather than to a team, every sow you make is also a gift, arranging pits that your opponent will run twenty seconds later. The fittest side on the hill can lose to five people who simply counted better.

# BIAS

**A fusion of *race walking* (a legally locked gait that must be maintained under judges' eyes, on pain of penalty), *lawn bowls* (weighted, biased bowls rolled at a jack, where the nearest bowl owns the head and nothing is ever safe), and *bingo* (a randomised card of numbers that must be completed in lines).**

### The Venue
A 1.5 km parkland loop with **sixteen numbered Rinks** — short strips of mown grass, each 25 m long with a white jack at its far end — set at intervals around the circuit, the low numbers on the flat opening kilometre and the high numbers strung along a hill nobody wants to climb twice. At the start/finish stands each team's **Bank**, holding its bowls, and a lit **Card Board** facing the crowd.

### The Card
Before the whistle, each team draws a **4 × 4 Card**: the numbers 1–16 shuffled into a grid, publicly displayed. Every team must claim the same sixteen rinks — but the *arrangement* is different for each side, so the four rinks that give you a line are not the four that give them one, and the hill numbers may land in the middle of your best row.

### Equipment
Biased woods (1.5 kg, standard bowls bias), soft flat shoes, and nothing else. Twenty-four bowls per team for the whole match, **no resupply**.

### Teams & Format
Five a side. Sixty minutes, running clock. The match ends at the horn — or instantly on a full house.

### Core Rules
1. **You may never run.** Race-walking law applies everywhere on the course: visible contact with the ground at all times, front leg straight from first contact to the vertical. Three **Walking Judges** patrol with red paddles; three cautions puts an athlete in the Box for two minutes. Everyone is doing this carrying two bowls, uphill, at 12 km/h — the ugliest, hardest, funniest athletic problem in sport.
2. **A bowl travels once.** Bowls are carried out from the Bank and delivered at a rink; they then lie where they stop for the rest of the match, becoming shot, guard, or nuisance. Bowls are never collected. Twenty-four woods, sixty minutes, sixteen rinks: a team that floods the easy flat numbers early will spend the last quarter defending a Card it can no longer change.
3. **Ownership is only ever borrowed.** At each rink the team with the **nearest bowl** flies the flag and that number lights on their Card Board. Any opponent who walks out and bowls closer takes it instantly. Nothing is banked; the Card is counted at the horn.
4. **The Drive.** A bowl fired flat and hard may smash the head apart, and a bowl that drives the **jack out of the rink** burns it: every wood there is dead ground, the number goes dark for *both* teams, and the rink is out of the match. Burning a rink your opponent needs for a line — and that you don't — is the sport's coldest and most despised tactic.
5. **Scoring.** Each rink owned at the horn = **1 point**. Each completed line on your Card — row, column or diagonal — = **8 points**. **Full house wins outright**, whatever the score.
6. **The Toucher bonus.** Claim a rink with your team's **first** bowl to that rink and it counts double if it ends up inside a completed line — the reward for the athlete who walked up the hill fresh enough to have steady hands at the top.
7. **No contact, no obstruction.** You may walk beside an opponent, read their load and sit on their shoulder all day; touching a person, a bowl or a jack costs a full penalty lap of the loop, unloaded, under the judges' eyes.

### Positions
Two *Engines* (the walkers — pure race-walk athletes who ferry woods and never bowl anything important), the *Hand* (the delicate draw bowler, deliberately spared the hill so her weight is right), the *Driver* (the heavy arm kept in reserve to burn a rink at the death), and the *Caller* — a non-walking captain at the board who watches both Cards and decides which number is worth somebody's legs and which one to leave sitting as bait.

### Why It Works
Race walking supplies an unfakeable, judged, gloriously punishing form of transit that keeps the whole sport at a legible human speed and makes every metre honest — you cannot sprint out of trouble. Lawn bowls gives a scoring act of pure touch performed with a heaving chest, and a head that any opponent can steal back with one better wood. And bingo is the masterstroke: because the two Cards are arranged differently, the same sixteen rinks are worth wildly different things to each side, so a team can own more ground than its opponent all afternoon and lose to five people who simply walked to the right four numbers. It needs a park, sixteen jacks and a crate of woods, involves no contact at all, and demands an athlete nobody currently trains: a race walker with a bowler's weight and a captain who is playing a bingo card with other people's quadriceps.

# DEADLIGHT

**A fusion of *caving / SRT rope work* (abseils, prusik ascents and squeezes through a vertical labyrinth), *orienteering* (finding numbered controls from a survey, with no marked route), and *cave rescue hauling* (a loaded stretcher lifted out of the system by a rope crew).**

### The Venue
A purpose-built **Stack**: a 30 m-deep artificial cave — four levels of concrete tubes, crawls, rift passages, boulder chokes and four vertical **Pitches** (8 m, 11 m, 6 m, 5 m) — sealed against daylight and wired with low-light cameras so the crowd upstairs watches on screens what the athletes can barely see. Scattered through it are **twenty Controls**, worth 5 points on the entrance series, 15 on the middle levels and 40 in the flooded-floor **Deep Chambers**. At the very bottom lies **the Casualty**: a 70 kg dummy in a rescue stretcher.

### Equipment
Helmet, harness, cowstails, descender, ascenders, and each team's own ropes, hangers and slings. One dibber. **And a metered battery pack: 9,000 lumen-hours for the entire match, shared by the whole team.** A sealed emergency lamp is carried by every athlete — breaking the seal is legal, safe and ends your scoring instantly.

### Teams & Format
Five per side, both teams underground at once, **90 minutes**. All five must exit together; 30 seconds late costs 20 points.

### Core Rules
1. **You get a survey, not a route.** A hand-drawn cave survey at the surface, studied for three minutes, then taken away. No maps below, no phones, no marshal's help. Controls are punched by touch.
2. **Rig your own rope.** Every Pitch must be rigged by the team itself — deviations, rebelays, knots past the rub points. A **rigging fault** called by the pitch marshal (rope on rock, no backup anchor, unprotected edge) freezes the team where it stands for two minutes while it re-rigs.
3. **Light is ammunition.** Every lamp burning drains the shared meter, and the meter is displayed to the crowd. Run it empty and you are escorted out in the dark by an official, scoring nothing further. So teams travel on one lamp, crawl blind through known passage, and argue constantly about whether the next chamber is worth the watts.
4. **The Deadlight bonus.** Punch a Control with every lamp in the team switched off — found by memory, feel and counting bends — and it scores **double**. It is the single most valuable and most terrifying act in the sport.
5. **The Haul (the rescue element).** The Casualty scores **100 points**, and can only be raised by a counterbalance haul that needs four bodies on the rope and one below the stretcher. It takes twenty minutes, burns light continuously, and means abandoning the Deep Chambers to do it — the whole match is a wager on whether you go for the load or the ledger.
6. **No contact, no interference.** Teams meet in the passages constantly; you may not touch an opponent, their rope or their rigging, and a rigged rope may be used by anyone (a team that rigs beautifully is also building a road for the enemy). Fouls cost five minutes sitting at a pitch head with lamps off.
7. **Safety is absolute and unarguable.** Marshals at every pitch head, a sump-free system, no free-climbing, and any athlete may call an abort at any moment — a called abort costs the team nothing at all.

### Positions
The *Rigger* (the technician who owns every pitch head and never navigates), the *Navigator* (holds the whole survey in their head and decides what the team can afford to look for), two *Engines* (the haul crew, and the bodies that drag the stretcher through the crawls), and the *Ghost* — the lightest, calmest athlete, sent alone into known passage with no lamp at all to farm doubled Controls while everyone else works in the light.

### Why It Works
Caving supplies a playing field with a real third dimension and a difficulty no organiser has to invent — rock, rope and gravity referee themselves. Orienteering makes the sport a thinking game where the strongest team routinely loses to the one that remembered the survey properly. And rescue hauling gives it a single, enormous, cooperative prize that cannot be won by a star. The masterstroke is the light meter: in every other sport the athletes can see, so darkness becomes a spendable resource, courage becomes literally purchasable, and the crowd watches five people decide, again and again, whether the next forty points are worth turning the lamps off for.

# SCRATCH

**A fusion of *Olympic weightlifting* (three-attempt clean & jerks judged by three white lights), *sprint hurdles* (every kilo of iron must be carried over a barrier lane before it can be lifted), and *Yahtzee* (five dice, two re-rolls, and thirteen categories that can each be filled exactly once — or scratched to zero forever).**

### The Hall
A 60 m hall. At one end, a competition **Platform** with a bar and judges' lights. At the other, the **Rack**, holding every plate in the building. Between them runs the **Lane**: 40 m of track with six 84 cm hurdles. Plates reach the bar one way only — carried, by hand, over the hurdles. Facing the crowd hangs the **Card**: thirteen Yahtzee categories per team, filling up in public.

### Equipment
A 20 kg bar, plates in 5 kg increments, chalk, and five oversized dice thrown into a padded pit at the Platform's edge. Nothing else.

### Teams & Format
Four per side, alternating turns. The match ends when both Cards are full — thirteen turns each, no clock, no substitutions.

### Core Rules

1. **The Roll.** A turn begins with five dice. As in Yahtzee, you may keep any dice and re-roll the rest **twice** — but **each re-roll costs a Lap**: one athlete must run the Lane, over six hurdles, out and back, before the dice may be picked up again. Luck is purchasable, and it is purchased in lactate by the same people who are about to load and lift.

2. **Dice become iron.** The final roll sets the bar: **bar weight = 20 kg + (sum of the five dice × 5 kg)**. A roll of 6-6-6-4-3 is a 145 kg clean & jerk; a roll of ones is an insult you still have to do something with.

3. **Declare a category.** Before loading, the Caller names one unfilled category — Fours, Full House, Large Straight, Chance, Yahtzee. The roll must legally satisfy it. Categories score their standard Yahtzee value **multiplied by the bar weight in tens of kilos**, so the same Full House is worth three times as much on a heavy roll as a light one.

4. **The Lane.** Plates are carried **one at a time**, one athlete at a time, over the hurdles. A knocked hurdle is a 10-second hold at the barrier. A 145 kg bar is eleven trips. The heaviest, most valuable rolls are the ones that arrive at the Platform with the loaders already emptied — which is the entire joke of the sport.

5. **Make it or scratch it.** The lifter has **one attempt**, judged as a standard clean & jerk: two white lights or better. Make it and the category is banked. Miss it and the category is **scratched at zero, permanently** — the most brutal rule in Yahtzee, now performed in front of a hall by someone whose forearms are gone.

6. **No lifter twice in a row**, and no athlete may lift more than four times in a match. Every appearance is chalked on a board both captains can read, so late in the match your opponent knows exactly which body you have left and how heavy it can go.

7. **The Bonus.** Fill all six number categories and the team banks **35 × the average bar weight of those six lifts** — which means a team that dumped its ones and twos on cheap rolls early has quietly capped its own ceiling.

8. **The Scratch bonus:** a **Yahtzee** — five of a kind, a 170 kg bar off five sixes — scores double and lets the team **erase one scratched category** and replay it later. It has happened eleven times, and every one of them is on film.

### Positions
