- **Guardrails.** DBS checks, references, infection-control and safeguarding training; ward staff always present and in charge; no photographs, no notes taken, no social media, ever; no money, gifts, inheritances or wills — an instant, permanent, non-negotiable ban; no proselytising; and an explicit line that volunteers supplement palliative staffing rather than excusing its absence.
- **Nothing scored.** No streaks, badges or counters. The only feedback is a line from the nurse in charge: *"She died at 5:20. Her hand was held the whole way. Thank you for staying."*

**Why it works:** Most kindness apps ask for money, tools, skills or a spare room, and people quietly decide they have none. Vigil asks only for presence — the one thing everybody owns — and points it at the loneliest, most universal event there is, at a moment when it can never be done later. It costs a volunteer one quiet evening, and it changes something irreversible: whether a person spent their last hours with a human being in the room, and whether the family who couldn't be there spends the rest of their lives knowing somebody was.

**Bench — an app whose act of kindness is making yourself *interruptible*: sitting somewhere public with a sign that says a stranger may come and talk to you, right now.**

**The core idea:** Almost every loneliness service works by appointment — refer, assess, match, wait three weeks. But loneliness isn't felt in three weeks; it's felt at 2pm on a Wednesday in an empty flat, and the people who feel it worst are exactly the ones who will never phone a helpline, join a group or admit they need "befriending." Meanwhile thousands of people are already sitting in parks, cafés and libraries with an hour to kill, perfectly willing to talk to whoever sits down. Bench simply tells each side where the other is.

**How it works:**
- **Go "open" for an hour.** A volunteer taps *open* and picks a spot — a park bench, a library table, a café corner, the seats outside the leisure centre — and props up a small card, or wears a clip badge, saying **"Happy to chat."** A map shows nearby open benches for the next hour only; nothing is ever booked, and nothing is ever more than a walk away.
- **No referral, no story, no name required.** Anyone can just turn up and sit down. No account is needed to *receive* company — a poster with a QR code and a phone number outside GP surgeries, pharmacies, job centres and supermarkets covers the people with no smartphone at all. The commonest users are men in their sixties, new mothers and recently bereaved people, none of whom will use anything with "lonely" written on it.
- **Ordinary conversation, deliberately.** Volunteers are trained in one skill and one only: talk about the weather, the football, the dog, the price of everything — and let the person raise anything else if they want to. No counselling, no advice, no "how are you *really*," no note-taking, no follow-up questions about someone's circumstances. It is a chat, not an intervention, which is precisely why people come.
- **The dog lane.** The most-used feature: dog walkers mark their route and time, because walking beside someone with an animal to talk about removes the eye contact and the awkwardness that stop people speaking at all. Nearby users join the walk; nobody has to sit face to face with a stranger.
- **Venues sign up.** Cafés, pubs, libraries, garden centres, mosques and community centres register a permanent **talk table** — a marked table where sitting down means you're open to company, with no obligation to buy anything and a member of staff briefed to seat someone there rather than leave them hovering by the door.
- **The first ten seconds.** A one-screen guide for both sides on the bit everyone dreads: how to sit down, how to leave after four minutes without insulting anyone, and the explicit rule that either person can say *"I'll leave you to it"* at any moment, and that this means nothing at all.
- **Onward, when it's wanted.** Volunteers carry nothing but a short list of what's actually nearby — a warm hub, a lunch club, a men's shed, a bereavement group, a walking football session — and offer it once, gently, never twice.
- **Everyone sits both sides.** Users who came to talk are quietly invited, months later, to go open themselves for an hour. Most of the network's volunteers arrived as the person on the other end of the bench.
- **Guardrails.** Public places in daylight only, never a private home, never a lift in a car; ID verification, references and safeguarding training for volunteers; women-only and faith-appropriate signalling available; no money, gifts, sales, romance, politics or proselytising — instant permanent removal; no contact details exchanged and no meeting arranged off-app; benches are never placed where they'd expose someone's identity, and no user's location or attendance is ever logged or shared; clear escalation training for anyone in genuine crisis, routed straight to statutory and crisis services rather than handled on a bench.
- **Nothing scored.** No streaks, badges, check-ins or leaderboards — the whole point is that nobody is being counted. The only thing a volunteer ever hears is an occasional line weeks later: *"That's the first conversation I'd had since the funeral."*

**Why it works:** Every other model of kindness asks you to schedule it, and every other model of loneliness support asks the lonely person to identify themselves as lonely — two requirements that between them exclude almost everybody who needs it. Bench asks for nothing but an hour you were going to spend sitting down anyway, in a place you were already going, and it converts that hour into the one thing there is enormous demand and zero supply of: a person nearby, right now, who is not in a hurry and would be pleased if you sat next to them.

**Truce — an app where the act of kindness is stepping into a neighbourhood argument as the calm, unrelated third person.**

**The core idea:** Neighbour disputes are one of the great avoidable miseries of ordinary life. A hedge, a bin, a barking dog, a parking space, a bass line at midnight, a boundary six inches out — and within a year two households who have never actually spoken are exchanging solicitors' letters, filing police logs, and being made ill by the sight of each other's front door. Almost none of it starts with malice; it starts with nobody feeling able to knock. Truce turns "I'm reasonable, I live three doors down, and I have no dog in this fight" into the thing that stops it.

**How it works:**
- **The grumble, converted.** You type the complaint the way you actually feel it — *"they've had scaffolding across my drive for five weeks"* — and the app does one job before anything else: it turns it into a concrete, specific, blame-free request the other household can say yes to, and asks you the question nobody asks themselves first: *what else might explain this?* (night shifts, deafness, dementia, a newborn, a tenant who doesn't know the bin day). A large share of cases close here, because the first draft was a declaration of war and the second was a note about scaffolding.
- **The neutral knock.** If it needs a person, a trained volunteer from a *different* street — never a friend of either side, never someone with a stake — makes the first approach. Trained with community-mediation charities in one skill: shuttling between two people who won't be in the same room, until each has heard the other's version without being interrupted by it.
- **Nobody has to meet.** Most agreements in the app are reached by relay, never face to face. Where both sides eventually want to sit down, it happens in a neutral venue with two volunteers present, and either person can walk out with no explanation owed.
- **The written deal, and the six-week check.** Whatever's agreed — the drum practice stops at eight, the hedge is cut in October, the van moves after 6pm, the cat is fed by one house only — is written down plainly, signed by both, and revisited once. Verbal peace collapses; a paragraph on a fridge doesn't, and the revisit stops slow drift becoming round two.
- **The problem fund.** The most-used, least glamorous feature. A pooled fund and merchant partners cover the cheap physical fix that ends things outright: felt pads under a bed, an acoustic panel, a fence board, a hedge trim for an 84-year-old who genuinely cannot do it, a dog-behaviour session, a doorbell that doesn't chime at 5am. A £40 solution routinely prevents a £6,000 dispute and eighteen months of hatred.
- **Before it happens.** A "good first move" lane for the moments that set the tone for a decade: a note through the door before your building work starts, a heads-up before a party, an introduction when someone moves in, a "we're not ignoring you, we're on nights" card. New arrivals, refugee families and young renters get the most benefit, because they're the ones assumed to be the problem.
- **The interpreter lane.** Where the two households share no language, or one party is deaf, autistic, or dealing with cognitive decline, a volunteer with the relevant language or communication training joins — because an enormous number of "hostile neighbours" are simply two people who have never once successfully exchanged a sentence.
- **Hard limits, stated on the first screen.** Anything involving violence, harassment, stalking, hate crime, coercive control, child protection or a landlord's legal repair duty is hard-blocked and routed immediately to police, statutory services or housing enforcement. Volunteers mediate disputes between equals; they never mediate abuse, and they never become a reason a council or landlord fails to act.
- **Guardrails.** Volunteers are ID-checked, referenced and trained, and are auto-excluded from any case on their own street or involving anyone they know; no legal or boundary advice — surveying, title and tenancy questions go to partner services; no recordings, no photographs of anyone's property, no evidence-gathering for court; nothing is ever shared with police, insurers or the council without both parties' consent; contact stays in-app; and there is no public feed, no map of "problem addresses," and no way whatsoever to shame a neighbour, because a naming function would be the single most popular feature and would poison the entire thing.
- **Nothing scored.** No streaks, badges or peacemaker leaderboards. The only feedback a volunteer ever gets is a line a month later: *"He came round with the hedge trimmer on Saturday. Twelve years and we'd never spoken."*

**Why it works:** Every other kindness app moves something from someone who has it to someone who doesn't — money, food, hours, a spare room. Truce creates value out of nothing at all, because the resource being wasted is goodwill that already exists on both sides of a fence and has no route across it. It costs a volunteer two conversations and a note through a door, and it prevents the specific, grinding harm that no charity, food parcel or befriending scheme touches: being frightened of your own home, over something that was never really about the hedge.

**Basics — an app whose act of kindness is keeping one toilet cubicle near you stocked, so nobody has to ask for the things people are most ashamed to need.**

**The core idea:** Food banks handle hunger. Nobody handles hygiene poverty — the girl missing two days of school a month because there are no period products at home, the man who can't go to an interview because he has no razor or deodorant, the mother rationing nappies, the older person hiding incontinence pads under the shopping. These items are cheap, unglamorous, rarely donated, and impossible to ask for out loud. Basics removes the asking entirely.

**How it works:**
- **Adopt a cubicle.** You claim one specific location within walking distance — a school toilet, a library, a GP waiting room, a leisure centre, a mosque, a café, your own workplace loo — and keep a plain, unbranded basket in it filled with period products, nappies, wipes, soap, toothpaste, deodorant, razors, laundry pods. One tap to adopt; the whole obligation is a top-up when the app tells you.
- **Anyone can say it's empty.** A small QR sticker inside the cubicle lets any user report the basket low, anonymously, in three seconds. The alert goes to the adopter and two backups, so a shelf is never bare for a week because someone went on holiday.
- **Buy one more, not a whole donation.** Scan a barcode as you shop and the app tells you whether your local baskets actually need that item — because they drown in shampoo and never see size 5 nappies, incontinence pads, XL underwear, or products for afro hair. Drop it at a partner shop's collection point on the way out; volunteer runners batch the deliveries.
- **Take what you need, no eligibility.** No form, no means test, no staff conversation, no voucher. The screen for restocking and the screen for finding a basket look identical, so nobody in the room can tell which one you're using.
- **Doorstep lane.** Referrals through schools, health visitors, refuges, hostels and social prescribers deliver a specific list to a door in a plain bag — the app names items, never circumstances, and the volunteer never learns why.
- **Guardrails.** Sealed, in-date, unopened goods only; infant formula handled solely by health professionals under the WHO code, never by volunteers; venues sign a dignity agreement (no logos, no signage announcing charity, no staff gatekeeping); a pooled fund covers the items nobody donates; no money, tips or brand sampling in either direction, so it can never become marketing; recipients are never counted, named or photographed.
- **Nothing scored.** No streaks, badges or leaderboards. Just an occasional line from the school: *"Attendance in Year 9 is up. Nobody has mentioned the basket once."*

**Why it works:** Most kindness apps ask for hours, courage or a spare room. Basics asks for £3 added to a shop you were already doing and a two-minute detour to a building you already use — and aims it at a form of deprivation that is invisible precisely because shame keeps people silent about it. By putting the supplies where the need is felt, in a cubicle where no one can see you take them, it turns a trivial act of restocking into whether a child goes to school, a man gets to the interview, or a person leaves the house at all.

**Reset — an app where the act of kindness is two hours of cleaning, washing up and laundry for someone whose home has got beyond them.**

**The core idea:** Depression, a new baby, chemotherapy, a broken hip, bereavement, ADHD, long covid or a chaotic week can leave a home in a state the person is far too ashamed to let anyone see — and the mess then becomes its own trap, keeping visitors out, keeping health visitors and district nurses at arm's length, and making everything worse. Nobody asks for help with it, because admitting it feels like admitting you've failed at being a functioning adult. Reset makes it a routine, unremarkable, two-hour job done by a stranger who will never mention it again.

**How it works:**
- **One room, two hours, no comment.** Requests are deliberately small and finishable: *"Kitchen only." "The washing-up and the bin." "Six loads of laundry."* Volunteers arrive in pairs, work to the requester's instructions, and follow the one absolute rule of the app — no remarks, no raised eyebrows, no advice, no "how did it get like this," and nothing said to anyone afterwards, ever.
- **Nothing is thrown away without permission.** Every item stays unless the person says so, out loud, item by item. This is non-negotiable, because a well-meaning stranger binning something precious is the fastest way to do real psychological harm — especially to people with hoarding disorder, who are routed only to volunteers trained with specialist charities and OTs, and who lead their own sessions at their own pace.
- **The laundry run.** The most-used lane and the easiest to give: you take a bag home, run it through your own machine while you get on with your evening, and return it clean and dry the next day. For families in temporary accommodation with no machine, a mother with a newborn, or someone incontinent and too embarrassed to use a launderette, it is the single most requested thing in the app.
- **Clean with me.** For people whose problem isn't inability but paralysis — depression, executive dysfunction, autistic burnout — a volunteer simply stays on a video call, doing their own washing-up, while the person does theirs. No instruction, no encouragement, no checking progress. Body-doubling costs the volunteer nothing and routinely unsticks a kitchen that's been untouched for a month.
- **The one-off big ones.** A rubbish run to the tip for someone with no car, a fridge cleared after a hospital stay, a flat made habitable before a discharge or a social-services visit, a deep clean before a landlord's inspection, or the hardest and most requested of all: clearing the home of someone who has just died, with the family choosing what is kept, boxed or donated.
- **Kit and products supplied.** A pooled fund and merchant partners provide cleaning products, bin bags, gloves and a vacuum where there isn't one — so a volunteer is never quietly paying, and a household isn't handed a sparkling kitchen and no way to keep it that way.
- **Guardrails.** Referrals through occupational therapists, health visitors, hospital discharge teams, mental health services, refuges and social prescribers as well as self-referral; DBS checks, references and training on hoarding, dementia, bereavement and infection control; never a lone visit; hard limits on hazards (needles, biohazards, faeces, pests and blood are routed to funded specialist services, never to volunteers); no photographs of anyone's home, ever, and no before-and-after shots for any purpose; no money, tips, or cleaning businesses touting for work — an instant permanent ban; no reporting to landlords, councils or social services except through agreed safeguarding routes; and a plain statement that this supplements funded home care rather than excusing its absence.
- **Nothing scored.** No streaks, badges or feeds. The only feedback a volunteer ever gets is a line a fortnight later: *"She let her sister come round on Sunday. First time in two years."*

**Why it works:** Most kindness apps ask for money, skills, courage or a spare room, and most people conclude they have none of them. Everybody can wash up, and almost everybody has a washing machine running half-empty. Reset points that at a form of suffering nobody names and no charity handles, because it's hidden behind a front door and buried under shame — and it produces something rare: a problem that is completely, visibly gone by teatime, and a home someone is no longer frightened to let another human being into.

**Wing — an app for the moment you find an injured animal by the roadside and have absolutely no idea what to do.**

**The core idea:** Almost everyone has stopped for a bird stunned by a window, a hedgehog out in daylight, a swan on a dual carriageway, a fox tangled in football netting — and then driven on, because they didn't know who to ring, whether it was even in trouble, or how they'd get it forty miles to a rescue centre. Wildlife hospitals aren't short of goodwill; they're short of *drivers*, foster space and people who know when to leave an animal alone. Wing turns a bewildered passer-by into the useful link in that chain.

**How it works:**
- **Triage before rescue.** You photograph what you've found and answer three questions. Most of the time the answer is *don't touch it* — the fledgling on the lawn has parents twenty feet away, the fawn is not abandoned, the seal pup is meant to be there — and the app says so plainly, with a picture, because well-meaning kidnapping is the single most common harm the public does to wildlife. Only genuine casualties go any further.
- **The relay.** The real bottleneck is transport: rescue centres are rural, understaffed and often two hours away. Wing pings drivers already heading that direction and splits the journey into legs — a cardboard box handed over in a supermarket car park three times until a barn owl reaches a hospital. Ten minutes of someone's commute each, and a bird that would otherwise have died in a hedge.
- **Hold the fort.** People with a spare shed, quiet garage or utility room register as overnight holders — dark, warm, silent, no food, no water forced in — so an animal found at 9pm isn't left on a doorstep until the centre opens.
- **Tiers, honestly enforced.** *Anyone* (a stunned songbird into a box, a hedgehog off a road, keeping a dog away from a casualty). *Trained* (swans, gulls, gannets, deer, anything with a beak or a hoof that can genuinely injure you). *Licensed only* — bats are hard-blocked to rabies-vaccinated handlers, seals, birds of prey and cetaceans to accredited medics. The app will refuse to let an enthusiastic amateur near a heron.
- **Foster the winter.** Hedgehogs too small to hibernate, orphaned birds needing four-hourly feeds — parcelled out to trained volunteer carers with equipment, food and vet costs from a pooled fund, and a firm rule that everything goes back out where it came from. Nothing becomes a pet, and nothing is released somewhere prettier.
- **The prevention lane, which matters more.** Seasonal, specific, five-minute jobs: toad patrols on wet March nights carrying frogs across a lane; checking a bonfire before lighting it; strimming a verge after walking it once; cutting discarded fishing line and can rings from a riverbank; taking down garden netting before it takes down a hedgehog; checking a rescue's "found bird of prey near this A-road" hotspot map.
- **Data as a by-product.** Anonymised casualty and roadkill locations build a live map handed to highways teams, councils and ecologists, so one strip of road that kills forty badgers a year eventually gets a tunnel. Individual kindness becomes evidence.
- **Guardrails.** Live-linked to registered rescues, the RSPCA/SSPCA and vets rather than freelancing; biosecurity and avian-flu protocols with hard stops on handling sick waterfowl; zoonosis and bite training; no entering water, roads, cliffs or private land; no photographs of distressed animals for social media; no money, tips or "rescue" fundraising by individuals; and firm legal guidance on protected species, what may lawfully be kept, and the duty to release at the site of capture.
- **Nothing scored.** No streaks, badges or rescue counters. The only thing you ever get back is a line a fortnight later: *"The tawny you drove the second leg for was released on Tuesday night, half a mile from the lay-by you found her in."*

**Why it works:** This is kindness with the motivation already fully installed and nowhere to go — people stop, they care, and then the practical wall (who do I call, can I lift it, how does it get there?) turns concern into guilt and a dead animal in a verge. Wing costs a cardboard box and a detour on a drive you were making anyway, tells you honestly when the kindest act is to walk away, and quietly builds the volunteer infrastructure that wildlife hospitals run on. It's also the easiest door into helping there is: people who won't join a befriending scheme or give money will absolutely drive a hedgehog to Aylesbury.

Give me a diet that a human should eat t.answer:
Eat like a bear in autumn: a several‑week phase of deliberate hyperphagia (a big calorie surplus, on the order of 1.5–2× normal intake) designed to lay down a large, high‑quality fat store, since fat is the fuel that a hibernator burns for months.

**Composition of the diet**
- **Fat ~50–60% of calories, emphasizing unsaturated fats**, especially moderate amounts of the polyunsaturated omega‑6 linoleic acid (nuts, seeds, sunflower/safflower oil, avocado, olive oil, fatty fish). Polyunsaturated fat stored in adipose tissue stays fluid and enzymatically usable at the low body temperatures of torpor, whereas heavily saturated fat "stiffens" and is harder to mobilize when cold — but don't go extreme, since too much PUFA raises oxidative/peroxidation risk, so include some monounsaturated fat and a little omega‑3 (fish, walnuts) for membrane and cardiac stability.
- **Carbohydrate ~25–35% of calories** from energy‑dense, easily converted sources (fruit, honey, grains, starchy vegetables) to drive insulin and efficient conversion into body fat and to top off liver/muscle glycogen for the entry into and arousal from torpor.
- **Protein ~15–20% of calories**, high‑quality (eggs, fish, dairy, meat, legumes) to build extra lean mass, since muscle will be catabolized slowly during the fast; adequate protein plus resistance training beforehand gives a bigger buffer against wasting.
- **Micronutrients loaded up in advance:** calcium and vitamin D (bone loss during immobility), iron, magnesium, potassium, B vitamins, and antioxidants (vitamin E, C, selenium, polyphenols) to protect the stored polyunsaturated fat from going rancid and to blunt oxidative stress on re‑warming.
- **Plenty of water and salt beforehand**, and a taper of fiber/food in the last day or two so the gut is largely emptied at the start of dormancy.

In short: a nut‑, seed‑, oily‑fish‑, fruit‑ and starch‑heavy "autumn fattening" diet — a large calorie surplus that is fat‑dominant (rich in unsaturated, mainly linoleic‑acid fats), with ample carbohydrate, sufficient protein and a strong micronutrient/antioxidant base.

The best plan is a 4–6 week "marine‑mammal gorge," i.e. a ketogenic‑style, blubber‑building feeding plan that finishes with a fasting/gut‑clearing taper:

**Weeks 1–4 (gorge phase, ~5,000–6,000 kcal/day, low‑carb/high‑fat):** Eat like a seal. Base every meal on oily cold‑water fish (salmon, mackerel, herring, sardines, cod liver), fatty ruminant meat and tallow/suet, egg yolks, full‑fat dairy (butter, ghee, cream, aged cheese), macadamia nuts and olive/avocado oil. This builds a huge subcutaneous fat depot while keeping you keto‑adapted, so your enzymes are already tuned to burn fat and make ketones before torpor begins — no metabolic "switchover" crisis on day one. Eat two or three enormous meals a day rather than grazing, so the body practices long inter‑meal fasts.

**Micronutrient loading throughout:** liver and other organ meats weekly (vitamin A, B12, copper, retinol), oysters/shellfish (zinc, selenium), bone broth and small bony fish plus vitamin D3+K2 (skeleton protection during months of immobility), leafy greens and sea vegetables (magnesium, potassium, iodine), and berries/dark chocolate/extra‑virgin olive oil for polyphenol antioxidants that keep the stored fat from oxidizing.

**Final 5–7 days (taper):** Drop fibre and residue almost to zero — clear broths, bone broth, cooked white fish, eggs, oil, plus a strong electrolyte load (sodium, potassium, magnesium) and generous water. Add creatine and a final protein‑rich meal to top up muscle stores. This empties the gut so nothing ferments or rots during dormancy, leaves you fully hydrated and mineral‑replete, and delivers you into hibernation already in nutritional ketosis, running smoothly on the fat you spent a month packing on.

Eat like a migratory bird fattening before a long flight — a high‑carbohydrate, plant‑forward "de novo lipogenesis" fattening plan rather than a fat‑gorging one.

**How it works:** For 6–8 weeks, run a steady moderate surplus (about +1,000–1,500 kcal/day, ~4,000–4,500 kcal total) built mainly on sugary fruit, dates, figs, honey, rice, potatoes, oats and other starches, with olive oil, avocado and macadamias as the main added fat. The large carbohydrate load keeps insulin high, which is exactly the anabolic signal that drives fat storage and simultaneously fills liver and muscle glycogen to the brim (a classic carb‑load in the final week), giving you the quick‑burn fuel needed for the shivering, high‑cost entry into and arousals from torpor, when fat alone is too slow to mobilise. Because most of the fat you deposit is made by your own liver, it comes out as palmitate and especially oleate — a monounsaturated blend that stays soft and mobilisable at low body temperature yet is far less prone to going rancid than a diet loaded with polyunsaturated oils.

**Round it out with:**
- Protein ~1.6 g/kg from beans, lentils, tofu, eggs, dairy and fish, taken with resistance training, so you enter dormancy with extra muscle to spend.
- Sodium‑, potassium‑ and magnesium‑rich foods plus plenty of water and beetroot/nitrate‑rich greens for circulation.
- Calcium + vitamin D3/K2, iron, B12, choline and iodine to survive months of immobility and fasting.
- A daily antioxidant/polyphenol base — berries, cocoa, green tea, olives, vitamin E‑rich seeds — plus a modest omega‑3 intake (a couple of oily‑fish meals a week) purely for membrane and heart function.
- Avoid alcohol and heavy seed‑oil intake, which impair fat quality and liver storage.

**Last 48 hours:** stop fibre, switch to low‑residue liquids, a final sugar/salt/electrolyte drink and creatine, so the gut is empty, glycogen is maximal, and you go under fully hydrated and mineral‑loaded on a body composition of soft, oleate‑rich fat over well‑preserved muscle.

Imagine a competition where contestants.answer: A contest like this would essentially be an "animal home-building challenge," where teams are given a specific species and must design and construct a habitat suited to it. Entries would typically need to include the essentials of that animal's natural environment: sturdy, weather‑proof shelter or den/nesting space; a clean water source and feeding station; appropriate substrate and native plants or vegetation for cover; enrichment features such as climbing branches, rocks, burrowing areas, or perches; space to roam and hide; and safety elements like secure fencing, drainage, ventilation, and temperature/humidity control. Judges would score on how closely the build mimics the animal's wild habitat, its safety and durability, use of sustainable or recycled materials, ease of cleaning and maintenance, creativity, and how well it supports the animal's natural behaviors and welfare.

Picture a community "Wildlife Hotel Challenge," where entrants build homes for small backyard creatures out of reclaimed materials. A typical entry might be a multi-storey bug hotel framed from an old pallet, with compartments stuffed with hollow bamboo canes and drilled logs for solitary bees, pinecones and straw for ladybirds and lacewings, bark, moss and dead leaves for beetles and woodlice, and broken terracotta pots for frogs and toads. Around it, builders could add a mini pond or shallow water dish, a green (sedum-planted) roof, a hedgehog box tucked into the base, and bird and bat boxes fixed on top, all sited on a bed of nectar-rich wildflowers. Prizes would go to whichever creation attracts and shelters the widest variety of species while looking good and standing up to the weather.

Think of a school/STEM "Zoo Exhibit Design Challenge," where teams build a scale model (diorama) of an enclosure for an assigned species and present it to judges. A strong entry would include a labeled floor plan and cardboard/foam‑board model showing: a naturalistic terrain with rockwork, a pool or stream, shade trees and browse plants; a heated rock or basking lamp and a cooler shaded retreat; a night house/holding den with a squeeze cage for vet checks; safe barriers such as a moat, hot‑wire, or laminated viewing glass; keeper service corridors, doors, drains and food‑prep area; enrichment features (climbing structures, puzzle feeders, digging pits, scratching posts); public viewing platforms and interpretive signage about the animal's conservation status; and a written rationale explaining how the design meets the animal's biological and behavioral needs, plus a budget and sustainability plan (solar power, recycled materials, water recycling). Judging would weigh scientific accuracy, animal welfare, visitor experience, safety, and creativity.

It could be a birdhouse-building contest — a woodworking competition where entrants craft nest boxes to be judged and then hung in local parks or gardens. Entries would typically include untreated cedar or pine walls with a sloped, overhanging roof; a species-appropriate entrance hole (e.g., 1⅛" for wrens, 1½" for bluebirds) with a metal predator guard and no perch; ventilation slots near the top and drainage holes in the floor; a rough or grooved interior wall so fledglings can climb out; a hinged or removable side panel for cleaning; a mounting bracket or pole with a baffle to deter raccoons and snakes; and decorative touches like carved shingles, weathered paint, or themed designs (a tiny cottage, barn, or lighthouse). Winners would be chosen for craftsmanship, bird-friendly and safe construction, durability outdoors, use of recycled or sustainable wood, and creative appearance.

It could be an aquascaping contest, where hobbyists compete to build the best aquarium habitat for fish and shrimp. A winning tank would typically include: a layered nutrient-rich substrate capped with sand or gravel; hardscape such as driftwood, seiryu stone or lava rock arranged along a focal point/"golden ratio" layout; live plants ranging from carpeting foreground species to mosses, midground bushes and tall background stems; caves, roots and dense planting for hiding and spawning spots; open swimming space and gentle current; and the life-support gear — filter, heater, CO₂ injection, spectrum-tuned LED lighting, and a stocking plan of compatible, appropriately sized fish, shrimp or snails. Judges would score naturalism and composition, plant and fish health, water quality and stability, technical execution (hidden equipment, clean glass), and the overall creativity of the underwater "landscape."

It could be a county‑fair style **chicken coop building competition**, where 4‑H clubs, carpenters or backyard‑poultry hobbyists compete to build the best backyard coop (often auctioned off for charity afterward).

A typical entry would include: a raised, weatherproof henhouse on skids or legs with a shingled or metal sloped roof; an insulated, draft‑free interior with vents up high for year‑round airflow; roosting bars set above tiered, curtained nesting boxes (one per 3–4 hens) with an exterior egg‑collection door for easy gathering; a droppings board or deep‑litter tray under the roosts and a big hinged clean‑out door; a ramp with cleats leading down to an attached run enclosed in ½" hardware cloth (not chicken wire) with a buried or aprons skirt to stop digging predators, plus raccoon‑proof latches; automatic pop‑door, gravity feeder and nipple waterer; a dust‑bathing area, perches and a shaded/sunny mix in the run; and finishing touches like a green roof, rain‑barrel gutter, solar light, and painted trim or a themed design (barn, cottage, "coop de ville").

Judges would score predator‑proofing and safety, ventilation and sanitation, square footage per bird, ease of cleaning and egg access, durability against weather, use of recycled or sustainable materials, craftsmanship, and overall creativity/curb appeal.

It could be a "Barkitecture" doghouse-building competition, where architects, builders and design students compete to create custom dog houses that are later auctioned off to benefit an animal shelter. A strong entry would include: a weatherproof, insulated sleeping chamber sized to the breed, raised off the ground on a floor deck with drainage; a shingled, metal or living/green roof with an overhang, plus a hinged or lift-off top for cleaning; an offset doorway with a wind-baffle or flexible flap to block drafts, and cross-ventilation for hot weather; cedar or reclaimed lumber with non-toxic, pet-safe finishes and no exposed nails or splinters; a washable cushion or bed, built-in food and water bowl station, toy/leash storage, and a small shaded porch or ramp for older dogs; and playful design flourishes—a miniature mid-century modern house, a fire station, a surf shack—often themed to match the owner's home. Judging would weigh comfort and safety for the dog, weather durability, craftsmanship, sustainability of materials, and architectural creativity, with bonus points for how much money the piece raises at the charity auction.

Think of a bioactive vivarium/terrarium building competition, where reptile and amphibian keepers (or a herp‑society club) compete to build the best living enclosure for a species like a crested gecko, dart frog or ball python. A winning entry would typically include: a properly sized glass or PVC enclosure with secure, escape‑proof screen ventilation; a drainage layer of LECA/lava rock topped with mesh and a naturalistic bioactive soil mix; a "clean‑up crew" of springtails and isopods in leaf litter to break down waste; live tropical plants (bromeliads, pothos, ferns, moss) plus cork bark, branches, vines and a background of carved foam or cork for climbing; humid hides, a water feature or misting/fogging system on a timer; correct heat gradient with a basking spot, thermostat‑controlled heat source and UVB lighting on a day/night cycle; and thermometers/hygrometers to prove stable temperature and humidity. Judges would score animal welfare and species‑appropriateness, self‑sustaining ecology, planting and hardscape artistry, hidden equipment and tidy technical work, and overall creativity of the miniature rainforest or desert scene.

Think of a winter shelter‑building contest for community/feral cats, the kind local rescue groups run each autumn: volunteers, scout troops or workshops compete to build the best outdoor cat house, and the finished shelters get placed at colony sites afterward.

A typical entry would include: a small, low‑ceilinged insulated box (just big enough for two or three cats so their body heat warms it) built from a plastic storage tote or plywood lined with rigid foam board or a nested styrofoam cooler; a raised base on bricks, pallet slats or legs to keep it off cold, wet ground; a sloped, overhanging waterproof lid — often shingled, tarped or covered with pond liner — that lifts off for cleaning and refilling; a 5–6" doorway (too small for dogs, coyotes or raccoons) placed high on the wall and off‑center, with a flexible flap or vinyl door and a second exit or escape hole so a cat is never cornered; a short vestibule or baffle wall inside to block wind; a small vent hole to release moisture; loose straw bedding — never hay, blankets or towels, which absorb damp and freeze; sealed seams and caulked edges; a heated or insulated water bowl station and a covered feeding area set slightly apart from the sleeping box; and camouflage paint in browns and greens so the shelter blends into hedges and yards without attracting attention.

Judges would score warmth and insulation value, predator‑ and weather‑proofing, correct doorway size and escape route, ease of cleaning and restraw‑ing, use of cheap recycled materials, durability through freeze/thaw, portability, and creativity — with bonus points for how many shelters the team can produce in a day for the colonies that need them.

It could be a video‑game build contest — for example a "Planet Zoo" (or Minecraft/Zoo Tycoon) habitat‑building challenge, where players are given a theme and a species and compete on the workshop/Discord for the best in‑game enclosure. A winning entry would include: a terrain‑sculpted habitat with correct climate, biome and land/water ratio for the animal; custom‑built rockwork, cliffs, waterfalls and a swimming pool made from stacked scenery pieces; authentic foliage of the right continent; barriers hidden behind natural‑looking moats, glass viewing windows and rock walls; enrichment items, feeders, shelters and a heater/chiller to keep welfare stats at 100%; a themed keeper hut, back‑of‑house animal house and staff paths; guest viewing platforms, education boards, benches, litter bins and photo spots; and decorative theming (a colonial ranger station, Southeast Asian temple ruins, etc.) built piece‑by‑piece with the advanced move tool. Judges score animal‑welfare stats, realism and species accuracy, guest experience and flow, theming/detail craftsmanship, and originality — with bonus points for hitting the challenge's material or budget restrictions and for the screenshots or timelapse video submitted with the build.

Picture a conservation group's **bat house–building competition**, where woodworking clubs, scout troops and school classes compete to build the best bat roost, with the winners mounted around local parks, farms and wetlands to control mosquitoes.

A typical entry would include: an untreated rough‑sawn cedar or exterior‑grade plywood box roughly 24" tall and 14–24" wide (bigger boxes hold more bats and buffer temperature swings); several internal partitions creating narrow ¾" roosting chambers, with all interior surfaces scratched, grooved or lined with plastic mesh so bats can cling; a landing pad extending 3–6" below the open bottom (no floor, so guano falls out and cleaning is unnecessary); a sloped, overhanging roof and caulked, sealed seams so the box stays dry and draft‑free; a narrow vent slit a few inches up the front for temperature gradients in hot climates; dark, medium or light exterior paint chosen to match the region's summer temperatures for proper solar heating; and a mounting plan — pole or building wall (not a tree), 12–20 feet up, facing south/southeast for 6+ hours of sun, near a water source and clear of branches and predator perches.

Judges would score thermal design and chamber spacing against Bat Conservation International specs, weather‑tightness and durability, safe non‑toxic materials, craftsmanship of the joinery and finish, use of reclaimed lumber, and creative touches like carved or painted bat motifs — with bonus points for entries that actually get occupied by a colony in the first season.

Picture an **artificial reef–building competition** run by a marine conservation group or engineering school, where teams design and cast reef modules that are then sunk offshore to create fish and invertebrate habitat.

A typical entry would include: a cast structure of pH‑neutral, marine‑grade concrete (often with limestone or crushed shell aggregate, sometimes reinforced with basalt or fiberglass rather than rusting steel), shaped as a dome, pyramid, "reef ball," or stacked oyster‑castle block; a heavy, wide, stable base designed to resist storm surge and prevent scouring or rolling on the seabed; numerous holes, tunnels and swim‑throughs of varied sizes to shelter everything from juvenile fish and lobsters to eels and octopus; a deliberately rough, pitted, textured surface to encourage settlement of coral larvae, oyster spat, sponges and algae; ledges and vertical relief that create shade, current breaks and feeding stations; optional coral or oyster nursery attachment points (plugs, mesh bags, spat‑on‑shell); a deployment plan noting depth, substrate, current, light and distance from natural reef so it enhances rather than damages existing habitat; and permits, buoy markers and a monitoring schedule with dive surveys or GoPro footage.

Judges would score ecological function (species diversity and settlement expected/observed), structural stability and longevity in saltwater, environmental safety of the materials (no toxins, no plastics or tires), cost and ease of casting and deployment, sculptural creativity — many are made as fish, turtles or art pieces to double as dive attractions — and bonus points for the module that recruits the most life during the follow‑up survey season.

Picture a small‑pet keepers' "cage makeover" challenge — say a hamster habitat contest run by a rodent‑welfare group or pet forum, where entrants photograph the enclosure they've built and are judged on how well it lets the animal behave naturally.

A winning entry would typically include: a large single‑level tank, bin cage or converted IKEA‑style glass/wood enclosure well over the minimum floor space, with a secure mesh lid for ventilation and no wire bars, high shelves or drop hazards; 10–12 inches (or more) of mixed burrowing substrate — paper bedding blended with hemp, coco fibre, soil and a little hay so tunnels hold their shape — with a "deep burrowing zone" built up against the glass so the owner can see the natural tunnel system; multi‑chamber wooden or cork hides plus mossy tunnels, cork bark, grapevine branches, bendy bridges and a dig box; a solid‑surface wheel of the correct diameter for the species and a flat‑bottomed sand bath of chinchilla sand for grooming; scatter‑feeding of a varied seed mix, foraging toys and safe chews (applewood, whimzees, loofah, willow balls) for dental wear; a ceramic or glass water dish or drip‑free bottle; live or dried safe plants, leaf litter, pinecones and clean rocks for enrichment and enclosure "theming" (a desert wadi, forest floor, or fairy‑garden look); spot‑cleaning access and a wipe‑clean base; and a written care plan explaining substrate depth, temperature, lighting/dark cycle and quarantine of foraged materials.

Judges would score animal welfare and species‑appropriate sizing first, then enrichment variety, burrowing depth, safety of materials, hygiene and ease of maintenance, budget‑friendliness or DIY resourcefulness, and finally the creativity and naturalism of the finished "scape" — with bonus points for before‑and‑after photos and video of the pet actually using every feature.

It could be a beekeepers' association **hive‑building competition**, where members and woodworking students compete to build the best home for a honeybee colony, with the winning hives given to new beekeepers or placed on club apiary sites.

A typical entry would include: a bee‑space‑accurate box built from untreated western red cedar, pine or reclaimed lumber — a Langstroth stack, a horizontal top‑bar hive, a Warré, or a woven/log‑style "skep" or hollow‑tree replica for a natural‑comb category; precisely cut box joints or rabbets, with frames or top bars spaced at exactly 1¼–1⅜" and a 3/8" bee space so the bees don't glue everything with propolis; a screened, mite‑monitoring bottom board with a removable sticky tray; an adjustable, mouse‑guarded entrance reducer and a landing board; a ventilated inner cover and a weatherproof telescoping or gabled copper/metal roof with an overhang; insulated or quilt‑box "moisture management" for winter; an integrated feeder, queen excluder and follower boards; and non‑toxic finishes — raw linseed oil, beeswax dip or milk paint — with bright painted patterns or landmarks on the fronts to help bees orient to the right hive.

Judges would score woodworking precision (especially bee‑space tolerances and square, interchangeable boxes), weather‑tightness and durability, ventilation and condensation control, ease of inspection and honey harvesting for the beekeeper, colony health features like mite screens and swarm‑management space, use of sustainable local timber, and decorative craftsmanship — with bonus points for the hive that a captured swarm actually settles into and overwinters in.

Think of a garden club or conservation district's **"Certified Pollinator Habitat" garden challenge**, where households, schools and businesses compete to turn a plot of lawn into the best butterfly-and-bee habitat, with an inspector scoring the finished garden.

A strong entry would include: a sunny, sheltered site with a windbreak hedge; **larval host plants** for specific species (milkweed for monarchs, dill/parsley/fennel for swallowtails, violets for fritillaries, native willows and oaks for moths); **nectar plants blooming in overlapping succession** from early spring through late fall, planted in big single-species drifts rather than dotted singly, in a range of flower shapes and colors for short- and long-tongued visitors; mostly regionally native, pesticide- and neonicotinoid-free stock; **flat basking stones** in the sun and a damp sand or mud "puddling station" with a pinch of salt for minerals; a shallow pebble-filled water dish for bees; **nesting resources** — a patch of bare, undisturbed sunny soil for ground-nesting bees, pithy stems and drilled hardwood blocks or reed bundles for cavity nesters, and a bumblebee tussock of unmown grass; brush piles, leaf litter and standing dead stems left over winter for overwintering chrysalises and eggs; a mowing/"leave the leaves" maintenance plan; a rotting log and fallen fruit feeding station for hackberry and comma butterflies; plus paths, benches and interpretive signage, a plant list/map, and a photo log of species observed.

Judging would weigh the number of native host and nectar species, continuity of bloom, provision of water, shelter and nesting sites, absence of chemicals, documented butterfly and bee visitation counts, sustainability of the design (rain garden, compost, no irrigation), and overall beauty and educational value — with bonus points for the garden that records the most different pollinator species during the survey.

Think of an ant‑keeping club's **formicarium (ant farm) building competition**, where hobbyists compete to build the best custom home for a colony, judged from photos and video of the ants actually living in it.

A typical entry would include: a cast **ytong/aerated concrete, plaster, acrylic or 3D‑printed nesting block** with hand‑carved chambers and tunnels of the right size for the species, sealed behind clear glass or acrylic with a red‑film cover so the ants tunnel against the viewing pane but still think they're in the dark; a **hydration system** — a water tower, sponge reservoir or wet‑plaster wall — giving a humidity gradient from damp brood chambers to a dry seed/refuse room, with a hygrometer and a heat cable or lamp on a thermostat at one end for a temperature gradient; a connecting tube or ramp to a naturalistic **outworld/foraging arena** landscaped with sand, soil, leaf litter, cork bark, twigs, moss or live plants, a shallow water and sugar‑feeder station, a protein dish, and a trash/midden corner; **escape‑proofing** — talcum or PTFE‑painted walls, a petroleum‑jelly or oil barrier, tight‑fitting mesh vents and plugged tube ends; ventilation screens to prevent mould; expandable modular design so extra nest modules can be added as the colony grows; and cleaning/access hatches plus a written care log noting species, queen date, colony size, feeding schedule and hibernation plan.

Judges would score species‑appropriate humidity, temperature and chamber design, colony health and brood growth, escape‑ and mould‑proofing, ease of feeding and cleaning, craftsmanship and clarity of the viewing panes, sustainability/DIY resourcefulness, and the artistry of the outworld "scape" — with bonus points for time‑lapse footage of the ants excavating and moving their brood in.

Picture an **aviary‑building competition** run by a bird club or parrot rescue, where entrants construct walk‑in flight aviaries that are judged on site (and often donated to the sanctuary afterwards).

A strong entry would include: a long rectangular flight — length prioritised over height so budgies, finches or conures can actually fly — framed in aluminium or rot‑resistant timber and clad in welded stainless/galvanised‑after‑weld mesh of a gauge and bar spacing matched to the species (small enough to exclude rats, snakes and wild birds, strong enough that a macaw can't bend it); a **double‑door safety porch** with self‑closing doors so nothing escapes when the keeper enters; a concrete footing or buried wire skirt/apron to stop foxes, cats and rodents digging in; a solid, insulated roofed shelter section with perching, a heat panel/thermostat and full‑spectrum UV lighting for winter, opening into an open‑mesh sunny flight with part‑solid roof for shade and rain cover; **natural branch perches of varied diameter, texture and orientation** (untreated eucalypt, willow, apple) plus rope perches and swings, sited so birds don't foul food below; foraging and enrichment furniture — puzzle feeders, browse and chew branches, shreddable toys, hanging baskets, a bathing pan or misting sprinkler; nest boxes or breeding logs of the correct dimensions with inspection hatches; safe planted greenery and non‑toxic sealants; hygienic, well‑drained flooring (river sand, gravel or sealed concrete falling to a drain) with a hose‑down clean‑out, service corridor and lockable feed store; and weather‑proofing such as windbreak panels on the prevailing side, guttering and a rain‑water butt.

Judges would score bird welfare and flight space per bird, escape‑ and predator‑proofing, ventilation, drainage and ease of daily cleaning, safety of every material (no zinc, no toxic timber, no gaps to trap toes or heads), craftsmanship and durability, sustainable/reclaimed materials, and the naturalism and visual appeal of the planted flight — with bonus points for the aviary whose occupants settle, breed and stay healthiest through a full season.

Picture a "Build a Wildlife Pond" competition run by a wildlife trust or garden show, where entrants dig and plant a pond in a garden, schoolyard or field margin and it's judged for the amphibians and insects it attracts.

A strong entry would include: a sunny but partly sheltered site away from overhanging trees and away from run‑off or fertilised lawn; a hole dug with **varied depths and profiles** — a deep zone (60–90 cm) that won't freeze solid for overwintering frogs and newts, marginal shelves at 10–30 cm for planting, and at least one long, gently sloping "beach" edge so hedgehogs, birds and froglets can get in and out safely; a puncture‑free butyl/EPDM liner (or clay/preformed unit) bedded on sand, old carpet or underlay, with the liner edge hidden under turf, stone or a bog‑garden overflow rather than a hard rim; **rainwater fill** from a diverted downpipe or water butt rather than chlorinated tap water; a natural planting scheme of native species only — oxygenators such as hornwort and water‑crowfoot, floating cover like frogbit and a small water lily for shade and dragonfly perches, marginals such as marsh marigold, water forget‑me‑not, flag iris and purple loosestrife for larvae to climb out on, and no invasive non‑natives; a sunken log, stones and gravel bottom for cover, plus a "dead hedge", log pile, rockery and long grass corridor around the edge as the terrestrial half of the amphibians' habitat; no fish, no pump or fountain (still water for tadpoles), and a partly shaded, partly sunlit surface; safety features such as a mesh grid or fence if children are around; and a monitoring log — spawn counts, newt torch surveys, dragonfly exuviae, visiting birds and mammals — plus a maintenance plan for autumn leaf netting and gradual blanketweed and silt removal.

Judges would score biodiversity value and species actually recorded, use of native and locally sourced plants, correct depth profile and safe sloping access, water quality and lack of chemicals, integration with surrounding habitat, sustainability and use of reclaimed materials, and how attractive and educational the finished pond is — with bonus points for the pond that records the most amphibian and invertebrate species in its first season.

Think of a watershed council or engineering‑school **stream habitat restoration challenge**, where teams design (and then actually build) a reach of river to bring salmon and trout back, judged after a season of fish surveys.

A typical entry would include: a survey and design plan of the reach — channel cross‑sections, gradient, flood modeling and a sediment‑transport analysis — showing how the straightened, incised ditch will be reshaped into a meandering channel with a reconnected floodplain and side channels; **engineered logjams and large woody debris** (whole trees with rootwads, ballasted and keyed into the bank rather than pinned with rebar) to scour deep resting pools and create cover; a **riffle‑pool‑glide sequence** with clean, washed spawning gravel of the right size for redds, plus boulder clusters and vanes to sort sediment and create current breaks; removal or retrofit of a perched culvert or small dam and installation of a step‑pool fishway so juveniles and adults can pass at all flows; undercut banks, root wads and beaver‑dam analogues for rearing habitat; bank stabilization by **bioengineering** — live willow stakes, coir logs, brush mattresses and fascines instead of riprap; a replanted riparian buffer of native trees and shrubs for shade (cooling water temperature), leaf litter and future wood recruitment, fenced from livestock with an off‑channel stock watering point; wetland and off‑channel ponds for high‑flow refuge and amphibians; nutrient enhancement (carcass analogs) and invasive‑weed control; and a monitoring package — temperature and dissolved‑oxygen loggers, redd counts, smolt traps, macroinvertebrate sampling and before/after drone imagery — plus permits, landowner agreements, a volunteer planting day and a maintenance budget.

Judges would score ecological benefit (documented spawning, fish density and macroinvertebrate diversity), hydraulic and structural stability through a big flood event, water quality and temperature improvement, use of natural, locally sourced materials over hard armoring, cost‑effectiveness per mile restored, community involvement and education, and long‑term self‑sustaining function — with bonus points for the reach that counts the most returning fish in its first season.

Picture a school garden club or council-run **"Build the Best Worm Farm" composting competition**, where classes, families or community gardeners construct a habitat for red wigglers and are judged on how healthy and productive the colony is after a few months.

A typical entry would include: a stacked-tray or repurposed container system (nested plastic totes, a cut-down wheelie bin, an old bathtub, or a timber "worm hotel" made from reclaimed pallet boards and a hinged lid) with a mesh-screened air-hole pattern for ventilation but no gaps big enough for the worms to crawl out; a tap, spigot or sump tray at the base to drain "worm tea" leachate, with a false floor or hardware-cloth screen so the worms don't drown; damp bedding of shredded newspaper, cardboard, coco coir, aged leaf litter and a handful of grit or crushed eggshell for their gizzards; a moist-but-not-soggy zone kept around 60–80% moisture and pH near neutral; a shaded, insulated, weather-proofed placement (foam board or straw jacket for winter, elevated on legs to deter rats and ants, with an ant moat on each leg); a burlap or damp-cardboard blanket over the surface to keep the top layer dark and moist; a feeding plan and pocket-feeding scheme for fruit and veggie scraps, coffee grounds and crushed shells with a "no meat, dairy, oil, citrus or onion" rule to stop odours and flies; upward-migration trays so finished castings can be harvested without hand-sorting; and a monitoring log of temperature, moisture, worm population growth, castings and liquid fertiliser yield, plus signage explaining the process.

Judges would score worm health and reproduction rate, absence of odour, flies and escapees, drainage and aeration design, ease of feeding and harvesting castings, durability and weather-proofing, use of recycled or salvaged materials and low cost, volume of kitchen waste diverted, and creativity of the build — with bonus points for the farm that produces the most castings and the liveliest colony by judging day.

It could be a 4‑H/FFA **rabbit hutch–building competition**, where members and ag‑shop students build backyard rabbit housing that's judged at the county fair (and often sold to benefit the club).

A typical entry would include: a raised, all‑weather hutch on legs or a wheeled stand, sized generously for the breed (roughly 4+ sq ft per adult, tall enough to sit up and take three hops); a wire mesh floor of the correct 1"×½" gauge with a resting board or mat to prevent sore hocks, sloping to a slide‑out galvanized dropping tray or manure board over a worm‑bin/compost catch; solid, insulated side and back walls with an overhanging, sloped, shingled or metal roof for shade and rain, and a hinged panel or drop‑down flap for winter windbreak; ½" hardware cloth (not chicken wire) on the open sides with predator‑proof latches and a skirt against digging dogs and raccoons; good cross‑ventilation up high to prevent ammonia buildup, plus a fan/misting option for heat; a nest box with a lip for kindling does, a hay rack, gravity J‑feeder and a nipple waterer or crock with a heater cup; an attached shaded run or ramp to a grazing tractor with a wire bottom so rabbits can graze safely; enrichment such as willow chew sticks, a digging box, tunnels and a platform; and easy‑clean touches — smooth sealed non‑toxic wood, removable trays, big access doors and a corner litter pan.

Judges would score animal comfort and health (floor type, space, ventilation, temperature protection), predator‑proofing and secure latches, sanitation and ease of daily feeding/cleaning, craftsmanship and durability, use of recycled or sustainable materials, cost, portability, and overall design creativity.

Think of a hermit‑crab keepers' "crabitat" contest, run by a pet forum or exotics expo, where entrants photograph the tank they've built for their land hermit crabs and it's judged on how well it mimics a tropical shoreline.

A winning entry would include: a large sealed glass tank (well beyond the "one crab per gallon" minimum) with a glass or plexiglass lid and weather stripping to hold humidity; at least 6 inches — or three times the biggest crab's height — of moist, sand‑castle‑consistency substrate (play sand mixed 5:1 with coco fibre) so every crab can dig down and molt undisturbed, sometimes with a deeper "molting corner" and a separate dry sand play area; **two pools** — one dechlorinated fresh water and one marine‑salt salt water — both deep enough to submerge in, with gently sloping ramps, bridges, or mesh so crabs can climb out and not drown; a heat mat/panel on the side wall with a thermostat keeping 75–85 °F and a hygrometer showing 75–85 % humidity, plus a low‑wattage LED on a day/night cycle; a jungle of climbing and hiding décor — cholla wood, cork bark, coconut caves, grapevine, lava rock, plastic or safe live plants, netting and moss pits; a "shell shop" of a dozen‑plus extra natural (never painted) shells in a range of opening sizes and shapes for shell swaps; food and calcium stations offering cuttlebone, crushed oyster shell, dried shrimp, worm castings, leaf litter, seeds and fresh fruit in shallow non‑metal dishes; and no toxic elements — no cedar, no metal, no painted shells, no copper.

Judges would score molting‑safe substrate depth and humidity/temperature stability first, then water setup and drowning safety, shell selection, climbing and enrichment variety, diet and safety of every material, cleanliness and ease of maintenance, and finally the artistry and naturalism of the "beach" scape — with bonus points for photos or video of the crabs actually digging, bathing, climbing and swapping shells.

Picture an architecture school's **"Urban Biodiversity Green Roof Challenge,"** where teams compete to convert a bare rooftop (or design a mock-up panel of one) into living habitat for city wildlife, judged after a season of wildlife surveys.

A strong entry would include: a load-assessed, waterproofed and root-barriered roof deck with drainage mat and filter fleece; a **varied-depth crushed-brick/recycled-aggregate substrate**, mounded from 60 mm up to 200 mm to create dry ridges, damp hollows and a "brown roof" mosaic of bare rubble, sand patches and gravel scrapes for ground-nesting solitary bees and rare invertebrates; a planting palette of drought-tolerant sedums plus native wildflowers and grasses chosen for long, overlapping bloom (thyme, bird's-foot trefoil, viper's bugloss, yarrow) and left un-mown over winter; **micro-habitat furniture** — log and stone piles, standing deadwood, bee hotels of reed bundles and drilled hardwood, a sand bank, and a shallow lined "sky pond" or seasonal wet scrape edged with pebbles; **nesting provision integrated into the fabric** — swift bricks and house-martin cups under the eaves, a kestrel or gull tray, sparrow terraces, bat access tiles and a bat box on the warm south wall, all sited away from access routes; predator-proofing and safety details (parapet or fall-arrest line, no cat access, non-toxic membranes, fire breaks); a maintenance and irrigation plan using harvested rainwater, plus stormwater-attenuation and building-cooling calculations; and a monitoring package — camera traps, bat detectors, pitfall traps and pollinator transects — with a public viewing terrace and interpretive signage.

Judges would score documented species richness and nesting success, ecological authenticity of the habitat mosaic, structural and drainage engineering, use of recycled and locally sourced materials, stormwater/energy co-benefits, buildability and cost per square metre, maintenance realism, and design flair — with bonus points for the roof that logs the most breeding birds and pollinator species in its first summer.

Think of a humane society's **"Catio Design Contest,"** where builders and DIYers compete to create the best outdoor cat enclosure attached to a house, with the winning catios raffled off or installed for adopters.

A strong entry would include: a weather‑resistant cedar or powder‑coated aluminum frame clad in escape‑proof welded wire or polycarbonate panels, with a solid roof section for rain/shade and an open mesh section for sun; a secure cat door, tunnel, or window box connecting it to the house, plus a double‑door human entry vestibule so no cat slips out; a solid floor or buried wire skirt so cats can't dig out and wildlife can't dig in; multi‑level shelves, ramps, catwalks and bridges to maximize vertical territory; sisal scratching posts, real (cat‑safe) tree branches for climbing, hammocks and cozy insulated hidey boxes; planters of cat grass, catnip, silver vine and valerian, with all toxic plants excluded; a hidden litter station and non‑spill water fountain; birdwatching perches positioned by a feeder placed safely out of pouncing range; and easy‑clean, hose‑down surfaces with drainage.

Judges would score cat safety and escape‑proofing, enrichment and vertical space, weather protection, ease of cleaning, use of reclaimed or sustainable materials, buildability on a modest budget, and how attractively it blends with the home's architecture — with bonus points for video of the cats actually using every level.

Think of an equine facility **"Design‑and‑Build the Best Barn" competition**, run by a horse council, agricultural college or trade show, where teams (or ag‑engineering students) design — and sometimes construct a full‑scale or scale‑model — stabling for horses, judged by vets, farriers and barn managers.

A strong entry would include: a well‑drained, elevated site plan with the barn oriented to catch prevailing summer breezes and block winter wind; roomy box stalls (about 12×12 ft, larger for foaling or drafts) with 8‑ft partitions topped by grills so horses can see and sniff neighbours without kicking through; rounded corners, flush latches and no protruding hardware, kick‑proof tongue‑and‑groove hardwood or rubber‑lined walls, and yoke or Dutch doors opening to the outside; a non‑slip, cushioned floor system — tamped stone dust or crushed limestone under rubber mats — sloped to a covered drain, deep‑bedded in straw or shavings; a wide (12–14 ft) centre aisle with even, dust‑free footing, cross‑tie areas, and doors at both ends for emergency evacuation; ridge vents, cupolas, ceiling fans and generous eave/window openings for the 4–8 air changes an hour that prevent respiratory disease and ammonia buildup; abundant natural light plus caged, dust‑tight fixtures, GFCI outlets, conduit run out of reach, lightning protection, fire extinguishers, sprinklers/smoke detectors and no hay stored overhead; automatic waterers or heated buckets, a hay and grain room sealed against rodents, a heated tack room, wash stall with hot water, feed/medication lockers and a manure‑management bunker; a farrier/vet stock area, quarantine stall, and attached paddocks with safe fencing (no barbed wire), run‑in sheds, gates that swing both ways, and a hard‑surfaced turnout lane; plus arena or round‑pen access, hay storage, and a budget, materials list and maintenance plan.

Judges would score horse health and safety first (ventilation, footing, injury‑proof fittings, fire escape routes), then labour efficiency for daily chores, biosecurity, durability of materials, cost per stall, sustainability features like solar panels, rainwater capture and composting, and finally craftsmanship and curb appeal — with bonus points for a design that a working barn manager says they could run single‑handed.

Picture a utility company or Audubon chapter's **osprey/raptor nesting‑platform competition**, where lineworker crews, welding shops and high‑school ag/engineering classes compete to build the best artificial nest structure, with the winners craned into place on marshes, lake shores and rights‑of‑way each winter before the birds return.

A typical entry would include: a tall (roughly 12–20 ft, or a retired 30–40 ft utility pole) galvanized‑steel or pressure‑treated wooden mast with a deep, concrete‑set or auger footing engineered to stay rigid under a 300‑lb nest plus wind and ice loading; a 4×4 to 5×5 ft platform deck of welded rebar grid, expanded metal or slatted lumber, slightly dished or with raised rails/perimeter lip so eggs and chicks can't roll off in a gale, and open enough to drain rain and shed guano; a starter nest of sticks, driftwood and sod wired down to convince the pair the site is "used"; sturdy side perch arms and a landing branch above the rim so adults have somewhere to eat and the fledglings can "helicopter" before first flight; a smooth conical or cylindrical **predator baffle** on the pole against raccoons and rat snakes, plus anti‑bird‑of‑prey competitor and anti‑climb hardware; no sharp edges, no loose baling twine or netting that can entangle chicks; safe electrical clearance if it's near a live line (the whole point is often to lure ospreys off transformers), and grounding/insulated standoffs; siting notes — within a mile of open fishable water, clear flight lines, away from trails, oriented for shade and prevailing winds; and optional extras such as a solar‑powered nest cam and Wi‑Fi link, band‑reading numbering, and a hinged or winch‑down top for annual maintenance and banding.

Judges would score biological suitability (dimensions, height, site choice, predator‑proofing), structural engineering and wind/ice load calculations, safety for both birds and the crew installing it, weld and carpentry craftsmanship, corrosion resistance and expected 20‑plus‑year lifespan, use of reclaimed poles and scrap steel, cost and ease of installation from a bucket truck, and the education/outreach package — with the grand prize going to whichever platform is actually occupied and fledges chicks in its first nesting season.

Think of a **botanic‑garden or design‑school "Build a Butterfly House" competition**, where teams design and construct a walk‑through tropical butterfly conservatory (full‑scale or as a scale model/greenhouse mock‑up), judged on how well the butterflies thrive and how much visitors enjoy it.

A strong entry would include: a glazed or ETFE‑clad greenhouse shell with automated vents, shade cloth, misters and heating to hold roughly 26–30 °C and 70–80 % humidity year‑round; a **double‑door airlock vestibule** with hanging curtains, mirrors and air curtains so no butterflies escape and no wild insects get in; a landscaped interior with a stream, waterfall and pond, winding paths and open sunlit "flyways" tall enough for swallowtails and morphos to patrol, plus sheltered, wind‑free corners for roosting; **nectar plants in continuous bloom** (lantana, pentas, ixora, buddleia, firebush) and species‑specific **larval host plants** (passionflower, citrus, milkweed, Aristolochia) for the on‑site breeding program; feeding stations of rotting fruit trays and sugar‑water wicks, plus mud/salt puddling patches and warm basking stones; a glass‑fronted **pupae emergence chamber** where visitors watch chrysalises hatch, backed by a quarantine/rearing lab, netted breeding cages and a sealed import‑permit protocol; pest‑ and predator‑control that's pesticide‑free (parasitoid screening, ant barriers, no spiders or geckos); benches, wheelchair‑accessible paths, interpretive signage and staff to check clothing on the way out; and sustainability features like rainwater harvesting, solar/geothermal heating and locally propagated plants.

Judges would score butterfly survival, longevity and natural behaviour (courtship, egg‑laying, emergence success), horticultural quality and plant–insect matching, climate‑control engineering and energy use, escape‑ and biosecurity‑proofing, visitor experience and education value, buildability and running cost, and the sheer beauty of the immersive tropical landscape — with bonus points for the design that sustains the most species without importing replacements.

Picture a racing‑pigeon club's **loft‑building competition**, where fanciers and woodworking students compete to build the best home for a team of birds, with the winning loft judged at the club show and handed to a junior member starting out.

A strong entry would include: a raised timber loft on legs or a concrete pad, sited facing the morning sun and sheltered from prevailing wind and rain, with a dry, draught‑free but generously ventilated design (louvred inlets low down, ridge or gable outlets high up) since respiratory disease is the fancier's biggest enemy; separate compartments for cocks, hens, young birds and a stock/breeding section, each allowing roughly 2 cubic feet of air space per bird; individual box perches or V‑perches for the racers and nest boxes with fronts, bowls and a closing gate for pairs; a "sputnik" or bob‑wire trap and landing board with an electronic clocking pad so returning birds are timed instantly; a wide aviary or wire flight for basking and open‑door training; a deep‑litter or slatted/grid floor over a slide‑out droppings tray for easy scraping and disease control; hopper feeders, grit and mineral pots and drinkers positioned so they can't be fouled; a sealed, rodent‑proof feed and grit store, plus a small sick‑bay/quarantine pen and a bath pan; smooth, non‑toxic sealed interior surfaces with no cracks for parasites, insulated walls and a felted, overhanging roof with guttering into a water butt; predator‑proofing against cats, rats and hawks (wire skirts, secure latches, mesh over vents); and touches like solar lighting, painted trim, a viewing window and a written management plan for ventilation, feeding and race‑day routine.

Judges would score bird health and ventilation first, then trapping speed and layout for training, ease of daily cleaning and feeding, predator‑ and vermin‑proofing, weather‑tightness and durability, use of reclaimed timber and cost, craftsmanship and appearance — with bonus points for the loft whose birds home fastest and stay healthiest through a full race season.

Think of a turtle‑and‑tortoise society's **"Best Outdoor Tortoise Pen" competition**, where keepers build a permanent outdoor habitat in their yard and submit photos, plans and a keeper's log for judging.

A winning entry would include: a large, sun‑drenched pen sited on well‑drained, gently sloping ground, walled with mortared block, timber or stone at least twice the tortoise's height, with the top course leaned inward and the walls **sunk 8–12 inches below grade** (or footed on buried hardware cloth) to stop digging escapes and burrowing predators; **opaque, solid sides** rather than wire mesh, since tortoises pace endlessly at any barrier they can see through; a secure wire or lattice top over part or all of the pen against raccoons, dogs, ravens and rats; a temperature/behaviour mosaic inside — an open **basking area of flat rock or packed earth**, deep shade from shrubs and a shade cloth panel, and a **humid hide or artificial burrow** (a half‑buried drainage pipe or dug‑out hillside den) that holds cool, damp air; a heated, insulated, thermostat‑controlled night box or cold‑frame shed with a lockable door and a ramp for chilly nights and early spring; a **shallow, sunken soaking dish** with a ramped edge and grippy bottom, sunk flush to the substrate and easy to tip and scrub daily; deep, diggable substrate of topsoil, sand and leaf litter for nesting females, plus a dedicated sunny **egg‑laying mound**; a living "salad bar" of grazing plants — grasses, clover, dandelion, plantain, hibiscus, mulberry, prickly pear, cactus pads — with all toxic ornamentals (oleander, azalea, foxglove, buttercup) removed, and a cuttlebone/calcium station; logs, rock piles, a small hill and winding pathways for terrain enrichment and exercise, with no steep drops or gaps a tortoise could wedge into or flip over on; drainage grading and gutters so it never becomes a mud pit; and a written care plan covering species, diet, brumation arrangements, quarantine and vet checks.

Judges would score species‑appropriate space and thermal gradients, escape‑ and predator‑proofing, safety (nothing to trap, drown or overturn the animal), quality and variety of edible planting, hydration and humidity provision, sanitation and ease of daily maintenance, use of natural/reclaimed materials and cost, and the naturalism and landscaping beauty of the finished habitat — with bonus points for photos or video of the tortoises grazing, basking, digging and behaving as they would in the wild.

It could be a **wildlife‑crossing design competition** (like the ARC International contest), where engineering and landscape‑architecture teams compete to design a structure that reconnects habitat split by a highway, with the winning concept actually built over a real road.
