A strong entry would include: a **vegetated overpass ("green bridge") or wide, open‑span underpass** sized to the target species — broad and shallow‑sloped enough for elk, moose or bears, with a high openness ratio so animals can see the far side; a modular, quick‑to‑erect superstructure (precast concrete arches, glue‑lam timber, fibre‑reinforced polymer, or gabion/soil‑nail abutments) engineered for deep soil and snow loads; **varied‑depth native soil and rock substrate** planted with locally sourced grasses, shrubs and trees to blend seamlessly into the surrounding terrain, plus log piles, brush, boulder clusters and a shallow wet swale so small mammals, reptiles and amphibians have cover the whole way across; **solid berms, earth mounds and vegetated parapets** to screen out headlights, traffic noise and human sightlines; several miles of **exclusion fencing with one‑way jump‑outs, escape ramps and cattle‑grid/ electrified mats** at access roads to funnel animals to the structure and keep them off the pavement; complementary smaller passages in the same corridor — box culverts with **dry ledges/benches** for otters and beavers, amphibian tunnels with slotted daylighting, arboreal rope bridges or canopy poles for squirrels and possums, and fish‑passable stream culverts; drainage, de‑icing‑salt containment and erosion control so run‑off doesn't poison the plantings; a construction‑staging and cost plan that avoids closing the highway; and a **monitoring package** — camera traps, track pads, GPS‑collar data and before/after roadkill counts — plus interpretive pull‑offs and public education.

Judges would score ecological effectiveness for the named target species, structural and cost efficiency, modularity/replicability on other highways, driver and animal safety, use of native and recycled materials, maintenance realism, and elegance of the design — with the grand prize going to the crossing that records the most species safely using it (and the biggest drop in vehicle collisions) in its first seasons.

It could be an agricultural‑engineering **"Design the Best Dairy Barn" competition**, where ag‑college teams, farm‑building contractors and FFA chapters compete (with plans, 3‑D models or a full built structure) to create the most cow‑friendly free‑stall barn, judged by dairy vets, nutritionists and producers.

A strong entry would include: a well‑drained site with the barn oriented east–west so the north–south open sidewalls catch the prevailing breeze and the roof shades the feed alley; **free stalls sized to the herd's frame** (roughly 48–50" wide, 8–9 ft long) with flexible loops, correct neck rail and brisket‑locator placement, and deep‑bedded sand or a thick mattress with sawdust so cows lie down 12+ hours a day without hock sores; **grooved, non‑slip concrete or rubber alley flooring** scraped by automatic alley scrapers or slats over a manure pit, sized 12–14 ft for the feed alley and 10 ft for crossovers; a **ventilation package** — tall open sidewalls with automated curtains, a wide ridge opening, and tunnel or cross‑ventilation fans plus soakers/misters and a heat‑stress cooling plan (target THI under 68) with LED lighting on a 16‑hour long‑day photoperiod; **generous feed‑bunk space** (24–30" per cow) with a smooth epoxy or tile bunk face, headlocks for sorting and vet work, and at least 3.5" of clean waterer perimeter per cow at every crossover; a **milking centre or robotic milking boxes** with a holding pen, footbath, and cow‑flow lanes designed on curved, no‑dead‑end handling principles; separate **special‑needs areas** — maternity/calving pens with clean straw packs, fresh‑cow and hospital pens, hoof‑trimming chute, and individual or group calf housing with its own biosecure airspace and positive‑pressure tube ventilation; **manure and nutrient management** (pit, lagoon, sand separator, digester, runoff containment), a feed centre with bunker silos and commodity bays, and sustainability features like solar panels, plate‑cooler heat recovery and rainwater capture; plus a labour‑flow diagram, biosecurity/visitor route, budget per stall and expansion plan.

Judges would score cow comfort and welfare metrics first (lying time, lameness and hock scores, stall and bunk space, heat abatement), then ventilation and air quality, milk quality and udder‑health design, labour efficiency and cow flow, biosecurity, manure handling and environmental compliance, worker and animal safety, construction cost per stall and durability, and sustainability — with bonus points for a design a real farm crew says they could run profitably and expand later.

Picture a nature‑centre or school science fair **"Build a Nest Like a Bird" challenge**, where contestants (kids, families or biology students) have to construct a working bird's nest using only materials a bird could actually gather — and, in the strictest version, using just one hand or a pair of chopsticks to mimic a beak.

A typical entry would include: a cup‑ or dome‑shaped structure woven from foraged twigs, dried grasses, pine needles, rootlets and long strips of bark; mud, clay or chewed leaf pulp used as mortar (robin‑ or swallow‑style) to bind the walls; a soft inner lining of moss, plant down, thistle fluff, animal hair, shed fur and a few feathers for insulation; springy anchoring "hooks" of vine, grapevine tendril or spider‑web substitute (thread or fine fibre) to lash the whole thing to a forked branch, a wall ledge, or a hanging position; the correct size and cup depth for the assigned species (a tiny hummingbird thimble, a robin cup, a weaverbird's woven hanging pouch, an eagle's stick platform, or a ground‑scrape with pebbles and camouflage); drainage and a slight rim so eggs don't roll out; and camouflage — lichen flakes, leaf litter and moss on the outside so it disappears into its surroundings. No glue, wire, string or plastic allowed, and nothing may be taken from a living plant or a real nest.

The finished nests are then tested: judges shake the branch or run a fan on it to simulate wind, pour water over it to check it sheds rain and drains, and load it with weighted plastic or hard‑boiled eggs (and sometimes a "chick" weight) to see whether it holds without collapsing or spilling. Scoring covers structural strength and stability, weather‑proofing and insulation, authenticity to the assigned species' real nesting style, use of only genuinely bird‑available natural materials, camouflage and craftsmanship under the "beak only" handicap, and a short presentation explaining the bird's nesting biology — with bonus points for the most convincing nest that a judge mistakes for the real thing, and extra credit if it's later mounted outdoors and adopted by an actual bird.

Picture a lake association / state fisheries agency **"Fish Attractor Build Day" competition**, where angling clubs, scout troops and shop classes compete to build the best fish‑habitat structure, which is then sunk through the winter ice or barged out to bare lake bottoms in spring.

A typical entry would include: a hardwood pallet or oak‑frame base ballasted with a poured‑concrete footing or cinder blocks so it lands upright and stays put in current and ice heave; a "porcupine crib" or spider‑block bristling with untreated hardwood stakes, cedar limbs or bundled hardwood slabs at varied angles to make dense, tangled cover; sections of large‑diameter PVC or corrugated pipe and stacked half‑logs forming shaded caves and ambush lanes for bass, walleye and catfish; smaller‑mesh brush bundles and evergreen tops lashed with biodegradable jute rather than plastic zip ties, giving fry and fingerlings a predator refuge; a clean gravel/cobble spawning bench on one face for nest builders; vertical "reef" columns of stacked crates or hollow blocks rising through the water column to hold suspended crappie and baitfish; deliberately rough, textured surfaces to grow periphyton, snails and insect larvae — the base of the food web; no tires, treated lumber, painted wood, foam or loose plastic; plus a deployment plan giving GPS coordinates, depth (usually within the photic zone), spacing from other structures, distance from boat lanes and navigation hazards, agency permits, marker buoys, and a monitoring schedule using side‑scan sonar and underwater camera drops.

Judges would score fish‑habitat value (cover complexity, size range of hiding spaces, spawning and forage benefit), structural stability and expected lifespan underwater, environmental safety of materials, use of donated or recycled wood and low cost per unit, buildability by volunteers in a day, safe handling/deployment weight, and creativity of the design — with the grand prize going to the structure that holds the most fish on the follow‑up sonar and camera survey.

It could be a hunting/conservation club's **"Farm Wildlife Habitat Improvement Contest,"** where landowners, FFA chapters or land‑management students compete over a season to turn a plot of cropland or old pasture into the best quail, rabbit and songbird habitat, judged by a wildlife biologist on a walk‑through and follow‑up covey counts.

A strong entry would include: **edge feathering** — half‑cutting or hinge‑cutting fencerow trees so they fall living into the field edge for escape cover; **brush piles** built the right way (a base of large logs, stumps or old fence posts laid in a crisscross "log cabin" so there are ground‑level tunnels underneath, then treetops and cedar limbs layered on top, sited every few acres within a covey's dash of feeding areas); a **rock‑and‑stump hibernaculum** dug below frost line for snakes, toads and salamanders; strips of **native warm‑season bunchgrasses** (little bluestem, indiangrass) with bare ground between clumps so chicks can run and dust‑bathe, plus a ragweed/partridge‑pea/lespedeza "weedy" disked strip for insects and seed; shrub thickets and a mixed hedgerow travel corridor of plum, dogwood, elderberry and hazel linking the woodlot to the field; a small food plot of grain sorghum, millet or sunflowers left standing through winter; a shallow wetland scrape, guzzler or livestock‑tank escape ramp for water; nest structures where they fit — wood duck and kestrel boxes, a bluebird trail, brush‑pile rabbit "hutches"; removal of fescue, autumn olive and other invasives, cattle fenced out of the creek with a riparian buffer, and a written management calendar of prescribed burns, strip‑disking on rotation and delayed mowing to protect nests.

Judging would weigh cover diversity and how the pieces are arranged (food, nesting, brood and escape cover all within reach of each other), use of native species and removal of invasives, quality of brush‑pile construction and durability, soil and water protection, cost per acre and use of on‑farm materials, compatibility with the working farm, and the written plan — with the trophy going to whoever's ground records the most coveys, nests and species on the fall survey.

Think of a **Purple Martin Society "Best Martin Housing" competition**, where clubs, woodshop classes and retirees compete to build the best colony house or gourd rack, with winners erected at parks, golf courses and lakeshores.

A typical entry would include: a multi-compartment aluminum, wood or PVC "condo," or a rack hung with natural/plastic gourds, mounted on a **telescoping or winch-down pole** so every cavity can be lowered for weekly nest checks; roomy compartments (at least 6"×6", ideally 6"×12" deep) with **crescent or starling-resistant entrance holes** about 1⅛" high placed low on the front wall, plus porch dividers and railings so fledglings don't fall; drainage holes, ventilation slots, a light-colored heat-reflective finish and a wide roof overhang for shade; subfloors or removable trays for easy nest replacement, and a scoop of pine needles/wood chips as starter nesting material; a **predator baffle** (stovepipe or cone) on the pole against snakes, raccoons and cats, plus owl/hawk guards of wire mesh over the entries; a placement plan — 30–100 feet from human housing, in the open with clear flight paths and no trees within about 40–60 feet, near water; and management extras like a sparrow/starling trapping plan, decoys and a dawnsong audio lure, plus a landlord's logbook of eggs and fledglings.

Judges would score biological correctness (compartment size, hole shape and height, ventilation, drainage), predator- and competitor-proofing, ease of lowering and cleaning for nest checks, weather durability and craftsmanship, use of lightweight/recycled materials and cost, and creative appearance — with the grand prize going to whichever house actually attracts martins and fledges the most young in its first season.

Picture an architecture firm's **"Design the Shelter" competition** for a humane society — teams compete to design (and the winner gets built) a new animal‑shelter building that houses homeless dogs and cats until adoption.

A strong entry would include: indoor–outdoor **double‑sided kennel runs** with guillotine doors so a dog is never disturbed during cleaning, solid (not chain‑link) dividers to block visual stress and disease spread, and sealed, sloped epoxy or trowelled‑concrete floors with trench drains and radiant heat; **cat colony rooms and multi‑compartment condos** with portals between litter and sleeping areas, window catios, climbing shelves and hiding boxes; a **zoned HVAC system** with 10–15 air changes an hour and no shared air between intake, isolation, adoption and surgery areas; separate intake/stray holding, quarantine and sick bays with their own entrance, foot baths and PPE stations; sound‑absorbing ceilings, baffles and acoustic panels to keep the notorious dog‑bark noise down; an on‑site spay/neuter surgery suite, treatment room, grooming/bathing area and food‑prep kitchen; homelike **"real‑life" get‑acquainted rooms**, play yards, agility lawns and walking trails for enrichment and adopter meet‑ups; laundry, storage, staff and volunteer space; and a welcoming, daylit public lobby with adoption counselling nooks, clear wayfinding and a memorial garden — plus sustainability features (solar panels, water recycling, easily disinfected non‑porous finishes) and a phased budget.

Judges would score animal welfare and stress reduction, disease control and biosecurity, noise and odour management, staff workflow efficiency, adopter appeal and length‑of‑stay reduction, durability and cleanability of materials, cost per animal housed, and architectural warmth and creativity.

It could be an **artificial penguin nest design competition** — the kind conservation groups have run for the endangered African penguin, where teams (engineers, ceramicists, design students, materials scientists) compete to build a burrow substitute to replace the guano the colonies lost, with winning prototypes trialled on real breeding islands.

A typical entry would include: a domed, burrow‑shaped shell moulded from fibreglass, ceramic, recycled plastic or geotextile‑and‑cement, sized for two adults plus two chicks with room to turn around and preen; a double‑layered or foam‑cored wall with a reflective white/pale exterior and insulating air gap so the interior stays below the lethal ~35 °C on a blazing summer day yet stays warm on cold, wet nights; a low, narrow, shaded entrance tunnel or hooded porch that keeps out direct sun, wind‑blown sand and, crucially, kelp gulls, ibis and other egg predators, while letting the parents shuffle in easily on their bellies; passive cross‑ventilation vents placed high and screened, plus a raised, ridged or perforated floor and a drainage lip so the nest never floods or puddles in rain; a sand/guano‑friendly base that can be part‑buried and anchored against gales, with a scoop of nesting material (twigs, feathers, pebbles) inside; UV‑stable, non‑toxic, guano‑ and salt‑spray‑resistant materials expected to last a decade or more; a removable lid or hatch for researchers to weigh chicks, check eggs and clean between seasons; camouflage colouring and a low profile so it blends into the colony; and a deployment plan (placement, spacing, orientation away from afternoon sun) with data loggers recording internal temperature and humidity.

Judges would score thermal performance against logger data first, then breeding success — occupancy rates, eggs laid and chicks fledged compared with natural burrows and surface nests — plus predator‑proofing, durability in a harsh marine environment, cost and ease of mass‑manufacture and transport by boat, use of recycled materials, and ease of monitoring, with the grand prize going to the design the penguins themselves choose most often and raise the most chicks in.

It could be an aerospace‑engineering student challenge — a "Design an Animal Habitat for Space" competition, where teams build a flight‑ready module to keep research animals (mice, quail, zebrafish, fruit flies or crickets) alive on the ISS or a Mars transit.

A winning entry would include: a sealed, launch‑rated enclosure that fits a standard payload locker and survives vibration and g‑loads; microgravity‑appropriate interior surfaces — grid‑mesh walls, grab bars, tethers and textured footholds instead of a "floor" — so the animals can cling, push off and orient themselves; a closed‑loop life‑support package with HEPA/charcoal‑filtered airflow, CO₂ scrubbing, oxygen supply, humidity and temperature control, and a slight negative pressure so dander and odour never escape into the crew cabin; capillary/nipple water dispensers and paste or gel food bars that won't crumble into floating debris; an airflow‑driven waste‑capture system with replaceable trays and antimicrobial liners; LED lighting on a programmable day/night cycle plus infrared cameras for filming behaviour in the dark; sensors and telemetry streaming temperature, humidity, O₂/CO₂, activity and body mass to the ground team; glovebox‑style transfer ports and a separation/quarantine compartment so crew can handle animals, dose them or remove one without releasing the others; radiation shielding and a centrifuge option to test artificial gravity; enrichment such as huddling nooks, chew material and shelters to reduce stress on a months‑long mission; and a full animal‑welfare protocol covering crew training, contingency plans and humane endpoints.

Judges would score animal survival, health and welfare, containment and crew safety, closed‑loop efficiency (mass, power and volume budgets), science return and data quality, serviceability by a gloved astronaut, and engineering elegance — with bonus points for a prototype that performs on a parabolic "vomit comet" flight test.

It could be a farm-and-conservation-group **barn owl nest box building competition**, where woodshop classes, young farmers and volunteers compete to build the best owl box, with the winners mounted in barns, on poles and in isolated trees to give the birds a home (and free rodent control) in place of lost hollow trees and old buildings.

A typical entry would include: a big, deep box of untreated exterior-grade plywood or rough-sawn timber (roughly 24–36" long, 16" wide and 16–18" tall — barn owls need far more room than a songbird box, since a brood can be five or six chicks); an entrance hole about 4½–6" square or oval, set high and off to one end so a wobbly owlet can't tumble straight out; an internal **exercise ledge or landing platform** outside the hole for branching youngsters, and a lip or sill at the front so eggs and pellets don't roll away; a sloped, overhanging waterproof roof with sealed seams, high ventilation gaps and small drainage holes in the floor; a rough or cleated interior wall and an inner baffle wall creating a dark, draught-free nesting chamber away from the entrance; a bedding layer of wood chips or shredded bark (owls build no nest of their own); a hinged side or end panel with a secure latch for annual cleaning and chick ringing; predator-proofing — a smooth pole with a stovepipe baffle, or an interior barn placement with a flight opening, away from raccoons, and sited well back from busy roads to prevent traffic deaths; and a mounting plan specifying 10–20 feet up, facing away from prevailing weather, overlooking rough grassland or field margins good for voles.

Judges would score biological correctness against wildlife-trust specifications (chamber size, hole dimensions, exercise ledge, drainage), weather-tightness and expected 15–20 year lifespan, safety and ease of access for cleaning and monitoring, use of non-toxic reclaimed timber, craftsmanship of the joinery, cost and how many a team can produce, and the quality of the siting/monitoring plan — with the top prize going to whichever box is actually occupied and fledges owlets in its first season.

It could be an Audubon chapter's **"Build a Chimney Swift Tower" competition**, where woodshop classes, master‑naturalist teams and scout troops compete to build artificial nesting/roosting chimneys for swifts, with the winners erected at nature centers, parks and schoolyards to replace the capped and demolished masonry chimneys the birds have lost.

A typical entry would include: a free‑standing tower roughly 8–12 feet tall (or a wall‑mounted "kiosk" version) framed of exterior‑grade plywood over a treated 4×4 or steel post, set in a deep concrete footing engineered against wind; an **interior shaft about 11×14 inches** — narrow enough for the birds to brace against opposite walls, tall enough for chicks to climb — lined with rough‑sawn, unsanded, horizontally grooved or scratched wood (no metal, no smooth or slick surfaces, no treated lumber inside) so swifts can cling with their tiny claws and stiff tail spines and glue their half‑saucer twig nests to the wall with saliva; a wide, open top with a **sun shield/rain cap and shade skirt** so downpours and heat can't cook or drown the brood, plus double‑wall or insulated construction and a light‑colored exterior to buffer temperature swings; ventilation gaps and a screened, angled floor with drainage and a removable clean‑out door for the annual sweeping of nests and droppings; **predator‑proofing** — a smooth pole with a stovepipe baffle, sealed seams and no ledges for raccoons, snakes, cats or starlings; a siting plan (open area, clear flight path, near water and insect‑rich habitat, away from lights and traffic) with a compass orientation; and finishing touches like cedar shingles, painted murals or interpretive signage and an inspection camera in the shaft.

Judges would score biological correctness against Driftwood Wildlife/Audubon specifications (shaft dimensions, wall texture, height, ventilation, rain protection), thermal performance, structural stability in storms, ease of annual cleaning and monitoring, use of reclaimed and non‑toxic materials, cost and how many a team can produce, craftsmanship and artistic appeal — with the grand prize going to whichever tower is actually occupied by a nesting pair or a migration roost in its first season.

Think of a wildlife charity's **"Build the Best Hedgehog House" competition**, where families, garden clubs and woodwork classes compete to make a hibernation home for hedgehogs, with the winners installed in gardens, allotments and school grounds.

A strong entry would include: a sturdy box roughly 40 × 30 × 30 cm made from untreated FSC or reclaimed timber (or thick recycled plastic/wicker), big enough for a hibernating adult and a litter of hoglets; a **short entrance tunnel about 13 cm square and 30 cm long**, angled or offset so badgers, foxes, cats and dogs can't reach in; an internal sleeping chamber separated from the tunnel by a baffle wall to block draughts and rain; small screened ventilation holes near the top and a slightly raised or slatted floor with drainage so the bedding stays dry; a sloped, overhanging, waterproof roof (roofing felt, tiles or a living sedum lid) that is hinged for annual checks and cleaning; no nails or screws poking through the inside, no treated wood, creosote or toxic paint, and no plastic netting the animal could snag on; a starter bed of dry leaves, straw and hay left in the chamber; a camouflage finish in browns and greens, plus a plan for siting it in a quiet, shady spot backed against a hedge, wall or log pile, half-buried in leaves and brushwood, near a supply of meat-based cat food and a shallow water dish, with a 13 cm "hedgehog highway" gap cut in the fence to let animals reach it.

Judges would score warmth, dryness and predator-proofing, correct tunnel and chamber dimensions to national hedgehog-society specifications, safety and non-toxicity of every material, ease of cleaning and monitoring, durability outdoors over several winters, use of scrap or sustainable materials and low cost, craftsmanship and decorative charm — with the top prize going to whichever house is actually occupied, ideally by a nesting or hibernating hedgehog caught on a trail camera or footprint tunnel that first season.

It could be a **"Refine the Cage" laboratory‑animal housing design competition** (the kind the NC3Rs, a veterinary school or a lab‑animal science association runs), where students, technicians and equipment designers compete to create better housing for research mice, rats, zebrafish or macaques, judged by welfare scientists and animal technologists.

A strong entry would include: an individually ventilated cage or tank with generous floor area and, crucially, **height for rearing and climbing**, allowing stable social groups rather than single housing; a deep layer of aspen/corncob bedding and a big wad of nesting material (nestlets, shredded paper, hay) so mice can build a proper insulating dome and thermoregulate; shelters, red translucent tunnels, cardboard huts, gnawing sticks, ladders, platforms, a running wheel or wading/climbing structures for enrichment, plus foraging/scatter‑feeding and puzzle feeders instead of only a hopper; species‑appropriate lighting on a dim, red‑shifted or reversed day/night cycle with dawn/dusk ramps, low‑noise and low‑vibration construction to avoid ultrasound and infrasound stress; HEPA‑filtered airflow with the correct air changes but no draughts, stable temperature/humidity, and ammonia control that still lets the animals keep some scent‑marked bedding at cage change; refined handling features — a tunnel or cupped‑hand transfer tube rather than tail lifting, transparent walls for non‑invasive observation, and video/RFID/home‑cage monitoring so data are collected without removing the animal; a divider or mesh partition for pair separation, breeding, quarantine or post‑surgical recovery, easy‑access water via bottle or automatic lixit, and autoclavable, durable, easy‑sanitising materials; plus a costing sheet, rack‑density calculation and a written justification citing welfare evidence and the 3Rs.

Judges would score animal welfare and expression of natural behaviours (nest scores, burrowing, climbing, social contact), stress and health indicators, scientific validity and reproducibility of data collected in it, biosecurity and hygiene, ergonomics and workload for the technicians, durability, cost and rack footprint, and originality — with bonus points for a working prototype and behavioural data showing the animals prefer it over standard housing.

Picture a falconry club or raptor‑rehab centre's **"Best Mews" building competition**, where apprentices, woodworkers and ag‑shop classes compete to build housing for a hawk, falcon or owl — judged against the state/federal falconry facility standards a licensing inspector would apply.

A strong entry would include: a solid, weather‑tight shed‑style mews big enough for the bird to hop and bate without hitting the walls, with **smooth solid walls or vertical wooden slats/bars (never wire mesh or chain link, which shreds feathers and cere)**; a sand, pea‑gravel or wood‑chip floor that drains and can be raked clean, sloped to a door sill; barred or shuttered windows for natural light and cross‑ventilation with no draughts on the perches; a **double‑door safety porch/vestibule** with self‑closing, lockable doors so a loose bird can't escape and thieves or predators can't get in; a buried wire skirt and sealed gaps against raccoons, rats, cats and snakes; a range of perch types at correct heights — bow perch, block perch, ledge/shelf perch and a padded screen perch, all with astroturf, cocoa‑mat or rope surfacing to prevent bumblefoot, spaced so tail feathers and leash can't tangle; a wide, shallow bath pan by the door for filling from outside; a covered **weathering yard** of grass or gravel with shade, wind‑break panels and an overhead net or roof against wild raptors; plus a scale/weighing perch, hooks for leashes and swivels, a food‑prep area with freezer and lockable equipment room, moulted‑feather storage, and a night light or camera for checking the bird.

Judging would weigh bird safety and feather protection first, then escape‑ and predator‑proofing, ventilation, light and sanitation, compliance with the legal facility requirements, ease of daily servicing and weighing, durability and craftsmanship, use of reclaimed timber and modest cost — with bonus points for a design an inspector would pass on the spot and that keeps a bird in perfect feather through a full hunting season.

Picture a post‑bushfire **"Nest Box Blitz" competition** run by an Australian wildlife group, where Men's Sheds, school woodwork classes and arborist crews compete to build replacement tree hollows for possums, gliders, microbats and parrots, with the winners installed in burnt bushland reserves.

A typical entry would include: a box (or a chainsaw‑carved "chainsaw hollow"/salvaged log section) built to species‑specific dimensions — a small, high‑entrance box with a slot for feathertail and sugar gliders, a deeper chamber with a 100 mm hole for brushtail possums, a narrow crevice box for microbats, a tall log box for cockatoos; untreated marine‑ply or reclaimed hardwood with non‑toxic glue and stainless screws, no chemicals or gap‑free plastic; **thermal buffering** — double walls, insulated lids, a light‑coloured or bark‑clad exterior and shaded orientation (south/east facing) so the box doesn't cook animals in a heatwave; a sloped, overhanging waterproof lid that hinges for monitoring, with drainage holes, high vents and a draught baffle; a roughened or grooved interior climbing strip and ladder to the entrance, plus a scoop of leaf litter, shredded bark or eucalypt leaves as starter bedding; predator‑ and competitor‑proofing — entrance sized to exclude larger possums, mynas and starlings, no perch, and a smooth trunk collar or metal band against goannas, cats and rats; **tree‑friendly mounting** using rubber‑padded straps, coach‑screws with spacers or a bracket that won't ringbark the trunk, at the right height and near feed trees and connective canopy; and a siting/monitoring plan with GPS points, a QR‑code tag, camera traps and spring occupancy surveys.

Judges would score species‑appropriate design against wildlife‑agency specs, internal temperature performance in summer, weather‑tightness and expected 10–20 year lifespan, safety and non‑toxicity, ease of mounting and inspection, use of salvaged timber and low cost per box, how many the team can produce in a build day, and craftsmanship — with the grand prize going to whichever box is occupied by breeding wildlife (glider, possum, bat or parrot) first.

It could be a grassland conservation group's **"Build a Better Burrow" competition**, where volunteers, FFA chapters and welding/shop classes compete to make artificial nesting burrows for burrowing owls (the winners installed on prairie preserves, airfields and reclaimed mine land where prairie dog and badger diggings have vanished).

A typical entry would include: a buried nest chamber — a plastic 5‑gallon bucket, milk crate, wooden box or half‑barrel roughly 12–18" across and tall enough for an adult to stand — set 2–3 feet down on a bed of gravel for drainage, with a bedding scoop of shredded bark, dry grass and cow/horse manure to mimic the natural burrow; one or two lengths of 4" flexible corrugated drain pipe or PVC forming a curved, 6–10 foot **entry tunnel** angled up to daylight so rain drains away and light doesn't reach the chamber, with a second tunnel as an escape exit; a low earthen apron/mound of loose soil at the mouth for the owls' habitual "porch," plus a nearby perch post, T‑stump or fence rail for the male to stand sentry; predator‑proofing — tunnel diameter narrow enough to exclude badgers, coyotes and dogs, a buried hardware‑cloth collar, and no large stones that could collapse the shaft; a screw‑down access lid or inspection tube with a soil cap so biologists can band chicks and clean it out annually, and a peephole or burrow‑cam port; UV‑stable, non‑toxic, chew‑ and freeze‑thaw‑resistant materials expected to last a decade underground; and a siting plan — short‑grazed open grassland, away from roads, tunnel facing away from prevailing storms, several burrows clustered as satellite roosts so a family can spread out.

Judges would score biological correctness against state wildlife‑agency specifications (chamber size, tunnel length/curve, drainage, escape route), predator‑ and flood‑proofing, internal temperature and humidity stability, ease of installation with hand tools and of annual monitoring, durability, cost and how many a team can produce in a build day, and use of salvaged materials — with the grand prize going to whichever burrow is actually adopted by a pair and fledges owlets in its first season.

It could be a garden club's "Toad Abode & Frog Hollow" contest, where kids and gardeners compete to build the best little home for backyard amphibians, with the winners installed in school gardens and allotments.

A typical entry would include: an overturned or half‑buried terracotta pot, hollowed log, stacked flat stones or hand‑built clay dome with a doorway roughly 3–4 inches wide, set on the shady, north side of the garden and sunk an inch or two into cool, damp soil; a floor of loose leaf litter, moss and damp soil so the toad can burrow and stay moist; a shallow, gently sloping saucer or sunken dish of dechlorinated water nearby (deep enough to soak in, shallow enough that nothing drowns), topped up daily; surrounding cover of dense low plants, ferns, mulch, a log pile and flat rocks for hiding and a sunny stone for the odd basking spot; a pesticide‑ and slug‑pellet‑free zone plus a night light set a little way off to draw in the moths, beetles and slugs the toads eat; smooth, non‑toxic, unglazed materials with no sharp edges, no treated wood and no gaps that could trap a leg; protection from cats and lawnmowers, and a route in and out of the garden (a gap under the fence, a log ramp out of any window well or pond); and decorative touches — painted mushroom roofs, mosaic tiles, pebble doorsteps or a whole "toad village" theme.

Judges would score coolness, dampness and shade of the interior, correct doorway size, water provision, safety and non‑toxicity of materials, weather durability and ease of siting, use of recycled pots and scrap, and charm of the decoration — with the top prize going to whichever abode is actually taken up by a toad or frog, caught on camera that summer.

It could be an elementary‑school **"Habitat in a Shoebox" diorama contest**, where students each draw an animal and biome and build a miniature scene of its natural home, displayed in the gym on science night.

A typical entry would include: a shoebox or cardboard flat painted with a background sky/horizon; a sculpted terrain of papier‑mâché, clay, foam or crumpled paper — sand dunes, tundra permafrost, a coral reef, a rainforest floor; ground cover of real twigs, moss, pebbles, sand, cotton "snow" or dyed rice; construction‑paper or pipe‑cleaner trees, tissue‑paper leaves and paper vines for the canopy layers; blue cellophane or resin for a river, pond or ocean; the animal itself modeled in clay, printed, or a small plastic figure, shown doing something real — a burrow, den, nest or web, and a food source (a prey animal, berries, plankton) plus predators and other species that share the habitat; hand‑lettered labels and arrows identifying the producers, consumers, food chain and adaptations; a fact card giving the biome's climate, rainfall and location on a small map; and often a flashlight "sun," a string‑hung flying bird, or a peephole viewing window for effect.

Judges would score scientific accuracy (correct plants, animals and climate for the biome), how well it explains the animal's adaptations and food web, neatness and craftsmanship, use of recycled or natural materials, the clarity of the labels and the student's short spoken presentation — with bonus points for creativity and for the most convincing miniature world.

It could be a koi club or garden‑show **"Best Koi Pond" building competition**, where landscapers, water‑garden dealers and backyard hobbyists compete to construct a pond for prize nishikigoi, judged on site by koi judges and pond builders.

A winning entry would include: a generously sized, deep pond (typically 1,500+ gallons and at least 4–6 ft deep, so the fish can grow, escape herons and overwinter safely under ice) built of concrete/shotcrete or EPDM liner over protective underlay, with vertical or steeply sloped smooth walls and no sharp edges or gravel bottom to trap waste; a bowl‑shaped, sloping floor feeding **bottom drains** with air domes, plus mid‑water and skimmer intakes so debris and settled solids are pulled out continuously; a gravity‑fed filtration train — settlement/vortex chamber or sieve, brush and matting mechanical stages, then a bakki shower, moving‑bed or trickle **biofilter** with plenty of cultivated bacteria surface area, backed by UV clarifiers for green water and a bead or drum filter; aeration via air stones and a venturi return that creates a gentle circular current for exercise, with the whole volume turning over every one to two hours; heating/chiller and a de‑icer or bubbler for winter, plus automatic top‑off, dechlorinator, easy‑access valves, backwash lines and a discharge point; a shaded pergola, water lilies or shade sail, plus a heron‑deterring net, wire, motion sprinkler or steep walls, and a fence/edge detail for child safety; a planted bog or wetland filter of iris, watercress and rushes for nutrient export, kept separate from koi mouths; smooth pebble beach or viewing window, underwater lighting, waterfall and stream for oxygenation and sound; and a quarantine/hospital tank, feeding station, test kits and a water‑quality log (ammonia, nitrite, nitrate, KH, pH, temperature, dissolved oxygen).

Judges would score fish health, growth and colour, water clarity and measured water quality, correct depth, volume and turnover for the stocking level, filtration and plumbing engineering, ease of maintenance and cleaning, predator‑proofing and safety, quality of the surrounding landscaping and viewing experience, and craftsmanship of the construction — with bonus points for the pond whose koi win at the next show.

It could be a toy‑brick building contest — say a LEGO store or fan‑convention "Build a Zoo Habitat" challenge, where kids and AFOLs get a limited pile of bricks and a set time to construct an enclosure for a chosen animal minifigure/creature.

A winning build would typically include: a baseplate landscaped with sloped and stacked terrain — grassy plates, rockwork made from slopes and cheese wedges, sand‑coloured tiles, or transparent blue plates and tiles for a pool, stream or waterfall; brick‑built trees, leaf/plant elements, logs and vines for climbing and shade; a den, cave or nest box the animal can shelter in; feeding troughs, hay bales, hanging enrichment toys, ropes, tyres and a scratching post; barriers appropriate to the species — a moat, trans‑clear glass viewing panel, fence pieces or rock wall — plus a lockable keeper gate and a back‑of‑house night quarters; and visitor touches like a viewing platform, benches, litter bin, information signs with printed tiles, minifigure keepers with buckets and a camera‑toting family.

Judging would weigh how believably it suits that animal's needs, creative use of unusual parts ("NPU"), sturdiness of the build, colour blending and landscaping technique, storytelling and detail at minifigure scale, and staying within the brick and time limits — with bonus points for a clever moving feature such as a lifting gate or rotating turntable.

Picture a coastal conservation group's **"Build a Sea Turtle Nesting Beach" restoration competition**, where school teams, dune-restoration volunteers and coastal-engineering students each adopt a stretch of eroded shoreline and are judged after a nesting season on how many loggerheads or greens crawl up and successfully hatch.

A strong entry would include: a graded, gently sloping beach profile with a wide, dry backshore and a rebuilt **primary dune** raised with sand fencing, brush matting and Christmas-tree/sandbag cores to trap wind-blown sand; a planting of native dune stabilizers — sea oats, panic grass, railroad vine, beach sunflower, sea grape — planted on the dune face and back, never on the open nesting strand itself; removal of exotic invasives (Australian pine, beach vitex) whose dense roots trap hatchlings and whose shade cools nests; a cleared, obstacle-free crawl corridor with all beach furniture, boats, ruts and tire tracks removed nightly and no seawalls, rip-rap or hard armoring; **dark-sky lighting retrofits** on adjacent buildings — shielded, low-mounted, long-wavelength amber LEDs, tinted windows and "lights-out" ordinances — plus screening vegetation so hatchlings orient to the sea rather than the road; **predator exclusion** self-releasing wire cages or screens over marked nests, raccoon/coyote/ghost-crab management and dog leash rules; sand of the correct grain size, moisture, and colour so incubation temperature yields a balanced hatchling sex ratio (with temperature data loggers buried in mock nests to prove it); a relocation/hatchery plan for nests laid below the high-tide line, with shaded, ventilated corrals; a wrack line left intact for moisture and nutrients; marked nests with stakes, signage and a public education kiosk; and a monitoring package — dawn crawl surveys, nest inventories, hatch-and-emergence success counts, disorientation reports and drone imagery of the dune's growth.

Judges would score documented nesting crawls, hatch and emergence success and reduction in hatchling disorientation, ecological authenticity and survival rate of the native plantings, dune volume gained and storm resilience, permit compliance and safe handling protocols, cost and use of donated/recycled materials, volunteer and community involvement, and long-term self-sustaining function — with the trophy going to the stretch of beach that sends the most hatchlings safely into the surf.

Picture a herpetological society or land‑trust **"Build a Snake Hibernaculum" competition**, where volunteer teams, scout troops and ecology students each construct an artificial overwintering den/basking refuge on a nature reserve, judged the following spring on how many reptiles and amphibians actually use it.

A strong entry would include: a **south‑ or southwest‑facing site** on a well‑drained slope above the water table, chosen for winter sun and no flooding; a pit dug **below the local frost line** (often 4–6 ft) and backfilled with a loose, airy core of clean rubble — broken concrete, rock, stumps, logs and coarse gravel — so there are frost‑free voids and drainage but no soil slumping in; several **angled entrance/exit tunnels** made of drain pipe, hollow logs or stacked flat stones opening at different heights and aspects so snakes can move up and down through a temperature gradient; a capping mound of soil and turf with a **sun‑warmed rock apron, log pile and flat stones** on top for basking, plus a brush pile and tussocky grass for cover; a shed/gravel "sloughing" area and a nearby **egg‑laying/nesting mound of compost, sawdust or manure** for grass snakes and turtles; a shallow scrape or pond within travel distance for amphibians and drinking; predator‑ and disturbance‑proofing (entrances too narrow for badgers/dogs, no mown edges, set back from roads and trails, wire mesh where needed); native, chemical‑free planting and a connective corridor of rough grass or hedgerow linking it to existing habitat; and no treated timber, plastic sheeting or loose netting that could trap or poison animals.

Entries would come with a site plan, temperature/humidity data loggers buried in the core, trail‑camera or coverboard/artificial‑cover‑object monitoring, permits and landowner agreement, plus interpretive signage.

Judges would score thermal performance (proof the core stays above freezing yet cool and humid), correct depth, drainage and void structure, predator and flood protection, use of donated or salvaged rock and timber, buildability by volunteers in a day and cost, integration with surrounding habitat, and the monitoring plan — with the trophy going to whichever hibernaculum records the most snakes, lizards, newts and toads emerging from it in its first spring.

Picture a lake association's **"Floating Nesting Island Build-Off,"** where cottage owners, scout troops and shop classes compete to construct floating rafts that give common loons, terns and turtles a safe place to nest on lakes with fluctuating, eroded or predator-heavy shorelines — the winners towed out and anchored before ice-out.

A typical entry would include: a roughly 5×5-ft cedar or reclaimed-timber frame lashed together with stainless hardware, floated on sealed closed-cell billets, cedar logs or capped PVC pontoons (never crumbling bare styrofoam) so it rides just an inch or two above water; a coconut-coir or burlap-lined deck filled with a shallow bed of natural sod, sedge, sweet flag, rush and marsh grass plugs transplanted from the lake so the raft looks and smells like a real bog hummock; a scooped-out nest bowl in the center with a rim of vegetation for concealment, plus overhanging plants and a low "canopy" of wire mesh or brush that hides the sitting bird from eagles and gulls while leaving the sides open; a gently sloping ramp or notched log at water level so chicks and turtles can climb aboard and adults can slide off quickly; anchor lines with slack and a pulley/counterweight so the raft rises and falls with water levels and doesn't drift into boat lanes, with concrete-block or mushroom anchors; a "no-wake / loon nesting" marker buoy and shoreline signage keeping paddlers and anglers back; no lead, no treated lumber, no loose monofilament or netting that could entangle a bird; siting notes — a sheltered cove out of wave fetch and wind, away from shore predators like raccoons and mink, near quiet nursery water; and a monitoring package of a trail camera, banding access and a season log of eggs and chicks.

Judges would score biological correctness (freeboard height, nest bowl, chick ramp, concealment), stability in wind and boat wake, durability through ice-out and multiple seasons, predator- and entanglement-proofing, use of natural and salvaged materials, buildability and cost per raft, and how naturally it blends into the shoreline — with the trophy going to whichever island is actually claimed by a pair and fledges chicks in its first summer.

Think of a bake‑off style **"Edible Animal Habitat" gingerbread challenge** — the sort of holiday or county‑fair pastry competition where teams (bakers, culinary students, families) must build a fully edible model of a chosen creature's home, judged on both engineering and artistry.

A typical entry would include: a structural gingerbread or shortbread base and framework held together with royal icing "mortar," strong enough to stand for the whole display period; a sculpted terrain of modelling chocolate, fondant and rice‑crispy treat — mountain cliffs, a desert dune, a hollow tree trunk of pretzel‑rod and cocoa‑powder bark, or an arctic ice floe of isomalt and sugar glass; the habitat's key features rendered in candy — a shimmering blue isomalt pond or "ocean" with gelatin waves, a waterfall of piped icing, a den, burrow or nest hollowed underneath, a coral reef of piped meringue and sour‑ribbon seaweed, or a rainforest canopy of green‑tinted coconut, matcha buttercream moss and spun‑sugar vines; food sources and enrichment details like marzipan berries, chocolate‑rock caves, wafer logs and a licorice liana; the animals themselves — hand‑modelled fondant or chocolate bears, penguins, frogs or bees, posed doing something true to life (nesting, denning, hibernating, foraging); and finishing touches such as edible‑ink signage, an LED light hidden behind the sugar "ice," dusted cocoa soil, powdered‑sugar snow and a labelled card explaining the biome and species.

Judges would score structural soundness (does it hold up without hidden wire or non‑edible supports?), the "100% edible" rule and food safety, biological accuracy of the biome and its plants and animals, sugar‑work and modelling technique, colour and composition, theme storytelling, and overall wow factor — with bonus points for pieces auctioned off or displayed to raise money for a wildlife charity.

Picture an aquaculture‑engineering **"Design‑and‑Build the Best Fish Farm" competition**, where fisheries students, hatchery technicians and equipment firms compete to build a recirculating aquaculture system (RAS) or sea‑pen home for tilapia, trout or salmon, judged by fish vets and producers after a grow‑out trial.

A strong entry would include: **circular or raceway tanks** with a dual‑drain, self‑cleaning conical bottom and a tangential inlet that sets up a gentle, exercise‑promoting rotational current at species‑appropriate velocity; conservative **stocking densities** and tank depth/diameter ratios that let fish school naturally; a full water‑treatment train — drum/microscreen filter for solids, moving‑bed or trickling **biofilter** for ammonia and nitrite, degassing column for CO₂, protein skimmer/foam fractionator, UV or ozone disinfection — sized for a 95–99 % daily reuse rate; oxygen cones or diffusers with dissolved‑oxygen probes, plus **backup aeration, alarms, generator and redundant pumps** so a power cut can't wipe out the stock; automated monitoring/dosing of temperature, pH, alkalinity, salinity, TAN, nitrate and TSS with data logging; smooth, non‑abrasive, light‑coloured tank surfaces, covers and shading, low‑noise pumps and dimmable LED photoperiod lighting to reduce stress; **enrichment and welfare features** — structure or substrate for benthic species, current refuges, and gentle fish‑friendly handling: swim‑through grading, fish pumps, crowding screens, and a humane percussive/electrical stunning station; biosecurity zoning with quarantine and hatchery/nursery rooms, footbaths, effluent treatment, and escape prevention (screened outfalls, predator netting and seal‑proof, storm‑rated moorings for the net‑pen version); plus sustainability elements — heat recovery, solar, sludge to biogas or hydroponic/aquaponic nutrient reuse — and a costed business plan with feed‑conversion and mortality targets.

Judging would weigh fish health and welfare indicators (growth, FCR, fin and gill condition, mortality, stress hormones), water‑quality stability, biosecurity and escape prevention, energy and water efficiency, humane harvest, environmental discharge compliance, capital and running cost per kilo produced, and design ingenuity — with bonus points for the system that finishes the trial with the healthiest, fastest‑growing fish.

It could be an agricultural show's **"Build the Best Pig Ark" competition**, where farmers, ag‑college teams and woodwork classes compete to build portable outdoor pig housing for a free‑range herd, judged in the show ring and then put to work on a real paddock.

A typical entry would include: a curved or A‑frame ark on skids or a towing eye, light enough to be dragged to fresh ground by quad or tractor but heavy/anchored enough that a boar can't shove it over; a galvanised or insulated ply shell with a reflective outer skin and an insulated inner lining so it stays warm on frosty nights and doesn't cook pigs in summer sun; a wide, low doorway with a canvas or rubber flap and a raised sill to keep bedding in and draughts out; adjustable roof or gable vents and a shaded, overhanging eave; a slatted or removable floor (or open earth base) with deep straw bedding and drainage so it never turns to mud; **farrowing rails around the inside walls** and a creep area with a heat lamp so the sow can't crush her piglets; smooth interior surfaces with no protruding nails, splinters or sharp edges; a hinged roof panel or lift‑off end for inspecting litters, cleaning and disinfecting; and an outdoor package around it — a shaded wallow or mister for cooling (pigs can't sweat), a rooting/digging zone, sturdy trough or spill‑proof ad‑lib feeder, a nipple drinker on a frost‑protected line, scratching posts and enrichment such as straw bales, logs and rooting balls, plus electric‑fence paddock rotation and a mucking‑out/composting plan.

Judges would score pig comfort and welfare first (temperature control, ventilation, dryness, crush protection, wallow and rooting provision), then durability against a determined pig, portability and one‑person handling, ease of daily feeding, bedding and cleaning, biosecurity, use of reclaimed timber and cost per sow housed, and craftsmanship — with bonus points for a design a working stockperson says they'd buy on the spot.

Think of an **insect‑farming "Build the Best Cricket Rig" challenge** — the kind of competition run at an entomophagy expo, ag‑tech incubator or engineering school, where teams build a modular rearing habitat for edible insects (crickets, mealworms, black soldier fly larvae) and are judged after a full grow‑out cycle.

A typical entry would include: stackable, escape‑proof rearing bins or a vertical rack of smooth‑walled tubs with mesh‑screened lids (fine enough to hold pinhead nymphs but freely ventilating); a huge amount of vertical surface area packed in as cardboard egg‑flat stacks, corrugated inserts or 3‑D printed lattice so thousands of crickets can perch, hide and moult without crowding and cannibalising; a controlled micro‑climate — heat mats or a room heater with thermostat holding roughly 28–32 °C, humidity around 50–70 % via misters or a humidifier, and gentle airflow with dust/ammonia extraction and HEPA/fine screening to stop escapes and mite or pathogen (densovirus) entry; a moisture‑without‑drowning water station — hydrogel crystals, wicking mats or gravity nipple pads instead of open dishes; feed hoppers dosed with a milled bran/soy/vegetable‑waste ration, with a food‑safety plan for the waste streams used; **breeding provision** — separate laying bins of damp coco coir or sand for egg deposition, a nursery/incubation drawer for the pinheads, and a staged bin rotation so cohorts are age‑separated; a frass screen and slide‑out collection tray so droppings and exuviae can be sieved off (and sold as fertiliser); easy‑clean, food‑grade, autoclavable or wash‑down surfaces with sealed corners and a biosecurity zone with footbaths and quarantine bins; sensors and a dashboard logging temperature, humidity, CO₂ and feed use; a humane freezing/harvest chill station and processing area; plus a costed plan showing kilos of protein per square metre per month and feed‑conversion ratio.

Judges would score insect survival and yield, growth rate and feed conversion, welfare/density and escape‑ and pest‑proofing, hygiene and food safety, energy and space efficiency, use of recycled feed and reclaimed materials, ease of daily labour and harvesting, scalability and cost — with the top prize going to the rig that produces the healthiest, heaviest crop of insects per watt and square metre by the end of the trial.

Picture a smallholders' show or agri‑college **"Best Snail Farm" (heliciculture) build‑off**, where teams construct a habitat for edible garden snails (*Helix aspersa*) and are judged after a growing season on how well the stock breeds and fattens.

A typical entry would include: a shaded outdoor pen or polytunnel/greenhouse module with fine‑mesh netting overhead against birds and rodents; an escape‑proof perimeter — smooth inward‑lipped boards, a copper strip or a low‑voltage electric fence wire along the top rail, plus a buried skirt against moles and beetles; a bed of loose, friable, well‑drained, **calcium‑rich soil** (limed to near‑neutral pH) deep enough for the snails to bury themselves and lay their eggs; ranks of angled wooden or corrugated **shelter boards, tiles and pallet "condos"** giving huge amounts of shaded resting surface per square metre; a living forage crop of chard, kale, sunflower, clover and dandelion for grazing and shade, topped up with a bran/calcium‑carbonate ration in shallow trays that don't drown the stock; an automatic **misting/irrigation line on a timer** to hold roughly 75–95 % humidity and 15–24 °C, with shade cloth for heatwaves and a frost/hibernation plan; separate **breeding and egg‑laying boxes** of damp compost, a hatchery/nursery bed for the tiny juveniles and size‑graded grow‑out pens so cohorts stay uniform; drainage, slug‑pellet‑free and pesticide‑free zoning, a footbath/biosecurity routine and traps for predatory beetles and flatworms; easy‑clean, food‑grade surfaces and a purging/fasting chamber plus chilled harvest station at the end; and a costed plan showing kilos harvested per square metre, feed conversion and mortality rate.

Judges would score snail survival, growth rate and shell quality, breeding and hatch success, humidity/temperature control, escape‑ and predator‑proofing, hygiene and food‑safety compliance, labour efficiency and ease of harvesting, use of reclaimed timber and recycled materials, and the ingenuity and scalability of the design — with the top prize going to the pen producing the heaviest, healthiest crop of snails per square metre.

It could be a Ducks Unlimited chapter's **wood duck nest box building competition**, where sportsmen's clubs, FFA chapters and shop classes compete to build the best nesting box, with the winners installed on marshes, beaver ponds and flooded timber before spring.

A typical entry would include: a deep box of untreated rough‑cut cedar or exterior plywood roughly 24 inches tall with a 10×10‑inch floor (hens need room for a dozen eggs and a big brood); an oval entrance about 3 inches high by 4 inches wide set near the top — sized to admit a hen wood duck but exclude raccoons; a rough, kerfed or hardware‑cloth "ladder" running from the hole down to the floor so ducklings can climb out on day one; 3–4 inches of wood shavings or sawdust as nesting material (never hay or straw); a sloped, overhanging, weather‑tight roof with drainage holes in the floor and vent gaps under the eaves; a hinged side or front panel with a hook‑and‑eye latch for the annual clean‑out and egg/brood check; predator‑proofing in the form of a smooth metal pipe or 4×4 post fitted with a cone or stovepipe baffle, no perch under the hole, and a metal plate around the entrance to stop squirrels chewing it wider; galvanized or stainless screws rather than nails so it can be reopened; and a siting plan — mounted 6–10 feet over water or 20–30 feet back on shore, facing open water, spaced apart or with baffled backs so hens don't "dump nest" in each other's boxes, near buttonbush and duckweed brood cover.

Judges would score biological correctness against state waterfowl‑agency specs (cavity size, hole dimensions, exit ladder, shavings), predator‑ and starling‑proofing, weather‑tightness and expected 15–20 year lifespan, ease of mounting and annual cleaning, use of donated or reclaimed lumber and cost per box, how many a team can turn out in a build day, and craftsmanship — with the top prize going to whichever box a hen actually uses and hatches a brood from that first spring.

It could be a **"Living Seawall" habitat-tile design competition**, run by a port authority, marine institute or design school, where teams design and cast panels that get bolted onto the flat, lifeless concrete of a harbour wall to turn it back into rocky-shore habitat, judged after a year of dive and quadrat surveys.

A strong entry would include: a 3D-modelled and 3D-printed mould used to cast a panel of low-carbon, pH-neutral marine concrete (often with crushed oyster shell, basalt or biochar aggregate, and basalt/GFRP reinforcement instead of rusting steel), sized and drilled to bolt onto standard seawall blocks with stainless or composite fixings and a corrosion-safe backing; a complex, biomimetic surface copying natural rock — deep crevices, overhangs, honeycomb pits, ridges and swim-throughs at a whole range of scales so everything from barnacle and mussel spat to juvenile fish, crabs, snails and blennies finds shelter from waves, sun and predators; **water-retaining "micro rock pools"** and shaded hollows that hold moisture through low tide so intertidal life survives desiccation; a deliberately rough, textured, alkaline-buffered finish to encourage algal turf, coralline algae and oyster/mussel settlement, sometimes seeded with spat-on-shell, kelp gametophytes or transplanted natives; tiles zoned and mounted at the correct tidal heights (splash, intertidal, subtidal) with a mosaic of different tile types rather than one repeated pattern; no toxins, antifoulants, plastics or microplastic-shedding materials; a fitting plan that doesn't compromise the wall's structural or navigation function, plus safe access for maintenance and monitoring quadrats, photo-quadrat markers and settlement plates.

Judges would score documented biodiversity gain and species recruitment versus bare-wall control panels, ecological realism of the surface complexity, structural durability and fixing safety in storms and boat wash, environmental footprint of the concrete mix, cost and repeatability of casting at scale, ease of installation by divers or from a barge, water-quality and filter-feeder benefits, and aesthetic/public-education value — with the trophy going to whichever tile design hosts the most species and the healthiest oyster and algal cover after its first year underwater.

It could be a river‑trust **"Build an Artificial Otter Holt" competition**, where volunteer groups, angling clubs and countryside‑management students each construct a breeding holt on a river bank, judged the following season on whether otters move in.

A strong entry would include: a bankside site above the highest flood line but within a few metres of the water, screened by scrub and away from paths, dogs and roads; an excavated chamber roughly 60 × 60 cm floored with dry sand or gravel for drainage and roofed by a "log cabin" of stacked hardwood logs, brushwood, root‑plates or old stumps (or a buried concrete/plastic chamber for a permanent version), capped with a geotextile or soil‑and‑turf mound so it disappears into the bank; **two or more low, narrow entrance tunnels of drainage pipe, hollow log or stacked stone** — one opening below the waterline or into a reed‑fringed slipway, one dry escape exit inland — sized to admit an otter but exclude dogs and badgers; a separate dry lying‑up couch and, above it, a hidden ventilation shaft of pipe or loose stone capped with brash so the chamber stays fresh but dark; a bed of dry grass, reed and leaf litter; a nearby sprainting rock, slide, and log pile/scrub corridor linking it to bankside cover; untreated timber only — no creosote, plastic netting or wire that could trap or poison cubs; and permits, landowner agreement, plus monitoring by camera trap, footprint tunnel and spraint surveys.

Judging would weigh siting and flood‑proofing, correct chamber and tunnel dimensions to wildlife‑trust specification, dryness, ventilation and darkness, disturbance and predator protection, use of locally sourced or salvaged timber and stone, buildability by volunteers in a day, how invisibly it blends into the bank, and the monitoring plan — with the trophy to whichever holt first records an otter (or better, a breeding female and cubs) in residence.

It could be a **"Closed Ecosystem Jar" (ecosphere) competition** — the kind run by a biology club, aquarium society or science‑YouTube challenge, where entrants build a sealed, no‑input miniature world and are judged months later on whether it's still alive.

A typical entry would include: a large, thick‑walled glass jar, demijohn or Kilner vessel, sterilised and sealed with a gasket lid (or left cracked for a "closed‑ish" class); a substrate layer of aquasoil, sand or pond‑mud capped with gravel, plus a handful of leaf litter, catappa/oak leaves and driftwood as a slow‑release carbon and biofilm source; "living water" collected from an established pond or mature tank, seeded with a whole microfauna community — green algae, diatoms, paramecia, rotifers, copepods, daphnia, ostracods, seed shrimp, detritus worms, ramshorn or bladder snails, and a few *Neocaridina* shrimp or scuds as the visible headline "animal"; oxygenating plants balanced to the bioload — hornwort, elodea, moss, subwassertang, duckweed or a marimo ball — with emergent plants or a mossy riparium shore in a half‑land version housing springtails and isopods; hiding and grazing structure of cholla wood, cork, lava rock and stone crevices so shrimp can moult safely; a source of calcium (crushed cuttlebone or shell) for shells and exoskeletons; and a stable, low‑tech life‑support plan — indirect natural light or a timed low‑wattage LED, a cool, steady room temperature, no feeding, no filter, no water changes, no top‑ups.

Judges would score survival and reproduction (bonus points for a berried shrimp or a second generation hatching), self‑sustaining nutrient cycling and water clarity, absence of algae blooms, ammonia spikes or die‑offs, biodiversity and the completeness of the food web (producers, grazers, detritivores, decomposers), the elegance and naturalism of the little "scape," documentation — a build log, photos, parameter tests and a written explanation of the carbon, oxygen and nitrogen cycles at work — and creativity in theming (a flooded forest floor, a rocky spring, a paludarium shoreline), with the trophy going to whichever sealed world is still thriving longest at the final judging.

Picture a wildlife trust's **"Build a Sand Martin Bank" competition**, where volunteer groups, gravel‑pit operators, engineering students and Men's Shed teams compete to construct an artificial nesting cliff for sand martins (bank swallows), with the winning banks erected beside lakes, quarry pools and restored wetlands where natural eroding riverbanks have been lost.

A typical entry would include: a solid, free‑standing tower or bunded earth‑and‑sleeper wall with a **vertical, overhanging face** (never a slope, so predators can't scramble down), raised at least 2–3 m above ground or standing in shallow water for extra protection from foxes, rats, cats and mink; rows of **entrance holes about 6–7 cm across**, spaced roughly 15–20 cm apart in staggered ranks near the top of the face, each leading to a horizontal **nest tunnel 45–60 cm long** made from plastic drainpipe, clay pipe or drilled timber, gently sloping upwards so rain drains out; **removable nest chambers** — wooden or plastic boxes bolted behind the face, filled with a scoop of sand, soil or dry grass and accessible from a rear service door or walkway so they can be cleaned of fleas and old nests each winter; a rendered or sand‑faced front (a compacted sand/clay mix behind a retaining mesh, or a textured concrete panel) so the birds land on something that looks and feels like a natural cliff; a wide, overhanging capping roof to keep the burrows dry and shaded; no perches, ledges or climbable vegetation on the face, plus a smooth metal skirt or moat and a fenced exclusion zone against disturbance; siting notes — facing away from prevailing weather (often south/east), with clear flight lines, open water and insect‑rich meadow or marsh within easy foraging distance; and finishing extras such as sound‑lure speakers playing colony calls, decoy birds, a ringing/monitoring hatch, nest cameras and interpretive signage.

Judges would score biological correctness against RSPB/wildlife‑agency specifications (hole size and spacing, tunnel length and gradient, chamber dimensions, drainage), predator‑ and flood‑proofing, structural stability and expected 20‑year lifespan, ease of annual cleaning and ringing access, use of reclaimed pipe, sleepers and quarry spoil, cost and buildability by volunteers, and how naturally it blends into the landscape — with the trophy going to whichever bank attracts the biggest colony and fledges the most chicks in its first season.

It could be a coastal community's **"Build a Mangrove Nursery Forest" restoration competition**, where school teams, fishing cooperatives and university coastal‑ecology clubs each adopt a degraded stretch of tidal mudflat or abandoned shrimp pond and are judged a year or two later on how much living fish‑nursery habitat they've created.

A strong entry would include: a site assessment showing the right **tidal elevation, salinity and inundation frequency** for each species, with breached pond walls, re‑dug tidal creeks and culverts to restore natural water flow (hydrology first, planting second); a community **propagule nursery** of locally collected seeds and seedlings raised in biodegradable coir or bamboo pots rather than plastic bags; a zoned planting scheme matching species to elevation — *Rhizophora* stilt‑root mangroves on the seaward fringe, *Avicennia* and *Sonneratia* with their pneumatophores on softer flats, *Bruguiera* and *Nypa* landward — planted at natural, mixed‑age spacing instead of monoculture rows; **wave‑attenuation and sediment‑trapping structures** such as permeable brushwood or bamboo fences, coir logs and oyster‑shell bunds to hold mud in place while the seedlings root; log tangles, root mats and shallow channels that give juvenile snapper, mullet, mud crabs, prawns and shrimp somewhere to shelter and feed; removal of invasive weeds and rubbish, exclusion of grazing livestock and boat traffic, and a mangrove‑friendly zoning agreement with local fishers; nest and roost provision for kingfishers, egrets, herons and monkeys as the canopy closes; plus a monitoring package — seedling survival counts, canopy cover, sediment accretion pins, water‑quality and salinity logs, fish and crab trap surveys, bird counts and drone imagery — and interpretive signs, boardwalks and school field‑trip programmes.

Judges would score seedling survival and natural recruitment rate, correctness of species‑to‑elevation matching and hydrological restoration, documented gains in fish, crab and bird abundance, sediment accretion and shoreline/storm‑surge protection benefit, carbon sequestration ("blue carbon") estimates, use of local, biodegradable and salvaged materials, cost per hectare, community involvement and long‑term stewardship plan — with the trophy going to whichever plot becomes a self‑seeding, self‑sustaining forest full of young fish rather than a field of dead sticks.

Picture a marine‑biology department or public‑aquarium **"Design the Best Octopus Enclosure" competition**, where aquarists, engineering students and DIY cephalopod keepers compete to build a tank a giant Pacific or common octopus can actually thrive in — famously the hardest animal in the aquarium trade to house.

A winning entry would include: a large, cold, deep tank (hundreds of gallons for a big species) with a chiller holding stable species‑appropriate temperature, high dissolved oxygen and pristine, fully cycled water — heavy protein skimming, oversized biofiltration and a big turnover rate to cope with an octopus's messy, high‑ammonia waste; **absolute escape‑proofing**, since an octopus can squeeze through any gap wider than its beak: a locked, weighted, gasketed lid, mesh or perforated covers over every overflow and standpipe, AstroTurf or artificial‑grass strips around the rim it dislikes crossing, sealed cable and plumbing penetrations, and a low‑voltage "hot wire" or lip in some designs; a naturalistic rockscape of live rock, ledges and caves with **several den options** — a barrel, clay pot, PVC lair or rock crevice with an entrance sized so it feels tight and secure — plus sand or shell substrate it can rearrange, since redecorating is natural behaviour; a smooth‑surfaced interior with no sharp edges, no copper anywhere in the system (lethal to invertebrates), and no coral or fish tankmates that would be eaten or that would nip the arms; a strong **enrichment programme built into the design** — puzzle feeders, screw‑top jars, Lego‑style boxes, mirrors, textured toys, live crabs and shrimp for hunting, varied feeding times and hiding of food so the animal forages rather than begs; dim, adjustable lighting on a natural day/night cycle with shaded areas, low‑noise pumps and vibration isolation to reduce stress; quarantine/holding and a separate acclimation tank, a service hatch and easy access for feeding and cleaning without releasing the animal; monitoring and welfare records — feeding logs, weight, colour/behaviour notes, senescence and end‑of‑life planning, and cameras for time‑lapse observation.

Judges would score escape‑proofing above all, then water quality and life‑support engineering, den and denning security, enrichment variety and evidence of natural behaviours (hunting, problem solving, exploring), safety of every material used, ease of maintenance and public viewing/interpretation value — with the trophy going to the design whose octopus stays healthiest, most active and, crucially, inside the tank.

Think of a fan‑convention or design‑school **"Habitat for a Mythical Beast" challenge**, where teams (creature designers, architecture students, biology geeks) invent a plausible, welfare‑minded enclosure for a fictional animal — a dragon, griffin, kraken or dire wolf — and present concept art, a scale model and a "keeper's manual."

A strong entry would include: an invented but internally consistent **species biology sheet** (mass, wingspan, thermal tolerance, diet, social structure, lifespan, reproduction) that every design decision is justified against; for a dragon, a fireproof habitat carved from basalt and refractory brick with geothermal vents and a heated lava‑rock basking shelf, a deep sand wallow and a cool cavern retreat for a full thermal gradient; a **hoard chamber/den** big enough to coil in, since nesting on treasure is a species‑typical behaviour; an enormous netted or canyon‑walled **flight paddock** with thermals from warm updraft grates, cliff launch ledges and perch pinnacles; containment engineered to the threat — ceramic‑composite mesh, blast doors, water cannons, a shift/holding chamber and hydraulic squeeze cage for vet work, plus firebreaks, sprinklers and a keeper airlock; enrichment such as whole‑carcass hoist feeds, scent trails, puzzle boulders, scratching monoliths and a swim lagoon (or, for the kraken, a deep chilled seawater basin with rockwork lairs and escape‑proof lids); a back‑of‑house quarantine barn, forge‑grade waste handling, and a written diet and training plan; and visitor infrastructure — armoured viewing galleries, interpretive signage on the beast's "conservation status" and folklore, and a night‑house webcam.

Judges would score how convincingly the design meets the invented creature's biology and behavioural needs, safety for animal, staff and public, engineering plausibility of materials and containment, enrichment and welfare, craftsmanship of the model and artwork, worldbuilding storytelling, and sheer imagination — with bonus points for the entry a real zoo curator says they'd actually be able to run.

It could be a **kennel club / vet‑school "Best Whelping Box" build‑off**, where breeders, woodworking clubs and animal‑science students compete to build housing for a mother dog and her newborn litter, with the winners donated to breeders, foster carers and shelter neonatal programs.

A strong entry would include: a box sized to the breed so the dam can stretch out fully with room to spare (roughly her length plus 50%), with walls high enough to contain crawling neonates but a **low, removable front panel or drop‑down door** so she can step in and out without jumping on pups; **"pig rails"/anti‑crush bars** set a few inches off the floor and walls so a puppy pushed against the side isn't smothered when she flops down; a warm‑zone gradient — an overhead heat lamp on a guard or a thermostat‑controlled heat mat under one corner (about 85–90 °F at birth, stepped down weekly), with a cooler area the dam can retreat to, plus a digital thermometer/hygrometer; non‑slip, washable flooring — vinyl or sealed marine ply topped with whelping fleece/vet bed over absorbent pads — for traction so pups don't splay their legs, sloped or trayed for fluid drainage; smooth, sealed, non‑toxic, fully disinfectable surfaces with rounded corners, no exposed screws, staples or splinters; a hinged or lift‑off lid and removable panels so it knocks down flat for storage and steam cleaning; an attached **weaning/exercise pen** with a low ramp, potty tray, chew‑safe toys and enrichment ("puppy culture" wobble boards, tunnels, varied surfaces) that clips on around week three; and extras like a scale/weight chart holder, whelping kit shelf, night light, and a discreet camera mount so the breeder can monitor the birth remotely.

Judges would score neonatal survival features first (crush prevention, thermal control, traction, hygiene), then the dam's comfort and ease of access, cleanability and biosecurity, durability through repeated litters and disinfection, safe non‑toxic materials, portability/knock‑down design, cost and use of reclaimed timber, and craftsmanship — with bonus points for a design experienced breeders say has raised a litter without a single crushed or chilled puppy.

It could be a wildlife charity's **"Build a Better Bumblebee Nest Box" competition**, where garden clubs, school woodwork classes and volunteers compete to make an artificial nest for queen bumblebees (very different from the usual solitary‑bee "hotel"), with the winners buried in hedge banks, allotments and school grounds and scored on whether a queen actually moves in.
